29:
* Piggott's Greatest Horse
Sir Ivor was bred in America and raised in Ireland, and at first his build didn't stand out. But after breaking his maiden in his second start, he won three straight to end his 2yo season. L. Piggott, who rode him in the last of those, felt his acceleration and said "it felt as if a horse had shot out from under the saddle." With 3 wins from 4 starts, he was ranked No. 2 on the ratings.
In 1968 Sir Ivor and Piggott took on the British classics. In the 2000 Guineas his rival was Petingo, also ridden by Piggott in his wins, unbeaten in 3 and top-rated. Some doubted Piggott's judgment in choosing Sir Ivor over Petingo. Petingo and others raced up front while Sir Ivor waited at the back. Petingo hit the lead 2 furlongs (400m) out, but Sir Ivor burst through with a lightning kick and beat him by a length and a half.
Next came the Derby. In a strong field Sir Ivor was the runaway favorite at 1.8, the shortest price for a post-war Derby. Again he raced at the rear. Connaught tried to hold on, but Sir Ivor swooped wide with tremendous acceleration and won by a length - a British double classic winner. The local press called his finish a "thrilling surge," and Piggott called him "the best horse I've ever ridden."
But in his next race, the Irish Derby, the 1.33 favorite lost to Ribero, an outsider at 17.67 - ridden by none other than his own partner Piggott. It was called the greatest upset of the 20th century. In the Eclipse S. Piggott was back aboard, but he was only 3rd. Skipping the St. Leger over doubts about the distance, he went to France for the Arc, but despite a good run he finished 2nd.
Yet Sir Ivor wasn't done. Just two weeks after the Arc he won the Champion S., beating Taj Dewan, who had finished ahead of him in the Eclipse. Riding that momentum he went to his native America for the Washington DC International. A Derby winner racing in America was very rare - the first since Papyrus in 1923, 45 years earlier. Japan's Takeshiba O also ran. Heavy rain made the going truly bad, and Laurel Racecourse (now Laurel Park) was a tight track favoring front-runners - everything was against a closer like Sir Ivor. Takeshiba O led, while Sir Ivor sat a bit further forward than usual, at the back of the midfield. In the straight he made a furious charge, swept past the field and won.
That was Sir Ivor's last race. Piggott, who rode on for over 20 more years, later said "he and I had a special relationship, unlike any other horse."

* All In on the Arc
The horse that beat Sir Ivor in the Arc was the Irish-bred Vaguely Noble. He had won 2 of 4 at 2 with two 2nds, but wasn't entered in the British classics, so the owners who bought him at the end of that season set the Arc as his 3yo goal. With no French classic entries either, the Arc was really the only target.
In 1968, after moving to France, Vaguely Noble won his first two races. He was 3rd in the Grand Prix de Saint-Cloud but won the Prix de Chantilly and headed for the Arc. In a field of stars like Sir Ivor and Ribero he was the favorite. He and Sir Ivor raced near the front. In the straight Vaguely Noble broke clear, and even Sir Ivor's kick couldn't close the gap. Vaguely Noble had won the Arc just as planned.
Many hoped for a second Arc, but he was retired at 3, to much regret. Rated 140 lbs, one of the highest ever, he was syndicated for a record $5 million and went to stud, where his first crop included the great mare Dahlia - success in his second career too.

* The First-Ever Triple Tiara
This year one filly swept the US fillies' classics: Dark Mirage. She was so small she was mocked as "pony-sized" at the sale and sold for the minimum, $6,000 (2.16 million yen then). She debuted at 2 and won 2 of 15 - unimpressive, but impressive given she weighed just 323 kg. Her real success came next. In 1968, at 3, she won from her second start on, took the Kentucky Oaks, and went for the Triple Tiara (New York fillies' triple crown). She won the first leg, the Acorn S., by 6 lengths, matching the course record of past Triple Crown winner Count Fleet. No one could touch her now: she took the Mother Goose S. by 10 lengths and the CCA Oaks by 12, becoming the first-ever Triple Tiara winner.
30:
* The Prince and the Rival Who Stood in His Way
In September 1967, at the Keeneland Sale in America, a yearling sold for $250,000, then a record: Majestic Prince. His commanding build, rare for a yearling, won buyers over, and he debuted to win both his starts at 2.
In 1969, at 3, Majestic Prince stretched his streak to 7 and went into the Kentucky Derby, the first leg of the Triple Crown, unbeaten. The field held stars like Top Knight, the previous year's champion 2yo colt, and Arts and Letters, who had won a prep by 15 lengths, so many rivals pulled out and only 8 ran. In the straight Majestic Prince and Arts and Letters fought it out, and the Prince held on by a neck. In the Preakness S. the two dueled again, and again he won, this time by a head. No horse had ever won both races unbeaten, and racing fans went wild. By now he was affectionately known as "The Prince."
Just as everyone expected him to go for an unbeaten Triple Crown, his connections held a press conference the morning after the Preakness and announced he would skip the Belmont S. America hadn't seen a Triple Crown winner in years, and Forward Pass had fallen just short the year before, so hopes were high; a sports magazine wrote that "the Prince ran away from the big one." Under the pressure of public opinion, his camp reversed course and entered the Belmont.
The third leg, the Belmont S. Majestic Prince was rumored to have leg problems, while Arts and Letters was in top form after beating older horses in the Metropolitan H. The betting was tight: the Prince favorite at 2.3, Arts and Letters second choice at 2.7. Arts and Letters went forward at the start and stayed ahead of the Prince throughout. In the straight Majestic Prince chased desperately, but Arts and Letters pulled away to win by five and a half lengths. The dream of an unbeaten Triple Crown was ended by the rival he had battled all along.
Majestic Prince then went on a long break and retired without racing again. With "The Prince" gone, Arts and Letters led American racing, winning 6 straight and taking champion 3yo colt.

* A Bargain Mare: Park Top
Born in Britain, the filly Park Top was bought cheaply and, due to health problems, couldn't debut at 2 - an ordinary horse. But when she debuted at 3 she won four straight. She kept running well, and in 1969, at 5, she took off.
That year Park Top had won the Prix de la Seine, the Coronation C. and the Hardwicke S. With L. Piggott aboard she took on the big stage of the King George VI & Queen Elizabeth S. and won in fine style. Aiming for the Arc, she also won the prep, the Prix Foy. Winning the King George and the Arc in the same year would be a first for a mare, and on Arc day she was 2nd favorite. But it was 14th choice Levmoss who broke clear. Overlooked because he had been racing over long distances, he held on with a long run as if to show off a stayer's stamina. He never tired, and as the others fell away only Park Top came at him wide - but perhaps because she was slow to get out of the pack, she couldn't catch him, losing by three-quarters of a length. She just missed history, but she was a mare who rose from bargain buy to brilliant runner.
31:
* Nijinsky, Dancing on the Turf
Nijinsky was a Canadian-bred, Irish-trained horse named after the legendary Russian ballet dancer Vaslav Nijinsky, who late in life reportedly said "if I am reborn, I want to be a horse." True to his name, Nijinsky ran with elegance on the turf. He won all 5 starts at 2 and was named champion 2yo colt in both Britain and Ireland.
In 1970 he opened in the Gladness S. against older horses. The bad going didn't suit a closer like him, but he won by 5 lengths without being asked. In the 2000 Guineas, the first classic, he was the overwhelming favorite at 1.57. Sitting at the back of midfield, he took off 3 furlongs (600m) out and won by two and a half lengths, so easily that jockey L. Piggott looked back over his shoulder. Some said the Derby's 1 mile 4 furlongs (2400m) was too far for him, and his odds drifted to about 2.4, the longest of his career. He also had colic two days before and went in barely eating. But he burst out of midfield to win comfortably by two and a half lengths, taking his second classic. Nijinsky's camp had invited Vaslav's widow Romola to the race; she was delighted with the horse and is said to have bet heavily on him every time he ran.
He kept rolling, winning the Irish Derby by three and a half lengths without being asked, then beat older horses easily in the King George VI & Queen Elizabeth S. as the only 3yo. But over the summer he caught ringworm (a fungal skin infection). At one point he lost all the hair on one flank and couldn't even be saddled. Thanks to devoted care he recovered and was ready to race. The Arc was his main goal, but Doncaster, home of the St. Leger S. - the third leg of the British Triple Crown - pleaded for him to run, so he did. At about 15 furlongs (about 3000m) it was further than he had ever gone, but hopes for the first Triple Crown winner in 35 years made him a heavy favorite. He raced at the back, made his move in the straight, took the lead easily and won by a length - the 15th British Triple Crown winner, and only the 4th unbeaten.
In Europe today, winning at each horse's best distance counts for more than versatility, so few horses aim for the Triple Crown, and none has won it since Nijinsky. But from 2025 Betfred, the big bookmaker sponsoring the 2000 Guineas, offers a GBP 2 million (about 410 million yen) bonus to a Triple Crown winner, so the trend may change.

* The Arc's Huge Upset
The favorite for that year's Arc was Nijinsky, who came to France to sweep Europe's three big races (called the "European Triple Crown" in Japan). But the St. Leger had taken a heavy toll: he had lost about 30 lbs (about 13.5 kg). Far from his best, his popularity no longer depended on form, and he was favorite at 1.4. The leading runners went forward while Nijinsky sat at the back. In the straight 4th choice Sassafras went to the front. Nijinsky chased and finally passed him with about 100m left. But the moment Piggott hit him right-handed to pull away, Nijinsky veered sharply left, and Sassafras seized the chance to fight back. After a photo finish Sassafras won by a head. Longchamp reportedly fell silent at the shock. It was the first defeat of the great Nijinsky's career.
Sassafras retired after the Arc, while Nijinsky tried to bounce back in the Champion S. But he sweated badly before the race and was beaten into 2nd again. That was his last race.
32:
* Mill Reef: First-Ever European Triple Crown
Racing goes back to ancient Greece, but "modern racing" - run at racecourses under formal rules - is said to have begun in 16th-century England. It spread across Europe and later to America and Asia.
As races developed around the world, by the mid-20th century three stood out as Europe's biggest: the Derby (founded 1780), the King George VI & Queen Elizabeth S. (1951) and the Arc (1920). Winning all three, arguably the world's top races, in one year is called the "European Triple Crown" in Japan, but from 1951 no horse managed it for a long time.
In 1970 the British colt Mill Reef won 5 of 6 at under a mile (1600m). In 1971 he tried his first mile in the 2000 Guineas and was 2nd (no shame - the winner was Brigadier Gerard, unbeatable at a mile), and since his sire Never Bend was a speed line, many expected him to stick to shorter races. Instead his camp stepped up to the 2400m Derby. Despite many doubts, he won clearly by 2 lengths. He then beat older horses by 6 lengths in the King George VI & Queen Elizabeth S., breaking Ribot's 5-length record for the biggest winning margin in the race's history.
The year before, Triple Crown winner Nijinsky had run in the St. Leger before the Arc and lost, so Mill Reef's camp gave him over two months' rest before the Arc. He won by 3 lengths in course-record time for Longchamp's 2400m. Mill Reef carved his name into history as the first European Triple Crown winner.

* The Legendary 2000 Guineas
Brigadier Gerard was a British colt named after Brigadier Gerard, hero of Conan Doyle's historical novels. Though he won all 4 starts at 2, the public's eyes were on two other stars of his crop, Mill Reef and My Swallow.
In 1971, at 3, his first race was the 2000 Guineas, the first leg of the British Triple Crown. With the crop's three best in the field, many rivals stayed away, and only 6 ran - the smallest field of the 20th century. My Swallow led with Mill Reef tracking him, but in the straight Brigadier Gerard unleashed an astonishing kick and won by 3 lengths. It is still remembered as "the greatest 2000 Guineas ever."
Brigadier Gerard won his first 15 starts unbeaten until losing to Roberto in the Benson & Hedges Gold C. the next year, becoming the miler of the century and an idol of British racing fans. In time he was called "Britain's national hero," as hugely popular as the hero of the novels.
33:
* Mill Reef Sets a European Record of 6 Straight G1 Wins
The year before, Mill Reef had won the first-ever European Triple Crown. Believing he still had room to grow, his camp kept him in training at 4 with a second Arc as the goal. In his first public workout of the year he ran 12 furlongs (2400m) and beat a stablemate who had been given a head start by fully 12 lengths, stunning the crowd.
He started in France in the Prix Ganay. The overwhelming favorite at 1.1, he exceeded even those hopes, winning by 10 lengths. Yuji Nohira, who rode another horse in the race, later praised him: "His build was nothing special - I thought we could produce one like that ourselves. But once he raced, he was something else. It may be rude to his jockey, but I thought anyone could have won on him."
Next, back in England, he ran in the Coronation C. Few camps wanted to face him, so only 4 ran. Again favorite at 1.1, he seemed sure to dominate. But in the straight he was locked in a duel with Homeric and only edged ahead near the line to win by a neck. A hard-fought win, but it was his 6th straight G1, a European record.
Still, his camp wasn't happy with the performance. A post-race check found a viral illness, and he had to skip the Benson & Hedges Gold C., where a rematch with Brigadier Gerard was planned (Brigadier Gerard suffered the only loss of his career in that race). The virus came back and leg problems followed, and just when a return seemed possible, he fractured a leg in training before the Arc. The injury was serious enough that he might have been put down, but treatment saved his life and he recovered enough to walk.
He never raced again, and the dream of a second Arc faded. But because his life was saved, he went to stud and later became leading sire. Even after leaving the turf, Mill Reef's name lived on in racing.

* Secretariat, Horse of the Year at 2
Secretariat was an American colt whose name means an administrative office. His camp had applied to the Jockey Club for many names, but all were rejected for various reasons, so the farm secretary handling the paperwork applied for "Secretariat" because she had once worked at one - and it was accepted. An unusual story.
In 1972 he debuted at 2 in a dirt maiden race. As his later nickname "Big Red" suggests, his size was remarkable, and he was favorite. He bumped another horse at the start, lost ground and finished 4th, but what followed was astonishing. In his next maiden he won by 4 lengths. After that, even when he started slowly, he made up for it with amazing late runs, finishing his 2yo year with 7 wins from 9 (one loss was a disqualification for interference).
The Eclipse Awards had begun the year before, when Ack Ack was named Horse of the Year. Secretariat was not only named champion 2yo colt but also Horse of the Year, ahead of La Prevoyante, a 2yo filly unbeaten in 12, and Riva Ridge, the 3yo Kentucky Derby winner. Some argued La Prevoyante deserved it on record, but so many had been captivated by Secretariat's thrilling late runs that he rose to the top of American racing.
34:
* Allez France vs Dahlia
This year mares stood out in Europe. Above all, the clash of two of the same crop who would go down as historic greats - Allez France and Dahlia - thrilled racing. Both were French-trained fillies. Allez France swept the French fillies' Triple Crown - the Poule d'Essai des Pouliches, the Prix de Diane and the Prix Vermeille - and was 2nd in the Arc. Dahlia was 3rd, 2nd and 5th in those races, but became the first 3yo filly to win the King George VI & Queen Elizabeth S., by a record 6 lengths. She also became the first filly to win the Washington DC International in America, and won the Irish Oaks too. Allez France finished ahead in all 8 of their meetings, but Dahlia was also highly rated for beating colts in big races abroad, and it was hard to say which was better.
In fact the two were linked even before their debuts: Maurice Zilber, who bought Allez France as agent for her owner, was then hired by Dahlia's connections as her private trainer before she raced. Zilber said Allez France was "ugly," and indeed she had a rugged, colt-like build, while Dahlia was said to be beautiful and elegant.
Overlooked behind these two greats was another filly of the crop who shone in Britain: Mysterious. She won the 1000 Guineas and the Oaks, the British fillies' double, plus the Yorkshire Oaks. She then met Dahlia in the Irish Oaks but was beaten 3 lengths into 2nd.
Kalamoun, whose grandson would be the great sire Tony Bin, was another star of this crop, winning three G1s - the Poule d'Essai des Poulains, the Prix Lupin and the Prix Jacques le Marois - and showing rare talent.
This was also the year legendary British jockey L. Piggott first won the Arc. At the time French horses won almost every Arc, and foreign-trained winners were rare. Piggott, Britain's champion jockey, rode in it nearly every year, but fell just short in 14 tries, finally winning at 37 this year aboard Rheingold.


* Secretariat's Astonishing 31-Length Win
1973 was the year the first oil shock caused stagflation and dealt a heavy blow to the world economy. In America, as if to blow away the gloom, good news came from racing: Secretariat, Horse of the Year at 2 the year before, won the first US Triple Crown in 25 years with overwhelming power.
He won the Kentucky Derby and the Preakness S. in record time, and in the Belmont S. he left the field far behind, winning by 31 lengths in a staggering world-record 2:24.0. The record still stands, and no one has even run in the 2:25s since. News of this unprecedented Triple Crown winner reached even people who knew nothing of racing and gave the country hope. With frustration at politicians high over the Vietnam War and Watergate, some joked that "if Secretariat ran for president, he'd win" - a sign of his popularity and influence.
Also, two years after Europe adopted its Group system, the US and Canada introduced graded races from this year. Japan followed in 1984.
36:
* Star Appeal's Arc Challenge
Star Appeal was born at the Irish branch of Germany's Rottgen Stud. He debuted in Ireland and won 5 of 13, a decent record, before moving to Germany. His first race there, and last of his 3yo season, was the Arc. Among Europe's stars like Allez France and Dahlia, he was naturally the outsider - least fancied of 27. He finished 13th, far behind winner Rheingold, clearly outclassed. The next year he won two G2s but no G1, and his 4yo year was a slump with 2 wins from 14.
In 1975, at 5, his camp kept trying G1s. He traveled to Italy for the Gran Premio di Milano, a high-class race with G1 winners like Dahlia - and he won it, his first G1. Next came England's Eclipse S. Even as a G1 winner his record was thin, and he was only 6th choice at 21, but he defied the odds and won.
Two straight G1s brought sudden attention, but he then lost three G1s in a row. His stock fell sharply, and in the Arc he was least fancied of 24 at 120.7. He trailed at the very back. Into the final turn he split the pack right down the middle, took the lead in mid-straight and won by 3 lengths. The 2nd was 13th choice, while last year's winner Allez France was 5th - a huge upset. Star Appeal is still the only horse to win the Arc as the least-fancied runner.
It was also the first Arc win by a German-trained horse, and German fans and media went wild. The excitement was immense: an Irish-born horse, trained in Germany and ridden by a British jockey, winning in France - the French president even remarked that "this is a victory for all of Europe."

* Grundy Wins Britain's Race of the Century
The British colt Grundy won a G1 unbeaten in 4 starts at 2 and carried high hopes. In 1975, at 3, a stablemate kicked him in the face and broke his nose, and he struggled to win for a while, but then took three straight classics in two countries - the Irish 2000 Guineas, the Derby and the Irish Derby - and was confirmed as the best of his crop.
Among the 4yos, the British colt Bustino drew attention after winning the Coronation C. in course-record time for his 2nd straight G1. The record was 2 seconds faster than Grundy's winning time on the same course, and many fans thought he could beat Grundy.
They met in the King George VI & Queen Elizabeth Diamond S., renamed this year. Grundy was favorite, Bustino 2nd choice, and Dahlia, going for a 3rd straight win, 3rd choice. Two pacemakers from Bustino's camp went to the front - a plan to set a fast pace so Bustino, the faster on the clock, would have the edge. It worked: the pace was blistering and Bustino took the lead. Grundy was about 3 lengths behind, but 2 furlongs (about 400m) out he surged level and went ahead with a furlong left. It seemed over, but Bustino fought back with amazing grit. The breathless duel went on, and at the last moment Grundy got half a length in front at the line. The time, 2:26.98, broke the race record by over 2.5 seconds and stood until 2010.
How fierce the duel was can be seen from the fact that both horses left the turf within two months. The race was called "The Race of the Century" and is still talked about by fans today.
37:
* The Greatest Handicap Horse Ever
Perhaps because American racing holds that "a truly great horse wins even while giving weight to others," there are still many G1 handicaps in the US. Back then horses were often assigned 130 lbs (about 59 kg) or more. Forego kept fighting through that adversity.
Forego debuted in 1973. Even as a foal he had a huge appetite - when hungry, he reportedly tried to eat people's hands. As a result he grew even bigger than Secretariat, the famous giant of his crop. In his debut year at 3 he ran an amazing 18 races. When Triple Crown winner Secretariat retired that year, Forego rose as if to take his place, piling up wins and ever-higher weights. At 4 he won a G1 or G2 at 12, 7 and 16 furlongs in a row - a feat no other horse could match. That year he was named Eclipse Horse of the Year, champion older horse and champion sprinter. At 5 he shrugged off still higher weights to win 4 G1s, again taking Horse of the Year and champion older horse.
In 1976, at 6, he didn't start until May, but nothing could stop him; he won the G1 Metropolitan H., which he had lost twice before. In his last race of the year, the G1 Marlboro Cup Invitational H., he won carrying 137 lbs (about 62 kg). With 4 G1 wins that year he was Horse of the Year and champion older horse for the third straight year.
He raced until 8, finishing with 34 wins from 57 starts. Those numbers suggest a very sound horse, but he actually suffered from chronic leg trouble. Even so, the sight of him winning under huge weights was spectacular, and fans call him "the greatest handicap horse of all time."

* "The Puerto Rican Fugitive" Bold Forbes
Since 1983 racing countries and regions have been graded Part I to Part III under standards set by the International Cataloguing Standards Committee (ICSC). Puerto Rico is currently Part II, and its famous horses include Galgo Jr., world record holder with 137 career wins, and Camarero, who won 73 of 77.
Bold Forbes was a colt born in America who debuted in Puerto Rico in 1975. He won his debut by 17 lengths and went on to win 5 straight. His owner believed he was good enough for a bigger stage and moved him to America, aiming for the Kentucky Derby.
In 1976, at 3, he didn't always win at first, but he quickly improved, won three graded stakes in a row and went into the Kentucky Derby. The favorite was Honest Pleasure, the previous year's champion 2yo colt, on a 9-race winning streak; Bold Forbes was 2nd choice. He broke sharply and set a fast pace in a big lead. The others closed gradually, but he never tired and beat Honest Pleasure by a length. In the Preakness S. he again went for a big lead, but Honest Pleasure pressed him hard, the pace fell apart, and he faded in the straight to finish 3rd.
Then came the third classic, the Belmont S. Crowds of Latino fans packed Belmont Park, waving Puerto Rican flags and cheering him on. Bold Forbes again set off in a big lead. In the straight the others drew level, but as if carried by the roar of the crowd he held on by a neck. He had won two legs of the US Triple Crown, to thunderous applause.
35:
* "Queen of Longchamp" Allez France
True to her name, "Go, France," Allez France had swept the French fillies' Triple Crown (Poule d'Essai des Pouliches, Prix de Diane, Prix Vermeille) the year before - France's top mare. But in the Arc, Europe's greatest race, she had tasted bitter defeat in 2nd.
In 1974, at 4, she began in the G2 Prix d'Harcourt and won easily. She took two straight G1s, won the G3 Prix Foy prep, and headed to the Arc for revenge.
All seemed set, but 10 days before the race her regular jockey Yves Saint-Martin fell and broke his hip. A substitute was lined up, but Saint-Martin refused to give up the ride and took painkillers to get in the saddle. She was expected to come from behind as usual, but from the final turn she swept past the field and hit the front early - perhaps because of Saint-Martin's injury. Pressed by others near the line, she just held on to win by a head. As a daughter of Sea-Bird, often called France's greatest horse, she completed a father-daughter Arc double,.
That year Allez France won all 5 of her starts at Longchamp and was named France's champion older mare and Horse of the Year. With 12 of her 13 career wins at Longchamp, fans came to call her "the Queen of Longchamp."

* "The Black Butterfly Dancing Around the World" Dahlia
The year before, the French filly Dahlia had stunned fans by winning the King George VI & Queen Elizabeth S. by a record 6 lengths. She also traveled to America and became the first filly to win the G1 Washington DC International, making her name known worldwide.
This year she opened in the Prix d'Harcourt, her 5th meeting with rival Allez France, and lost by six and a half lengths. In the Prix Ganay she was well beaten again, 5th behind her rival. Traveling to England for the Coronation C., she was only 3rd - three straight losses, a poor start.
But back in France, in the G1 Grand Prix de Saint-Cloud, with Allez France absent and a weaker field, she won convincingly. Dahlia then flew back to England for the King George VI & Queen Elizabeth S. Despite a strong field including Highclere, winner of the 1000 Guineas and Prix de Diane, she cruised out of the back of midfield to become the first horse ever to win the race twice.
She kept racing around the world, winning 10 G1s in her career. At a time when shipping horses abroad was still far from routine, she raced in six countries with great success - truly one of the horses who opened the road for international racing.
38:
* Seattle Slew, Carrying Dreams of Freedom
A cheaply bought horse with an unremarkable pedigree runs like a champion and sets a historic first - there is no more thrilling American dream in racing. Seattle Slew was its embodiment.
When he was born, he was not much to look at. He was entered in the yearling sale at Keeneland in Kentucky, America's famous breeding region, but his pedigree and looks kept him out of the select sale, so he went to the general sale in Lexington and sold for only $17,500 (about 5.18 million yen then). His trainer even nicknamed him "the ugly duckling," but once he debuted he ran brilliantly, quickly winning twice. He then won the G1 Champagne S. easily in 2yo record time and was named champion 2yo colt.
In 1977, at 3, his camp believed in him and chose the classic path. They expected the Belmont S., the longest leg at 12 furlongs (2400m), to be the hurdle to the Triple Crown. Thinking he needed to calm down mentally to handle the extra distance, they rested him through the winter in warm Florida. The plan seemed to work: he won two G1s and went into the Kentucky Derby unbeaten. He hit his head on the gate and lost about 2 lengths at the start, but quickly recovered, took the lead around the final turn and won with ease. He won the Preakness S. safely too, and went to the last classic, the Belmont S. His camp had always worried about the distance, and more doubts piled up: the horse van arrived 20 minutes late, and it was his first race on heavy going. But as if shrugging it all off, he shot to the front from the start and, never letting anyone near, won by 4 lengths. It was the moment the first unbeaten US Triple Crown winner was born.

* British Fillies' Double Winner Dunfermline
The British royal family founded Ascot, Britain's flagship racecourse, and still owns it - royalty and racing are inseparable. Of all the royals, Elizabeth II was said to be the most passionate about racing.
The Queen owned many racehorses, and one of the most remarkable was Dunfermline, a filly named after a beautiful Scottish town. At 2 she was twice 2nd in G3s, a fair record, and she won her first race in the Pretty Polly S. on her 3yo debut. After that she went the classic route and took on the Oaks. Before the race the favorite Durtal bolted and was withdrawn; in that chaotic mood, 4th choice Dunfermline showed a sharp turn of foot in the straight to win a classic.
In the St. Leger S., Alleged, unbeaten in 5, was a heavy favorite, with Dunfermline only 3rd choice. Alleged went to the front early and tried to hold on. But Dunfermline, biding her time behind, surged up alongside. After a duel she pulled clear a furlong out and won by a length and a half. She completed the British fillies' double and became the only horse ever to beat Alleged, who would go on to win the Arc twice.
39:
* Two US Triple Crown Winners Collide
At this time America had Triple Crown winners two years in a row, and racing was booming. One was Seattle Slew, who won it in 1977 - the first to sweep the Triple Crown unbeaten, and still named among the greatest American horses ever. The other was Affirmed, who swept it in 1978. Beaten only twice in 16 starts, both 2nds at 2, he was a giant with 8 G1 wins.
The two Triple Crown winners finally met in September's Marlboro Cup Invitational H. It was the first-ever clash of Triple Crown winners in American racing history and drew fierce attention from across the country and the world. Affirmed, riding high after his Triple Crown, was favorite, while Seattle Slew, who had won only two allowance races that year, was 2nd choice. But once the race began, Seattle Slew grabbed the lead, kept it all the way and held off Affirmed in 2nd to win by 3 lengths - the senior Triple Crown winner showing his class.
The next month they clashed again in the Jockey Club Gold C. This time Affirmed hung onto Seattle Slew early, but couldn't keep up and faded. Seattle Slew seemed set to dominate, but Exceller came from behind and the two fought a fierce duel, Exceller winning by a nose. Seattle Slew won their head-to-head 2-0, but Exceller, who beat them both, became famous overnight.
Maruzensky, brought from America to Japan with off-the-charts power, was the same age as Seattle Slew. It was whispered in America at the time that had he debuted there, Seattle Slew's Triple Crown might have been in danger.

* The Rival Who Threatened Affirmed's Triple Crown
Affirmed became the 11th US Triple Crown winner, but the road was far from smooth, because his crop included the formidable Alydar. They clashed again and again from their debuts; in G1s at 2 they met four times, Affirmed winning three and Alydar one. In the 3yo Triple Crown races Alydar was 2nd every time, but by margins of a length and a half, a neck and a head - razor-thin - so Affirmed's Triple Crown was won through battle after battle. Affirmed's trainer Barrera said: "Affirmed is better than Secretariat (the 9th US Triple Crown winner in 1973), because he won the Triple Crown by beating a great rival in Alydar."
Affirmed's jockey Steve Cauthen was just 18, the youngest jockey ever to win the Triple Crown, and was later inducted into the US Racing Hall of Fame.
Both Affirmed and Alydar made their mark as sires too, but Alydar's offspring, including two Kentucky Derby winners, far outperformed Affirmed's.

* Alleged Wins Back-to-Back Arcs
In Europe Alleged became the 5th horse ever to win the Arc twice and was rated 140 lbs in the International Classification (later revised to 134). He retired after this year and became a leading sire of the Ribot line.
This was also the year the first crop of future great sire Mr. Prospector debuted. It included It's in the Air, who won the Eclipse Award for champion 2yo filly right away - a brilliant start that made him North America's leading first-crop sire.
40:
* Affirmed, US Horse of the Year Two Years Running
The year before, Affirmed won the US Triple Crown and Horse of the Year, but in the second half he couldn't win, losing three straight. Starting this year in January, he still couldn't win, and his losing streak stretched to 5. Everyone feared he would never run like a Triple Crown winner again. But in the G1 Charles H. Strub S. he won by 10 lengths. Affirmed was fully back, and after an allowance race he won 5 more G1s in a row. With his win in the Hollywood Gold C. during that streak, his career earnings passed $2.03 million, making him America's first $2 million horse and breaking the world record then held by Kelso.
His farewell race was the Jockey Club Gold C., in which he had been 5th a year earlier. It was then the autumn championship for the best dirt horse, a race he badly wanted. Perhaps scared off, only 4 ran, but they included US double classic winner Spectacular Bid, a field worthy of a farewell. Affirmed led with Spectacular Bid chasing, but he held on to win, ending his career in style.
After faltering once, Affirmed ran on with rare fighting spirit, winning 6 G1s that year, and was named Horse of the Year for the second year running.

* Exceller, "Maker of Great Races," Retires
Exceller was a champion without a crown. With two Triple Crown winners, Seattle Slew and Affirmed, around at the same time, he was often overlooked, but his strength was real - as the 1978 Jockey Club Gold C. proved.
In the earlier Marlboro Cup, Seattle Slew had won the clash of Triple Crown winners, and the two met again in the Jockey Club Gold C.
As fans thrilled at the rematch, the race became a blistering match race between the two Triple Crown winners fighting for the lead. Exceller ran more than 20 lengths back. But when Affirmed faded, Exceller charged forward. Seattle Slew showed astonishing grit for a horse who had set such a fast pace, but Exceller won the fierce duel by a nose - the only horse ever to beat two Triple Crown winners in the same race.
Exceller retired in 1979 at 6. He went to stud at a famous American farm, where his high fee showed the hopes placed on him, but his offspring did poorly and he was sent to Sweden to continue as a sire. After his owner went bankrupt, Swedish law prevented him from even covering mares, and he was slaughtered. His death shocked racing people and fans, and led to groups protecting retired racehorses such as the "Exceller Fund."
41:
* Only the Second Filly to Win the Kentucky Derby
Genuine Risk was a filly born in Kentucky. She joined the stable of L. Jolley, who had trained Kentucky Derby winner Foolish Pleasure. She was very stubborn and hard to train, but her trainer, thrown off again and again, patiently built her trust. It paid off: debuting in 1979, she won 4 straight unbeaten, beating even Smart Angle, that year's champion 2yo filly, in her last race, the Demoiselle S.
In 1980, at 3, her winning run continued to 6. Jockey J. Vasquez, convinced she was as good as any colt, proposed taking on the colts' classics, but Jolley was reluctant. In 1975 he had watched his colt Foolish Pleasure run a match race against Ruffian, the best filly of the time, in which Ruffian broke down and had to be put down. Vasquez still believed in her and persuaded Jolley, and Genuine Risk stepped onto the colts' battlefield.
First she ran in the Wood Memorial S., a prep full of colts. Sitting 3rd and waiting for a gap, she was blocked by a horse who veered badly and finished 3rd. After this Jolley suggested switching to the Kentucky Oaks, but the owner, impressed that she still held 3rd despite the interference, chose the Kentucky Derby. In fact, a filly even placing in the Wood Memorial was only the 4th time ever, and the first in 33 years.
Then came the Kentucky Derby. Genuine Risk was the first filly to run in 21 years. Against 12 colts and geldings, including Wood Memorial winner Plugged Nickle, she was a respectable 6th choice of 13. She broke well and tracked the leaders. The pace was slow, and as the front-runners struggled, she made her move around the third turn, passed horse after horse to take the lead, and held on. She was the first filly to win the Kentucky Derby in 65 years.
She went on to the Preakness S. and the Belmont S., but was 2nd in both. Still, Genuine Risk remains the only filly ever to place in all three US Triple Crown races.

* Spectacular Bid's World Record
The year before, Spectacular Bid had just missed the US Triple Crown and lost Horse of the Year to Affirmed. But this year he was in peak form.
He won his first two races, then in the Charles H. Strub S. ran 10 furlongs (2000m) on dirt in 1:57.80, breaking the world record for the first time in 30 years. The record still stands. He kept winning and retired unbeaten in 9 starts that year. He also broke the career earnings world record set by Affirmed the year before and was the undisputed Horse of the Year.
42:
* That Finishing Kick: Pure Delight
Pleasant Colony was born in Virginia. Debuting in 1980, he finished 6th, 16 lengths behind winner Summing. A poor start, but he ended his 2yo year with a decent 2 wins from 5.
In 1981, on his 3yo debut in the Fountain of Youth S., he was beaten a nose into 2nd. In the Florida Derby he was a distant 5th, 13 lengths back. After this the owner decided to move him to Italian-born trainer John P. Campo. From then on he showed his true worth.
His first race for the new stable was the Wood Memorial S. In a strong field he won by 3 lengths. Unnoticed until then, Pleasant Colony suddenly emerged as a leading classic contender. In the Kentucky Derby the favorite was Proud Appeal, 8 wins from 9, with Pleasant Colony 2nd choice. Proud Appeal and others battled for the lead at a blistering pace. When it slowed down the backstretch, Pleasant Colony, waiting at the back, swept past the tiring leaders in delightful fashion and won by three-quarters of a length. In the Preakness S. he was favorite at 2.6 and lived up to it, winning by a length for his second classic.
Then the last classic, the Belmont S. With hopes of a Triple Crown his support grew, and he was favorite at 2.0. He waited at the very back, made up ground fast down the backstretch and was 3rd into the straight, but couldn't reach the leader and finished 3rd. The front-runner who held on was 3rd choice Summing. Afterwards Campo blamed the waiting tactics, calling it "the worst ride in history" to the media. Pleasant Colony had to settle for two legs of the US Triple Crown.
He ran three more times and retired. At stud, despite few matings, he sired Irish Derby winner St. Jovite and Pleasantly Perfect, winner of the Breeders' Cup Classic and Dubai World Cup, becoming the leading sire of the direct line of Ribot, one of the great horses of the 20th century.

* South Africa Adopts Graded Races
In modern racing, races have been ranked since 1970, when Britain, Ireland and France introduced the "Group system," ranking some races by level as Group 1, Group 2 and Group 3. Italy and Germany followed, and race programs took shape.
The "graded" system, familiar to Japanese fans, began in the US and Canada in 1973. It works like the Group system, but the ranks are called Grade I, Grade II and Grade III. Most countries followed Europe with Group systems, but in 1981 South Africa adopted grades. The reason is unclear, but South Africa had long imported mostly British-bred thoroughbreds, and by then imports were mainly North American, which may have played a part. Today the only Part I countries (the top level set by the International Cataloguing Standards Committee) using graded races are the US, Canada, South Africa and Japan.
43:
* An Unbeaten Derby Win in Just 4 Starts
Golden Fleece was by British Triple Crown winner Nijinsky. Born in America, he was owned by famous British owner Robert Sangster and, like Nijinsky, trained in Ireland. On his debut in September at 2 he met Assert, another Sangster horse, and won by 6 lengths. But he didn't race again that year and went on a long break.
He finally returned in April 1982 in the Ballymoss S. (now the Tattersalls Gold C.). Against a field including future Japan Cup winner Stanerra, he won easily by 3 lengths. Then in the Nijinsky S. (later the Derrinstown Derby Trial S.), named after his sire, he met Assert again and won by two and a half lengths.
He went into the Derby unbeaten. Far back in the straight, he swept past the field with a tremendous kick and won by 3 lengths, a Derby winner unbeaten in 4 starts. Jockey P. Eddery called him "the best horse I've ever ridden."
But Golden Fleece was injured in training and had to retire, leaving the turf after just 4 races despite his enormous talent. His strength is clear from the fact that Assert, the rival he beat twice, became the first horse to win both the French and Irish Derbies.

* A 14-Length Belmont Romp
Conquistador Cielo was an American colt whose name means "conqueror of the sky" in Spanish. True to it, he ran as if flying, leaving the earthbound field behind.
Injured the year before, he was 4th on his 3yo comeback, but then bounced back with a 4-length win. A recurring fracture ruled out the Kentucky Derby, so he went for the Metropolitan H., America's championship mile. He won an allowance race on the same course by 11 lengths and was ready. The Metropolitan included Star Gallant, who had beaten him in his 3yo debut, but Conquistador Cielo was favorite. He went straight to the lead, set his own pace, and by the straight was running alone, winning by over 7 lengths in course-record time. It was the first win by a 3yo in this race against older horses in 13 years.
After this, his camp announced he would run in the Belmont S., the last classic, stunning racing people and fans. The Belmont was just 6 days after the Metropolitan, and the distance jumped from 8 to 12 furlongs (1600m to 2400m) - an unheard-of schedule. On a day of heavy rain, Linkage, 8 wins from 11, was favorite, with Conquistador Cielo, doubted for the quick turnaround and the distance, 2nd choice. Right after the start he again went to the front. He dropped to 2nd once, but as the sloppy track sapped the others' stamina, he never weakened and kept extending his lead, winning by a record 14 lengths. Winning the impossible on an impossible schedule, he was named Horse of the Year.
44:
* British Filly Sun Princess
Sun Princess was born in Ireland and trained in Britain. True to her name she was proud, and as a youngster often acted up in training. She ran only once at 2, finishing 2nd.
In 1983 she opened in the Sir Charles Clore Memorial S., an Oaks trial, finishing 2nd to earn her place in the Oaks. The favorite was French-trained Alexandrie. Held up early, Sun Princess came wide and took the lead half a mile (about 800m) out. Into the straight she drew away with every stride and won by 12 lengths, the biggest margin in Oaks history (broken in 2021 by Deep Impact's daughter Snowfall, by 16 lengths). So dominant was she that racing people speculated she would have won the Derby against the colts.
She then ran in the King George VI & Queen Elizabeth Diamond S. against colts and older horses, but could only finish 3rd. Back among fillies in the Yorkshire Oaks, she led from the start and stretched her lead to 4 lengths in the straight. The press wrote that she ran with "tremendous zest."
Riding that momentum, she took on the colts again in the St. Leger. The going was bad, and French Derby winner Caerleon was withdrawn, so her own participation was in doubt until just before the race. But her camp stood firm and she ran. Again she hit the front early in the straight and won by three-quarters of a length. Winning the Oaks and the St. Leger, the Sun Princess claimed a fillies' double.

* Legendary Jockey Lester Piggott
L. Piggott was Britain's greatest jockey. Born into a family of jockeys - his father, grandfather and maternal grandfather all rode - he grew up around horses and debuted as a jockey at 12. He was hailed as a prodigy, and in 1954 he won his first Derby at 18 on Never Say Die. He kept winning, including the Triple Crown with Nijinsky, and became a true star. He was especially popular with housewives, and helped spread racing's appeal to the general public at a time when it was still seen as a pastime of the upper class.
In the 1983 Derby he rode Teenoso, winner of the Derby Trial S. After a thunderstorm the night before, the going was extremely heavy. Teenoso settled in a good position, struck the front early and won safely by 3 lengths. It was Piggott's 9th Derby win, breaking his own record, which still stands today.
Piggott died in 2022 at 86. Champion jockey in Britain 11 times, with over 5,000 wins at home and abroad, he was a true legend.
45:
* John Henry, US Horse of the Year Again
John Henry was named after a legendary working-class folk hero. With a poor pedigree and plain looks he was rated low. Worse, he had a terrible temper - when offered as a yearling at auction, he had banged his head against a wall and his face was covered in blood. To fix his temperament he was gelded before he even raced.
Debuting in 1977, he started well with 3 wins from 6, but then lost 10 straight from autumn into the next year. The turning point was a claiming race - a race where every runner is for sale. Japan has none, but in America, where racehorses are traded actively, they make up about half of all races. In one such race John Henry, who had always run on dirt, tried turf for the first time. He took the lead at the final turn, never let anyone near, and won by 14 lengths. No one claimed him, but his rise had begun. In 1980 he switched to turf, won a G3 and G2s three in a row, took his first G1 in the San Luis Rey S., and won 4 G1s that year. The next year he became the first champion of the Arlington Million, the world's first race worth $1 million. With 5 G1 wins that year he was named US Horse of the Year, the first unanimous choice.
At 7 and 8 he didn't get the results he wanted, but in 1984, at an amazing 9 years old, John Henry recaptured his peak form. In May he won the G3 Golden Gate H. in course-record time, the first graded-stakes win by a 9yo in US history. Through September he won 4 more G1s and was named US Horse of the Year for the second time, a fitting finale.
John Henry won 16 G1s from 83 career starts, and lived to 32 - the grit of a horse who rose from the bottom.

* The Breeders' Cup, a Festival of Racing, Is Born
In 1970s America, Triple Crown winners like Secretariat, Seattle Slew and Affirmed thrilled racing fans. But racing struggled to win new fans, and with lotteries and casinos being legalized, its popularity was fading. Worried breeders from across the US came together and created the Breeders' Cup in 1984. Seven races were held in one day, including the "Classic" for older horses at middle distances and the "Distaff" for fillies and mares 3 and up, each with huge prize money. Staked on the breeders' pride, the event was a huge success and is now a festival of racing that draws top horses from around the world.
46:
* Oh So Sharp's British Fillies' Triple Crown
Oh So Sharp was a filly owned by Sheikh Mohammed, later ruler of Dubai. Born in Ireland and trained in Britain, her pedigree was packed with great European and American sires - a true blueblood. On debut she was favorite in a field of 21 and lived up to it, winning. She won 3 straight, including a graded stakes, to end her first year.
In 1985, after 7 months off, she started in the Nell Gwyn S., a 1000 Guineas prep, and won by a length and a half, heading for the 1000 Guineas two weeks later. In a field including Triptych, a French G1 winner the year before, Oh So Sharp was favorite at 3.0. Instead of her usual forward tactics, she raced in a good spot in midfield. With 100 yards (about 91m) to go she was about 2 lengths behind the two leaders, but she surged and just caught them on the line, winning by a short head (a margin used abroad, smaller than a head). The runner-up Al Bahathri was owned by Mohammed's brother Sheikh Hamdan, so Oh So Sharp beat her owner's brother's horse to give Sheikh Mohammed his first British classic.
In the Oaks she met Triptych again, the first filly to win the Irish 2000 Guineas, but Oh So Sharp was favorite at 2.5. On soft going she came wide on the best ground, breezed past Triptych and won by 6 lengths, one step from the fillies' Triple Crown.
Next she took on older horses and colts in the King George VI & Queen Elizabeth Diamond S. Against a field including Japanese Derby winner Sirius Symboli, who had traveled all the way from Japan, she was 2nd to outsider Petoski at 13. After that first loss she was 2nd again in the Benson & Hedges Gold C., and went into the big one, the St. Leger, on two straight defeats. Hopes were high for the first fillies' Triple Crown winner since Meld in 1955, and she was favorite at 1.73. She outdueled stablemate Lanfranco, a two-time G1 winner, in a fierce fight and won - the first British fillies' Triple Crown winner in 30 years. As she was already past her peak, she then retired: favorite in all 9 of her races, 7 wins and two 2nds, a brilliant record. No filly has won the British fillies' Triple Crown since.

* A Bitter Disqualification
Sagace was a French horse who debuted in 1983. In his 4th start he won the G3 Prix Niel, his first graded win, and from then on raced only at Longchamp. He was a well-beaten 11th in his first Arc, but won it the next year.
In 1985, riding that momentum, he won the Prix Ganay and Prix d'Ispahan with ease for 3 straight G1s. He won the Prix Foy prep and went for a second Arc. With Oh So Sharp and Derby winner Slip Anchor absent, Sagace was favorite. Running 2nd, he took the lead just before the straight. Rainbow Quest, 18th in the previous Arc, charged up beside him and it became a two-horse battle. After a fierce struggle Rainbow Quest weakened at the end and Sagace finished half a length ahead. But after the race P. Eddery, Rainbow Quest's jockey, protested furiously that Sagace had interfered with him. The protest was upheld, Sagace was placed 2nd, and the back-to-back Arc that had been within his grasp slipped away in a way no one expected.
47:
* The Horse With the Highest Rating Ever
1986 was the year Dancing Brave, called the best in Europe in the 80s, swept the racing world. With an astonishing finishing kick he won the 2000 Guineas, the King George VI & Queen Elizabeth Diamond S. and the Arc. His rating of 141 lbs in the International Classification, the highest ever, has never been beaten, making him arguably the greatest horse of all time, not just the 80s. (In 2013 past ratings were reviewed and his was cut to 138, but the change was later reversed.)
The only horse to beat Dancing Brave in Europe was Shahrastani. In the Derby he held off Dancing Brave's mighty finish by half a length. Dancing Brave came from a hopeless position and fell just short, and his ride drew criticism, with jockey Greville Starkey taking the brunt. Starkey had confidently said beforehand that the distance was no problem for a horse who had only ever run a mile, which fueled the criticism. On the other hand, the race showed Dancing Brave's power, closing his last furlong (200m) in an astonishing 10.3 seconds. Shahrastani proved he was no ordinary horse either, winning the Irish Derby by 8 lengths next time out.
Dancing Brave then won an Arc with what was called the best field ever, in record time of 2:27.7, cementing his place as the greatest.
Curiously, Mill Reef, hailed as Europe's best 15 years earlier, died this very year, as if handing over to the new champion.

* "Iron Ladies" of America and Europe
Meanwhile in America, a mare was drawing attention with a North American record of 8 G1 wins in a year: Lady's Secret, arguably Secretariat's finest offspring. She won 8 G1s including the Whitney H. and the Breeders' Cup Distaff, and was a fine 2nd against colts in the Woodward S. She was only the second filly or mare named Horse of the Year since the Eclipse Awards began. For her toughness, running 15 times that year, she was called "The Iron Lady."
Europe had its own tough "Iron Lady" at the same time: Triptych, who won 8 G1s against colts in 41 career starts. She drew attention as Dancing Brave's rival; this year she was 2nd in the Eclipse S. and 3rd behind Dancing Brave in both the King George VI & Queen Elizabeth Diamond S. and the Arc. She later traveled to the Breeders' Cup Classic in America and the Japan Cup in Japan, becoming known around the world.
Lady's Secret and Triptych never met, but two great mares both called "Iron Lady," famous at the same time in America and Europe, may be a curious twist of fate.
48:
* Reference Point's British Double
Mill Reef was the first to win the European Triple Crown (as Japan calls it), and his son Reference Point aimed for it too. In his first season he won the William Hill Futurity S., the 2yo mile championship, for his first G1.
In 1987 he was aimed at the 2000 Guineas, the first classic, but a nasal infection forced him out. On his return he won a G2 easily and went for the Derby, the second classic. He led from the start, and when a rival drew level in the straight he found a second wind and pulled away to win by a length and a half, joining his sire as a Derby winner.
He lost to older horses in the Eclipse S., but was favorite for the King George VI & Queen Elizabeth Diamond S. Again he made the running, never gave up the lead and won by 3 lengths, one step from the European Triple Crown.
His camp then planned the St. Leger before the Arc. In the past 50 years only 3 Derby winners had run in the St. Leger - an unorthodox plan. But fans were excited, and he was a heavy favorite at 1.36. Again he led all the way to the line, completing a British double.
Then, for his first trip abroad, the Arc. Expected to be the first European Triple Crown winner since his sire Mill Reef, he was again a clear favorite at 1.73. As usual he went to the front, but Sharaniya took him on. Their duel made the pace furious. Reference Point just held the lead into the straight, but had no stamina left to hold off the field, sank back into the pack and was a well-beaten 8th. Winner Trempolino broke the Arc record set the year before by Dancing Brave by 1.4 seconds.
Founded as an unusual race for 3yos only in an era when 5- and 6-year-olds dominated, the St. Leger had long been prestigious. But after Triple Crown winner Nijinsky lost the Arc two weeks after the St. Leger in 1970, its prestige fell, and Reference Point's heavy Arc defeat is said to have finished it off. His loss may have had other causes, such as the blistering pace or an abscess in his foot, but in fact no Derby winner ran in the St. Leger for the next 25 years.
49:
* A Legendary Breeders' Cup Distaff
This year's Breeders' Cup Distaff brought together the three best fillies and mares of the time in a fierce battle still remembered as a race of the century.
One was Personal Ensign, unbeaten in 12 starts - a seasoned 4yo with 7 G1 wins. Another was Winning Colors, only the third filly to win the Kentucky Derby. The third was Goodbye Halo, who had won the fillies' G1 series: the Kentucky Oaks, Mother Goose S. and CCA Oaks. To see the three clash, crowds packed Churchill Downs despite bad weather.
Winning Colors went to the front and tried to make the sloppy track work for her, but Personal Ensign came with a stunning finish to win by a nose. Goodbye Halo, who closed with her, was 3rd by half a length. Personal Ensign retired after this race, the first horse in 80 years to retire unbeaten after 10 or more starts.
At the Eclipse Awards, Horse of the Year went to Breeders' Cup Classic winner Alysheba, but Personal Ensign was named champion older mare and Winning Colors champion 3yo filly.
That year's Breeders' Cup also saw the great European mare Miesque win the Breeders' Cup Mile for the second time, a first. It was her only race in America that year, but her dominant performance earned her the Eclipse Award as champion turf mare. That day brought together the great mares of America and Europe - a historic day.

* Italy's Great Tony Bin Wins the Arc
In Europe the big story was Tony Bin, the first Italian-trained Arc winner in 27 years. Italy had produced greats like Nearco and Ribot, but its racing declined from the 1970s and fell behind Britain, Ireland and France. No Italian horse had won the Arc since Molvedo in 1961. Tony Bin appeared as if to blow away that gloom.
Tony Bin was no star prospect at first; he was a late bloomer who only came into his own at 4. The year before he was 5th in the King George VI & Queen Elizabeth Diamond S. and 2nd in the Arc, showing world-class ability, and this year he became the first Italian-trained Arc winner in 26 years, bringing joy to his homeland.
Mtoto, beaten into 2nd by Tony Bin, was Britain's undisputed ace, having won the King George VI & Queen Elizabeth Diamond S. and the Eclipse S. Losing to a horse from Italy, seen as a lesser racing nation, left Britain in deep dismay.
Soon after, Tony Bin announced he would run in the Japan Cup. The first Arc winner ever to run in the race was big news in Japan. Sadly he couldn't keep up with the epic battle between Pay the Butler and Tamamo Cross and finished 5th, just behind the fight for 3rd.
50:
* After Four Battles...
In the year Secretariat, the legend hailed as America's greatest, passed away, two new heroes appeared who would carve their names into US racing history: Sunday Silence and Easy Goer, both familiar to Japanese fans.
In American racing at the time, Sunday Silence was just an "ordinary horse" with nothing special in his birth or pedigree, who won over doubters by winning races. Easy Goer, by contrast, came from a great farm with a first-class pedigree - an elite path promised before he was born. Sunday Silence's home, Stone Farm, was even an offshoot of Claiborne Farm, where Easy Goer was born, which says something about their relationship.
The two clashed in the classics, and Sunday Silence won both the Kentucky Derby and the Preakness S., with Easy Goer 2nd behind him. But in the Belmont S., the third leg, Easy Goer vented his frustration with a powerful run, crushing Sunday Silence by 8 lengths to take the last classic and show his pride. The most talked-about of their clashes was the Preakness: the fiery match race of the two, who broke clear early, was called "the race of the half-century."
Having split the Triple Crown, they clashed again in the Breeders' Cup Classic, and Sunday Silence held off Easy Goer by a neck to win the race of the century. As a result, Sunday Silence was named Horse of the Year and champion 3yo colt by a near-unanimous vote. Easy Goer had a flawless record too, 6 G1 wins and three 2nds, but got almost no votes and won no titles.
US racing's new stars weren't only horses but a jockey too: K. Desormeaux, in his 4th year, won an astonishing 598 races that year alone and was named Eclipse champion jockey. The record of 598 wins in a year still stands and remains a Guinness World Record.

* Nashwan, Acclaimed in Britain
Meanwhile in Britain, one horse drew attention rivaling legends like Nijinsky and Mill Reef: Nashwan. Unbeaten since his debut, he won the 2000 Guineas and the Derby, brushed aside older horses by 5 lengths in the Eclipse S., and went on to win the King George VI & Queen Elizabeth Diamond S. - a remarkable feat. Rather than the St. Leger and the Triple Crown, he chose the Arc, but in the Prix Niel prep he was a shocking 3rd. That was his last race. Nashwan, once hoped to be the first British Triple Crown winner in 19 years, divided opinion after the baffling loss and sudden retirement, and was rated a middling 131 lbs in the International Classification.
Two of his crop were rated higher: Old Vic and Zilzal. Old Vic won the French and Irish Derbies; he skipped the Derby for the French Derby, so he never met Nashwan. Zilzal was a dominant miler who debuted in May and retired in November, appearing and vanishing like a gust of wind.
Nashwan's camp objected to being rated below these two, and trainer D. Hern praised him above all: "the best horse I have ever trained."

* A Southern Hemisphere Mare Makes Her Name Worldwide
Also big news that year: a New Zealand mare set a world record for 2400m on turf - Horlicks, winner of the 9th Japan Cup.
Until the year before she had raced only in New Zealand, and had only just won her first G1 in neighboring Australia that year. She then traveled to Japan for the Japan Cup and, after an epic battle with Oguri Cap, won in a world-record 2:22.2. The first Southern Hemisphere-trained winner of the Japan Cup, she made her name known worldwide with that astonishing time. Japan was in the middle of its second racing boom, and because she beat Oguri Cap, the idol horse of the era, the name "Horlicks" became known even to people who knew nothing about racing.
51:
* Salsabil's British Fillies' Double
The British-trained filly Salsabil was from the second crop of Sadler's Wells, a sire well known in Japan, and one of the offspring who made him a great sire. She debuted in 1989 and won her first G1, the Prix Marcel Boussac, in her 3rd start as 4th choice.
In 1990 she started in the G3 Fred Darling S. Dead Certain and Chimes of Freedom, seen as leading classic fillies, were in the field, and Salsabil was 3rd choice behind them. Dead Certain led, but faded badly late, and Salsabil swept past to lead, then pulled away to win by 6 lengths.
Now the top classic prospect, she was favorite for the 1000 Guineas. She won a fierce duel with 2nd choice Heart of Joy by three-quarters of a length. Naturally she was favorite again in the Oaks. She was blocked at one point, but once clear she pulled away to win by 5 lengths, her second classic.
After resting until autumn, she skipped the St. Leger and the fillies' Triple Crown and aimed for the Arc. She won the Prix Vermeille prep by a neck and was favorite in the Arc. But she couldn't show her true form and was well beaten in 10th. She retired after this race.
Salsabil left the turf to much regret, but her 4 G1 wins helped make her sire Sadler's Wells leading sire for the first time.

* Great Sire Northern Dancer Dies
This year the great Canadian-born sire Northern Dancer died. He produced many top horses, including British Triple Crown winner Nijinsky from his second crop, and was leading sire twice in America and four times in Britain.
He was retired from stud in 1987 due to falling fertility and died in 1990, much mourned. In his place his son Sadler's Wells rose as a sire. In Japan his son Northern Taste was leading sire 10 times, and his blood has spread around the world.
52:
* "Precocious Genius" Arazi
In 1991 the Cartier Awards were founded as Europe's annual honors, modeled on America's Eclipse Awards. The very first Horse of the Year was, remarkably, a 2yo: Arazi.
Arazi was American-bred and French-trained. He debuted early, in May at 2, finishing 2nd. After winning a listed race he took the G3 Prix du Bois and the G2 Prix Robert Papin in a row. With an overwhelming kick that swept past the field in the straight, he went on to win the Prix Morny, the Prix de la Salamandre and the Grand Criterium.
Having swept France's 2yo G1s, he went to his native America for the Breeders' Cup Juvenile, the 2yo colts' championship. His first race on dirt and a wide draw raised doubts, but he was still favorite at 3.1. He sat at the back early, hit the front around the final turn, and kept pulling away to win by 5 lengths - the first European-trained winner of the race.
With 7 wins from 8 that year, including 4 G1s, Arazi was named the first-ever Cartier Horse of the Year.

* Generous: From Huge Upset to Top Class
The Irish-bred colt Generous was, true to his name, said to be a gentle horse. He debuted early, in May at 2. He won first time out, but in his first G1, the Prix Morny, he was well beaten in 10th, and in his next G1 try, the Dewhurst S., he was 7th choice at 51. Held up at the back, he came with a tremendous kick to win by three-quarters of a length - a huge upset.
In 1991 he opened his 3yo year with a respectable 4th in the 2000 Guineas, enough to show his win wasn't a fluke - and from there his run began. In the Derby, perhaps because it was his first try at 12 furlongs (2400m), he drifted to 5th choice. Tracking in 3rd, he broke clear about 2 furlongs out and pulled away to win by 5 lengths, a rare rout even for the Derby.
Now in the top class, he won the Irish Derby as favorite, then crushed older horses by a race-record 7 lengths in the King George VI & Queen Elizabeth Diamond S. He seemed off form in the Arc and was a well-beaten 8th, and illness afterwards forced his retirement. At the new Cartier Awards, Horse of the Year went to Arazi and champion 3yo colt to Suave Dancer, but in the International Classification he was rated 137 lbs, above both.
At stud he stood 4 years in Britain before moving to Japan, where he sired Erimo Harrier, three-time winner of the Hakodate Kinen.
53:
* User Friendly's British Fillies' Double
User Friendly was a filly bred in Britain by W. Gredley. By Slip Anchor, part of three generations of Derby winners, out of a mare by Derby winner Blakeney, her pedigree was excellent - yet she found no buyer as a yearling, so Gredley kept her.
She finally debuted in April 1992 at 3, an outsider at 26, and won by two and a half lengths. Two weeks later she won the Oaks Trial S. and suddenly became a classic contender. In the Oaks she was 3rd choice at 6. She raced near the front and took the lead early. By the time the others began to close it was too late: she won by three and a half lengths, with the 3rd another 20 lengths back. Beating the favorite in dominant style, she received great applause. She went on to win the Irish Oaks and Yorkshire Oaks, three Oaks in all (in Japan the winner of all three is sometimes called an Anglo-Irish Oaks Triple Crown winner).
Next was the St. Leger. She was the only filly among 7 runners, yet favorite ahead of the colts. Again she raced forward, led about 2 furlongs (400m) out, and won by three and a half lengths, completing the British fillies' double. She also finished 2nd in an Arc packed with top older colts, and with such a brilliant record was named Cartier Horse of the Year.

* Nijinsky's Legacy
After racing, British Triple Crown winner Nijinsky succeeded Northern Dancer as a top sire, and in 1986, thanks to his son Shahrastani, he was champion sire in Britain and Ireland. Through horses like Maruzensky his influence on Japan was also great.
In 1992, as his illness worsened, Nijinsky was put down. As the great horse departed, his son Lammtarra, born that year, would go on to achieve what even his sire could not.
54:
* First European-Trained Breeders' Cup Classic Winner
Sagace missed a second Arc by a whisker after a bitter disqualification. He went to stud in America but died young at 9, leaving only three crops. One of his few offspring was Arcangues. Trained in France, Arcangues began with a dismal last of 19 on debut, and by 4 had a plain record of 3 wins from 11, including a G2 and a G3.
At 5 he started in the Prix Ganay and was 7th of 8. Still he kept running in G1s, choosing the Prix d'Ispahan next. After his poor run he was only 5th choice of 7. Usually a closer, this time he raced forward, never weakened in the straight, and won his first G1 by a length and a half. Encouraged, he traveled to England to avenge his loss in the Eclipse S. the year before, but was a dismal 6th. Back home in the G2 Prix Dollar he was a distant 4th, 10 lengths back.
After all those losses, his camp chose the Breeders' Cup Classic, which gathers the world's best dirt horses. After a heavy defeat, from a bad wide draw and, above all, in his first dirt race, he was given no chance: least fancied at 134.6. His regular jockey was unavailable, so J. Bailey rode at short notice. Unable to speak French, he couldn't understand the trainers, and reportedly said, "I know nothing about this horse - I don't even know how to pronounce his name." With everything pointing to defeat, the race began. Favorite Bertrando took the lead and set a fast pace into the straight. No one seemed able to catch him, but Arcangues came flying wide with a superb finish, swept past and beat Bertrando by 2 lengths. The least-fancied horse became the first European-trained winner of the Breeders' Cup Classic. The commentator called it: "Absolutely shocking! Impossible victory!" His 134.6 odds are still the biggest payout in Breeders' Cup history.
55:
* "The Conquering King of Steel" Carnegie
Carnegie was named after A. Carnegie, the American industrialist known as the "King of Steel." By the great sire Sadler's Wells out of Arc winner Detroit, he was a blueblood, born in Ireland and trained in France.
He debuted late, in March 1994 at 3, and won first time out. But he then lost twice, and gave up on classics like the French Derby. Improving from summer, he won a listed race and then his first graded race, the G2 Prix Eugene Adam.
In autumn he aimed at the Arc and took on the Prix Niel prep. The favorite was French Derby winner Celtic Arms, with Carnegie 2nd choice. He turned in 6th, unleashed his kick to lead with 200m left and won by a length and a half.
Then the Arc, with stars like King George VI & Queen Elizabeth Diamond S. winner King's Theatre and Italian Derby winner White Muzzle. King's Theatre and others raced up front while Carnegie sat in a good midfield spot. In the straight he swept past the tiring leaders to take the lead, then held off the late chargers by a short head. Sire-and-son Arc winners had happened before, but this was the first-ever dam-and-son double.

* The Growth of Hong Kong Racing
Thoroughbred racing took hold in Hong Kong from the 1960s under British rule. After Sha Tin Racecourse opened in 1978, Hong Kong racing grew fast, and in 1988 its first international race, the Hong Kong Invitation Cup, was founded.
In 1994 the Hong Kong International Vase, a new 2400m international race, began, and excitement grew further. In time the Hong Kong International Races became a festival of four G1s on one day: the Vase, the Sprint, the Mile and the Cup.
Today Hong Kong even sells bets on which jockeys and trainers will do best in some races - its racing has evolved its own brand of entertainment.
56:
* First-Ever Unbeaten European Triple Crown Winner
This year an unprecedented horse appeared: just 4 starts and 4 wins in his life, three of them the European Triple Crown. Lammtarra, well known in Japan too. He debuted the year before, was off for nearly a year with illness, then won the Derby on his return. He went on to beat strong fields with ease in the King George VI & Queen Elizabeth Diamond S. and the Arc, taking Europe's top titles without fuss. He was the first European Triple Crown winner since Mill Reef in 1971, 24 years earlier, and the first ever to do it unbeaten. For his miraculous record and his name (Arabic for "the invisible"), he was called "the horse of God."
Yet Lammtarra was not named Cartier Horse of the Year, and was rated only 130 lbs in the International Classification, low for his record. Reasons given were the modest quality of the horses he beat and his unspectacular style, but even more important was Ridgewood Pearl, a star of the mile division.
Ridgewood Pearl, a filly of the same crop, won mile G1s in four countries: the Irish 1000 Guineas, Britain's Coronation S., France's Prix du Moulin de Longchamp and America's Breeders' Cup Mile. She ran impressively too, setting a record time in the Coronation S. In the end the Cartier Awards named her Horse of the Year, while Lammtarra took champion 3yo colt.
The decision was controversial, with claims that Lammtarra was held back for being owned by Dubai's powerful Maktoum family, while Ridgewood Pearl, raised by a small Irish breeding couple, was favored. Even so, Lammtarra was a great horse, and he was later imported to Japan as a leading heir to Nijinsky for 4.4 billion yen (at the time's exchange rate).

* Cigar, America's Best of the 1990s
At the same time, America had a horse on an incredible winning run: Cigar, who set an unprecedented 16-race winning streak from 1994 to 1996. This year, at 5, he won all 10 starts, including 8 G1s (equaling the record then), and was named Eclipse Horse of the Year almost unanimously. Most stunning was the Breeders' Cup Classic, where he clocked 1:59.58 on a sloppy track, overwhelming everyone with his astonishing potential. He was rated 132 lbs in the International Classification this year and 135 the next, and is called America's greatest horse of the 1990s.
The 3yo crop had a star too: Thunder Gulch, winner of the Kentucky Derby and Belmont S., and his clash with Cigar in the Jockey Club Gold C. drew great attention. But Cigar won easily, and Thunder Gulch was a well-beaten 5th, over 10 lengths back. It was his last race.
Another standout that year was Inside Information, who won the Breeders' Cup Distaff by a record thirteen and a half lengths - a margin still unbeaten some 30 years later.
57:
* A Victory Signal Rising From the Dust
The year before, Cigar won all 10 starts, including 8 G1s, and was Eclipse Horse of the Year. In 1996, at 6, he raced on, starting in the G1 Donn H., which he had won before. In a strong field including 8-time G1 winner Heavenly Prize, he was overwhelming favorite at 1.2. He won so easily he was eased down in the straight, winning the race for the second time. Next he was invited to the new Dubai World Cup, founded that year. He beat horses like Japan's best dirt horse of the time, Lively Mount, with ease to become its first champion.
In America at the time, racecourse after racecourse announced bigger purses only for races Cigar entered, trying to lure him - that is how big his impact on American racing was. Back home he won a listed race to stretch his streak, which began two years before, to 15. One more win would equal the American record of 16 straight set by Triple Crown winner Citation in 1950. For this historic attempt a special race was staged, the Citation Challenge Invitational S. Cigar won it, and the crowd applauded his 16th straight win for a full 20 minutes.
He lost his next race, ending the streak, but by retirement his earnings totaled $9,999,815. The world's leading money earner, Cigar was Eclipse Horse of the Year for the second straight year.

* The Dubai World Cup Is Founded
Since its first racecourse was built in 1969, racing culture spread quickly in Dubai. Sheikh Mohammed did most to drive it. He owned British fillies' Triple Crown winner Oh So Sharp and Arc winner Carnegie, and founded the Godolphin racing operation with a training base in Dubai - a tireless champion of racing.
In 1996 he founded the Dubai World Cup, an international race at Nad Al Sheba Racecourse. Its defining feature was being the world's richest race ($4 million in total). The first running being won by Cigar, hailed as America's best, may have helped cement its status.
More races were added to the same day, including the turf Dubai Turf Classic (now the Dubai Sheema Classic), and today Dubai World Cup Day is an event that draws top horses from around the world.
58:
* A European-Trained Dubai World Cup Winner
The Japan Cup, made an international G1 in 1992, was booming. In 1996 stars came from around the world, including Helissio, fresh from a dominant Arc win, and Pentire, Europe's best older horse and King George VI & Queen Elizabeth Diamond S. winner. But the race was snatched by Singspiel, a British horse with just one G1 win, 4th choice.
In 1997, at 5, Singspiel rose even higher. He opened in the second Dubai World Cup. Rare torrential rain delayed the meeting by 4 days, and it was his first race on dirt, but he shrugged it all off to become the first European-trained winner of the Dubai World Cup. For Japanese fans, though, it was a sad race: Japan's "Queen of the Sand" Hokuto Vega fell during the race and had to be put down. She was due to retire after it, so the grief of her camp and fans was all the greater.
Singspiel then won two more G1s at home in Britain, the Coronation C. and the International S. He traveled again for the Breeders' Cup Turf, but fractured a leg in training the day before, was withdrawn and retired.

* Young Genius Trainer A. O'Brien
A. O'Brien, influenced by his father, a former jockey and trainer, became an assistant trainer and took over his trainer wife's stable in 1993. He first shone over jumps, champion jumps trainer in Ireland for five straight seasons from his first in 1993.
Soon his talent shone on the flat too. He won his first G1 with Desert King in 1996, and an Irish double with him the next year. That year, at 26, he became the youngest-ever champion flat trainer in Ireland. He kept it up, developing greats like Galileo and Rock of Gibraltar, and was champion trainer 10 years running from 1997 to 2006. With 10 Derby wins and 16 Irish Derby wins by 2024, he is one of modern racing's leading trainers.
59:
* Swain Defies the Odds
Swain was a good horse who had won the Coronation C. and the Prix Foy. But the 1997 King George VI & Queen Elizabeth Diamond S. was packed with stars like French Horse of the Year Helissio and US Horse of the Year Singspiel, and Swain was only 6th choice. The race was later called "The Race of the Decade." In heavy rain, Swain passed leader Helissio 2 furlongs out and held off the rest to win by a length.
As older stars like Helissio and Singspiel left the turf, Swain raced on at 6 in 1998. But wins dried up, and he came into his second King George on a 5-race losing streak. Despite being the previous winner, he was only 4th choice.
