In mid-straight he won a duel with High-Rise and went on to win by a length - only the second horse ever to win the King George VI & Queen Elizabeth Diamond S. twice, and the first since Dahlia 24 years earlier.

* The Charm of the Grey
Greys often become idols in Japan, and it's the same abroad. Silver Charm was a grey who captivated American fans with his beautiful build and fighting spirit. In 1997, at 3, he ran in the Kentucky Derby and held off the late charge of favorite Captain Bodgit by a head. In the Preakness S. he just won a three-way photo with Free House as well, taking two legs of the Triple Crown. He narrowly lost the Belmont S., but was named Eclipse Horse of the Year.
Winning two G2s early in 1998, Silver Charm headed to the Dubai World Cup on a roll. He faced the formidable Swain, but was favorite with British bookmakers (betting isn't offered in Dubai for religious reasons). Silver Charm led with 100m left, then Swain launched a fierce attack. They hit the line almost together, but Silver Charm won by a short head. Afterwards jockey G. Stevens praised his spirit: "He got passed once, but he put his head down and fought to get back in front." All three of his G1 wins to that point came by a head or less - proof of his extraordinary will to win.
60:
* Montjeu Stands in Japan's Way
Montjeu was an Irish-bred, French-trained colt. He won both starts at 2, and in his first race of 1999 took the G2 Prix Greffulhe for his first graded win, becoming a classic contender. He was narrowly 2nd in the G1 Prix Lupin, but crushed the field by 4 lengths in the big one, the French Derby. On a roll, he ran in the Irish Derby. Held up at the back, he moved up between the third and final turns and swept past the field in the straight to win by 5 lengths, confirming himself as Europe's best 3yo.
In autumn he started in the Prix Niel, the Arc prep, as overwhelming favorite at 1.1. Bienamado went for home early and almost held on, but Montjeu just got by him by a head. Then the Arc, on a 3-race streak since the French Derby. Montjeu was favorite, with Japan's El Condor Pasa, on a roll after winning the Grand Prix de Saint-Cloud and the Prix Foy, a close 2nd choice. The going was extraordinarily heavy, and the race was seen as a duel between the two mud-lovers. El Condor Pasa broke well and led alone. In the straight he showed no sign of tiring and tried to leave the field behind, but Montjeu alone closed in. With about 100m left Montjeu went by, and held off El Condor Pasa's fightback by half a length. Japanese fans had hoped for Japan's first Arc win, but Europe showed the true depth of its racing.
The next year Montjeu won 3 G1s and retired. At stud his powerful kick passed on to his offspring, and he sired four Derby winners.

* Mr. Prospector, Working to the End
As a racehorse Mr. Prospector won 7 of 14 with no graded wins - hardly top class. His true worth showed at stud. He started in Florida, but his first crop produced 5-time G1 winner It's in the Air, his reputation soared, and he moved to Kentucky, the heart of American breeding. His son Conquistador Cielo became US Horse of the Year, and his standing as a sire kept rising.
His defining trait was toughness. In 1999 he was put down at 29 due to severe colic, yet he covered 47 mares that very year. He left many offspring, who succeeded hugely as racehorses and as sires, so his blood still has a major influence on world racing.

* The WSRC Is Founded
This year, sponsored by a Dubai-based airline, the World Series Racing Championship was founded, awarding points for placings in the world's major G1s. The original races were the King George VI & Queen Elizabeth Diamond S., Irish Champion S., Cox Plate, Breeders' Cup Turf, Breeders' Cup Classic, Japan Cup, Canadian International S., Hong Kong Cup and Dubai World Cup. The Arc was added in 2001. The first champion was Daylami, who won 3 of the races for 38 points, still the series record. Created to develop racing internationally, it was renamed the World Racing Championship in 2005, but ended that year after 7 editions.
61:
* Two Contenders for Cartier Horse of the Year
This year Europe had two worthy candidates for Cartier Horse of the Year: Giant's Causeway, a 3yo star over short-to-middle distances, and Sinndar, also 3, the best over middle-to-long distances.
Giant's Causeway won 5 straight G1s over about 8-10 furlongs (1600-2000m), including the St. James's Palace S., the Eclipse S. and the International S., then traveled to America for a fine 2nd in the Breeders' Cup Classic. Sinndar won the Derby and Irish Derby plus the Arc, utterly dominant at 12 furlongs (2400m). It was hard to choose between them: Giant's Causeway was named Cartier Horse of the Year, but Sinndar won champion 3yo colt - a split that had never happened before in the awards' history.
Beyond these two, many stars emerged in 2000. Montjeu, who beat El Condor Pasa in the previous year's Arc, won 3 straight G1s including the King George VI & Queen Elizabeth Diamond S. Kalanisi, 2nd to Giant's Causeway in races like the Eclipse S., won the Champion S. and the Breeders' Cup Turf. And Dubai Millennium, named to be "the millennium's Dubai World Cup winner," won the 2000 Dubai World Cup just as his name promised. A match race between Dubai Millennium and Montjeu was proposed and drew great interest, but Dubai Millennium fractured a leg and retired, and the dream clash never happened.

* The US and European Horses of the Year Clash
In America, Breeders' Cup Classic winner Tiznow was at the center of racing this year. He only broke his maiden at the end of May and missed the classics, but he improved rapidly through summer and autumn and won 3 straight, capped by the Breeders' Cup Classic. That remarkable run earned him Eclipse Horse of the Year. That Breeders' Cup Classic also featured Cartier Horse of the Year Giant's Causeway from Europe, so the future Horses of the Year of America and Europe met head-on in a star-studded race (Giant's Causeway ran a superb 2nd in his first dirt race).
Another headline: Fusaichi Pegasus became the first son of Mr. Prospector to win the Kentucky Derby. Mr. Prospector had sired many G1 winners and won the Preakness S. and Belmont S. early on, but the Kentucky Derby had always eluded him until his 22nd crop, when Fusaichi Pegasus finally fulfilled the long-held dream.
Also, Yutaka Take was on a long stint in America this year and rode 2yo Point Given on his debut. Point Given would be Eclipse Horse of the Year the next year, but back then he was an unknown, still developing 6th choice of 11, and Take's skill shone in bringing him home 2nd.
62:
* Hong Kong Horse of the Year Two Years Running
With its international races established, Hong Kong racing was booming. But Hong Kong-trained horses long failed to win outside Hong Kong, Japan included, with near misses like Oriental Express's 2nd in the 1998 Yasuda Kinen and Indigenous's 2nd in the 1999 Japan Cup. Fairy King Prawn broke through. In the 2000 Yasuda Kinen he was only 10th choice of 18, but he burst through wide in the straight to win, defying the odds to become the first Hong Kong-trained winner of a Japanese G1. With his Hong Kong Sprint win also counted, he was named Hong Kong Horse of the Year for the 1999/2000 season (Hong Kong's season runs from September to early July).
The next season he won two Hong Kong G1s, then traveled to the Dubai Duty Free, running a superb 2nd by a neck to French horse Jim and Tonic and showing the world Hong Kong's strength. Back home he won another G1. He was 9th in the Yasuda Kinen and couldn't repeat, but with 3 G1 wins that year he was named Hong Kong Horse of the Year for the second straight season.

* First-Ever Back-to-Back Breeders' Cup Classic
The year before, Tiznow beat Giant's Causeway and Fusaichi Pegasus to win the Breeders' Cup Classic and was named Eclipse Horse of the Year. In 2001 he opened with a win in the G2 San Fernando BC S. He was 2nd in his next G2, but won the big Santa Anita H. by 5 lengths for his 3rd G1.
Then he was injured in training and went on a long break. The injury was serious enough that many expected him to retire, but his camp set a second Breeders' Cup Classic as the goal and kept him in training. Soon after his return, an event shook the world: the September 11 attacks.
With New York's World Trade Center devastated, the Breeders' Cup a month and a half later was, by fate, held at Belmont Park in New York State. The track was under tight security with soldiers and police dogs, an eerie atmosphere. With European stars like Sakhee and Galileo in the field, Tiznow, 3rd in both races since his return, was only 4th choice despite being the defending champion. In the straight he, Sakhee and Albert the Great fought fiercely. Sakhee went ahead, but as if showing American pride, Tiznow fought back to win by a nose - the first horse ever to win the Breeders' Cup Classic twice, lighting a spark of hope for American fans in their darkest hour. The commentator's cry as he crossed the line, "Tiznow wins it for America!", is still remembered as a classic call.
63:
* Rock of Gibraltar's World Record
Rock of Gibraltar was named after the great rock on the Strait of Gibraltar, which links the Mediterranean and the Atlantic. True to his name, his running was rock solid. He stumbled to 6th in a G3 in his second start, but that was the only time in his life he finished out of the top two, and he ended his 2yo year with two straight G1 wins.
After six months off, his first race of 2002 was the 2000 Guineas itself. Stablemate Hawk Wing was favorite; Rock of Gibraltar was only 4th choice, perhaps due to a jockey change and his first mile without a prep. Sitting in midfield, he led a furlong (200m) out, but Hawk Wing burst out of the pack and drew level at the line. After a photo, Rock of Gibraltar won by a short head. From then on he stuck to the mile division, winning the Irish 2000 Guineas and the St. James's Palace S. easily. Winning both 2000 Guineas was a first in 10 years, and adding the St. James's Palace S. a first in 33.
Now Europe's best miler, no one could stop him. He won the Sussex S., his first race against older horses, without a scare. Then in the Prix du Moulin de Longchamp he won a fierce battle with French star filly Banks Hill for his 7th straight G1, breaking Mill Reef's record. The streak ended in the Breeders' Cup Mile, where he was 2nd after being hampered by an injured horse, and he retired. His reputation stood firm, and he was named Cartier Horse of the Year.

* German-Bred Kazzia Wins the British Fillies' Double
Meanwhile in Britain the German-born filly Kazzia was shining. After debuting in Germany in 2001 and winning her first graded race in her second start, she was bought by Godolphin (the racing operation led by Dubai's Sheikh Mohammed) and moved to Dubai.
In 2002 her first 3yo race was the 1000 Guineas. She was only 6th choice at 15, but she led a furlong out, held on and won by a neck - the first British G1 win by a German-bred. She kept rolling and won the Oaks too, completing the British fillies' double.
Her camp planned the St. Leger for the Triple Crown, but a leg abscess forced her out. The Triple Crown dream was over, but she won one more G1, retired with 3 G1 wins, and was a great success as a broodmare too.
64:
* "A Spear Through the Pack" High Chaparral
The year before, High Chaparral won the Derby and the Irish Derby with a spear-sharp finish. He was 3rd in the Arc, but won the Breeders' Cup Turf and was Eclipse champion turf male.
Horses with records like that often retire early, but his camp kept him in training in 2003. With a shoulder injury, his first 4yo race was the G2 Royal Whip S. in August, which he just won by three-quarters of a length. In the Irish Champion S. he was only 3rd choice behind King George winner Alamshar and 3-time G1 winner that year Falbrav. He won by a neck from Falbrav, showing his power was intact.
Next he took on the Arc. The year before a viral illness had ruined his summer preparation, so this time, fully prepared, he carried high hopes and was favorite. But unluckily the going was heavy. A closer by nature, he couldn't quicken in the straight and sank to 3rd.
He then traveled to America again for the Breeders' Cup Turf. Despite being the defending champ, perhaps because of the Arc loss, he was only 4th choice of 9. High Chaparral and Falbrav, sitting in good spots in midfield, surged up together in the straight. It looked like a two-horse fight, but Johar came charging from behind and all three hit the line together. After a 12-minute photo, High Chaparral and Johar dead-heated for the win, with Falbrav 3rd by a head - a thrilling finish, and High Chaparral became the first horse to win the Breeders' Cup Turf twice.
He retired after this race. With 3 wins from 4 that year, he was Eclipse champion turf male for the second straight year. At stud he succeeded in both Europe and Oceania, spreading the blood of his sire Sadler's Wells around the world.

* Great Horsemen Retire, and a New Record
This year two great jockeys of Britain and America retired: P. Eddery and L. Pincay Jr.
P. Eddery won 4,632 races, 2nd most in British history, and was champion jockey 11 times. He was especially famous for partnering Dancing Brave, whose 1986 Arc is called "the greatest Arc ever."
L. Pincay Jr. was a great American jockey who broke the world record for career wins in 1999, with achievements such as three straight Belmont S. wins and 7 Breeders' Cup wins. He retired with 9,530 wins.
Meanwhile, a trainer set a new record: America's R. Frankel won 25 G1s this year, including the Belmont S. with Empire Maker - a new world record, breaking the 23 set in 2001 by himself and Ireland's A. O'Brien.

* The BHB Summer Triple Crown and Grand Slam
This year the BHB (The British Horseracing Board), Britain's racing authority, created bonus series called the BHB Summer Triple Crown and Grand Slam, aiming to boost British flat racing's most prestigious races. The first leg was the Oaks or Derby for 3yos, or the Coronation C. or Prince of Wales's S. for older horses; the second the Eclipse S.; the third the King George VI & Queen Elizabeth Diamond S. Winning all three earned the Summer Triple Crown and a GBP 1 million bonus, and also winning the fourth leg, the International S., completed the Grand Slam, raising the prize to GBP 5 million. The next year the rules changed: a horse that won the first leg needed only 2 wins from legs 2-4 for the Summer Triple Crown (the Grand Slam was scrapped after trainers said it put too much pressure on top horses). Under these rules, past horses like Nashwan and Opera House would have qualified, so it was expected to be achievable, but no horse did it in either year, and the series was dropped after 2004 to cut costs. Had it continued, four horses would have won the Summer Triple Crown: Duke of Marmalade in 2008, Sea the Stars in 2009, Ghaiyyath in 2020 and City of Troy in 2024 - but three wins in just over two months is a tall order.
65:
* The Indomitable Late Bloomer
The American mare Azeri debuted very late, in November of her 3yo year. She shrugged off long odds of 18.3 to win, and by the end of her 4yo year had won 10 of 11, including 5 G1s like the Breeders' Cup Distaff - a dominant record that made her 2002 Eclipse champion older mare and Horse of the Year. She was only the third filly or mare to be Horse of the Year, and the first in 16 years since Lady's Secret in 1986.
She kept rolling in 2003. Aiming for the Breeders' Cup, she followed the same path as the year before, winning 4 races again including the Apple Blossom H., then ran in the G2 Lady's Secret H., which she had also won before. But perhaps due to her 128 lb (about 58 kg) weight she was 2nd, and afterwards she was found to have a tendon injury. She had to skip the Breeders' Cup, and her trainer even announced her retirement. But owner M. Paulson didn't give up: he consulted several vets, found a path back, and moved her to a new stable. Named Eclipse champion older mare for the second time while recovering, Azeri finally returned in April 2004 at 6 in her third Apple Blossom H. After a long layoff and as top weight with 128 lbs, she was only 3rd choice, but she ran like her old self to win the race for an unprecedented third time. She didn't always win after that, but added 2 more G1s before retiring, and was Eclipse champion older mare for the third straight year - a perfect finale.


* A Historic Record After 200 Years
Sadler's Wells, heir to the great sire Northern Dancer, dominated European and indeed world racing. After first becoming champion sire in Britain and Ireland in 1990, he lost the title to Caerleon the next year, but then held it 13 years running from 1992 to 2004. That broke the record of 13 British sire titles set by Highflyer, the great horse of the 18th century, in 1798 - unbeaten for over 200 years.
Sadler's Wells stood at stud until 26, retiring in 2008 due to falling fertility. But many heirs, such as Galileo, were already succeeding, and his blood remains strong in racing.
66:
* A Meeting Born of the Name Alex
Afleet Alex had an unremarkable pedigree and build, and was sold and resold before he ever raced. He ended up with an ownership group, and since two members' daughters were named "Alex," he was named by combining that with his sire, Northern Afleet.
Shortly before his debut, the owners heard about another girl named Alex. She was fighting childhood cancer, yet was selling lemonade to raise money for other children with cancer. Moved, the owners decided to donate part of his winnings. But just three days after Afleet Alex won a graded stakes in his third straight win from debut, the girl passed away. Her work continued as the Alex's Lemonade Stand Foundation, and the owners pledged part of his earnings to it.
In 2005, at 3, Afleet Alex took on the US Triple Crown. On the Triple Crown race days that year, tracks across the country promoted the foundation. Carrying those hopes, he narrowly finished 3rd in the Kentucky Derby. In the Preakness S. he raced in a good midfield spot, but as he moved up at the final turn another horse bumped him and he stumbled so badly his jockey nearly fell. Yet as if someone had reached out a hand, he quickly regained his balance, surged again, took the lead and won by four and three-quarter lengths. He then won the Belmont S. by 7 lengths, taking two legs of the Triple Crown and bringing hope to many. He was named Eclipse champion 3yo colt, and his owners received a special award for their charity work.

* The Global Sprint Challenge Is Founded
This year the Global Sprint Challenge was founded, the world's first international sprint series to crown a world sprint champion. At first four countries took part - Australia, Britain, Japan and Hong Kong - with six international graded races at 6 furlongs (1200m) or less. Points were awarded for placings, and the first champion was Hong Kong-trained Cape of Good Hope, winner of the Australia S. and Britain's Golden Jubilee S.
The series continued with changing countries and races, but was suspended in 2018 when new transport rules made shipping horses between Australia and Hong Kong difficult.

* The Asian Mile Challenge Is Founded
To raise the level of Asian milers and their international competitiveness, the Asian Mile Challenge was also founded in 2005. At first it covered two races, Japan's Yasuda Kinen and Hong Kong's Champions Mile; the next year Australia's Futurity S. and Dubai's Dubai Turf were added. Until 2010 a bonus was paid to any horse winning two or more of the races; in 2011 the bonus was replaced by a luxury car. The series ended after 2011. In 7 editions the only bonus winner was Bullish Luck, who won the Champions Mile and Yasuda Kinen in 2006; no horse qualified in any other year. With schedules, travel and other hurdles, winning two was clearly very hard.
67:
* The Lady Who Reads the Future
Ouija Board was a British racehorse. Her name comes from the "Ouija board," inspired by her granddam Ouija and dam Selection Board.
She won 1 of 3 at 2, but blossomed at 3. She won a listed race by 6 lengths, then tried graded company for the first time in the Oaks. Only 4th choice, she left the field behind to win by 7 lengths. She added the Irish Oaks, the 10th filly ever to win both. She ran well in the Arc but was only 3rd. Straight after she traveled to America for the Breeders' Cup Filly & Mare Turf and won. With 3 G1 wins that year she was Cartier Horse of the Year.
2005 was a year of trials. In her first race, the G1 Prince of Wales's S., she lost a shoe at the final turn and was a distant 7th, 30 lengths back. After the race she was found to have a stress fracture and a split hoof in her left foreleg and had to rest. Back in action, she was narrowly 2nd in the Breeders' Cup Filly & Mare Turf. She then went to Japan for the Japan Cup, finishing 5th, 2 lengths behind record-breaking winner Alkaased. With no time to rest, she flew to Hong Kong for the Hong Kong Vase and won convincingly by 3 lengths with a late surge from the back. Wins had been scarce, but she showed her power in the end.
In 2006, at 5, she kept traveling to big races. She came up short in the Dubai Sheema Classic and the Queen Elizabeth S., but avenged her heavy defeat in the Prince of Wales's S. by winning it. In autumn she ran in the Breeders' Cup Filly & Mare Turf again and won by two and a quarter lengths with a tremendous finish, her second win in the race. With 3 G1 wins that year she was Cartier Horse of the Year again - the first horse to win it twice since the awards began.

* Speed Carried Into the Future
This year the great sire Danzig was put down due to old age, dying at 29. As a racehorse he won all 3 starts with blazing speed, but a knee injury forced early retirement. At stud, offspring who inherited his speed succeeded one after another, and he was US champion sire three years running from 1991 to 1993. His heirs include Danehill, three-time champion sire in Britain and Ireland, spreading his blood worldwide.
68:
* Rags to Riches Wins the Belmont
Rags to Riches was an American filly by Belmont S. winner A.P. Indy, and grandaughter of Belmont winner Seattle Slew. On the very day she finished 4th on her 2yo debut, her half-brother Jazil won the Belmont S. - perhaps her own Belmont was destiny.
She raced just once at 2 and returned in January at 3 after a long break. She broke her maiden and went straight on to win her first G1, the Las Virgenes S. She kept rolling, winning the Santa Anita Oaks by five and a half lengths. In the Kentucky Oaks, where she was the clear standout, she lived up to it with a four-and-a-quarter-length win.
For her next race her camp chose not a fillies' race but the Belmont S., the last leg of the colts' classics. Against strong colts, she was 2nd choice at 5.3. It became a duel with Preakness winner Curlin, going for a double. After a fierce battle Rags to Riches won by a head. The commentator called it: "She beats Curlin and a hundred years of Belmont history!" She was the first filly to win the Belmont in 102 years, since Tanya in 1905, and only the third ever. Her feat was widely celebrated: besides Eclipse champion 3yo filly, she was even nominated in the athlete category of the "Teen Choice Awards," where American teenagers pick their favorite artists and celebrities.

* French Racing Legend, Trainer A. Fabre
Andre Fabre is France's leading trainer, who developed many great horses including Arc winners Carnegie and Peintre Celebre. He has close ties with major owners like Dubai's Sheikh Mohammed and trains many of their horses. He first became champion trainer in France in 1987 and then held the title 21 years running until 2007. He has won it many more times since - a true legend.
69:
* Zarkava, Unbeaten Arc Winner in 7 Starts
Zarkava was an Irish-born, French-trained filly owned by H.H. Aga Khan IV of France. After an easy debut win at 2 she ran in the G1 Prix Marcel Boussac. Though blocked in the straight, when a gap finally opened she shot through it with a piercing kick to win by two and a half lengths.
In 2008, at 3, she won a prep and ran in the Poule d'Essai des Pouliches. On the strength of her powerful runs she was a heavy favorite at 1.3. She won by 2 lengths in a time 0.4 seconds faster than the colts' Poule d'Essai des Poulains the same day - astonishing. She won the Prix de Diane as a heavy favorite too, so easily that jockey C. Soumillon blew kisses to the crowd before the line. In the Prix Vermeille she missed the break badly and had to sit last, but she swept past the leaders wide to win, completing the French fillies' Triple Crown for the first time in 35 years, since Allez France in 1973.
Her run wasn't over. She took on the big stage of the Arc. The only filly among 16, she was favorite, unbeaten in 6. As in the Marcel Boussac at 2, she was blocked in the straight, but again she threaded through gaps in the pack to win clearly by 2 lengths. It was a record-filled win: the first unbeaten Arc winner in 13 years, the first filly winner in 15 years and the first 3yo filly winner in 26 years. As she headed to the presentation, the commentator and crowd cried "Quelle pouliche! Extraordinaire!" (What a filly! Extraordinary!) Zarkava retired after this race and was named Cartier Horse of the Year.

* Curlin, US Horse of the Year Two Years Running
Curlin debuted late, in February at 3, but won his first 3 starts, including a G3 and a G2, and quickly became a Kentucky Derby contender. No horse who debuted at 3 had ever won the Derby, but he was 2nd choice. He couldn't catch Street Sense and others, finishing 3rd. In the Preakness S. he met Street Sense again. Street Sense led in the straight and seemed set to win, but Curlin charged wide and won by a head for his first G1. He was 2nd to the filly Rags to Riches in the Belmont S., but in autumn won the Jockey Club Gold C. and the Breeders' Cup Classic, now a two-day event, and with 3 G1 wins was Eclipse Horse of the Year.
In 2008 Curlin traveled to the Dubai World Cup. He took the lead 400m out and just kept pulling away, winning by a race-record seven and three-quarter lengths. His run was so overwhelming that the stands reportedly fell silent for a moment. Back in America he won 3 more G1s, becoming North America's first $10 million horse. Beating horses like Zenyatta, unbeaten in 7 that year, he was Eclipse Horse of the Year for the second straight year.
70:
* Sea the Stars' British Double
Sea the Stars was named after "See the stars," words his owner's mother often said to him as a child, and his dam, Arc winner Urban Sea. Half-brother to the great Galileo and G1 winner Black Sam Bellamy, he was a true blueblood. He was 4th on debut, but then won twice, including a G2, living up to his breeding.
In 2009, at 3, he charged down the classic path. A fever meant he went into the 2000 Guineas without a prep, and he was only 6th choice. It became a duel with favorite Delegator, but Sea the Stars pulled clear at the end to win by a length and a half. Afterwards his camp said the Guineas had been the main goal, since his sire Cape Cross was a miler. But ignoring his camp's worries about the distance, he also won the Derby (12 furlongs = 2400m) clearly by a length and three-quarters, the first British double in 20 years, since Nashwan in 1989.
He raced through summer, only in G1s, and won 3 straight. Then he went for the Arc, the race his dam had won. After a good start he tossed his head, keen to go, but jockey M. Kinane managed to settle him in midfield. At the end he unleashed a powerful finish to win - only the second dam-and-son pair to win the Arc. Sea the Stars retired after this race. Running only in G1s, he won all 6 that year and was the undisputed Cartier Horse of the Year. At stud he has sired many G1 winners, living up to his blood.

* Yeats, Europe's Champion Stayer Four Years Running
Yeats debuted at 2 in 2003, won 3 straight and was the hot favorite for the Derby. But days before the race he was injured, not only missing the Derby but losing a full year to recovery. Returning in May at 4, he won his first G1 in the Coronation C., but then couldn't win.
In 2006, in his first race at 5, he tried a true marathon for the first time in the 20-furlong (4000m) G1 Gold C. and won by 4 lengths. He added the 16-furlong (3200m) G2 Goodwood C. and was named Cartier champion stayer.
His talent as a stayer now in full bloom, Yeats kept racing over long distances at 6 and 7, winning the Gold C. three years running. But in 2009, at 8, age began to show: in his first race, a listed event, he faded badly late and finished 6th, 32 lengths back. Hopes were high for a first-ever 4th Gold C. in its 200-plus-year history, and he was favorite. He settled in a good spot in midfield, took the lead early at the third turn, and held on to win by three and a half lengths. Over the last furlong a huge roar of cheers rang out for him. That was his only win that year, but he was champion stayer for the 4th year running, a perfect finale - the first horse ever to win a Cartier Award four years in a row.
71:
* Zenyatta, America's Hard-Charging Heroine
Zenyatta was named after an album by the British rock band The Police. Using her big frame and long stride to charge from the back, she had won 14 straight since her 2007 debut.
Her camp first announced she would retire after winning the 2009 BC Classic and even held a grand farewell, but in January the next year they suddenly said she would race on. The public's surprise and confusion soon turned to excitement: calls were growing for a clash with Rachel Alexandra, 2009 Horse of the Year.
To make it happen, April's Apple Blossom H. changed its purse and conditions, becoming the Apple Blossom Invitational H. under set weights. Both camps declared, but Rachel Alexandra lost her prep in 2nd and skipped the race. Without her rival, Zenyatta won by over 4 lengths.
Calls for the clash never stopped, but Rachel Alexandra announced her retirement that September, and the two never met.
Zenyatta added 3 more G1 wins, and her camp headed for the BC Classic to win it again. She was overwhelming favorite, and racing fans worldwide hoped for the queen's 20th straight win.
She missed the break badly and had to trail at the very back - a tough race. But she was the queen: she steadily closed the gap and in the straight charged with a furious finish. She ran down leader Blame... but fell short by the narrowest of margins, 2nd by a head. After this agonizing loss, her camp announced her retirement for good.
Despite that final defeat, she won 19 of 20 starts. Her overwhelming record still shines in American racing history.

* Goldikova Wins a Third BC Mile
Goldikova had already won the BC Mile twice and was famous worldwide. She lost Cartier Horse of the Year to Sea the Stars, but no one could stop her run in the mile division.
In 2010 she opened with a win in the Prix d'Ispahan and kept winning. She was 2nd in August's Prix Jacques le Marois, but in the Prix de la Foret she broke well, led and held off all challengers. Some had feared she couldn't handle Longchamp's soft ground, but the win blew those fears away.
Then came the BC Mile. The last two years it had been held at Santa Anita Park, but in 2010 it was at Churchill Downs. Goldikova was favorite at 1.3, with Gio Ponti, previous year's Eclipse champion older male and champion turf male, next in the betting.
The pace was fairly slow, and Goldikova watched the leaders from midfield. In a grueling race where the front-runners wouldn't stop, she made her move in the straight and swept past the others in an instant. Gio Ponti charged from behind with a tremendous kick, but she shrugged off his challenge to win her third straight BC Mile.
It was an unprecedented feat in Breeders' Cup history on the flat. Goldikova became a champion whose name will live on in world racing history.
72:
* Frankel: The Legend Begins
This year a "monster" dominated European racing: Frankel, a British-bred colt named after great trainer Robert Frankel, who died in 2009.
His sire was Galileo, winner of the Derby and Irish Derby. Carrying enormous expectations as his son, Frankel debuted and beat Nathaniel, a future winner of the King George VI & Queen Elizabeth S. and the Eclipse S., by half a length. His run continued, and in 2011 he went into the G1 2000 Guineas unbeaten.
Overwhelming favorite, he won by 6 lengths from Dubawi Gold. That untouchable style - like his 10-length win in the Royal Lodge S. the year before - is Frankel's trademark.
Seeing such power, people hoped for a father-son Derby double. But his camp chose the St. James's Palace S. in the mile division instead, where he gave a controversial performance.
Running in the second group, he made an early move mid-race, took the lead and kept pulling away. The crowd gasped at what looked like a runaway. Everyone thought he'd be swallowed up. But he didn't tire as expected and held off Zoffany's fierce charge by three-quarters of a length. The narrow win drew criticism, but holding on through sheer ability was impressive in itself.
Then came the Sussex S. Frankel was favorite again, with Canford Cliffs, who had beaten mile queen Goldikova, close behind in the betting. Billed as the "Duel on the Downs," it drew huge attention.
But when it came to it, Frankel made the running and won without letting anyone near, showing the crowd his tremendous power.

* Great Hoofprints Left at Longchamp
This year a Cinderella story was written into racing history. Its heroine was Danedream, a filly bred at Germany's Brummerhof Stud. She was naturally small, and sold as a yearling for 9,000 euros (about 1 million yen) - a sign of how little she was rated.
She won her debut, but then only ran well without winning. She bravely tried G1s like the Prix Marcel Boussac, but victory wouldn't come.
Looking for a breakthrough, her camp took her to Italy. Her third race there, the Italian Oaks at San Siro, was the race of destiny. Racing in midfield, she kicked from the final turn and blew past her rivals with an explosive finish, winning by six and a half lengths. It was the moment the 9,000-euro filly's sleeping talent awoke.
Now soaring, she won the Grosser Preis von Berlin and the Grosser Preis von Baden, and finally took on the Arc. She had shown her ability, but the field included defending champion Workforce, last year's runner-up Nakayama Festa from Japan and many other stars, and she was only 10th choice.
But whoever she faced, her kick never dulled. In the straight she accelerated, swept elegantly past the leaders and won by 5 lengths from Shareta.
It was the first Arc win by a German horse, and jockey A. Starke became the first German jockey to win it. Helped by unusually good ground at Longchamp that year, she won in record time. Setting so many records, Danedream marched on as Europe's queen.
73:
* The "Monster" Rated 140 lbs
Unbeaten since his debut and winning race after race in the mile division, Frankel - known worldwide as "the monster" - soared even higher this year.
He ran only in G1s and won all 5, every one by a wide margin. In the Queen Anne S. he won by an incredible 11 lengths, earning a rating of 140 lbs in the World Thoroughbred Rankings. He also won the International S. by 7 lengths and the Sussex S. by 6; over 8-10 furlongs (1600-2000m) he was simply unbeatable, and was Cartier Horse of the Year for the second straight year.
The extraordinary Frankel even shook the ranking system itself. 140 lbs was normally the ceiling; only Dancing Brave, at 141 in 1986, had ever exceeded it. There had long been criticism that past ratings were too generous, and Frankel's arrival led to the drastic step of lowering all past ratings across the board.
This drew a strong backlash. Harwood, trainer of Dancing Brave, who was "downgraded" from a record 141 to 138, fumed: "Utter nonsense. If they want Frankel on top, just rate Frankel higher." Former jockey W. Swinburn agreed, questioning the rewriting of history.
In the end the review was made unofficial, and it was announced that Dancing Brave's 141 remained the highest ever. Frankel's 140 became the second highest, but horses from different eras and distances can't simply be compared - both are once-in-a-generation greats.

* Camelot Tries for the British Triple Crown
Another talking point this year was Ireland's Camelot trying for the British Triple Crown. The last horse to win the 2000 Guineas, Derby and St. Leger was Nijinsky in 1970, and with the long St. Leger's prestige declining, most horses now aimed for the Arc instead. But having won the 2000 Guineas and the Derby, Camelot ran in the St. Leger, trying for the first Triple Crown in 42 years.
He just failed to catch front-runner Encke and was 2nd - no Triple Crown. Still, he also won the Irish Derby that year and was named Cartier champion 3yo colt.

* Black Caviar's Winning Streak Down Under
In the Southern Hemisphere, Australian mare Black Caviar set an unprecedented record: 25 straight wins unbeaten from her debut, 15 of them G1s. Rated 130 lbs in the World Thoroughbred Rankings, she was ranked 3rd in the world behind Frankel (140) and Cirrus des Aigles (131).
The Australian season runs from August to the following July, and in the 2013 end-of-season rankings she became the first Australian-trained horse ever to top the world.
74:
* America's Turf Titan
Wise Dan. To explain his achievement, we must start with how turf and dirt racing are ranked in America.
Dirt racing has long been mainstream in America and considered above turf. Indeed, almost every Horse of the Year has been a dirt winner, and even turf winners tended to handle dirt as well. Wise Dan was the first "turf miler" to be named Eclipse Horse of the Year in America - and the first turf-based horse to win it two years running.
From his 2010 debut through 2011, Wise Dan showed ability on all-weather, dirt and turf, but won 8 of 14, with just one G1, the Clark H. A fine record, but something was missing.
The turning point was the 2012 Stephen Foster H. After losing to Ron the Greek there, he was switched to turf only.
The decision seems to have paid off. He won the Fourstardave H. and the Woodbine Mile S. in a row, and from there began to dominate the turf mile division. Favorite for the BC Mile, he lived up to it, breaking a 15-year-old course record. For this unmatched run he won three Eclipse Awards.
2013 was his golden age. His only loss was a 2nd in the Shadwell Turf Mile S. He won the Woodbine Mile again in record time and the BC Mile again, a 14-race turf winning streak, and won three Eclipse Awards for the second straight year.
Wise Dan won 23 of 31 in his career. Of his 8 losses, only one came on turf, before the switch. No horse deserves the title "Titan of the Turf" more.

* The Sprint Queen Leaves the Turf
Who is the world's greatest sprinter? Many names come up, but many would say Australia's great mare Black Caviar. Since her 2009 debut, 25 starts, 25 wins - an unbeaten sprinter in the truest sense.
Australia has a rich program of sprint races, with fierce competition. Yet Black Caviar kept winning from her debut on.
With no rivals left at home, in June 2012 she traveled to faraway Britain for the Diamond Jubilee S. at Royal Ascot. She had an unexpectedly hard fight but won. Some were puzzled by such a narrow win, but the next day it emerged she had injured a leg - perhaps the strain of travel.
She then rested, and in February 2013 ran in the Black Caviar Lightning, named after her. She never gave up the lead and won in track-record time. Running like a champion despite the long break, she left great hoofprints on Flemington's straight course, "The Straight Six."
She kept winning, set a record 25-race winning streak, and after winning the T.J. Smith S. suddenly announced her retirement, leaving the turf with many legends behind her.
This year she was rated 130, level with Arc winner Treve, becoming the first Australian-trained horse to finish the year No. 1 in the world rankings.
75:
* Treve Wins Back-to-Back Arcs
A brilliant comeback - no words fit the 2014 Arc better. The star was Treve, a filly who won the 2013 Arc by 5 lengths over Japan's Orfevre and was named Cartier Horse of the Year.
Treve was an unbeaten Arc winner. But after that Arc her glittering record began to dim. She was 2nd in the Prix Ganay, 3rd in the Prince of Wales's S., then 4th in the Prix Vermeille. After three shock defeats, the public turned critical and some doubted her ability. Facing that headwind, she headed for the Arc again.
German Derby winner Sea the Moon, expected to run, suddenly retired after losing the Grosser Preis von Baden, and with strong runners from Britain and Japan the betting was wide open. The favorite was Taghrooda, winner of the Oaks and the King George VI & Queen Elizabeth S. - curiously, a 3yo filly like Treve the year before. Stars like Japan's Just a Way, who romped in the Dubai Duty Free, and Prix Niel winner Ectot were also well backed, and Treve was only 12.0.
Under a chilly autumn sky, very different from the days before, the Arc began. Treve settled in the pack, watching the leaders and never getting too keen. Out of the false straight, as the field fanned out and kicked, she slipped up the inside and gradually moved forward. With 400m left she swept past the others and pulled away, coasting home by 2 lengths. She was only the 6th horse ever to win the Arc twice.
Fans worldwide cheered her brilliant comeback. The champion's form that silenced all doubts was back.

* The Kentucky Derby: A Dream 52 Years in the Making
This year one horse achieved a remarkable feat: California Chrome, a racehorse born, as his name says, in California on the West Coast.
American racing history reveals an East-West rivalry. In the late 19th century, the center of American racing was Kentucky in the East. Led by Kentucky, organizations were formed and laws put in place modeled on British racing, rapidly modernizing American racing.
The West Coast - California and other western states - didn't like this. Western power brokers pushed modernization to rival the East. In 1937 Del Mar Racetrack opened, backed by Hollywood actor Bing Crosby and others.
But with transport problems and more, West Coast-bred horses struggled to win in the East. No California-bred had won the Kentucky Derby since Decidedly in 1962.
Against this background, a West Coast-bred winning the Kentucky Derby carried special meaning. In 2014 California Chrome went into the Derby carrying the West Coast's pride and hopes. Fresh from winning the Santa Anita Derby, he was favorite at 3.5, though some dismissed him simply for being West Coast-bred.
The pace was slow. Sitting 3rd and moving up, he passed the leader at the final turn and powered away in the straight. It's easy to imagine the cheers in California and across the West Coast at this first win in 52 years.
76:
* American Pharoah's Triumphant Run
American racing had gone without a Triple Crown winner since Affirmed in 1978. Twelve horses won two legs - Spectacular Bid, Pleasant Colony, Alysheba, Sunday Silence and more - but all fell in the final leg, the Belmont S. Then this year, at last, a Triple Crown winner appeared: American Pharoah.
His Kentucky Derby was a close win, but he won the Preakness S. by 7 lengths and the Belmont S. by five and a half - beyond dispute. On Belmont day an overflowing crowd packed Belmont Park to see the first Triple Crown winner in 37 years and witnessed the historic moment in a frenzy.
He went on to win the Breeders' Cup Classic too, completing the "Grand Slam." When Affirmed won the Triple Crown 37 years earlier the Breeders' Cup didn't exist yet, so American Pharoah became the first Grand Slam winner in US racing history.
That year's Breeders' Cup Classic also promised a clash with Beholder, then called the best mare in training - unbeaten in 5 that year, with 9 G1s in all and invincible even against colts. Excitement ran high, but Beholder fell ill just before the race, and the showdown never happened.
With his great rival absent, American Pharoah won the Classic easily by six and a half lengths. For this stunning run he was unanimously named Eclipse Horse of the Year and rated world No. 1 at 134 lbs in the World's Best Racehorse Rankings.
By the way, "Pharoah" was meant to be "Pharaoh," after the kings of ancient Egypt, but was misspelled when registered. Thanks to his success the story became widely known, and the misspelled name is simply pronounced "Pharaoh" by commentators and in Japanese.

* Treve Goes for a Third Arc
In Europe all eyes were on Treve's attempt at an unprecedented third straight Arc. She had become famous in Japan two years earlier by beating Orfevre in the Arc. This year she won three straight from the start of the season and went into the Arc as overwhelming favorite. But she was beaten by the new 3yo star, Golden Horn, and the hat-trick was not to be.
Golden Horn had won 6 of 7, including three G1s: the Derby, the Eclipse S. and the Irish Champion S. He won the Arc clearly, holding off Treve's charge, and more was expected, but after a 2nd in the Breeders' Cup Turf he retired.
With both stars, Treve and Golden Horn, gone from the turf, European racing entered a wide-open era the next year.
77:
* The West Coast Hero, Horse of the Year Again
In 2015 California Chrome ran a fine 2nd in the Dubai World Cup, but injuries kept him sidelined most of the year. He returned in January 2016 in the San Pasqual S. As favorite he won safely, and after a handicap at Meydan he headed for the Dubai World Cup, the race he had missed out on the year before.
He sat in a good spot, came wide into the final turn, accelerated to the front, pulled clear from 300m out and won by over 3 lengths from Mubtaahij.
Behind the win was a mishap: his saddle slipped badly during the race. Jockey V. Espinoza said, "It was all I could do to keep my balance." Yet it was a stunning run, as if nothing had happened - the West Coast hero showing his class. The win made him North America's all-time leading money earner.
His run continued. He won two more G1s, including the Awesome Again S. In the BC Classic he was beaten half a length by 3yo Arrogate's fierce charge, but no one in the world doubted his strength anymore.
The California-born hero won Eclipse Horse of the Year for 2016, his second after 2014, carving his name into American racing history.

* The Pegasus World Cup Is Born
In 2016 the world's richest race was the Dubai World Cup at $10 million (total purse). But in May, the Stronach Group, an American racing business, announced the Pegasus World Cup, with an even bigger $12 million purse - for 4yos and up, 9 furlongs (1800m) on dirt. Its name comes from the Pegasus statue at the host track, Gulfstream Park.
In January 2017 the first Pegasus World Cup was held. Among many stars, including Dubai World Cup winner California Chrome, the winner was Arrogate, who had beaten California Chrome in the BC Classic. Setting a track record of 1:46.83, he dazzled the world with a champion's run.
In 2018 the purse rose to $16.3 million. But in 2019, with the new Pegasus World Cup Turf ($7 million) added, it fell to $9 million, and from 2020, with entry fees abolished, to $3 million.
Though the prize is smaller than at first, the winner earns priority entry to the Saudi Cup in February, so it remains a big race drawing many top horses. As a showcase for American racing, its future is worth watching.
78:
* Fated Rivals
The horse who dominated this year's BC Classic was Gun Runner, named Eclipse Horse of the Year. A blueblood, he was out of a mare by Giant's Causeway, "the Iron Horse," and his uncle was BC Classic winner Saint Liam.
His rival was Arrogate, from the same crop, who beat Horse of the Year California Chrome in the 2016 BC Classic and was top-rated at 134 lbs. Comparing their 3yo records, Arrogate was far ahead. Gun Runner ran consistently well but often fell short, and in their meeting in the Travers S. he was crushed by 15 lengths.
Then came their 4yo season. They met again in March's Dubai World Cup, and Arrogate won by two and a quarter lengths. Gun Runner was again shown the gap between them.
But after this race things changed. Gun Runner won G1 after G1, as if his sleeping talent had awoken, while Arrogate's form faltered.
They met once more in the BC Classic. Gun Runner, the challenger trying to stop Arrogate repeating, made the running and pulled away in the straight to win, finally getting revenge on his rival. After the race his owner said, "I was confident we could beat Arrogate, but sitting there I started getting nervous." Taking on the champion clearly brought enormous pressure.
Arrogate retired after this race. The next January Gun Runner won the Pegasus World Cup, which Arrogate had won in 2017, and also ended his career. So ended the era built by the two rivals.

* Enable, First British-Trained Filly to Win the Arc
The British filly Enable was from the first crop of Nathaniel, winner of the 2011 King George VI & Queen Elizabeth S. and more. When she debuted at 2 she wasn't highly rated, nor did she show eye-catching power.
It was the 2017 Cheshire Oaks and her meeting with jockey L. Dettori that led her to the big stage. She won safely and went on to the Oaks, winning by 5 lengths in record time.
Her winning run kept going. She romped in the Irish Oaks to complete the Anglo-Irish Oaks double, then ran in the King George VI & Queen Elizabeth S., once won by her sire Nathaniel, beating Eclipse winner Ulysses by four and a half lengths. She added the Yorkshire Oaks and moved on to the Arc.
The 96th Arc was held under cloudy skies at Chantilly. Among 18 runners from many countries, Enable was overwhelming favorite. The pace was surprisingly slow - 1:27.10 for the first 1400m - but she raced calmly in 3rd or 4th. In the straight she broke clear and pulled away from runner-up Cloth of Stars, showing the world her power and brilliance.
Dettori called her "a superstar." She was the first British-trained 3yo filly ever to win the Arc.
79:
* Winx Sets New Records
43 starts, 37 wins, 25 G1s - an unprecedented, unbreakable record held by one great mare: Winx, an Australian-bred by Dubai World Cup winner Street Cry.
From May of her 3yo year, when she won the Sunshine Coast Guineas and the Queensland Oaks, no one could stop her. In her first Cox Plate she won by four and three-quarter lengths. Her trainer C. Waller said after the race, "I never imagined she'd become a horse like this." She went on to win graded races including G1s, one after another - the Chipping Norton S., the George Ryder S. and the Doncaster Mile - reigning over the turf with crushing power, and was named Horse of the Year.
In 2016, at 5, the Cox Plate was hers alone again. Racing with the leaders, she hit the front at the final turn and pulled away to win by 8 lengths.
In 2017 she won the Cox Plate in record time, the first to win it three times running since Kingston Town in 1982. She kept winning, and her Chipping Norton S. win broke Black Caviar's Australian record of 15 G1 wins.
Then came 2018. At 7, with retirement in sight, she showed no sign of slowing. Besides extending her winning streak every time she ran, she set records like a third straight George Main S. and back-to-back Turnbull S. wins. Then she went for an unprecedented fourth straight Cox Plate.
She faced many strong rivals, including Dubai Turf winner Benbatl, but brushed them aside. Moving up from midfield, she took the lead with ease and won by 2 lengths, and was named Horse of the Year for the fourth straight year.

* An Unbeaten US Triple Crown, But...
Justify. His name means "to show to be right." 6 starts, 6 wins, an unbeaten US Triple Crown - who could have guessed that after such a brilliant career his own name would turn ironic?
After debuting at 3, Justify aimed for the US Triple Crown: the Kentucky Derby, the Preakness S. and the Belmont S. Earning enough qualifying points by winning the Santa Anita Derby, he went for the Triple Crown fully prepared.
He won the Kentucky Derby from the front in commanding style. Two weeks later he won the Preakness S., then went to the Belmont S. unbeaten.
He led and set a fast pace. In the straight no one could go with him, and he drew away to the line. He was the 13th US Triple Crown winner - only the second unbeaten one, after Seattle Slew in 1977, and the first ever to debut at 3. Just 112 days after his debut, the fastest Triple Crown ever.
He was then prepared for the BC Classic in autumn, but an injury forced his retirement, to much regret. After shining like a brilliant shooting star, he went to stud.
But in 2019 a scandal emerged: after his Santa Anita Derby win, a banned substance had been detected in his sample. Had he not won the Santa Anita Derby, he could not have run in the Kentucky Derby. The scandal grew into a huge affair involving many people.
His camp denied using any drug, claiming it came from a plant growing wild. The legal battle dragged on, and in March 2024 he was officially disqualified. Even so, his Triple Crown that followed was not taken away. His record and achievement will remain.

* The Stayers' Million Is Founded
With British racing shifting toward shorter races, the BHA (British Horseracing Authority) founded the Stayers' Million this year, a long-distance race series to protect the breeding of stayers. A horse that won one qualifier, such as the Sagaro S. or the Yorkshire C., and then won all three main races - the Gold C., the Goodwood C. and the Lonsdale C. - earned a GBP 1 million bonus, a huge sum for British racing then. Before the series began, no horse had ever won all three main races in the same year, and a winner was expected to be rare. But a monster stayer, Stradivarius, not only did it with ease but did it two years running. Whether that was the direct cause is unclear, but the series was scrapped after just two years.
80:
* Australia's Great Mare Leaves With One More Feat
In April 2019 the great mare Winx, who had left so many legends on the world's turf, was about to run her final race, the Queen Elizabeth S. at Royal Randwick.
Six months after her unprecedented fourth Cox Plate, she had also won the Chipping Norton S. and the George Ryder S. for the fourth straight time, stretching her winning streak to 32 and her G1 tally to 24 - truly unbreakable records.
In the Queen Elizabeth S. she was overwhelming favorite at 1.1. After the start she waited in midfield to the rear, saving her energy, then came wide at the final turn and swept past the whole field. Japan's Kluger charged hard up the inside, but couldn't match her explosive finish. She ran out the last furlongs of her career and won by a length and a half.
33 straight wins, 25 G1s. And with this race's prize money she passed Arrogate, the previous record holder, to become the world's all-time leading earner: A$26,451,174 (about 2.124 billion yen). No one threatened her record until Hong Kong's Golden Sixty broke it in 2023.
Having finished her last race, Australia's hero and undisputed queen left the turf - with a win so dominant some said she shouldn't retire yet. Perhaps no one, her camp included, ever found the limit of her ability.
Her regular jockey H. Bowman later said, "She has nothing left to prove."

* A Shock Arc Finish
Having won two Arcs, Enable ran in the 2019 Arc going for a third. As people hoped for a historic record, an assassin stood in her way: Waldgeist, a colt who had been 4th in the 2018 Arc.
Unremarkable early in his career, he came into his own as an older horse, winning G1s like the Grand Prix de Saint-Cloud and the Prix Ganay. In the King George VI & Queen Elizabeth S. he trailed stars like Enable and Crystal Ocean, but still ran a fine 3rd. He then won the Prix Foy, the Arc prep, and went into Arc day on a roll.
On the day, Longchamp was all about Enable. Fans were handed boards to cheer her on, and of course she was favorite. Everyone hoped for an unprecedented third win. Her expected rivals were Prix Niel winner Sottsass and Grand Prix de Paris winner Japan. Waldgeist was only 5th choice.
Rain since the day before had left the ground soft. The 12 runners ploughed through the heavy going. Enable, racing just off the leaders, burst out of the pack after the false straight. But perhaps drained by the tough ground, she faltered just short of the line. Pouncing was Waldgeist, who had been biding his time in the pack. Unleashing his kick in the final furlong, he caught the queen 50m out and pulled away to the line.
It was the first Arc win by a colt aged 5 or older in 17 years, and the first by a Prix Foy winner in 35 years. Having set new records, Waldgeist left the turf after this race.
82:
* Snowfall Wins the English and Irish Oaks
Snowfall was a filly by Japanese Triple Crown winner Deep Impact, born in Japan and trained in Ireland, out of a Galileo mare - a blueblood. But at 2 she won just 1 of 7. In her last 2yo race, the G1 Fillies' Mile, there was a bizarre mix-up: Snowfall and stablemate Mother Earth ran in each other's colors without anyone noticing. It came to light after the race, and the correct result was announced: Mother Earth 3rd, Snowfall 8th.
After drawing attention for that odd incident, she seemed like a different horse at 3 in 2021. In her first race, the G3 Musidora S., she was 4th choice at 15 but won by three and three-quarter lengths. Her stock rose to 3rd choice for the Oaks. On good-to-soft ground she waited at the back of midfield, surged when a gap opened, took the lead and kept pulling away, winning by 16 lengths - the biggest margin in the Oaks' 200-plus-year history. Jockey L. Dettori, a 20-time classic winner, said, "I've won many Classics but not one as easy as that." In the Irish Oaks she was overwhelming favorite at 1.3 and won by eight and a half lengths. She then won the Yorkshire Oaks for 3 straight G1 wins.
She tried races like the Arc afterwards but didn't win again. Still, her dominant wins that year earned her Cartier champion 3yo filly. But early the next year came sad news: while on a break she was found to have a fractured pelvis, and despite treatment her condition worsened until she had to be put down. The snow that fell so heavily in summer melted away in the cold winter sky, mourned by all.

* Arlington Park Closes
The Arlington Million S., founded in 1981 as the world's first race worth $1 million, was held at Arlington Park, opened in 1972 in Illinois. It suffered a fire in 1985 and changed owners repeatedly from the 1990s, and in 2021 the site was sold and the track closed. It was also known for being among the first to introduce technologies now taken for granted, like the odds board and photo-finish camera - a track that contributed greatly to racing.
83:
* 6 Starts, 71 Lengths: A Shock
Flightline, by top American sire Tapit, stood out even as a foal and sold for $1 million at the 2019 Saratoga yearling sale, the top price on day one. No real rival ever emerged in his career - his greatest enemy was injury. Before his debut he was startled at the farm and slammed his hindquarters into a stall door, badly injuring himself. Then the coronavirus pandemic delayed his development, and he didn't debut until April at 3. Though he was never asked, he won his 6-furlong (1200m) debut by thirteen and a quarter lengths, drawing great attention. Then he injured a hoof and had to rest through summer. But as if layoffs meant nothing to him, he won his comeback and then the G1 Malibu S. by over 10 lengths each, ending his 3yo year unbeaten in 3.
In 2022, at 4, all eyes were on him, but another training injury held him back. He finally ran in June's Metropolitan H. and, despite a slow start, won easily by 6 lengths. Next came the 10-furlong (2000m) Pacific Classic S. Some wondered whether the longer trip would trouble a horse whose weapon seemed to be speed, but such logic meant nothing to him. He took the lead down the backstretch and simply kept pulling away. Even easing up over the last 100m, he beat Dubai World Cup winner Country Grammer by an astonishing 19-plus lengths. Trainer J. Sadler said, "This is an exceptional horse. He has speed and keeps going."
Then, at last, the Breeders' Cup Classic. In a star field where all 8 runners were G1 winners, he was a clear favorite at 1.44. So sure was everyone of his win that his show odds (top 2) of 1.46 were actually higher than his win odds - a rare oddity. He sat right on Life Is Good, who set a blistering pace, passed him easily at the final turn and ran away from the field, winning by a race-record eight and a quarter lengths.
Plagued by leg trouble all along, Flightline retired unbeaten, having won his 6 races by a combined 71 lengths. After his stunning Pacific Classic his rating was 139 lbs, raised to 140 the next January - level with Frankel at the top, and far above Cigar's 135, by far the highest ever for a North American-trained horse. Despite just 3 races that year he was named Eclipse Horse of the Year almost unanimously. A great horse who carved his name into American racing history, he will be talked about for years to come.
84:
* Golden Sixty Becomes the All-Time Money Earner
The big news this year was Hong Kong's Golden Sixty setting a world earnings record. In recent years the record had been about $17.1 million, set by America's Arrogate at the end of 2017, until Australia's Winx broke it in April 2019 with about A$26.45 million (about $18.6 million then). Then in April of this year, Golden Sixty reached about HK$167.17 million (about $21.27 million then) to become the new world leader.
Golden Sixty raced only in Hong Kong, winning 10 international G1s, including three Hong Kong Miles and three Champions Miles. He kept running through about five tough years, from late in his 3yo season to late at 8, to earn that much. He was Hong Kong Horse of the Year three years running from 5 to 7 - a great horse of modern Hong Kong racing.
But the next year his record was broken by fellow Hong Kong horse Romantic Warrior. Romantic Warrior also won G1s abroad, like Australia's Cox Plate and Japan's Yasuda Kinen, and at the end of 2024 won his third straight Hong Kong Cup to pass Golden Sixty in career earnings.
Also in the news: jockey Z. Purton, who has also ridden Romantic Warrior, won 173 races in a season, a new Hong Kong record.
By the way, Japanese racing has high prize money overall, and several Japanese horses, like Equinox and Almond Eye, rank near the top of the world earnings list.

* Ace Impact Wins the Arc Unbeaten
In Europe, Ace Impact won the Arc unbeaten from his debut, and attention turned to the birth of a new young star. Ace Impact debuted in January this year and won the French Derby just four and a half months later. Unbeaten in 5, he went into the Arc as a well-deserved favorite and won. His seemingly limitless power shocked European racing, but this was his last race: after a career of just 9 months he went to stud, stepping onto a new stage to pass on the great blood of his grandsire Frankel and sire Cracksman.
A star of Ace Impact's crop was Ireland's Auguste Rodin. From Deep Impact's final crop, he won 4 G1s: the Derby, the Irish Derby, the Irish Champion S. and the Breeders' Cup Turf. He never met Ace Impact, but the two competed as candidates for Cartier Horse of the Year.
In the end Ace Impact won both Horse of the Year and champion 3yo colt, the No. 1 horse of the year.
85:
* City of Troy, Europe's Horse of the Year
City of Troy is by US Triple Crown winner Justify, out of a mare by European great Galileo. Living up to his blood, he won 3 straight at 2, capped by the G1 Dewhurst S. In 2024 his first 3yo race was the 2000 Guineas, where he was overwhelming favorite at 1.6. He raced up front but was easily passed and finished a well-beaten 9th. Still, trainer A. O'Brien announced he would go straight to the Derby. In the big race, favorite again, he slipped out from the back of midfield and won clearly by two and three-quarter lengths - the first American-bred Derby winner in 21 years. Having overcome that heavy defeat, he beat older horses clearly in the Eclipse S., then won the International S. in course-record time. He was 8th in his last race, the Breeders' Cup Classic, but his 3 G1 wins earned him Cartier Horse of the Year.
City of Troy went to stud after the Breeders' Cup Classic. Even O'Brien, who has trained so many greats, said, "He's definitely the best we've ever trained, no doubt about it." His future at stud is eagerly awaited.
His stablemate Auguste Rodin also grew after a heavy defeat. He debuted in 2022 and soon won a G1, but in his first 3yo race, the 2000 Guineas, he sank to 12th as favorite. He then won the Derby and the Irish Derby, and even the Breeders' Cup Turf. In 2024, at 4, he wasn't as dominant, but won the G1 Prince of Wales's S. For his last race his camp chose the Japan Cup. He finished 8th, but at the retirement ceremony afterwards Japanese fans gave a huge ovation to Auguste Rodin, from Deep Impact's last crop.

* A New World Earnings Record
By the previous year Hong Kong's Romantic Warrior had won 6 Hong Kong G1s and even Australia's G1 Cox Plate. In 2024 he traveled to Japan for the Yasuda Kinen and won, beating Namur and others. He ended the 2023/2024 season (Hong Kong's season runs from September to early July) with 5 straight G1 wins and was named Hong Kong Horse of the Year. In December he ran in the Hong Kong Cup, which he had won the two previous years. Beating Japan's fillies' Triple Crown winner Liberty Island and Derby winner Tastiera, he became the first to win the Hong Kong Cup three times running. With this win his career earnings reached $22.8 million, passing fellow Hong Kong horse Golden Sixty to become the world's all-time leader.
81:
* Enable Leaves the Turf
The year before, Enable narrowly missed a third straight Arc. Her camp kept her racing at 6, aiming for a third Arc win.
After more than six months off, she returned in the Eclipse S. in July 2020. Because of the coronavirus pandemic, Britain's flat program was partly irregular, and for the first time the Eclipse was closed to 3yos. Hopes for her comeback made her favorite, but she was beaten into 2nd by Ghaiyyath, who had won the Coronation C. in record time.
Next she ran in the King George VI & Queen Elizabeth S. Perhaps to avoid facing a two-time winner of the race, rivals pulled out one after another, leaving just 3 runners, the smallest field ever. She easily ran down front-runner Sovereign in the straight and won by five and a half lengths, the first horse ever to win the King George three times. In autumn, as planned, she tried a fourth Arc but sank to 6th, her first and only finish out of the top three. It was her last race. No third Arc, but her running left its mark on fans worldwide.

* A Solo on the Turf
Stradivarius was a British colt named after the world's finest violins. After winning the 16-furlong (3200m) G1 Goodwood C. at 3, he made long distances his domain. At 4 he won all 5 of his long-distance graded races, including the 20-furlong (4000m) Gold C., and was named 2018 Cartier champion stayer. At 5 he won the Gold C., the Goodwood C. and the Doncaster C., the first stayers' triple crown in 24 years, and was champion stayer again.
In 2020, at 6, he won his third straight Gold C. and a record fourth straight Goodwood C., proving he was still the best and taking champion stayer for the third straight year. He kept running long races until 8, winning 18 graded races in a long career.

* Love's British Fillies' Double
The year before, Love won the G1 Moyglare Stud S. and became a leading contender for the British fillies' classics. After over six months off, she went straight into the 1000 Guineas for her first 3yo race. She was 2nd choice behind unbeaten 2yo queen Quadrilateral, but won by four and a quarter lengths. As favorite in the Oaks she lived up to it, winning by 9 lengths in a race-record 2:34.06 to complete the British fillies' double. She then beat older horses easily in the Yorkshire Oaks, ending the year unbeaten in 3, and was named Cartier champion 3yo filly.
86:
* Veteran Voyage Bubble Shines
Voyage Bubble was a Hong Kong miler who won two G1s the year before, the Hong Kong Stewards' C. and the Hong Kong Mile. But on trips abroad he was 13th in the Dubai Turf and 17th in the Yasuda Kinen. This year, with him now 6, his camp decided to skip travel and focus on Hong Kong, especially the Hong Kong Triple Crown.
He won the first leg, the Stewards' C., easily by 2 lengths, his second straight win in the race. The second leg, the Hong Kong Gold C., was a race he had lost in 2nd the year before, but this time he won safely by over 3 lengths. The third leg, the Champions & Chater C., was 2400m. With no experience beyond 2000m it looked tough, but he swept past the field in the straight to win by three and a half lengths. Jockey J. McDonald said afterwards, "Voyage Bubble switched off nicely and handled the trip." He became only the second Hong Kong Triple Crown winner ever, and the first in 31 years.
Also, in January jockey Z. Purton rode his 1,814th winner, breaking Hong Kong's all-time record. It was a year full of headlines for Hong Kong racing.

* Minnie Hauk Wins the English and Irish Oaks
Minnie Hauk is an Irish-bred filly by the unbeaten Frankel, and she ran every bit as well as her "monster" sire. She opened this year by winning the Cheshire Oaks, an Oaks trial, then went for the real thing. Desert Flower, unbeaten winner of the 1000 Guineas going for the second leg of the fillies' double, was favorite, with Minnie Hauk 2nd choice. 4th choice Whirl went clear in front. As Desert Flower struggled, Minnie Hauk made her move, drew level with Whirl and it became a two-horse battle, which she won by a neck.
In the Irish Oaks she was overwhelming favorite at 1.1 and lived up to it with a sharp finish - only the 16th filly ever to win both Oaks. Next she took on Europe's third Oaks, the Yorkshire Oaks. Perhaps to avoid her, only 4 ran. She pulled away easily to win by three and a half lengths, her third Oaks (sometimes called the European Oaks Triple Crown). She then went to France for the Arc, her camp's long-held goal. With three Oaks wins she was 2nd choice, but 10th choice Daryz won for his first G1, and Minnie Hauk was 2nd by a head. Still, running so well on the big stage against colts showed her true strength.
87:
* The Birth of the "Big Three"
Many groups of rivals from the same crop have been called a "Big Three," but this year the first-ever "Big Three" rose in Japanese racing: Takeshiba O, Asaka O and Marchis.
Takeshiba O was by China Rock, later a leading sire, but his dam never raced and his granddam was a maiden at local tracks - hardly a blueblood - and as a youngster he wasn't well built. He lost his first two starts, won his third, then won 6 straight from his fifth. In his first graded win, the Asahi Hai Sansai S., he won by a race-record 7 lengths and became the top classic contender.
Asaka O, by contrast, was by Hindostan, the great sire of five-crown winner Shinzan, and closely related to British Derby winner Pinza - a blueblood called "the young prince."
Marchis was the only one of the three from the Kansai region. His striking chestnut coat made him a fan favorite, and he was favorite in 21 of his 31 starts. He had the ability to match, winning the Hanshin Sansai S. to become the West's 2yo champion.
The three first met in the Yayoi Sho, a classic trial. Favorite was Takeshiba O, who had won his last race, the Tokyo Yonsai S. (moved to dirt due to snow), by 8 lengths in record time. He and the speedy 2nd choice Cadmus fought for the lead at a blistering pace. Takeshiba O got in front down the backstretch but ran out of steam and was caught by Asaka O before the line: Asaka O 1st, Takeshiba O 2nd, Marchis 3rd. Marchis then won the Spring S. With top contender Takeshiba O beaten twice, the race for the crown was now seen as a three-way battle.
The first classic, the Satsuki Sho, was run in the rain. Takeshiba O, who loved heavy ground, was favorite. He was slow away but took the lead before the third turn. In the straight he dueled with Asaka O, but the race went to Marchis, charging from the back. The top 3 were the same as in the Spring S.
The second leg, the Japanese Derby, was held a month late on July 7 due to stand renovations at Tokyo Racecourse, and was called the "Tanabata Derby." It also fell on the day of the House of Councillors election, so only 8 races were run instead of the usual card. Favorite was Marchis, who had won the Satsuki Sho and also beaten Takeshiba O in the NHK Hai, followed by Takeshiba O and Asaka O. When the race began, 9th choice Tanino Hello More, using gate 1, shocked everyone by going to the front. Normally Takeshiba O and Asaka O would follow, but perhaps wary of Marchis after the Satsuki Sho, they stayed stuck in midfield. In the straight Takeshiba O surged up the inside, threatening to take the lead, but it was too late. Tanino Hello More never weakened and led all the way to the line. Takeshiba O was 2nd, 5 lengths back, Asaka O 3rd and Marchis 4th - bitter for all three. Some called it luck, but Spartan training had made his talent bloom.
For the last classic, the Kikuka Sho, Takeshiba O had accepted an invitation to the Washington DC International in America, so it looked like a duel between Marchis and Asaka O. Tanino Hello More led again, but Asaka O, held up at the back, swept past him and Marchis in the straight to win his first classic. The Big Three's battle remained even, carried over to the next year.

* Southern Kanto's Champion Shines in the JRA
The Southern Kanto local racing triple crown began in 1964. In 1967 Hikaru Takai became the first horse to win all three.
The next year he moved to the JRA, finished 2nd in all three open races, and went into the Tenno Sho (Spring) as favorite. On heavy ground he tracked the leaders, took the lead at the top of the straight and drew away to win by 2.8 seconds - officially "a distance," about 17 lengths. A rout like that was no fluke of the rain. He then won the Takarazuka Kinen in record time, proving to the racing world that his power was real.

* Great Sire Hindostan Dies
This year the great sire Hindostan passed away. A British-bred who won the Irish Derby and more, he went to stud in Ireland but did little in five years there. The Hidaka Light Horse Promotion Association in Hokkaido spotted him, formed the first stallion syndicate in Japanese racing history, and imported him for 12 million yen, a huge sum then.
In 1961, his 6th year at stud in Japan, his offspring won an amazing 4 of the Big Eight races, and he became leading sire. He went on to sire five-crown winner Shinzan and more, winning 7 sire titles in all. His offspring's 117 graded wins still ranks near the top.
Hindostan died in 1968, while his son Asaka O was starring in the classics. His body was preserved and donated to the Japan Racing Association, and can still be seen at the horse museum in Urakawa, Hokkaido.
88:
* Takeshiba O at His Peak
The year before, Takeshiba O was seen as the leader of the "original Big Three," but never won a single head-to-head with them. He opened this year 2nd again in the Nanakusa S., his 7th straight 2nd in Japan.
But from here his real worth emerged. He ran in the Tokyo Shimbun Hai on dirt, a surface he had raced on only twice, and won by 6 lengths in record time. In a dirt open race he won by a distance, again in record time, carrying 60 kg. That Japanese record for 1700m on dirt stood for 37 years.
He then won the Kyoto Kinen on turf and an open race carrying 60 kg or more. Finally, in the Tenno Sho (Spring), he faced Asaka O and Marchis in a Big Three showdown for the first time in a while. Takeshiba O, on a winning streak, was favorite, followed by Asaka O and Marchis. The pace was slow; Takeshiba O led in the straight and held off the charging Asaka O by 2 lengths - his first win against the Big Three, and his first Big Eight race.
He won twice more, including an open special carrying a career-high 65 kg, and became the first "100-million-yen horse," passing 100 million yen in career earnings.
That year he won 8 straight, 4 in record time. Dominant at any distance and on any surface, setting record after record, he was called "the monster" by fans. Later horses would be called "the grey monster" and "the shadow-roll monster," but Takeshiba O is said to be the "original monster," the first in racing history to bear the name.

* A First Step Toward the Arc
Speed Symboli did little in the classics - 21st in the Satsuki Sho, 8th in the Japanese Derby - but ran 2nd in the Kikuka Sho, and the next year won 3 straight, including the Tenno Sho (Spring).
He kept running well and raced on this year at 7 (old age system). He was 3rd in his first race, then won the Meguro Kinen and the Diamond S. Seeing this, his camp decided on a trip to Europe, with the ultimate goal of the Arc - the first Japanese horse to try it. First he went to Britain for the King George VI & Queen Elizabeth S., but caught the equine flu then spreading in Britain, his preparation suffered, and he was 5th. He was 10th in the Grand Prix de Deauville prep and unplaced in the Arc itself - a crushing trip.
He recovered on a break and ran in the Arima Kinen. The field included Akane Tenryu, who had improved rapidly over summer to win the Kikuka Sho and was called "the greatest late bloomer since the war." The two dueled down the straight, and Speed Symboli won by a nose - the first 7yo ever to win the Arima Kinen.
His trip showed Japan's best were still far from world class, but his daring challenge was a huge achievement.

* Ritto Training Center Opens
Racehorses had always been trained at stables at each racecourse. But as racing boomed and the number of horses grew, the courses' stables could no longer cope, and dedicated "training centers" for managing and training racehorses were planned. This year Ritto Training Center finally opened, changing how racehorses were developed.
89:
* The Epic Duel of Arrow Express vs Tanino Moutiers
The 1970 classics were thrilled by an East vs West clash.
From the East came Arrow Express. The year before he won his debut in record time and the Asahi Hai Sansai S., the Kanto 2yo championship, breaking the 2yo record for 1600m on turf by 0.8 seconds. Unbeaten in 5, he was named champion 2yo colt.
From the West came Tanino Moutiers. He lost some races in his first year, but won the Kyoto Sansai S. and the Hanshin Sansai S. in a row to become the undisputed Kansai 2yo champion.
They first met in the Spring S., a trial for the Satsuki Sho. Billed as the "A-T Showdown" after their initials, it drew a crowd of over 100,000 to Nakayama. 2nd choice Arrow Express went forward, with favorite Tanino Moutiers chasing. In the straight Arrow Express took the lead about 200m out, but hopes of a win were short-lived: Tanino Moutiers came wide with an astonishing finish and swept past him before the line. The margin was three-quarters of a length, but it was a clear win. In the Satsuki Sho, Tanino Moutiers won the duel from 200m out by a head. In the NHK Hai, their third meeting before the Derby, Tanino Moutiers was slow away and Arrow Express won by two and a half lengths.
Then came the big one, the Japanese Derby. Perhaps because it was in Tokyo, Kanto horse Arrow Express was a heavy favorite with 41.8% of win bets, and Tanino Moutiers 2nd choice.
