But perhaps due to that morning's workout, Arrow Express was fretful and sweating in the paddock, while Tanino Moutiers was in perfect shape. As usual Arrow Express went forward, but struggled to get through the pack around the third and fourth turns and began to look in trouble. Tanino Moutiers glided forward wide, had the leaders in range at the final turn, and from about 200m out dueled with front-runner Date Tenryu, getting the better of him by half a length to complete the double. Arrow Express was 5th. Kansai horses took the top 3, a bitter result for Kanto.
Neither won again before retiring. At stud, as if avenging his own defeat, Arrow Express's offspring did brilliantly, while Tanino Moutiers's did little. Arrow Express was leading sire in 1980 and 1981.

* Masato Shibata's Bitter Replacement
This year Masato Shibata, a young jockey in his 3rd year, had ridden Arrow Express since his debut. But before the Satsuki Sho, he was told the owner wanted another jockey. Unable to accept it, Shibata asked the trainer why, and the trainer, in tears, told him: "Arrow is already Kanto's star. To beat Moutiers from Kansai, he needs Kanto's top jockey. If it hurts, then prove yourself better." Shibata turned that frustration into fuel, resolving to become a jockey who would never be taken off, and in 1988 he became Japan's champion jockey. He later said, "Because I couldn't ride Arrow, I became a real jockey."

* Speed Symboli, Old Warrior
Speed Symboli had nearly retired, but raced on this year at 8 (old age system). His camp had heard the JRA might create an international invitational race, and were determined: "We can't stop without running Speed Symboli, who has fought the world." In the end the plan was shelved after breeders protested the decision to free up horse imports, and it was delayed over 10 years until the Japan Cup. But Speed Symboli paid no attention and ran superbly.
In his first race, the American JCC, he won in Japanese record time carrying 60 kg, and he won the Takarazuka Kinen in record time too, showing no signs of age. At year's end he ran in his 5th straight Arima Kinen. Favorite was Akane Tenryu, whom he had beaten by a nose the year before; Speed Symboli was 3rd choice behind autumn Tenno Sho winner Mejiro Asama. He boldly took the rough inside, led at the top of the straight, and though nearly spent, held off Akane Tenryu's fierce charge with grit to win by a neck again - the first horse to win the Arima Kinen twice. He retired after this race and was named Horse of the Year for the second time, three years after the first.
90:
* The Little Filly Tomei's Challenge
Described as "like a mouse," Tomei sold for just 1.65 million yen. She was small even for a filly, weighing under 400 kg even in her racing days. Naturally she was rated low, but after debuting in 1968 she turned her fiery temper into fighting spirit, winning 4 of 6 that year. The next year she didn't win a classic, but won races like the Kyoto Yonsai Tokubetsu. In 1970 she improved further, winning twice in a row including the Milers C. She was favorite for the Hankyu Hai but finished 2nd, then split a hoof and had to rest for a long time.
Then came 1971. After over six months off, she returned in an open race. She didn't win at first, but after finally winning in her 4th start she seemed to awaken, reeling off 4 straight wins including the Milers C. and the Hankyu Hai. In autumn she tried her first long race, the Tenno Sho (Autumn). Her longest race had been the 2400m Japanese Oaks, and as a proven miler she was seen at a disadvantage, but she won anyway. For her final race she chose the Arima Kinen. With top horses out due to equine flu, Tomei was 2nd choice behind Tenno Sho winner Mejiro Musashi. She raced from last, took the lead at the final turn and held on to win clearly by a length and a half. It was the first Arima Kinen win by a filly or mare in 11 years, and she became the first filly or mare ever named Horse of the Year. None followed for 26 years, until Air Groove in 1997.

* The Upstart's Brilliant Run
In racing, a horse whose pedigree is uncertain and not recognized as a thoroughbred is called a "thoroughbred-type." Hikaru Imai was one of them, born not on a racehorse farm but on a rice farm that bred horses on the side. His price was just 1.5 million yen - and he was bought for only 750,000 yen, on the promise that "the other half will be paid if he wins his debut." He won his debut as 5th choice, and the breeder received the promised 750,000 yen. He kept winning and ended his 2yo year with 3 wins and two 2nds from 5.
In 1971, at 3, his form was erratic, but he won his first graded race, the Kisaragi Sho. In the first classic, the Satsuki Sho, he was 4th choice, but he swept past the leaders in the straight to win. In the Japanese Derby he raced around 23rd, far behind the so-called "Derby position" (top 10 at the first turn), but again his superb finish swept him past the field for his second classic. He never won again, and retired after a tendon injury. Rising from thoroughbred-type to double classic winner before soon leaving the turf, the upstart captivated racing fans.
91:
* The Kansai Big Three and the Shining Kick
The classic crop of 1972 (Showa 47) was packed with stars, one of the strongest generations in Japanese racing history, known as "the brilliant class of '47."
The classics were seen as a duel of the Kansai Big Three: Land Prince, Long Ace and Taiteem. The first classic, the Satsuki Sho, went to Land Prince, from the first crop of Tesco Boy. The Japanese Derby was pushed back to July by the flu, and also called the "Tanabata Derby." The Big Three fought it out, and favorite Long Ace won by a neck.
The final classic, the Kikuka Sho, was also seen as a Big Three battle, but 5th choice Kanto horse Ishino Hikaru, running for the second week in a row, ran down Taiteem to win. Suddenly the center of attention, he topped the fan vote for the Arima Kinen despite being only 3. That year's Arima Kinen drew three Tenno Sho winners - Mejiro Asama, Mejiro Musashi and Bell Wide - plus Big Three member Long Ace, and fans were thrilled; betting on the Arima Kinen passed 10 billion yen for the first time. Ishino Hikaru burst through wide with a superb finish to become the first 3yo colt to win the Arima Kinen. In the end Horse of the Year went not to the Kansai Big Three but to Ishino Hikaru.
The next year Taiteem, called "the uncrowned prince" after missing the classics, won the Takarazuka Kinen, and the year-end Arima Kinen went to Strong Eight of the same crop - "the brilliant class of '47" kept shining. Grand Marchis, who won the Nakayama Daishogai four times and became the first jumper inducted into the Hall of Fame, and Tanino Chikara, who overcame a serious injury to battle Haiseiko and Take Hope, were also of this crop.
92:
* Idol Horse Haiseiko's Triumphant Run
Haiseiko was a national idol who even appeared on the cover of a boys' manga magazine, and who sparked Japan's first racing boom. His power and popularity were truly monstrous.
He debuted at Oi, a local track, and won 6 straight, by a total of 56 lengths - unbeatable at Oi. Back then the wall between local and JRA racing was high, but Haiseiko moved to the JRA in style. As this "ronin" from local racing cut down the chosen elite one after another, the Japanese people saw themselves in him and went wild.
His JRA debut was the Yayoi Sho. Over 120,000 fans packed Nakayama, and fans at the front of the stands by the outer rail, trying to see him up close, were nearly crushed by the crowd surging from behind and fled onto the track. It wasn't the dazzling rout of his local days, but he won his first race for his new stable on turf for the first time, then won the Spring S. to stretch his streak to 8, and won the Satsuki Sho - the first ever by a horse from local racing.
He went into the Japanese Derby unbeaten with an incredible 66.7% of win bets. He tried to break clear from his usual forward spot, but couldn't quicken in the straight and was a shock 3rd. The Derby went to Take Hope - the horse Haiseiko would battle as his lifelong rival until retirement.
The Derby loss ended Haiseiko's myth of invincibility, but his popularity only grew - that is what makes him the original idol horse.

* Take Hope Proves Himself With a Double
Take Hope, meanwhile, was an unlucky horse, cast as the villain - "the Derby winner who beat the idol horse by a fluke." Angered at being called a fluke, his camp vowed to "beat Haiseiko!" in the Kikuka Sho.
In the Kikuka Sho, Haiseiko led 5 or 6 lengths clear at the final turn and kept going in the straight, but in mid-straight Take Hope charged and closed fast. The two pulled clear in a duel and hit the line together. The photo showed Take Hope had won by a nose. Beating Haiseiko "on ability, not popularity," Take Hope was finally accepted as Haiseiko's true rival.
He was named Horse of the Year (and champion 3yo colt), and the fact that he is the only colt besides Triple Crown winners to win both the Derby and the Kikuka Sho (he didn't run in the Satsuki Sho) proves his strength better than anything.

* Betting Machines Arrive
In June this year, prototype betting machines began operating at Nakayama. Today buying tickets from machines at the track is normal, but back then people usually bought them at windows, handing over a slip with their selections or telling the clerk out loud. At some tracks there were even separate windows for each bet type, such as win and place.
Being able to bet more easily may have been one reason the racing boom caught fire.
94:
* Battle of the Generation's Best Colt and Filly
Even after Haiseiko, leader of the first racing boom, retired, attendance kept rising, and in 1975 JRA racing drew a record 15 million fans. The filly who drew them more than any was Tesco Gaby, famed for her overwhelming speed.
From birth she was noted for a muscular build rare in a filly and a very calm temperament, and after debuting she won 4 straight with blazing front-running. In 1975 she kept rolling in the classics, leading all the way to win the Oka Sho easily. Fast Oka Sho winners often ran out of stamina in the Oaks, but she led all the way again with rare speed. Japanese racing then prized stamina - both Tenno Sho races were 3200m - but it gradually shifted toward speed, and some say Tesco Gaby, who swept the racing world with natural speed, was the turning point.
Among colts, Kabuto Yao drew attention for front-running so extreme it was called "madman's pace." Kicked by another horse as a youngster, he became a timid horse terrified of others, but his camp turned that to their advantage, training him to run fast from the front. Born healthy with superb heart and lungs, he grew into an elite front-runner. Years later jockey Yukio Okabe, a devotee of unbeaten Triple Crown winner Symboli Rudolf, said: "Against Kabuto Yao in his Derby, I don't know if even Rudolf could have won."
Before the classics, the two met once, in the Tokyo Yonsai S. (now the Kyodo News Hai), billed as a clash between two contrasting front-runners - one a hope since before her debut, the other awakened after his.
Tesco Gaby went forward at the start, but Kabuto Yao, refusing to yield the lead, shot out wide while fighting his rider. In that order they rounded the final turn. Mid-straight, as the field spread out, Kabuto Yao, hating the whip, veered so badly he almost hit Tesco Gaby. As he lost his balance she drew level, and a fierce duel followed, but Kabuto Yao held on by a neck. Both went on to win two classics each, proving their power. The race is remembered as the first and last great duel between two future double classic winners.

* "Mr. Keiba" Hangs Up His Whip
Jockey Yuji Nohira achieved many feats - the first 100 wins in a year in JRA history, the first win abroad by a Japanese jockey - and was known for partnering Speed Symboli. This year he retired to take over his late father's stable, winning his farewell race, the Meguro Kinen. He never won a colts' classic (he won the Oka Sho and Oaks with filly Kane Keyaki).
But as a trainer he met the great Symboli Rudolf and won the unbeaten Triple Crown with him. For his great contribution to Japanese racing as both jockey and trainer, Nohira was called "Mr. Keiba."
95:
* Epic Battle: "Pegasus" vs "Prince of the Blaze"
More than a year after Haiseiko left the turf, fans longed for a new star to fill the void. Then came the pair later called "TT."
Tosho Boy, called "Pegasus" for his flying stride, and Ten Point, the "Prince of the Blaze" for his beautiful chestnut coat and straight white blaze. Their clash gripped fans throughout this year's classics. Their first meeting was the Satsuki Sho, an East-West clash between Kansai's Ten Point and Kanto's Tosho Boy. Tosho Boy won by 5 lengths from Ten Point. Kansai courses then had few uphill straights compared with Kanto's. After the loss Ten Point's camp tearfully said, "Unless Ritto builds a hill course, we'll never beat Kanto horses" - which is said to have led to the hill training course at Ritto and today's Kansai dominance.
TT's first battle was settled, but their rivalry went on. In the Japanese Derby and Kikuka Sho both lost to outsiders, but at year's end they went into the Arima Kinen as the stars against older greats like spring Tenno Sho winner Erimo George, with fillies' double winner Teitania also from their crop. Sitting just ahead of midfield behind the front-runners, TT closed on the lead at the final turn and slipped clear in the straight. Tosho Boy passed Erimo George first and held off Ten Point by a length and a half. It was the first Arima Kinen with 3yos 1st and 2nd. Winning the fated TT duel, Tosho Boy broke the race record by 1.1 seconds and was named Horse of the Year and champion 3yo colt.
But TT's battle wasn't over. The next year a new assassin joined, and it grew even fiercer.

* New Ways to Enjoy Racing
Telephone betting, trialed since 1974, was fully introduced this year: members could place bets by phone. Push-button phones were rare, so most bets were placed by telling an operator. Taken for granted now, betting from home was revolutionary then. It later evolved into voice-guided and internet betting, widening how fans enjoy racing.
96:
* A Race for the Ages: TTG's Arima Kinen
In the previous year's Kikuka Sho, while all eyes were on TT and Derby winner Climb Kaiser, the winner was Green Grass, who had barely scraped in as the lowest earner in the field. A late bloomer with just one win during TT's spring classic battles, he crashed the TT rivalry as "the green assassin." The three became known as TTG and are still talked about.
In 1977 TTG, now older horses, clashed in the Takarazuka Kinen. Tosho Boy had been off since the previous Arima Kinen with leg trouble. Fresh off the break, his workouts were dull and his stable said he "lacked spirit," so he drifted and Ten Point was favorite. Ten Point had never beaten Tosho Boy - most fans thought his chance for revenge had come. But master jockey Kunihiko Take held Tosho Boy to a perfect slow pace in front, then ran the last 1000m faster than the then-record for 1000m on turf, winning with a long sustained run. After this race Ten Point declined an invitation to America's Washington DC International, vowing to "beat Tosho Boy" and become Japan's best.
In autumn Tosho Boy's camp announced he would retire after the Arima Kinen - Ten Point's last chance to beat his nemesis and TTG's final battle. Tosho Boy had the better record, but fans again made Ten Point favorite, as in the spring Grand Prix. TT broke clear early and fought a match race, neither giving up the lead - a clash of pride that set Nakayama roaring. The two stayed in front into the straight with no one near. Green Grass charged from behind, but TT kept going, and after a fierce duel Ten Point crossed the line three-quarters of a length ahead. Beating Tosho Boy at last, he was unanimously named Horse of the Year, the first unanimous winner in 21 years since Meiji Hikari.
This Arima Kinen, where TTG gave everything, is still hailed as the greatest race in Japanese history. Tosho Boy retired and TTG's era ended. In every race all three ran, they took 1st to 3rd - proof of how far above the rest they were.

* Tragedy of the "Mochikomi"
As TTG thrilled the nation, an extraordinary horse was born a year younger: Maruzensky, later called "the supercar." By British Triple Crown winner Nijinsky out of a mare by US Hall of Famer Buckpasser, he was a blueblood "mochikomi."
A mochikomi is a foal conceived abroad and born in Japan. Back then, Japanese stars like Speed Symboli and Takeshiba O were no match for foreign horses abroad, and Japan was thought far behind the world. So when trade was liberalized in 1971, to protect domestic breeders, mochikomi, like foreign-bred horses, were barred from the Big Eight races except the Arima Kinen.
Maruzensky swept the racing world with overwhelming speed, and fans badly wanted him in the Japanese Derby. But despite desperate appeals from his jockey Nakanowatari, he never got the chance. He retired injured, unbeaten in 8. He passed his speed to his offspring and produced many G1 winners as a sire and broodmare sire, hugely influencing racing.
From 1983 mochikomi were treated as domestic horses and the restriction ended. The regret of those who never saw Maruzensky run in the Derby may have paved the way for later mochikomi stars like Nishino Flower and Biwa Hayahide.
98:
* Avenging His Sire in the Derby
Katsurano Haiseiko, from the first crop of idol horse Haiseiko, who sparked the first racing boom, carried great hopes. Leg trouble meant it took him 4 starts to break his maiden, but he won 3 straight at 3 and joined the classics. He was narrowly 2nd in the Satsuki Sho, where a father-son double was hoped for, then went into the Japanese Derby - the race where his sire lost to Take Hope - as favorite.
With well over 20 runners in the Derby then, horses left behind at the start had little chance, and a top-10 spot at the first turn was called the "Derby position." He settled right at the edge, in 10th. He moved up to 3rd at the final turn and burst clear in the straight. Drawing alongside came Rindo Purban - who, as fate would have it, had won the Yonsai Chukyori S. like Take Hope, and was ridden by Isao Shimada, the very jockey who beat Haiseiko with Take Hope in the Derby. But as if shaking off that fate, Katsurano Haiseiko showed his pride and won by a nose.
His fine run avenging his sire thrilled many fans. In an era dominated by imported sires, it was the first Derby win by a son of a Japanese-bred sire in 20 years, since Komatsu Hikari (by Tosa Midori) in 1959.

* TTG's Last Stand
Green Grass, one of the TTG Big Three, often fell short compared with TT and was seen as the plain one. But after TT left the turf he kept running alone as No. 3, winning the Tenno Sho (Spring) the year before. This year, at 7 (old age system), he rested after two spring races, ran once in autumn, and with chronic leg trouble chose his third Arima Kinen (3rd and 6th before) as his farewell - the year-end showpiece his rivals had won (Tosho Boy in 1976, Ten Point in 1977). With them gone, it was a race he couldn't lose.
Sitting in midfield on the rail, he began a long run down the backstretch and was already level with the leaders before the third turn. Leading into the straight, he found a second wind and drew away, but Mejiro Phantom closed fast. Green Grass dug in and held him off by a nose - a run of pure grit, as if carrying TT's spirit.
Green Grass achieved the fairytale finish TT never had, bringing a glorious close to the TTG story.
93:
* Fated Rivals and a Third Assassin
The previous year's Horse of the Year was double classic winner Take Hope, while Haiseiko received a special "People's Award". In summer 1973, while both were resting, a horse returned from a 20-month layoff after surviving a life-threatening illness: Tanino Chikara. Half-brother to double classic winner Tanino Moutiers, he had been watched since before his debut but had just one win. Running with a unique low-headed style, he won race after race all the way to the Tenno Sho (Autumn). Just four months after his return, a "power crawling along the ground" had broken into the Big Two.
Haiseiko and Take Hope, who had carried the racing boom, both announced the year-end Arima Kinen as their final race. Favorite was Take Hope, Tenno Sho (Spring) winner, who now finally topped Haiseiko in popularity too. Haiseiko, beaten in all 6 starts at 2400m or more, was 3rd choice, with Tanino Chikara 2nd. Kitano Kachidoki, winner of the Satsuki Sho and Kikuka Sho and that year's Horse of the Year, didn't run.
Tanino Chikara took the lead at the start. The year before he had watched Haiseiko too closely, couldn't catch the leaders and was 4th - this bold tactic was the lesson learned. Haiseiko closed from mid-race, Take Hope surged from behind, and it came down to three. In the straight Tanino Chikara pulled away from both and won by 5 lengths from Haiseiko. But all eyes were on the battle for 2nd and 3rd between Haiseiko and Take Hope, after 9 epic battles. Fans felt an era ending with the retirement of the two who had led the boom.

* "Single-Bracket" Designation, Mark of a Favorite
Betting then was mainly bracket quinella, and if a favorite was scratched, bettors could only hope for the outsider in the same bracket. Haiseiko's huge support in the previous year's Japanese Derby exposed the problem, and in 1974 "single-bracket designation" was introduced, placing a horse expected to draw heavy betting alone in its bracket. It was first used in that year's Satsuki Sho, where unbeaten Kitano Kachidoki was given a single bracket and won.
97:
* Farewell, Ten Point
The year before, TTG had thrilled racing. Having finally beaten his nemesis Tosho Boy, who retired after the Arima Kinen, Ten Point set out this year on his long-planned trip abroad. But many Kansai fans wanted to see him once more before he left, so his camp entered him in the Nihon Keizai Shinshun Hai (now the Nikkei Shinshun Hai) at Kyoto. Everyone believed it would be a send-off win.
In falling snow, carrying a massive 66.5 kg, Ten Point led from the start down the backstretch. Erimo George and others pressed him, but just as everyone thought he was in a different class, he suddenly dropped back before the final turn. It was a severe fracture. Despite desperate treatment, 43 days later Ten Point passed away.
His tragic death was widely reported, bringing grief to racing and raising many issues, such as whether to assign excessively heavy weights. Two days after his death a farewell ceremony was held at Ritto Training Center - the first funeral ever held for a thoroughbred in Japan.
Farewell, Ten Point... Shuji Terayama, a poet and playwright who loved racing, dedicated a poem to him, and many fans grieved.

* Hatsushiba O, Toward an Unprecedented Fourth Crown
Southern Kanto's classics, the spring Haneda Hai and Tokyo Derby plus the Tokyo Okan Sho founded in autumn 1964, were modeled on the JRA's European-style classics (first two legs in spring, third in autumn).
This year Southern Kanto's star was Hatsushiba O, son of Takeshiba O, who ran on turf or dirt at any distance. He won the Haneda Hai and Tokyo Derby in spring, then the Tokyo Okan Sho by 6 lengths in autumn, the third Southern Kanto triple crown winner ever.
But he didn't stop. Aiming for a fourth crown that the two previous triple crown winners (Hikaru Takai and Golden Ribot) never managed, he ran in the year-end Tokyo Daishoten and won by two and a half lengths, the first Southern Kanto quadruple crown ever. The European-style format lasted until 1995, but only two others won all four (San Oi in 1983 and Rosita in 1989).

* Miho Training Center Opens
Japanese racing originally did everything at racecourses nationwide, from development and training to racing. But as racing's popularity and horse numbers grew, racecourse stables neared their limits, and urban sprawl around tracks made keeping horses there harder. So "training centers" dedicated to training and developing racehorses were planned.
In Kansai a site was found smoothly and Ritto opened in 1969, but in Kanto choosing and buying land dragged on. Finally, 17 years after it was planned, Miho opened in 1978. With both centers open, the East-West battle intensified and racing developed further.
99:
* Hagino Top Lady of the "Glamorous Clan"
Myrtle was a broodmare imported from Britain in 1957. Thanks to her offspring Oaks winner Yamapit and two-time champion mare Itto, her family was dubbed the "Glamorous Clan" after a popular novel of the time.
Itto's first foal, Hagino Top Lady, made a dazzling debut, setting a Japanese record of 57.2 seconds for 1000m on turf. It stood as Hakodate's 2yo record for over 45 years until 2025.
In 1980, at 3, she ran in the Oka Sho in just her third career start. Against rivals like previous champion 2yo filly Laughontes, she set a furious pace from the start and never gave up the lead. No other horse won the Oka Sho in its third start until Daring Tact in 2020. She later won the Queen Elizabeth II Cup too, was named champion 3yo filly, and raised the "Glamorous Clan's" fame.

* Birth of a White Horse
White horses command attention with their beauty. Japanese racing first recognized them around this time.
In 1979 a pure white foal, Hakutaiyu, was born on a farm in Urakawa, Hokkaido. Grey horses, also white-coated, aren't born white (they whiten with age), and neither of his parents was grey, so he couldn't be grey. Some suspected albinism, since a pure white horse had never been seen in Japan, but as white racehorses already ran abroad, he was registered as Japan's first white thoroughbred.
In 1980 Japan's first "Coat Color Council" recognized "white" as the 8th coat color, with Hakutaiyu as No. 1. Sports papers and TV covered him, and as "Hakuba-kun" he was loved far beyond racing - laying the groundwork for the white horses' popularity that continues today.
100:
* Breeding Horses That Can Compete With the World
Compared with Britain, birthplace of modern racing, and other countries, Japanese racing started late - a developing racing nation. Rules limiting foreign runners and burdensome quarantine made it so closed to foreign horses that it was mocked as "isolationist racing."
Calls grew to "breed horses that can compete with the world," and in 1981 Japan's first international invitational race, the Japan Cup, was finally held.
Seven foreign horses came from America, Canada and India. Japan's defenders included Hoyo Boy, winner of the Arima Kinen and Tenno Sho (Autumn), and Monte Prince, the uncrowned prince twice 2nd in classics. But foreign horses took 1st to 4th - a rout. The winner, American mare Mairzy Doates, hadn't even won a G1-level race at home, and she broke the course record by a full second. Japanese racing was shown just how high the world's wall was.

* Tenno Sho "Win and Out" Rule Abolished
The Tenno Sho has been run twice a year, spring and autumn, since the first running in 1937 (then the Teishitsu Gosho Ten). It used a "win and out" rule: a horse that won could never run in it again - reportedly so that a past winner losing wouldn't hurt the race's prestige. But as a result, the autumn field was sometimes weaker than the spring one.
Perhaps for that reason, the rule was finally abolished this year. Naturally horses then tried to win it twice, but in 1984 the autumn race was cut from 3200m to 2000m, making a spring-autumn double very hard. Only 6 horses have ever done it (same year: Tamamo Cross, Special Week, T.M. Opera O, Meisho Samson, Kitasan Black; across years: Super Creek).
101:
* Mejiro Titan: Father and Son Tenno Sho Winners
Mejiro Asama, autumn 1970 Tenno Sho winner, disproved the belief that "Partholon's offspring are precocious milers," and went to stud in 1973 with a syndicate and high hopes. But in his first year he covered 28 mares and none conceived, leaving his owners in despair. They kept trying, and in his 5th year at stud came Mejiro Titan.
Mejiro Titan debuted at 3. It took 4 starts to win, but he improved rapidly and won the St. Lite Kinen, a graded race, in September. In 1982, at 4, he went for a father-son double in the Tenno Sho (Autumn). He launched a long run from the third turn of the second lap, led in the straight and held on, completing the double in Japanese record time, a full second faster than last year's winner Hoyo Boy.
He was first trained by Tokichi Ogata, called "the Great Ogata" for his huge contributions to racing. Tokichi, who had also trained his sire Mejiro Asama, rated Mejiro Titan highly, but died just before the St. Lite Kinen. His son Moritsugu took over, and together he and Mejiro Titan won the Tenno Sho as if carrying on their fathers' wishes - a win built on the bond between man and horse.

* Northern Taste, Japan's Greatest Sire
Northern Dancer won two legs of the US Triple Crown and became a world-famous sire. His son Northern Taste was bought at an American sale by the Shadai Group. He raced in France and Britain with a respectable record, including the G1 Prix de la Foret. He then went to stud in Japan, though some breeders doubted him because of his big head and short legs.
But once his offspring raced, opinions changed completely. His first crop included Arima Kinen winner Amber Shadai, his runners did brilliantly, and in 1982 he became leading sire. His offspring kept showing such development that people said "Northern Taste's runners change three times," and he was leading sire 10 times in all (JRA and local combined).
His sire line has since died out in Japan, but he undoubtedly contributed hugely to Japanese racing - truly "the horse who changed Japanese breeding."
102:
* Mr. C.B., Flawless and Free
Tosho Boy, "Pegasus." C.B. Queen, who won the Mainichi Okan in record time. Two outstanding horses who, by a strange twist of fate, debuted in the same race. Their son was Mr. C.B. (C.B. Queen's first foal).
The first classic, the Satsuki Sho, was run on heavy ground, seemingly bad for a closer like him, but he charged boldly from last to win. In the Japanese Derby he ignored the jinx that "you can't win unless you're in the top 10 at the first turn," closing from third-last to win.
In the Kikuka Sho, going for the Triple Crown, he again raced at the back, but moved on the uphill of the third turn and passed the leaders. Then, on Kyoto's downhill, where the rule is to go easy, he accelerated against all convention, stunning the crowd. He took the lead at the final turn and won with no one near - the third Triple Crown winner ever and the first in 19 years, since Shinzan. He was also the first Triple Crown winner by a Japanese-bred sire.

* Farewell, Shuji Terayama
Poet Shuji Terayama, known as "the alchemist of words," loved racing so much he became an owner, and is known for the memorial poem "Farewell, Ten Point" he wrote when Ten Point died.
Among jockeys he favored Masato Yoshinaga, known for the extreme "Yoshinaga Special" tactics, often writing about him and vowing to "keep writing until he wins the Derby." But Terayama died suddenly this year. Yoshinaga won the Japanese Derby with Mr. C.B. about three weeks later.
Terayama's book "Uma Yabure te Sogen Ari" contains this line: "I don't necessarily think racing is a metaphor for life. On the contrary, I think life is a metaphor for racing." It shows his own racing philosophy: those who watch racing are what matter.
103:
* The Unbeaten Triple Crown
In the year the JRA introduced graded races, ranking 15 races as G1, a historic first was achieved.
Symboli Rudolf was rated highly even before his debut. When trainer Yuji Nohira asked jockey Yukio Okabe to ride him, he said, "If you ever find a horse stronger than Rudolf, you can switch anytime." As if to prove that confidence wasn't overblown, Rudolf won his first 3 starts with Okabe.
In 1984 he took on the classics and won the Satsuki Sho clearly. At the ceremony Okabe raised one finger high - "first crown." In the Japanese Derby Rudolf ignored his rider's cues and ran his own race to win, and Okabe raised two fingers. Afterwards he said, "Today Rudolf taught me." After the Derby his camp planned a trip abroad for the Arc, but a shoulder injury scrapped it, and he stayed in the classics. In the Kikuka Sho he showed the "Emperor's" style, bursting clear in the straight to become Japan's first unbeaten Triple Crown winner. At last Okabe thrust three fingers to the sky.
One can't help imagining how he'd have run in the Arc - but had he gone, there might have been no unbeaten Triple Crown.

* A Japan Cup Clash of Triple Crown Winners, and a Shock Ending
In the three years since the Japan Cup was founded under the slogan "horses that can compete with the world," Japanese horses kept losing to foreigners. But the year before, Kyoei Promise finished 2nd, and fans felt victory was within reach.
In October 1984 Tokyo Racecourse installed "Turf Vision," the JRA's first giant screen, changing the old style of watching through binoculars. Then last year's Triple Crown winner Mr. C.B. and Symboli Rudolf, unbeaten Triple Crown winner just two weeks earlier, both entered. Everyone focused on the first-ever clash of Triple Crown winners and how they'd take on world-class foreign horses. Early on, as the others watched each other, Takarazuka Kinen winner Katsuragi Ace went for broke, opening a lead of over 10 lengths. At the final turn it shrank to about 3 lengths, and Rudolf and the foreigners closed in the straight, but Katsuragi Ace, who had saved plenty at the slow pace, found a second wind and held on to win as 10th choice.
In its 4th year, Japan's long-held dream of a first Japan Cup win was achieved not by the two Triple Crown stars, but by supporting actor Katsuragi Ace. With this shocking win he earned the title "Triple Crown killer."

* The "Hall of Fame" Horses Who Built Japanese Racing
This year the Hall of Fame was created to honor horses who contributed greatly to JRA racing. The first 10 were Kumohata, St. Lite, Kurifuji, Tokitsukaze, Tosa Midori, Tokino Minoru, Hakuchikara, Shinzan, Haiseiko and Tosho Boy. Mr. C.B. was inducted in 1986 and Symboli Rudolf in 1987. The "Hall of Fame Corner" in the JRA Racing Museum at Tokyo Racecourse displays bronze statues and more, telling the story of the great horses who built Japanese racing.
106:
* Sakura Star O, Blooming in Autumn
Sakura Star O was born with part of a leg bent inward. He won his second start, but favoring the leg led to an injury, and he was out for 4 months.
Returning in 1987, he ran down the field from 4th, widest of all, with a powerful finish in the Yayoi Sho. Little noticed as 6th choice, he suddenly became a classic contender. In the Satsuki Sho his astonishing finish won it by two and a half lengths, in the third-fastest time ever after Symboli Rudolf and Tosho Boy. But his legs couldn't take the speed, another injury needed 4 months to heal, and he missed the Derby.
With a return in sight, his camp set the Kikuka Sho as his first autumn race. Before the grueling 3000m race, a prep was standard, so this was highly unusual. But his camp felt strongly: "We couldn't even give him the Derby - at least let him run in the Kikuka Sho." Far from 100%, and doubted after six months off, the Satsuki Sho winner was only 9th choice. But he burst up the inside in the straight to win clearly. No horse had ever won the Kikuka Sho in his first autumn race; after 202 days off, it was the longest gap ever for a Kikuka Sho or any classic winner. The announcer's cry before the line - "Cherry blossoms in full bloom in chrysanthemum season!" - is still remembered as a classic call.

* Improving Racing's Image
After the first racing boom raised its social standing, some still saw racing as gambling and stayed away. The Japan Racing Association tried many ways to change that image. This year it adopted the abbreviation "JRA" (Japan Racing Association).
Its off-track betting sites were also given the friendlier name "WINS," a double meaning of "WINning Spot" and "Weekend IN Spot."
Racing's better public image today may be the result of such steady efforts.
107:
* The "Common Sense" About Greys
"Grey horses don't win" was racing's common sense. Even after grey father and son Mejiro Asama and Mejiro Titan, the belief remained deep-rooted.
One grey struggled from his debut: Tamamo Cross. But from autumn of his 3yo year, switched from dirt, where he had done nothing, to mainly turf, he showed his true worth. In 1988 he won the Tenno Sho (Spring), drawing attention as "the late-arriving star."
Another grey also emerged: Oguri Cap, who joined the JRA after dominating at local Kasamatsu. His power was overwhelming, and some likened him to Haiseiko, who also moved from local racing and sparked the first boom.
The two greys met in the Tenno Sho (Autumn). The clash drew such buzz that some fans camped overnight at Tokyo's gates. Tamamo Cross surprised everyone by racing forward, then held off Oguri Cap's desperate charge to win - Oguri Cap's first loss since joining the JRA. In their second meeting, the Japan Cup, both lost to foreign horse Pay the Butler, but Tamamo Cross was 2nd and Oguri Cap 3rd. Afterwards it was announced Tamamo Cross would retire after the Arima Kinen.
Then came the final grey duel, the Arima Kinen. Determined to win, Oguri Cap's camp brought in master jockey Yukio Okabe. Late in the race Oguri Cap led in the straight, and Tamamo Cross drew level from last, widest of all. After a fierce duel Oguri Cap won by half a length, avenging two defeats - the first Arima Kinen win by a grey.
After seeing this grey duel, called "the last great race of the Showa era," no one believed "grey horses don't win" anymore.

* A Festival for Jockeys
This year the Golden Jockey Cup, an invitational jockeys' race at Sonoda Racecourse in Amagasaki, Hyogo, was founded. Only jockeys with 2,000 or more career wins, JRA or local, are invited to compete. Jockeys who usually wear their owners' silks ride in their own original colors - a treat for fans. It is still held today.

* Kansai Strikes Back
Since the hill training course opened at Ritto in 1985, Kansai horses had steadily improved. This year they finally passed Kanto horses in total wins - and Kansai horses have out-won Kanto horses every year since. It was the turning point when the East-West balance flipped.
110:
* From Emperor to King
The bubble economy that thrilled Japan ended this year. With Oguri Cap retired the year before, the boom seemed set to end with the downturn - but a new hero heated it up even more: Tokai Teio, son of seven-crown "Emperor" Symboli Rudolf, given the title "King."
At birth Tokai Teio was rated low for his slender frame. But once training began, his rare suppleness changed everyone's minds. Using that flexibility for a long, flowing stride, he won his first 4 starts without his jockey ever using the whip. By now everyone saw his sire in him.
Unbeaten, he won the Satsuki Sho despite the widest draw. Jockey Takayuki Yasuda, following Yukio Okabe, who won the Triple Crown on Symboli Rudolf, raised one finger - "first crown." In the Japanese Derby he sat in a good spot and broke clear at the final turn to win, the first Kansai winner since Bamboo Atlas in 1982. Yasuda proudly raised two fingers.
But afterwards Tokai Teio was found to have a fracture needing 6 months to heal. The dream of a father-son unbeaten Triple Crown ended without even a chance to try.

* Toward Clean Racing
This year both JRA and local racing introduced demotion rules. If a horse that finished ahead is judged to have interfered with another, it is placed just behind the horse it hampered. Europe and America had used such rules since the 1950s, so Japan now matched international rules.
Before that, interference meant disqualification. But more disqualifications meant fans holding back bets for fear of wasted tickets, hurting sales. So in practice disqualifications were rare, and most cases ended with penalties for jockeys. Rough riding increased, but the new rules improved things.
That spring, champion older horse Mejiro McQueen won the Tenno Sho, completing three generations of winners. He also finished first in the Tenno Sho (Autumn), but was judged to have cut inside right after the start and blocked several horses, including the last-placed one, and was demoted to last.

* Quinella Betting Begins
This year the JRA began selling "umaren," quinella bets by horse number. With this the single-bracket system of 1974 was abolished. Since bracket quinella began in 1963 no new bet types had been added - only win, place and bracket quinella.
The same year the "PAT" system for betting from home by computer was introduced. As racing flourished, ways to bet and enjoy it gradually widened.
105:
* "Bewitching Dark Bay" Mejiro Ramonu
In the year free "racing programs" began being handed out so every visitor could enjoy racing more, a new heroine was born: Mejiro Ramonu, a filly with a beautiful dark bay coat.
She won her debut by 20 lengths, showing her talent, but her true power emerged the next year when she teamed up with jockey Hiroshi Kawachi. In the 1986 Yonsai Himba Tokubetsu (West) (now the Fillies' Revue), she dropped to last when the leaders faltered, then burst clear in the straight with an astonishing late charge. She went on to win the Oka Sho, the Yonsai Himba Tokubetsu (East) (now the Flora S.) and the Oaks for an easy double. Kawachi compared her to Tesco Gaby, famed as the greatest filly ever: "I think she's surpassed her."
In autumn she won the Rose S. and went for the Triple Crown in the Queen Elizabeth II Cup. Hopes for the first fillies' Triple Crown made her 1.3. She moved from the third turn and drew level with the leaders. Used to winning from behind, her early move looked premature to crowd and commentator alike, but she held off the rest in the straight to win by half a length - the first fillies' Triple Crown in JRA history. Having also won every trial, she was hailed as a "perfect Triple Crown." Several fillies have since won the Triple Crown, but she alone did it perfectly.
With no graded wins against colts, some rate her only "the best filly," but the next year her Triple Crown earned her a Hall of Fame place alongside seven-crown winner Symboli Rudolf - the first female inducted.

* Japan's First Night Racing
Southern Kanto local racing runs mainly on weekdays to avoid clashing with weekend JRA racing. At first it ran on weekday afternoons, which salaried workers couldn't attend. So in 1986 Oi Racecourse began "Twinkle Races," night racing that people could attend after work - the first night racing not just in horse racing but in all public betting sports, including keirin. Night racing proved popular and is now held at many local tracks.
109:
* The Wonder Brought by "the Wind God"
The second racing boom, which began in the late 1980s, peaked this year.
After wins like the Asahi Hai Sansai S. the year before, Ines Fujin was seen as the top classic contender. But he lost the Yayoi Sho to Mejiro Ryan and the Satsuki Sho to Hakutaisei. Some called for jockey Eiji Nakano, his rider since his debut, to be replaced, but trainer Shusuke Kato kept him on.
Then came the Japanese Derby. In the middle of the boom, with fans excited by the clash of Mejiro Ryan, Hakutaisei and Ines Fujin, over 190,000 people packed Tokyo Racecourse. It far exceeded the first boom's record and still stands as the world record for racecourse attendance.
As the gates opened, Ines Fujin went to the front. He never slowed; Hakutaisei and others closed, but he pulled away again, kept his lead in the straight and won from the front. Having run a stunning time that broke the race record by a second, he could only walk slowly afterwards, returning to the stands alone, far behind the rest. Seeing the winner's calm return, the huge crowd chanted "Nakano! Nakano!" for the jockey's superb ride and the horse who answered it. Chanting a winner's name was unheard of then - a new culture was born. It may have been the moment racing was accepted as a sport.
After the race Ines Fujin suffered a tendon injury. He tried to return but couldn't, leaving the turf as if he had burned out in the Derby.

* Oguri Cap's Miracle Last Race
Oguri Cap led the second boom. In his first race this year, the Yasuda Kinen, he was ridden by Yutaka Take, another pillar of the boom. Two of racing's biggest stars together drew huge attention, and Oguri Cap won in course-record time.
But he was 2nd in the Takarazuka Kinen, then a poor 6th in the Tenno Sho (Autumn). Aiming to bounce back in the Japan Cup, he ran a dismal 11th, his first double-digit finish. People whispered "Oguri Cap is finished," and some fans, unable to bear seeing him lose, pleaded, "Please just let him retire."
His camp chose the Arima Kinen as his farewell. They asked Take to ride him again, the first time since the Yasuda Kinen, and say they'd have withdrawn him had he refused. Over 170,000 fans packed Nakayama to see Oguri Cap's last race, but he was only 4th choice, and few thought he could win.
Just before the start, Take reportedly encouraged his partner: "Hey, you're Oguri Cap, remember." The pace was unexpectedly slow, and many horses fought their riders. But the experienced Oguri Cap and Take saved their energy. Moving up from the third turn, he took the lead in the straight and held off the rest on sheer guts. The miracle last race, defying all predictions, set the crowd roaring, and soon chants of "Oguri! Oguri!" rang out. The idol horse who sparked the boom left the stage with the perfect finale.
104:
* Beyond Shinzan
The year before, Symboli Rudolf became unbeaten Triple Crown winner, and though beaten in the Japan Cup, won the Arima Kinen. Now he set out on the older horses' main path, aiming to be the first five-crown winner since Shinzan in 1965.
In the Tenno Sho (Spring), the third clash of Triple Crown winners with Mr. C.B., Rudolf let Mr. C.B. go ahead for the first time, then easily ran him down as he tired. Jockey Yukio Okabe raised five fingers.
Then he was injured before the Takarazuka Kinen. On his return in the Tenno Sho (Autumn) he was beaten by outsider Gallop Dyna. Still, trainer Yuji Nohira declared, "They say there are no certainties in racing, but with Rudolf there are," showing total faith in him. As if in reply, Rudolf shrugged off bad weather to win the Japan Cup, a sixth crown, beyond Shinzan.
With a trip abroad planned for the next year, the Arima Kinen was set as his last race in Japan. Nohira asked Okabe not just to win but to "win impressively." As told, Rudolf calmly took the lead at the third turn and won by 4 lengths from that year's double classic winner Miho Shinzan. He was the first to win two Arima Kinens since Speed Symboli in 1970 - and Japan's first seven-crown winner.

* Nihon Pillow Winner Dominates the Mile
While the older horses' main path was thrilled by Triple Crown clashes, one horse kept fighting over a mile: Nihon Pillow Winner. In 1982 he won his first 3 starts, showing his talent, but in the next year's Satsuki Sho he was last of 20, nearly 5 seconds behind winner Mr. C.B. Giving up on the classics, his camp turned to the mile division, which now had new G1s thanks to graded races. There he showed his full talent, piling up wins including the G1 Mile Championship.
In '85 he won two sprint G2s, the Milers C. and the Keio Hai Spring C., then won the Yasuda Kinen, which he had missed the year before with a fracture. In his farewell race, the Mile Championship, he won clearly by 3 lengths, winning it twice and bowing out in style. That year he was champion sprinter for the third straight year.
A great miler who starred from the very first year Japan's sprint and mile program was established, he was called "the Emperor of the Mile" after Emperor Symboli Rudolf. His trainer boasted, "At a mile he wouldn't lose even to Symboli Rudolf," but they met only once, not at a mile but in the 2000m Tenno Sho (Autumn). Rudolf was 2nd and Pillow Winner 3rd, just 0.1 seconds behind. On a stage that favored Rudolf, that shows his strength.

* Racing Tilts West
Back then Kanto horses were far stronger. In the Japanese Derby, for example, winners from 1973 to 1985 were 10 from Kanto and just 3 from Kansai.
Western trainers believed "Kanto horses are strong because they train on the uphill straights at Tokyo and Nakayama." In response, in 1985 a hill training course opened at Ritto Training Center.
Within a few years its effects became clear, shaping the "strong West, weak East" balance that followed.
108:
* The Heisei Big Three
The year before, racing was thrilled by the grey duel. In this, the first year of Heisei, the epic battles of three horses sparked the second racing boom: Oguri Cap, Inari One and Super Creek, the "Heisei Big Three."
Inari One moved from local Oi. While Oguri Cap and previous Kikuka Sho winner Super Creek rested in the first half of the year, he won the Tenno Sho (Spring) and the Takarazuka Kinen, rising fast on the main path with fierce fighting spirit. In autumn he met Oguri Cap for the first time in the Mainichi Okan: Oguri Cap won by a nose, showing the pride of "the idol horse of the age."
In the Tenno Sho (Autumn) Super Creek joined, and the future Heisei Big Three met for the first time. From the widest draw, thought a disadvantage, Super Creek raced forward with ease and held off Oguri Cap's charge by a neck.
All three met again in the Arima Kinen. Thanks to recent form, Oguri Cap and Super Creek got single brackets, and it was billed a "Big Two." As expected, the two raced forward and rounded the final turn together. But in the straight Inari One charged as if to prove he was one of the "Big Three," hitting the line level with Super Creek, and won by a nose after a photo.
The Heisei Big Three thrilled racing with neck-and-neck battles, and kept leading the boom with more fierce clashes the next year.

* Causes of the Second Racing Boom
The bubble economy was of course a big factor. But unlike the first boom, driven by horses like Haiseiko, this one was also boosted by attention on jockeys. Most popular of all was Yutaka Take, who rode all three of the Heisei Big Three. At first he was known as "Kunihiko Take's son," after his father, a top jockey until a few years before. But breaking the rookie wins record and becoming the youngest classic winner ever, he quickly became the star of the boom. He is still riding at the top today as racing's "living legend."
This year also saw the birth of Turfy, the JRA mascot. Perhaps helped by such efforts, child fans who couldn't even bet - unheard of in the first boom - surged.

* A First for Greys
Greys were starring, but late bloomer Tamamo Cross and Oguri Cap, who wasn't nominated for the classics, never ran in the Japanese Derby.
But this year a new grey, Winner's Circle, emerged. 2nd in the Satsuki Sho, he became the first grey ever to win the Derby. It was also the first Derby win by a horse bred in Ibaraki, where few are foaled, which made big news.
111:
* Teio vs McQueen: Their First and Last Showdown
After his Tenno Sho (Autumn) demotion the year before, Mejiro McQueen kept losing: 4th in the Japan Cup, 2nd in the Arima Kinen. But he opened this year with a 5-length win in the Hanshin Daishoten. In the Tenno Sho (Spring), going for a repeat, he faced the year-younger genius Tokai Teio, back from a 10-month layoff.
McQueen, famed as the best stayer, against Teio, still unbeaten after winning the Osaka Hai on his return. The clash of the two who carried the second boom after Oguri Cap's retirement was billed "the showdown of the century." Over 3200m at Kyoto, McQueen's record made him look the better bet. But Teio's jockey Yukio Okabe, usually measured, said Teio "could run to the ends of the earth." Not to be outdone, McQueen's jockey Yutaka Take replied, "Mine will climb to heaven," fueling the hype.
Teio was favorite and McQueen 2nd - the first time McQueen wasn't favorite since Take began riding him. McQueen sat in a good spot with Teio glued to his left flank. McQueen kicked from the third turn and Teio chased, but faded in the straight. McQueen won easily; Teio was 5th. The showdown ended with McQueen the first horse ever to win the Tenno Sho (Spring) twice in a row.



* The Assassin Who Stopped an Unbeaten Triple Crown
The hill course built at Ritto in 1985 was influential enough to flip the East-West balance. The most famous horse it produced was Mihono Bourbon, "child of the hill course." Put through hard hill training by trainer Tameo Toyama, known for Spartan methods, he gained rare speed.
In 1992, unbeaten, he led all the way to win the Spring S. and the Satsuki Sho. In the Japanese Derby he drew wide (gate 15), bad for a front-runner, but grabbed the lead and kept it, beating Rice Shower by 4 lengths.
Then the Kikuka Sho, unbeaten. With Tokai Teio having just missed an unbeaten Triple Crown the year before, hopes were sky-high. Kyoei Bowgun, who had vowed to lead, went to the front. Mihono Bourbon, who had led in every race that year, fought his rider in this new situation. He finally took the lead after the third turn, but Rice Shower surged past in the straight. With nothing left to fight back, he was 2nd, missing the unbeaten Triple Crown.
He was injured before the Japan Cup, newly made an international G1. He tried to return but kept getting hurt, and the double classic winner called "child of the hill course" and "the precision machine" retired, to much regret.
112:
* The Dramas of B, N and W
This year's classics were seen as a two-horse fight: Biwa Hayahide, ridden by Yukio Okabe, and Winning Ticket, ridden by Masato Shibata. In their first meeting, the Satsuki Sho, Winning Ticket passed the forward-running Biwa Hayahide, only for Biwa Hayahide to retake the lead in the straight. It seemed settled - until Narita Taishin flew from last and widest to win by a neck. Ridden by Yutaka Take, he had been a distant third on record. After this the classics were seen as a Big Three, dubbed "BNW" from their initials.
In the Japanese Derby, BNW's odds were tight at 3.6 to 4.0. Shibata, aboard favorite Winning Ticket, had won many big races but never the Derby, and wanted it more than anyone. Usually happy to talk to the press, he refused interviews the week before. He stayed on the rail the others avoided, broke clear in the straight and won a duel with the charging Biwa Hayahide. Winning Ticket was a "one-way ticket to victory," giving Shibata his first Derby.
2nd in both spring classics, Biwa Hayahide's camp took two steps to win the Kikuka Sho. Deciding the quick acceleration he lacked against his rivals, they added hill training as with Mihono Bourbon, and he gained the solid frame that powers acceleration. Then they removed his ear covers. Sensitive to noise, he had worn them since his debut, but they took the risk to sharpen his response when it counted.
In the Kikuka Sho he sat near the front and led at the final turn. In the straight he showed a burst that left Winning Ticket, who was tracking him, far behind, winning by 5 lengths in Japanese record time - a reward for the efforts of horse and camp.
This year's classics ended with each of BNW winning one - a true Big Three.


* The "King's" Miracle Comeback
The year before, Tokai Teio won the Japan Cup like his sire, but was a shock 11th in the Arima Kinen. This year he aimed for the Takarazuka Kinen, but suffered his third fracture and went on another long break. Most thought "we'll never see the King of old again," but his camp didn't give up. Trainer Shoichi Matsumoto later said, "I knew that if we got him fully ready, he could show his power straight away."
His comeback was the Arima Kinen, his first race in a year. With 8 G1 winners in a star field, including Kikuka Sho winner Biwa Hayahide and Derby winner Winning Ticket, he was only 4th choice. He sat in a good midfield spot, broke clear at the final turn and drew level with Biwa Hayahide in the straight, winning the fierce duel to the line. Winning the Arima Kinen after 364 days off was called "the miracle comeback," and it remains the longest layoff before a G1 win.

* "Weekly Gallop" Launches
This year the racing magazine "Weekly Gallop" was launched as a special edition of Sankei Sports. Its first cover featured Mejiro McQueen, hot favorite for that week's Tenno Sho (Autumn) (sadly scratched with leg trouble). Its big selling point was color photos, details and reviews of Sunday's main race on sale the very next day, while the excitement was still fresh. Covering JRA, local and overseas racing, with columns by active jockeys Yukio Okabe and Masayoshi Ebina and trainer Yuji Nohira from the start, it became a must-read and is still popular today.
113:
* Chasing His Brother to the Triple Crown
Narita Brian drew attention as half-brother to the previous Kikuka Sho winner Biwa Hayahide, but his early form was erratic. Unlike his brother, who won the Kikuka Sho after his ear covers came off, he was so timid he feared his own shadow, so he was fitted with a shadow roll - and then won the Kyoto Sansai S. and the Asahi Hai Sansai S. in brilliant style, becoming champion 2yo colt.
In spring 1994 he kept winning easily. He won the Satsuki Sho in course-record time and the Japanese Derby as a huge favorite with 61.8% of win bets. After Tokai Teio in '91 and Mihono Bourbon in '92 had both just missed the Triple Crown, fans longed to see one. All their hopes rested on Narita Brian.
But he fell ill in summer. Undertrained, he was 2nd in the Kyoto Shimbun Hai. Fans still trusted him, making him favorite at 1.7 for the Kikuka Sho. As Steel Cast set off in a huge lead like his dam, Brian waited calmly in midfield. In the straight he pulled 7 lengths clear to win in a race-record time, 0.1 seconds faster than his brother's record the year before - the 5th Triple Crown winner ever and the first in 10 years, since Symboli Rudolf.
He won his three classics by a total of 15 lengths. With no rival left in his crop, fans hoped for a clash with his brother on the older horses' main path, but Biwa Hayahide's injury in the Tenno Sho (Autumn) ended that dream. In the Arima Kinen, without his brother, Brian took the lead early at the final turn and won, keeping stars like Hishi Amazon and Rice Shower at bay.

* Hishi Amazon: From the Back Roads to the Top Mare
From 1984, "mochikomi" (foals born from mares imported in foal, or imported with their dams before age 1) could run in the classics. But "foreign-bred" horses, bred abroad and registered in Japan, still couldn't.
That unavoidable wall blocked Hishi Amazon. She drew attention by winning the Hanshin Sansai Himba S., but as a foreign-bred she couldn't run in the classics. As if channeling her frustration into her running, she won 5 graded races in a row. Then in the Queen Elizabeth II Cup, a G1 she could run in, she met Oaks winner Chokai Carol. After a fierce duel down the straight she won by a nose, showing the pride of a queen forced onto the back roads. With 6 straight graded wins, she was named champion 3yo filly.

* Sakura Bakushin O, a Born Sprinter
With a first-class classic pedigree, Sakura Bakushin O carried big hopes. But after a heavy defeat in 12th in the Spring S., a Satsuki Sho trial, his camp gave up on the classics and moved him to sprints to use his speed.
There he showed his true worth, winning the Sprinters S. in 1993 and '94 and dominating the sprint division, and was named champion sprinter in '94. He won 11 of 12 at 1400m or less, but 0 of 9 beyond 1400m - a true born sprinter.
He also succeeded at stud, passing his overwhelming speed to his offspring.
114:
* The Great Sire Sunday Silence
Sunday Silence went unsold as a youngster for his awkward looks, but as a racehorse he won 6 G1s, including two legs of the US Triple Crown and the BC Classic, and was Eclipse Horse of the Year. But his success story didn't end there.
Retiring in 1990, he was imported by Shadai Farm to stand in Japan. His sire Halo was a great horse, but his dam Wishing Well was no blueblood. With that pedigree, his sire's fiery temper, and his failure to sell for much at 2, American breeders scoffed that he'd never succeed at stud, and at first he wasn't rated highly in Japan either.
But his first crop, including Fuji Kiseki, did well in 1994, and in '95 Genuine and Dance Partner won classics, and he shot to leading sire - the fastest ever in Japan, with just two crops. His offspring kept succeeding, and he was leading sire 13 years running until 2007. In that time Still in Love won the fillies' Triple Crown in 2003 and Deep Impact the Triple Crown in 2005, making him the first sire of both a colt and a filly Triple Crown winner.
With stars among his grandchildren and great-grandchildren too, he redrew the bloodlines of Japanese thoroughbreds, and his blood keeps spreading worldwide. It's fair to say Sunday Silence alone raised the level of Japanese racing.

* Japanese Horses Abroad
The Japan Cup, founded in 1981 under the motto "breed horses that can compete with the world," helped raise Japanese horses' level by letting them face foreign rivals. But since they could meet foreign horses without traveling, it also made Japanese racing reluctant to race abroad. Some, like Sirius Symboli and Gallop Dyna, tried, but none won.
When the Hong Kong International Races began taking shape from '88, interest in racing abroad grew. In '95 Fujiyama Kenzan finally won the Hong Kong International Cup (local G1, international G2) - the first Japanese win in a major flat race abroad in 36 years, since Hakuchikara made the first postwar trip.

* Rice Shower Falls at Yodo
Rice Shower, "the black assassin from Kanto," won fame as a villain for denying Mihono Bourbon an unbeaten Triple Crown in 1992 and Mejiro McQueen a third straight Tenno Sho (Spring) in '93. But after that Tenno Sho he slumped, as if burned out.
In '95 he returned to the Tenno Sho (Spring) after two years, only 4th choice despite being a past winner. In a surprise attack he launched a long run from the third turn, took the lead and won by a nose. Fans rejoiced at his comeback - not as a villain, but as a hero who fought on after his old rivals had gone.
But tragedy struck in his next race, the Takarazuka Kinen. Mid-race he suffered a dislocation and collapsed. Judged beyond saving on the spot, he was put down. By fate, that year's Takarazuka Kinen was held at Kyoto, scene of his comeback. The tragic end of the great stayer at Yodo left racing in deep grief.
115:
* Queen of the Sand, Hokuto Vega
Hokuto Vega won the 1993 Queen Elizabeth II Cup, but after that did little beyond winning the Sapporo Kinen, then a G3. But after winning the Empress Hai at Kawasaki in '95 by 18 lengths, she switched to dirt full-time the next year, and her winning run began. In her first race, the Kawasaki Kinen, against elites like Lively Mount, then seen as the best dirt horse, and '93 Japan Cup winner Legacy World, she won by 5 lengths. She kept winning JRA-local graded races, and for her 5th, the Teio Sho, over 70,000 fans came to see her. She won all 8 of her dirt races that year and was named champion dirt horse.
No one then imagined that two years after this brilliant switch to dirt, tragedy would strike her in Dubai.

* Shinzan Passes Away
In 1964 Shinzan became the second Triple Crown winner ever and the first postwar, and also won the Tenno Sho (Autumn) and Arima Kinen to be called the five-crown winner. So dominant was he that "Beyond Shinzan" became Japanese racing's motto, the goal for horsemen for 20 years until unbeaten Triple Crown winner Symboli Rudolf. As a sire he produced classic winners like double winner Miho Shinzan and Kikuka Sho winner Minagawa Manna, and set a record of winners in 24 straight years.
While many racehorses give their all and die young, Shinzan lived very long after retiring from stud. In '95 he set the Japanese longevity record for a thoroughbred, then for all light horses (breeds improved for speed, including thoroughbreds), and this year he died at 35, much mourned.

* The "Brilliant Class 12" Debuts
This year the rookie jockeys called "the brilliant Class 12" of the racing school debuted. Leading them was Yuichi Fukunaga, son of great jockey Yoichi Fukunaga, who won his first two rides. Others included Ryuji Wada, later regular rider of T.M. Opera O; 5 of the 10 who debuted went on to win G1s.
Class 12 also included the JRA's first three female jockeys. One of them, Junko Hosoe, is still active today as a racing analyst ("horse collaborator").
116:
* Air Groove: First Female Horse of the Year in 26 Years
Air Groove won the Oaks the year before to become the best filly of her crop. In the new Shuka Sho she was too keyed up and finished 10th, and a fracture found afterwards kept her out a long time. Returning this year as an older mare, she won the Mermaid S. easily, then beat Satsuki Sho winner Genuine with ease in the Sapporo Kinen. In autumn her camp believed she could match the colts and chose the Tenno Sho (Autumn), her first G1 against males.
She was 2nd choice behind last year's winner Bubble Gum Fellow. Silence Suzuka set a fast pace in a big lead, with Bubble Gum Fellow near the front and Air Groove in midfield. In the straight, as Bubble Gum Fellow went to lead, Air Groove came powerfully alongside on the outside; they fought a dead heat from 200m out, and she won by a neck. It was the first win by a female in 17 years, since Pretty Cast in '80, and the first since the race was cut to 2000m in '84. She was then 2nd in the Japan Cup and 3rd in the Arima Kinen, matching the best colts, and came to be called "the Empress." That year she was named Horse of the Year, the first female since Tomei in 1971, 26 years earlier, and reigned as the best mare.

* Mayano Top Gun Wins the Big Three Clash
In 1995 Mayano Top Gun won the Kikuka Sho and Arima Kinen and was named champion 3yo colt. He won the Takarazuka Kinen the next year, but then was 4th in the All Comers and 7th in the Arima Kinen, and some said he was finished.
In '97 his camp kept him racing but decided he'd retire at year's end, targeting the Tenno Sho (Spring). He was seen as a front-runner, as when he led all the way in the '95 Arima Kinen. But jockey Seiki Tabara noticed he no longer wanted to go forward after the start, and in the Hanshin Daishoten prep let him do as he liked, waiting at the very back. He ran away from the field in the straight for his first win in six months. Many still said "Top Gun is at his best up front," but Tabara believed putting the horse's feelings first meant better running.
The Tenno Sho (Spring) drew Sakura Laurel and Marvelous Sunday, who both beat him in the last Arima Kinen. Billed as a Big Three clash, Sakura Laurel, going for a repeat, was favorite, followed by Top Gun and Marvelous Sunday, with tight odds. Tabara let Top Gun settle at the back as he wished. As the other two broke clear early and dueled in the straight, Top Gun unleashed an astonishing kick from far back and wide, from where it seemed impossible, caught both just before the line and won by over a length - in Japanese (and world) record time for 3200m.
As it turned out, this was the Big Three's final clash. The win, achieved with Tabara and Top Gun as one, is etched as one of the great races in Japanese history.

* Dirt Graded Races Established
With JRA-local racing exchange in full swing from 1995, this year JRA-local dirt graded races were renamed "dirt graded races." The JRA's February S. and local races like the Tokyo Daishoten (Oi) and Nambu Hai (Morioka) were made G1, new races like the Hokkaido Sprint Cup (G3, Sapporo) and Marine Cup (G3, Funabashi) were created, and a unified G1-G3 system covered local exchange races too. The February S., newly a G1, crowned Shinko Windy as its first champion. In the first Teio Sho (Oi) as a G1, Concert Boy and Abukuma Poro showed local pride with a local 1-2.
Nationwide grading boosted JRA-local exchange and greatly helped dirt racing develop.
117:
* Taiki Shuttle and Seeking the Pearl Go Abroad
In 1995 Fujiyama Kenzan won the first graded race abroad by a Japanese horse (the G2 Hong Kong International Cup), but a top European G1 remained out of reach. Two foreign-bred horses took up the challenge: Taiki Shuttle and Seeking the Pearl.
Taiki Shuttle dominated the sprint-mile division in '97, winning 2 G1s and champion sprinter. In '98 he kept rolling, winning the Keio Hai Spring Cup and the Yasuda Kinen, and set off on his long-planned trip to France.
Seeking the Pearl, a filly from the same division who won the NHK Mile Cup the year before, was also headed to France. She was first aimed at the G1 Prix Jacques le Marois over a mile, but was well beaten by Taiki Shuttle in the Yasuda Kinen just before the trip. With Taiki Shuttle now set for that race, she avoided him and targeted the G1 Prix Maurice de Gheest, 1300m on the straight, a week earlier. She was 5th choice. She broke well and, instead of racing from midfield as in Japan, easily settled near the front. Past 500m out, as the others began to push, she cruised to the lead with so much in hand her jockey could wait, then held off the rest to win from the front in course-record time - Japanese racing's long-held dream of a first European G1 for a Japan-trained horse. Her trainer Hideyuki Mori said afterwards, "Taiki Shuttle, who runs next week, is even stronger."
In the Prix Jacques le Marois, with top rivals out and buoyed by Seeking the Pearl's win, Taiki Shuttle was expected to win and was a clear favorite. Local fans flocked to see the Japanese horse said to be stronger than her. It was his first straight-course mile. Early on he reportedly looked around curiously (at the rail), but he made his move about 300m out, and past 200m out five horses fought side by side. Near the line he got half a length clear to win the battle.
Japan-trained horses winning European G1s two weeks running shocked racing worldwide, gave Japanese horsemen courage and laid the foundation for later G1 challenges abroad. About 40 years after Japan-trained horses first raced overseas, a new chapter opened for Japanese racing, so long rebuffed by the world's high walls.

* Silence Suzuka Never Comes Home
After debuting in 1997, Silence Suzuka showed flashes of talent but didn't deliver in graded races, and his form was erratic. But at year's end, teamed with Yutaka Take for the first time in the Hong Kong International Cup, he went for a big lead, and though 5th, Take saw something.
In '98, sensing promise in front-running, Take guided him to an easy win in the Valentine S. He led by a mile again in the G2 Nakayama Kinen and won, never letting anyone near. With his natural speed now in full flow, no one could catch him: with unheard-of runaway tactics, he won 5 graded races in a row, including the Takarazuka Kinen.
Then came the Tenno Sho (Autumn). Foreign-breds El Condor Pasa and Grass Wonder weren't even eligible then, and many, including Air Groove, avoided him, so only 12 ran in a field of 18 spots. He was overwhelming favorite at 1.2. Everyone expected another dazzling escape.
He broke perfectly, led alone and was over 10 lengths clear before the third turn. Just as everyone was sure of victory, he sank back. A murmur swept the crowd. He had shattered a leg. Unable to stand, he was judged beyond saving and put down on the spot.
If he had run in the Japan Cup... if he had made his planned trip to America... many fans still dream of how "the shadowless runaway" might have run.

* The Rise of the '98 Generation
The "'98 generation," 3yos in 1998, was packed with stars and called "the strongest generation" or "the golden generation." It always comes up in debates over the best crop ever.
Double classic winner Seiun Sky (Satsuki Sho and Kikuka Sho), Derby winner Special Week, who beat him there, El Condor Pasa, who won the Japan Cup at 3, and Arima Kinen winner Grass Wonder fought fiercely, none giving an inch. Together they won every flat G1 of the time, and many fans call them the greatest generation in Japanese history.
They kept up their fierce battles in the following years, thrilling racing.
118:
* The Arc Challenge and the "Commander-in-Chief's" Revenge
The '98 generation, which ran riot the year before, kept thrilling racing as older horses. In fact '99 may have been their most brilliant year.
El Condor Pasa, a foreign-bred barred from the classics, went abroad. The final goal was the Arc, the world's greatest race. No one wins it fresh off the plane, so a campaign was planned backwards from it. He was 2nd in the Prix d'Ispahan, then won the Grand Prix de Saint-Cloud, his first G1 abroad - and the first French middle-to-long-distance G1 ever won by a Japan-trained horse.
The Prix Foy prep had just 3 runners; he won it and moved on to the Arc. Favorite was French and Irish Derby winner Montjeu, with El Condor Pasa 2nd choice, already highly rated by locals. Using his inside draw, he took the lead. Leading the field into the straight with plenty in hand, he gradually extended it to about 2 lengths and seemed safe, but from about 400m out Montjeu closed relentlessly from behind. About 100m out Montjeu went by; El Condor Pasa fought back but fell half a length short. The Arc dream was over, but local fans warmly applauded the Japanese horse's brave run.
El Condor Pasa then retired, and Montjeu's next race was, of all things, the Japan Cup. Waiting for him was Special Week, winner of both Tenno Sho races that year. Arc winner and Europe's best Montjeu was favorite, with Special Week only 2nd choice, but Special Week, racing at the back, produced the fastest finish to win, keeping Montjeu and the rest at bay. As "Japan's commander-in-chief," he avenged his great rival.

* Grass vs Special: The Last Epic of the 20th Century
Grass Wonder won his first races easily after debuting in 1997, took the Asahi Hai Sansai S. in record time, and was seen as the best of his crop. But a fracture kept him out the next spring, and after returning he lacked sparkle, until in the year-end Arima Kinen he beat double classic winner Seiun Sky, Tenno Sho winner Mejiro Bright and empress Air Groove to make a full comeback.
In '99 he met Derby winner Special Week for the first time in the Takarazuka Kinen. One was rated the best of the crop at his debut; the other had become it by winning the Derby and Tenno Sho (Spring). Their clash drew huge attention, and the betting split between them, well ahead of the rest - a two-horse showdown. Special Week sat just ahead of midfield, with Grass Wonder right behind, marking him. Past 600m out Special Week took the lead, with Grass Wonder chasing. A match race loomed at the final turn, but Grass Wonder easily passed Special Week and won by 3 lengths, as if saying he had never given up the title of best of the crop.
They clashed again in the Arima Kinen. Grass Wonder had skipped the Japan Cup after a setback following his Mainichi Okan win, while Special Week came in fully prepared after winning the Tenno Sho (Autumn) and the Japan Cup, seeking revenge. Grass Wonder was 2.8 and Special Week 3.0. The new wide bet on the pair was hugely popular at 4.7. The pace was very slow, with Grass Wonder near the back and Special Week last. The race came alive after the third turn: Grass Wonder swept forward wide with Special Week chasing, and the battle went into the straight. Tsurumaru Tsuyoshi briefly led, T.M. Opera O, the Satsuki Sho winner, came up the inside, and Grass Wonder and Special Week flew wide; four horses hit the line almost together, in the same time. After a long photo, Grass Wonder won by just 4 cm. After enduring an era unkind to foreign-breds, he had won three straight Grand Prix races.

* The Hero Comes From the North
Meisei Opera won 9 straight at places like Iwate, beat JRA horses in the '98 G1 Nambu Hai, and was hailed as the second coming of Iwate's "monster" Tokei Nisei. This year he chose the JRA's G1 February S. for his first race. Some called a local horse taking on a JRA G1 reckless, but local fans believed "Meisei Opera can do it." Against JRA dirt stars like Washington Color and M.I. Blanc, he was a confident 2nd choice. He handled the turf start easily, sat in a good spot, surged powerfully down the middle of the track in the straight, took the lead easily past 200m out and won by 2 lengths. He was the first local-based horse ever to win a JRA G1, and none has done it since.
119:
* "End-of-Century King": An Era of One
The year before, T.M. Opera O fought a fierce Big Three battle in the classics with Narita Top Road and Admire Vega and was named champion 3yo colt. In 2000, with "strongest generation" stars like Special Week and El Condor Pasa gone, he ran riot among the older horses.
He won the G2 Kyoto Kinen and Hanshin Daishoten, then went to the Tenno Sho (Spring). Foreign-breds could run from this year, so a clash with Grass Wonder of the "strongest generation" was hoped for. But Grass Wonder hadn't been right since the last Arima Kinen and skipped it to focus on the Takarazuka Kinen. Opera O beat Rascal Suzuka and others easily for his second G1, his first since the Satsuki Sho a year before.
In the Takarazuka Kinen he finally met Grass Wonder. Opera O was 1.9 and Grass Wonder 2.8 - a two-horse fight. But Opera O came wide at the final turn and ground down the field with a dogged finish to win. Grass Wonder couldn't quicken and sank to 6th. Having won the older horses' spring G1s, he was now the best horse in training.
He kept rolling, winning the Tenno Sho (Autumn) safely. In the Japan Cup he drew a record 50.5% of win bets, and lived up to it, winning a fierce duel with Meisho Doto by a neck. His career earnings passed 1.2 billion yen, beating Special Week's record to become world No. 1.
He went into the Arima Kinen unbeaten in 7 that year, topping the fan vote with over 100,000 votes. He broke well, but several horses marked him, his path was blocked, and he dropped to 10th or worse into the straight. Boxed in and late to move, he seemed beaten; the crowd groaned. But in mid-straight he threaded through the pack, passed about 10 horses and snatched victory. Meisho Doto was 2nd again - beaten by Opera O in all four G1s that year. Their many great duels are still talked about.
With the Arima Kinen, Opera O became the first to sweep the older horses' middle-to-long G1s. He also set records like a record 5 G1s in a year and the first 8 straight graded wins as favorite, and was unanimously Horse of the Year - truly the "end-of-century king" who ruled the turf.

* Beyond the Border Between Japan and the World
This year Hong Kong's Fairy King Prawn won the Yasuda Kinen, the first Japanese G1 won by a Hong Kong horse. Meanwhile Junko Hosoe, one of the "brilliant Class 12," became the first JRA female jockey to win abroad. Foreign horses racing in Japan, and Japanese horses and jockeys going abroad, grew year after year.
120:
* Agnes Tachyon, Who Ran at the Speed of Light
Agnes Tachyon, full brother to the previous year's Derby winner Agnes Flight, was watched from the start. His workouts weren't eye-catching, so he was only 3rd choice on debut, but he won by three and a half lengths. In the Radio Tampa Hai Sansai S. (now the Hopeful S.), against fellow classic hopes Jungle Pocket and Kurofune, he won in record time and became the classic favorite.
His first race of 2001 was the Yayoi Sho. When he entered, others pulled out one after another - his strength was already recognized.
