The going was bad, seen as a disadvantage for a horse who won with a finishing kick. But he won easily by 5 lengths, with future Kikuka Sho winner Manhattan Cafe 4th.
Then the first classic, the Satsuki Sho. With stablemate Agnes Gold, another classic hope, out injured, the betting piled onto Tachyon, who took 59.6% of win bets - the second-highest in Satsuki Sho history after Tokino Minoru (1951). Sitting in a good spot, he took the lead easily in the straight. Dantsu Flame and Jungle Pocket closed hard, but near the line he pulled away again with plenty left.
With hopes high for brothers winning the Derby, bad news came in May: he had a tendon injury. He was retired that summer, leaving the turf after just 4 races. That Kurofune later won the NHK Mile C. and the Japan Cup Dirt, and Jungle Pocket the Derby and the Japan Cup - both 2-time G1 winners - shows how strong Tachyon was. At stud he passed that strength on, siring many G1 winners like Daiwa Scarlet and Deep Sky.

* The Relentless Challenger, Meisho Doto
The year before, T.M. Opera O won 5 G1s (8 straight graded races) among older horses. Four of those times, Meisho Doto was 2nd. The public called him "the silver collector who can never beat Opera O." But only in the Tenno Sho (Autumn) was he beaten clearly; the rest were by a neck twice and a nose once - defeats that still showed his strength.
At 5 this year, Meisho Doto didn't give up. He met Opera O for the 5th time in the Tenno Sho (Spring). Having always lost by racing ahead and being passed in the straight, he tried sitting behind Opera O for the first time. But despite a desperate drive in the straight, he fell short and was 2nd again.
His next try was the Takarazuka Kinen, where a year before, in his first G1, he had first lost to Opera O. As Opera O was hampered and couldn't get clear, Meisho Doto raced forward and led at the final turn. The gap closed in the straight, but he held on, finally beating Opera O at their 6th meeting. It was also his first G1 title.

* Japanese Racing Goes International
This year Stay Gold won the Dubai Sheema Classic, the first graded win in Dubai by a Japan-trained horse. As this shows, Japanese racing was catching up with the world year by year, and international trading of racehorses had grown since the 1990s.
Japan had counted horses' ages by the traditional system, counting a horse as 1 at birth. But the world used actual age, causing a one-year gap (a horse aged 2 worldwide was 3 in Japan). To avoid confusion in international trade, from 2001 Japan switched to the current actual-age system.
Racing itself also opened up. This year the Japanese Derby and the Kikuka Sho were opened to foreign-bred horses, and the other classics followed in later years as Japanese racing rapidly internationalized.
121:
* A 3yo's Challenge
The foreign-bred wave that began in the 1990s kept going into the 2000s. Foreign-breds like Eagle Cafe (2000 NHK Mile C.), Agnes Digital (2001 Tenno Sho (Autumn)) and Kurofune (2001 Japan Cup Dirt) were still thrilling racing. The best of them in the 2000s was Symboli Kris S.
He won his debut the year before, but a fragile constitution kept him from winning again, and he couldn't get into the Satsuki Sho. So he aimed for the Derby via a trial, winning his first graded race, the Aoba Sho (Derby trial), and went into the Japanese Derby 3rd choice behind 3-time graded winner Tanino Gimlet and Satsuki Sho winner No Reason. The Derby had been opened to foreign-breds the year before, when Kurofune was 5th. Hopes were high that he'd be the first foreign-bred Derby winner, but Tanino Gimlet swooped just before the line and he was 2nd. By fate, Gimlet was ridden by Yutaka Take, who had guided Kris S. to victory in the Aoba Sho.
His true worth showed in autumn. After a smooth summer he won the Kobe Shimbun Hai, then skipped the Kikuka Sho, the last classic, for the Tenno Sho (Autumn) against older horses. He was good enough to win the 3000m Kikuka Sho, but his camp felt he had a better chance in the 2000m Tenno Sho, even against older horses.
The 2002 Tenno Sho (Autumn) was held at Nakayama for the first time in 35 years, since 1967, due to renovation at Tokyo. The field held seasoned older horses like Narita Top Road, 3 graded wins that year and 3rd in the Tenno Sho (Spring), and T.M. Ocean, the previous year's fillies' double winner, fresh from winning the Sapporo Kinen. Kris S. was the only 3yo. He broke well and raced on the inside just ahead of midfield. Hemmed in by the leaders at the final turn, he forced his way through a tiny gap in the straight and burst clear with a powerful finish, beating Narita Top Road, who came wide, by three-quarters of a length for his first G1. Only the third 3yo ever to win the Tenno Sho (Autumn).
In the Japan Cup a slow start cost him, and he couldn't catch two lightly-regarded foreign horses who broke clear first, finishing 3rd. Perhaps because of that loss, he was 2nd choice for the Arima Kinen behind 3yo filly Fine Motion, unbeaten in 6 with wins in the Shuka Sho and Queen Elizabeth II Cup - two 3yos as top two choices, a strange situation. Tap Dance City raised the pace down the backstretch to open a gap, and as the others moved early to close it, Kris S. waited until the straight, then charged and caught Tap Dance City alone to win. He became the first horse to win the Tenno Sho (Autumn) and the Arima Kinen at 3, and was named Horse of the Year.

* Sunday Silence Dies
Since becoming leading sire in 1995, when his first crop swept the classics (Satsuki Sho: Genuine, Derby: Tayasu Tsuyoshi, Oaks: Dance Partner), Sunday Silence reigned on, redrawing Japan's bloodline map. But this year he developed laminitis and died, much mourned. His offspring kept winning after his death, and he stayed leading sire for 13 years until 2007. His blood lives on in his descendants and has recently begun spreading worldwide - truly a great sire Japan can be proud of.

* IPAT Begins
By now mobile phones with web browsers were spreading fast. The JRA began running "IPAT," internet betting for mobile phones. Betting from home already existed, but now buying tickets became even easier, which helped racing spread further.
122:
* Still in Love: The Second Fillies' Triple Crown
This year's fillies' classics were split between two daughters of Sunday Silence. Favorite in all three legs was Admire Groove, a blueblood out of "noble empress" and Horse of the Year Air Groove; she won 3 straight against colts before the Oka Sho. 2nd choice in all three was Still in Love. With a graded-winning brother (Big Bayamon, winner of the Radio Tampa Sho), she was watched early, won her first two, and was a gallant 2nd despite trouble in the Tulip Sho trial to earn her Oka Sho spot.
In the Oka Sho, Admire Groove shockingly missed the break and had to race from behind. Still in Love raced in a good spot, burst powerfully out of the middle of the track in the straight and won by a length and a half. Admire Groove closed wide but could only finish 3rd - a clear win for Still in Love.
The Oaks held special meaning for Admire Groove: a chance for three generations of winners after her granddam Dyna Carl and dam Air Groove. Three generations or a fillies' double? Again Admire Groove missed the break - in her 3yo spring this habit was her great trial. She was nearly last at the final turn, and the gap to Still in Love, who surged sharply from midfield to win, only grew. A double won on ability over popularity - it was clear to all that the true heroine was Still in Love.
Both camps chose the Rose S. for their autumn start. Still in Love was favorite for the first time, but Admire Groove won and she was 5th. The heroine's crown seemed to pass to Admire Groove. Then came the last leg, the Shuka Sho. Still in Love stuck to her own style, going forward, breaking clear and holding on, holding off Admire Groove by three-quarters of a length. Showing unmatched big-race grit, she became only the second fillies' Triple Crown winner, after Mejiro Ramonu in 1986. The Shuka Sho was created in 1996 as the third leg when the Queen Elizabeth II Cup opened to older mares; this was the first Triple Crown since.
Among colts, Neo Universe won the Satsuki Sho and the Japanese Derby but missed the Triple Crown, so no colt-and-filly double Triple Crown. Still, double classic winners among both colts and fillies in the same year was a first in 28 years, since 1975 (Kabuto Yao and Tesco Gaby).

* Hishi Miracle's Two Long-Shot Wins
In the previous Kikuka Sho, with favorite No Reason losing his rider at the start, Hishi Miracle swept forward from around the third turn and held on to win as 10th choice - a "miracle" true to his name. But he was 11th in the Arima Kinen, 12th in the Hanshin Daishoten and 7th in the Osaka Hai this year, and was being branded a "fluke Kikuka Sho winner."
Then came the Tenno Sho (Spring). Despite a weak field with only one other G1 winner, Dantsu Flame, he was only 7th choice. But he defied the odds, holding off Sunrise Jaeger's charge by half a length.
The Takarazuka Kinen drew a stellar field, including last year's Horse of the Year Symboli Kris S. and Agnes Digital, a G1 winner on turf and dirt. The day before, one person's huge bet made Hishi Miracle the 1.7 favorite (the bet did win), though he settled at 6th choice (16.3). Racing in midfield, he rounded the final turn 8th, then charged to the front in the straight. Turu Maru Boy came flying wide and drew level at the end, but he held on by a neck. As if to say "don't call it a fluke anymore," he won his third G1, proving his ability.

* Symboli Kris S. Wins the Tenno Sho (Autumn) and Arima Kinen Again
The year before, Symboli Kris S. won the Tenno Sho (Autumn) and Arima Kinen at 3 and was Horse of the Year. Big things were expected, but in his first race, the Takarazuka Kinen without a prep, he ran into Hishi Miracle's long-shot win and was a surprise 5th. But again he came good in autumn. In the Tenno Sho (Autumn), shrugging off the widest draw and the fast pace set by Lohengrin and Go Steady fighting for the lead, he burst clear a third of the way out from the rail in the straight to become the first to win the Tenno Sho (Autumn) twice (Mejiro McQueen and T.M. Opera O had won the spring race twice).
In the Japan Cup he let Tap Dance City get away alone and was well beaten in 3rd, over 9 lengths back. Then his farewell, the Arima Kinen. Racing in midfield, he moved up from before the third turn, drew level with the leaders easily at the final turn, and simply drew away, winning by 9 lengths - the biggest margin in a G1 since graded races began in 1984.
The first to win the Tenno Sho (Autumn) and Arima Kinen twice each, he was Horse of the Year for the second straight year, matching his great namesake Symboli Rudolf (1984 and 1985), and left the turf in glory.
123:
* "The Greatest Great King" King Kamehameha
Trainer Kunihide Matsuda was known for racing horses with their future breeding careers in mind. For top colts, to raise their stud value, he aimed for G1 wins at two different distances: the 1600m NHK Mile C. and the 2400m Japanese Derby. Some called it an odd schedule, but it would showcase early maturity and versatility. Still, with just two weeks between the races and an 800m jump in distance, few horses could manage it. His Kurofune in 2001 and Tanino Gimlet the next year tried, but each won only one.
This year, after seeing King Kamehameha (by Kingmambo) run on debut, Matsuda thought, "I want to go for the Derby with this horse," and planned the double. After winning his first graded race, the Mainichi Hai, he went to the NHK Mile C. Despite doubts as he'd never run a mile, he settled smoothly in midfield, tracked the fast pace with ease and won by 5 lengths - a race record margin, against strong rivals like the previous Asahi Hai FS 1-2, in race-record time.
Then, two weeks later, the Japanese Derby. His NHK Mile win made him favorite despite the 800m step up. The pace was fast again, and as the front-runners faded one by one, he swept forward widest of all and simply held on, winning by a length and a half from Heart's Cry. His time broke Ines Fujin's 1990 race record by 2 seconds. The first to win the NHK Mile C.-Derby double, he was, just as Matsuda planned, highly valued at stud and sired many G1 winners.

* "Star of Local Racing" Takes On the Classics
Cosmo Bulk, based in Hokkaido local racing, made headlines by taking on the JRA classics. He debuted at 2 in Hokkaido, then ran in the JRA's Hyakunichiso Tokubetsu. In his first turf race he won in course-record time, then won the Radio Tampa Hai 2yo S. at year's end, drawing huge attention.
In 2004 he set out on the JRA classics. His earnings were ample, but as a local horse he needed priority entry, so he won the Satsuki Sho trial, the Yayoi Sho, easily. With two graded wins and the excitement of a local horse in the classics, he was Satsuki Sho favorite. He closed in the straight but couldn't catch Daiwa Major, losing narrowly in 2nd. In the Derby he faced NHK Mile C. winner King Kamehameha. He led briefly but faded in the straight, finishing a well-beaten 8th behind the double winner. In autumn he won the St. Lite Kinen but was 4th to Delta Blues in the Kikuka Sho, and his classic dream ended.
He kept showing his pride, finishing 2nd in that year's Japan Cup. He kept trying JRA and even overseas G1s, and at 5 finally won a G1 in Singapore. He raced on until 8. No local-based horse has yet won a JRA classic, but his relentless challenges against the JRA's best stirred many fans.

* Durandal, Who Changed the Rules of Sprinting
In sprints, front-runners often hold on even at a fast pace, so racing forward was the rule. Durandal (by Sunday Silence) changed that, charging from the back in a class of his own.
Very hot-tempered, he had trouble at the start. Yutaka Take suggested to his trainer, "This horse should come from behind and go wide," and that became his style.
When Ikezoe became his jockey in autumn of his 4yo year, he came into his own, winning the Sprinters S. and the Mile CS from the back, and was named champion sprinter. In 2004 he was narrowly 2nd in the Takamatsunomiya Kinen and Sprinters S., unable to catch the leaders. But in the Mile CS he again swept past the field with an amazing kick for his third G1, and was champion sprinter for the second straight year.
The sharpness of his finish truly deserved his name, a legendary "famed sword."

* Trifecta Betting Begins
The trifecta - picking 1st, 2nd and 3rd in order - is hard but pays big. Hugely popular today, it was introduced in JRA racing in September this year, at first only on the last 4 races of a day. From 2008 it was sold on all races.
124:
* Deep Impact: Unbeaten Triple Crown
Born on March 25, the same birthday as his sire Sunday Silence, Deep Impact shocked Japanese racing even more than his sire and became a social phenomenon.
In his second start, the Wakakoma S., he was about 10 lengths behind the leader at the final turn, then surged to win by 5 lengths. So dominant was he that people already called the Triple Crown a certainty. In the Satsuki Sho he was favorite with 63.0% of win bets, second only to Tokino Minoru in 1951. He stumbled badly at the start, nearly losing his rider, and dropped to last, but won clearly by two and a half lengths. No one doubted the Triple Crown now. Yutaka Take's description, "he runs as if flying," became his trademark.
In the Japanese Derby he drew 73.4% of win bets, far beyond Haiseiko's 1973 record. He missed the break again, but led with 200m left and pulled away to win by 5 lengths, equaling King Kamehameha's record time from the year before.
Then the Kikuka Sho, unbeaten. Over 130,000 fans (182% of the year before), a Kikuka Sho record, packed Kyoto to see the Triple Crown. He drew 79.03% of win bets, and paid just 1.0 - money back. He broke well and waited in midfield. In the straight Norihiro Yokoyama on Admire Japan broke clear early and it seemed over, but again he flew home, winning by 2 lengths. The first unbeaten Triple Crown since Symboli Rudolf in 1984 was covered by media far beyond racing and grew into a true social phenomenon.

* Cesario Wins the Japanese and American Oaks
Cesario, by Special Week, who walked the royal road, won her first two starts, then the Flower C. prep in race-record time. But in the Oka Sho she was 2nd to Rhein Kraft, a future NHK Mile C. winner.
From here she shone. With Rhein Kraft absent from the Oaks (going to the NHK Mile C. as the distance didn't suit her), Cesario was heavy favorite. Racing from the back, still 12th at the final turn, she split the pack in the straight and caught Air Messiah to win by a neck.
Now the best 3yo filly, she was sent to the American Oaks. Oka Sho winner Dance in the Mood had been 2nd the year before, so it was a chance for revenge. Favorite was American filly Melhor Ainda, unbeaten in 4, with Cesario 2nd. She was keyed up before the race at her first foreign track and the huge crowd, but broke well. Moving early from the third turn, she led into the straight and kept everyone away, beating Melhor Ainda by 4 lengths - race records for both time and margin.
The first Japan-trained horse to win a US G1, Cesario was expected to do more and further trips were planned, but after returning she suffered a suspensory injury, went on a long break, and retired the next year without racing again.
126:
* Father and Daughter Derby Winners
The Japanese Derby is open to both sexes, but with the Oaks run over the same distance, very few fillies try it. The last filly to win was Kurifuji in 1943. Vodka boldly took on the race everyone avoided.
Her sire was Derby winner Tanino Gimlet. She was named "Vodka," stronger than a gimlet, and without the owner's usual prefix - a stylish touch.
The year before, she won the Hanshin JF in a Japanese 2yo record for 1600m on turf and was JRA champion 2yo filly, heading into the 2007 classics as the star. But in the Oka Sho she couldn't catch Daiwa Scarlet, whom she had beaten in the Tulip Sho prep.
Everyone expected the Oaks, but she went to the Japanese Derby. Her camp longed "to win the Derby again with a child of Derby winner Tanino Gimlet," and Vodka was chosen. But no filly had run in the Derby in 11 years, since Biwa Heidi in 1996, who was a well-beaten 13th, and some called it "reckless." Still, she was 3rd choice. She waited at the back, then in the straight swept past leader Asakusa Kings before he could react and burst down the middle to win - the third filly ever to win the Derby, the first in 64 years since Kurifuji. Of course, it was also the first father-daughter Derby double. Her powerful finish at Tokyo convinced everyone she would be at the center of racing.

* Japan Promoted to Part I
Racing countries and regions are graded Part I to Part III by the International Cataloguing Standards Committee (ICSC), based on how open their races are to foreign-trained horses.
Since founding the Japan Cup in 1981, Japan gradually opened up to foreign-trained horses, and this year it was promoted from Part II to Part I - a turning point in Japanese racing's worldwide recognition.
127:
* A Three-Way Tenno Sho (Autumn)
In the 2008 Tenno Sho (Autumn), all 17 runners were graded winners, yet the betting centered on a Big Three.
Favorite was Vodka. After her Derby win the year before she lost 7 straight (excluding a scratch), but won the Yasuda Kinen this year, her first win in a year. 2nd choice was her nemesis Daiwa Scarlet, who had beaten her in the previous Oka Sho and Shuka Sho - 7 wins and three 2nds from 10, never out of the top two. Next came 3yo colt Deep Sky, winner of this year's NHK Mile C.-Derby double.
Daiwa Scarlet set a fast pace, with Vodka tracking in midfield. In the straight Deep Sky joined and the three broke clear, spread across the track. Vodka seemed to edge ahead, but Daiwa Scarlet fought back and the two hit the line together, with Deep Sky just behind in 3rd. The photo took a full 13 minutes; it looked like a dead heat. As the crowd buzzed, Vodka was declared the winner by a nose - just 2 cm. Many fans name this duel between two mares as the greatest race ever. Winning this epic, Vodka was named Horse of the Year.

* Yukichan: World's First Graded Win by a White Horse
Oguri Cap and Tamamo Cross in the late 1980s disproved "greys don't win." But white horses were so rare and none had succeeded, so the belief that "white horses don't win" remained strong.
Then came Yukichan (by Kurofune), a white filly out of white mare Shirayuki Hime. She stumbled on debut, but won the Mimosa Sho in her first 3yo race, the first turf win by a white horse. She aimed for the classics but gave up after a 7th in the Flora S., and targeted the dirt graded Kanto Oaks. Her entry made huge news; Kawasaki drew 127% of the previous year's attendance, and a special window was set up just for bets on her. She led from the start, set a slow pace, pulled away from the third turn and won by 8 lengths - the first graded win by a white horse, not just in Japan but in the world. Yukichan overturned "white horses are weak." But the white horse story wasn't over: later, Shirayuki Hime's family would produce even greater stars.
125:
* Japan's Greatest Takes On the Arc
The year before, Deep Impact won an unbeaten Triple Crown and became a social phenomenon. As an older horse this year he kept running in a class of his own. In the Hanshin Daishoten he handled good-to-soft going for the first time with ease. In the Tenno Sho (Spring) he drew a race-record 73.5% of win bets. He missed the break again, then launched a long run before the third turn and led at the final turn. Still he produced the fastest finish in the straight, showing that wherever he moved, it didn't matter. His time was a world record for 3200m on turf. In the Takarazuka Kinen he again drew a race-record 75.2% of win bets and won easily; in the photo afterwards Yutaka Take raised five fingers for five crowns.
His camp, long planning a trip abroad, set his next race as the Arc, the world's greatest. Many Japanese fans traveled to Longchamp dreaming of glory. As favorite he broke well, and unlike his usual style, sat 2nd or 3rd. He led 400m out, but in the straight Rail Link, on a 4-race winning streak, passed him after a fierce duel, and he crossed the line 3rd. He was praised for his effort on his return, but over a month later he was disqualified from the Arc: ipratropium, a drug used for respiratory problems, had been detected. It wasn't banned in Japan then, but was added the next year after this. Japan's greatest horse's Arc challenge ended in an unexpected way.
Back home, announcing his retirement at year's end, he ran in the Japan Cup and Arima Kinen. As if to vent his frustration, he won both easily, leaving the turf with the pride of Japan's best intact. His overwhelming power lives on in his offspring, still making a huge impact on racing.

* Taking On G1s Abroad
Besides Deep Impact, many other horses took on G1s abroad this year.
Local horse Cosmo Bulk, who stormed the classics in 2004, ran in the Singapore Airlines International Cup on his first trip abroad. Racing forward, he won - the first G1 abroad by a local-based horse.
Among JRA horses, Delta Blues traveled to Australia. He was narrowly 3rd in the Caulfield Cup, then won the Melbourne Cup, called the greatest festival of Australian racing (Japan's Pop Rock was 2nd) - the first G1 in the distant Southern Hemisphere won by a Japan-trained horse.
128:
* "To the Top of the View" Buena Vista
Her sire was Derby winner Special Week, who walked the royal road; her dam was G1 winner Biwa Heidi, and half-brothers Admire Japan and Admire Aura shone in the classics. Buena Vista lived up to expectations, sweeping past the field in the straight to win the Hanshin JF and champion 2yo filly.
In her first race this year, the Tulip Sho, she drew a race-record 72.3% of win bets and won easily with a powerful kick. In the Oka Sho she was a clear favorite. Nearly last into the straight, over 10 lengths behind the leader, she surged wide to win. In the Oaks she again unleashed a devilish finish from the back, beating Red Desire, who had broken clear first, by a nose after a photo for the double.
An Arc trip was scrapped after a 2nd in the Sapporo Kinen prep, and she aimed for the fillies' Triple Crown in the Shuka Sho. She sat in midfield, marking Red Desire. In the straight they dueled again and hit the line together. In another photo, this time Red Desire won by a nose. Not only did Buena Vista miss the Triple Crown, she was judged to have interfered and was demoted to 3rd.
She was 3rd in the Queen Elizabeth II Cup behind the runaway Queen Spumante and T.M. Precure, and narrowly 2nd in the Arima Kinen after a duel with Dream Journey, proving she could match older horses. Named champion 3yo filly, she carried great hopes as a future star of Japanese racing.

* Vodka, the Greatest Mare Ever
The year before, Vodka won an epic duel with Daiwa Scarlet in the Tenno Sho (Autumn) and was Horse of the Year. This spring she tried the Dubai Duty Free (G1) again after a 4th the year before, but was 7th.
Back home her first race was the Victoria Mile. She had lost 3 straight since the Tenno Sho, but fans never doubted her, making her 1.7 favorite. She won by 7 lengths in record time for her 5th G1, and passed Air Groove to become the top-earning female ever.
But she wasn't done. In the Yasuda Kinen she waited in midfield. In the straight she tried to come up the inside but was walled in by a crowd of horses. Just when all seemed lost, she shot through a tiny gap, surged forward and caught double winner Deep Sky, who had broken clear first, before the line. With this win she became the first female to win the Yasuda Kinen twice, set a new record for G1 wins by a female with 6, and became the first female to earn 1 billion yen.
In autumn she narrowly lost the Mainichi Okan and the Tenno Sho (Autumn). The big one, the Japan Cup, was a race she longed to win after finishing 4th and 3rd before. She led early in the straight and broke fully clear at one point. Kikuka Sho winner Oken Bruce Lee charged at the end, but she held on by a nose - the first Japan-trained female to win the Japan Cup. Her 7th G1 tied the record held by Symboli Rudolf and others, and she was Horse of the Year for the second straight year.

* Dream Journey Returns to Glory
Dream Journey was by Stay Gold out of a Mejiro McQueen mare. This cross later produced Orfevre and Gold Ship and was called the "golden cross" - and Dream Journey was its pioneer. He won the Asahi Hai FS at 2 and was seen as a future star, but went through the classics without a win, and G1 titles stayed out of reach.
At 5 this year he beat favorite Deep Sky in the Sankei Osaka Hai for his 5th graded win. He ran well for 3rd in the Tenno Sho (Spring), then went for his spring goal, the Takarazuka Kinen. Favorite was Deep Sky again, at 1.6; 2nd choice Dream Journey was far behind at 7.1. But in the straight he swept wide past Deep Sky and Sakura Mega Wonder, who were driving hard, to win his first G1 in about two and a half years.
After a 2nd in the All Comers and 6th in the Tenno Sho (Autumn), he went to the Arima Kinen. After those losses, favorite was double winner Buena Vista. Waiting nearly last, he swept forward, and in the straight fought a fierce duel with Buena Vista, who had broken clear from a good spot, catching her by half a length. He became only the 6th horse since graded races began to win both the spring and autumn Grand Prix. With his great partner Kenichi Ikezoe, "Mr. Grand Prix," he is a horse remembered in both records and memories.
129:
* Apapane: A Triple Crown Won by "Studying at Ritto"
Apapane is named after a beautiful red Hawaiian bird, a nod to her sire King Kamehameha, named for the king who united Hawaii. She was 3rd on debut, then after over three months off gained a whopping 24 kg and won her maiden with a powerful run that belied her cute name. She won the Akamatsu Sho in a 2yo course record, then the Hanshin JF, and was unanimously champion 2yo filly.
In 2010, at 3, the Miho-based Apapane moved to Ritto in mid-February for training. Her trainer Kunieda devised this to spare horses the stress of shipping right before a race - a method called "studying at Ritto," first used with her dam Salty Bid. She was 2nd in the Tulip Sho at Hanshin but stayed at Ritto for the Oka Sho, which she won with a sharp run from up front in race-record time.
For the Oaks there were doubts about the distance: she had never run beyond 1800m and often fought her rider. She raced in midfield and surged wide in the straight together with Flora S. (Oaks trial) winner Saint Emilion. Apapane got clear about 200m out, but Saint Emilion fought back on the inside and drew level at the line. After a 12-minute photo, it was a dead heat - a first in JRA G1 history. Winning her second classic this way, she was the first Kanto-based fillies' double winner in 24 years, since Mejiro Ramonu in 1986.
In autumn she went back to Ritto for the Rose S. (Shuka Sho trial), having grown another 24 kg. She led briefly but was caught, a shock 4th. Still she was 2.3 favorite for the Shuka Sho. She broke well, sat at the back of midfield, and came wide with a powerful finish to win - only the third fillies' Triple Crown winner ever.

* Oguri Cap Dies
Idol horse Oguri Cap, who led the second racing boom, stood at stud at the Yushun Stallion Station in Niikappu, Hokkaido, after retiring in 1990. He was open to the public until 2002, a tourist spot visited by many fans.
In July 2010, after public viewing resumed, he was found lying in the viewing paddock. He had apparently slipped in the mud and suffered a compound fracture of his right hind leg, and was put down. About 800 racing people and fans from across Japan attended his farewell - a reminder of how deeply he moved racing.
130:
* Orfevre Wins the Triple Crown
Full brother to Grand Prix double winner Dream Journey, Orfevre was watched from before his debut. He won his debut easily, showing rare power, but also a fiery temper, throwing jockey Kenichi Ikezoe after the line. Perhaps because of that he sometimes fought his rider, and was a heavy-beaten 10th in the Keio Hai 2yo S.
His second win came in 2011, in his third 3yo start, the Spring S., earning priority entry to the Satsuki Sho. Due to the March Great East Japan Earthquake, the Satsuki Sho, usually at Nakayama, was moved to Tokyo. Despite winning the prep, doubts about his temper left him 4th choice at 10.8 (favorite was Yayoi Sho winner Sadamu Patek). But he settled at the back of midfield, burst out on the inside in the straight and won by 3 lengths from Sadamu Patek.
His rout made him 3.0 favorite for the Japanese Derby. A typhoon left Tokyo's track in terrible shape, but he powered through the heavy going to win the double. Ikezoe said, "Riding him all along is our strength," showing the bond of a pair who rose from that heavy defeat at 2.
In the Kobe Shimbun Hai he settled well, raced forward and broke clear early to win in commanding style. Then the Kikuka Sho, for the Triple Crown, with 68,000 fans at Kyoto. Unfazed when the horse next to him acted up in the gate, he broke well, sat in a good midfield spot, took the lead early at the top of the straight and ran away, beating Win Variation by two and a half lengths - the 7th Triple Crown winner ever. His running showed further growth, but after the line he again threw Ikezoe - his temper unchanged.
With no rivals left in his crop, he met older horses for the first time in the Arima Kinen. Against a superb field of 9 G1 winners, including double classic filly Buena Vista in her final race, he won the Grand Prix for his fourth crown and was named Horse of the Year.

* JRA Direct and WIN5 Begin
This year ways to bet and enjoy racing widened greatly.
One was JRA Direct: with a JRA-designated credit card, anyone could easily bet online, including on smartphones, which had spread from the late 2000s. Betting became easier than ever, and it's still widely used.
The other was a new bet type, the "five-race pick," known as WIN5: picking the winners of 5 designated races. It's very hard to hit, but the big payouts make it a popular bet.
131:
* The "Lady's" Triple Crown, Beating the Colts Too
Gentildonna, a filly by Deep Impact, was full sister to 2-time graded winner Donau Blue. She broke her maiden at the end of the previous year, then chose the G3 Shinzan Kinen against colts for her first 2012 race, her camp believing she could match the colts. As hoped, she won by over a length for her first graded win.
She was 4th in the Tulip Sho, partly due to illness, and 2nd choice for the Oka Sho behind previous 2yo queen Joie de Vivre. Waiting at the back of midfield, she came wide in the straight and ran down Verxina and I'm Yours, who had broken clear first, for her first classic.
In the Oaks she was only 3rd choice despite her Oka Sho win (favorite was Flora S. winner Midsummer Fair). Her dam Donna Blini was a sprinter, sister Donau Blue a miler, and she had only run at 1600m in 5 starts, raising doubts. But she closed from behind and won by 5 lengths from Verxina, breaking the race record by 1.7 seconds. With the distance doubts gone, she was overwhelming 1.3 favorite for the Shuka Sho. In the warm-up she was startled by the roar of fans who had come to see the Triple Crown and threw her jockey, but no harm was done. Her obstacle in the final battle was again Verxina, 2nd in both earlier classics. Under 100m out the two dueled, and Gentildonna won by a nose - 7 cm - becoming the 4th fillies' Triple Crown winner.
The best filly of her crop then took on the Japan Cup. Waiting was last year's Triple Crown winner Orfevre. This year he won the Takarazuka Kinen and was 2nd in the Arc, but in spring went berserk in the Hanshin Daishoten and had to retake a training exam (for horses judged insufficiently trained) - a true maverick, "the golden tyrant." It was the first clash of Triple Crown winners in the Japan Cup in 28 years, since 1984 (Symboli Rudolf vs Mr. C.B.). Again it came down to the straight. Under 200m out Gentildonna broke clear on the inside and Orfevre on the outside, fighting fiercely. Gentildonna held on by a nose - the first 3yo filly ever to win the Japan Cup, earning her Horse of the Year.

* Gold Ship, the Great Eccentric, Wins Two Classics
Gold Ship came from the same golden cross as Triple Crown winner Orfevre and Grand Prix double winner Dream Journey: by Stay Gold out of a Mejiro McQueen mare. He was 4th choice for the Satsuki Sho (favorite was Spring S. winner Grandezza). He left the gate slowly and sat last, but while the others avoided the rough inside, he alone charged up it, quickly gaining ground. He burst clear in the straight and beat World Ace by two and a half lengths. His unorthodox long run and deliberate choice of the rough inside stunned fans.
In the Derby he couldn't catch the leaders from the back and was 5th, but he romped in the Kobe Shimbun Hai and went to the Kikuka Sho. Again at the back, he launched a long run down the backstretch on the second lap, led at the top of the straight and won with no one near. A double of the Satsuki Sho and Kikuka Sho, 1000m apart, is rare - the first since Air Shakur in 2000. He then won the Arima Kinen at 3 as well.
With 3 G1 wins that year he was unanimously champion 3yo colt. He was clearly among the best in training, but from the next year people said whether he showed his power depended on his mood. Yet fans came to love him precisely for his eccentricity.
132:
* Sprint King Lord Kanaloa
Lord Kanaloa inherited top-class speed from his sire King Kamehameha and won his debut by 6 lengths. But he was 2nd in his second start, the Junior C. over a mile, and from then on his camp kept him to sprints. It paid off: at 4 the year before, he won the Sprinters S. in record time, then became the first Japanese horse to win the Hong Kong Sprint.
In 2013 he was invited to the Dubai Golden Shaheen, a sprint G1, but declined to try again for the Takamatsunomiya Kinen, which he had lost to Curren Chan the year before. He was overwhelming 1.3 favorite and, despite a slightly slow start, won in record time in a class of his own - the first Japanese horse to win three straight sprint G1s. Next was the Yasuda Kinen, his first mile since the Junior C. 2 years and 5 months earlier, and he won with a powerful late run, as if to say "I'm not the horse I was."
In autumn he won the Sprinters S. again and chose the Hong Kong Sprint as his farewell. He was 1.8 favorite in Hong Kong too. Tracking the leaders, he took the lead mid-straight and kept pulling away, winning by 5 lengths, rare for a sprint - the biggest margin in Hong Kong Sprint history, a parting record.
He was named Horse of the Year, the first sprinter since Taiki Shuttle 15 years earlier. Never out of the top three in his career, he went to stud and sired nine-G1 winner Almond Eye in his first crop, achieving great things as a sire too.

* Orfevre's Second Arc Challenge
The year before, Triple Crown winner Orfevre, "the golden tyrant," went to France, won the Prix Foy prep, but just missed in the Arc, finishing 2nd.
This year, with the Arc still the goal, he focused on Japan in spring. Careful training aimed to fix his habit of veering, which cost him the Arc, and to help him settle. It worked: in the Sankei Osaka Hai (then a G2) he settled perfectly and won easily, though by just half a length. He targeted the Takarazuka Kinen, a clash with stars like fillies' Triple Crown winner Gentildonna and the eccentric double winner Gold Ship that drew huge attention, but he bled from the lungs after his final workout a week before and was withdrawn.
Luckily it was mild, and the French trip went ahead. In the Prix Foy he settled perfectly and won so easily his jockey looked back in the straight, winning it again. Hopes for Japan's first Arc win soared, and he was favorite. With that year's Derby winner Kizuna also running, about 5,800 Japanese fans came to Longchamp. He tracked at the back of midfield. In the straight 2nd choice Treve, a French 3yo filly, burst clear, and Orfevre chased, but against her powerful finish the gap only grew, and he was 2nd, beaten 5 lengths.
He missed the Arc again, but two straight 2nds are something to be proud of, and he was warmly welcomed home. And he wasn't done: in his farewell, the Arima Kinen, he won by 8 lengths from Win Variation. Shining a dazzling golden light for the over 120,000 fans who came to see him one last time, Orfevre left the turf.
133:
* Just a Way: To the Top of the World
Just a Way, by Heart's Cry, ran in the classics but kept falling just short. But in the previous Tenno Sho (Autumn), as 5th choice, he beat fillies' Triple Crown winner Gentildonna by 4 lengths for his first G1 in his 4th try - a stunning leap.
In 2014, at 5, he announced a trip to Dubai. He won the Nakayama Kinen, his prep and send-off, proving his Tenno Sho was no fluke. The big race, the Dubai Duty Free, drew a stellar field with 7 G1-level winners. He missed the break and sat at the back, but in the straight unleashed a stunning finish, passed the whole field and kept going, winning by six and a quarter lengths - the biggest margin in the race's history, in a course record a full 2.41 seconds faster than the old one. The rout was hailed worldwide, earning him 130 in the international ratings (World's Best Racehorse Rankings) - far above the 125 of Deep Impact, called Japan's greatest ever, and second among Japan-trained horses only to El Condor Pasa's 134. Just a Way became the first Japan-trained horse ranked world No. 1. And No. 2 that year was Epiphaneia, rated 129 after winning the Japan Cup - Japan-trained horses 1st and 2nd in the world.

* Back-to-Back G1 Feats
Gold Ship, loved as "the grey idol horse," was crushed by Triple Crown winner Orfevre, by the same sire, in the previous Arima Kinen. Verxina set an odd record, 2nd to Gentildonna in all three fillies' classics. These two, humbled by champions, both shone this year.
Gold Ship, who won the Takarazuka Kinen the year before, topped both the fan vote and the betting this year. He dropped to last after the start, but moved up to about 4th before the first turn. He took the lead in the straight and pulled away to win by 3 lengths - the first to win the Takarazuka Kinen twice, and in a row. With 5 G1s he passed Oguri Cap and Mejiro McQueen's 4 to become the grey with the most G1 wins. But in his first race abroad, the Arc, he did nothing from the back and was 14th, and going for a third Takarazuka Kinen the next year he reared up in the gate at the start and was crushed - truly a horse "beyond common sense."
Verxina, a Deep Impact filly, won her long-sought G1 in the previous Victoria Mile. But she then lost 6 straight without making the top five, and despite being the defending champ was only 11th choice for this year's Victoria Mile. Her camp, believing her poor runs came from a lack of fighting spirit, decided to send her to the front to light a fire. As planned, once in front her fighting spirit blazed and she led all the way - the first to win the Victoria Mile twice in a row.
134:
* Father-Son Derby Winners, and a Kikuka Sho Without Its Star
Duramente, by King Kamehameha out of Admire Groove, was one of Japan's finest bluebloods. Named after a musical term meaning "harshly," he stormed this year's classics with fierce running.
In the Satsuki Sho he was 3rd choice behind Yayoi Sho winner Satono Crown and Kyodo News Hai winner Real Steel. Racing from behind, he botched the final turn and veered from inside to the far outside. But he regained his balance in the straight and unleashed an explosive finish, sweeping past Real Steel, Kitasan Black and others before they could react, and won with ease. The win completed an extraordinary four generations of G1 winners: his dam Admire Groove, granddam Air Groove and great-granddam Dyna Carl. Jockey Mirco Demuro was suspended 4 days for the interference.
In the Japanese Derby, the big race his sire had won, his brilliant win made him overwhelming 1.9 favorite. This time he settled well, led early in the straight and held on, winning the father-son Derby double and breaking his sire's race record by 0.1 seconds.
Everyone expected the Triple Crown after such wins, but while resting after the Derby he was found to have fractures in both forelegs and missed the Kikuka Sho. In the Kikuka Sho without its star, the winner was Kitasan Black, who later won many G1s.

* Maurice's Triumphant Run
Maurice was by Screen Hero (Japan Cup winner) out of a mare by Carnegie (Arc winner) - not a pedigree that drew attention. Still, he won his debut in a 2yo course record. But he could barely make the top five in graded races after that, and went on a long break before summer at 3, during which his painful back was carefully treated.
In 2015, at 4, he took off. After winning two allowance races, he took on the G3 Lord Derby Challenge Trophy. Despite missing the break in a mile race, he burst clear in the straight to win by three and a half lengths in race-record time, his first graded win.
Next was his first G1, the Yasuda Kinen. The field was far stronger, with 5 G1 winners, but his last run made him favorite. This time he broke sharply, sat in a good spot, led in the straight and held off Vincennes by a neck for his first G1. After summer he went straight to the Mile CS, five months on, a schedule that raised doubts and left him 4th choice. But he won anyway - only the 6th horse to win both the spring and autumn mile G1s.
With no rivals left among Japan's milers, he ran in the Hong Kong Mile at year's end. Favorite was Able Friend, "Hong Kong's hero," hugely popular at home; Maurice was 2nd choice. Maurice tracked in midfield with Able Friend right behind. In the straight he was passed once, but fought back to cross the line first, adding the Hong Kong Mile to his spring and autumn mile G1s. After losing all 4 starts the year before, he won all 6 this year and became only the third sprinter-miler named Horse of the Year, after Taiki Shuttle (1998) and Lord Kanaloa (2013).
135:
* Kitasan Black vs Satono Diamond
This year's Arima Kinen became a clash between last year's Kikuka Sho winner Kitasan Black and this year's, Satono Diamond.
Kitasan Black, owned by enka singer Saburo Kitajima, drew more attention the more he won. Sold for just 3.5 million yen, he won the Kikuka Sho the year before, and this year took the Tenno Sho (Spring) and Japan Cup to reach the top among older horses. His sire Black Tide, full brother of Deep Impact, was a graded winner but lived in the shadow of his brother, hailed as the greatest ever - yet as a sire he produced a huge star.
Satono Diamond, by Deep Impact out of Malpensa, a 3-time G1 winner in Argentina, was a blueblood sold at the Select Sale for 230 million yen. 3rd and 2nd in the spring classics, he won the Kikuka Sho as favorite by two and a half lengths and was seen as the best of his crop.
The clash of two contrasting Kikuka Sho winners drew huge interest, with Satono Diamond 2.6 and Kitasan Black 2.7. Kitasan Black sat in a perfect 2nd, while Satono Diamond moved right behind him down the backstretch, marking him all the way. At the third turn stablemate Satono Noblesse swept forward and the pace quickened. In the straight Kitasan Black led and tried to hold on, but Satono Diamond kept coming and won by a neck. The younger Kikuka Sho winner took the much-anticipated duel.

* Hokko Tarumae, Most G1-Level Wins Ever
Hokko Tarumae, owned by a Tomakomai owner and named after the city's Mt. Tarumae, debuted at 3 and ran steadily on dirt, then from 4 went on a tremendous run, winning 9 G1/JpnI races in three years to 6.
In 2016 he raced on at 7. He went for a third straight Kawasaki Kinen (JpnI) and won as favorite - only the second to win it three times running, after Countess Up (1985-87). It was his 10th G1/JpnI win, passing Vermilion and Espoir City's 9 for the most G1-level wins ever. He then tried Dubai again (Dubai WC) but was 9th, and retired at year's end. He has since done well at stud while serving as Tomakomai's tourism ambassador, helping his hometown.
136:
* Chasing a Triple Crown: 7 G1 Wins
Kitasan Black lost a thriller to Satono Diamond in the last Arima Kinen, but in 2017 he showed no sign of slowing.
Spring had only two G1s for older horses at middle-to-long distances (the Tenno Sho (Spring) and Takarazuka Kinen) - one fewer than autumn, and weighted to long races. So the 2000m G2 Sankei Osaka Hai was chosen, renamed the Osaka Hai and made a G1 this year. Kitasan Black took on this new "spring older horses' triple crown." In the Osaka Hai some had doubts, as he was a long-distance horse and had been 2nd the year before. But he didn't chase the runaway leader, sat in a good spot and coolly took the lead in the straight. The others closed but he never tired, becoming the first G1 Osaka Hai champion.
The Tenno Sho (Spring) was a two-horse clash with his nemesis Satono Diamond. Kitasan Black was 2.2, Satono Diamond 2.5. But favorites had lost the race 10 years running since Deep Impact in 2006. Runaway leader Yamakatsu Raiden set a blistering pace. As others tired, Kitasan Black led early and built a lead, and held off Satono Diamond and others in the straight. He avenged his defeat and set a record nearly a second faster than Deep Impact's. Having won two spring legs, perhaps tired, he was a dismal 9th in the Takarazuka Kinen as 1.4 favorite, just missing the first spring triple crown.
In autumn he started in the Tenno Sho (Autumn). On the first heavy track in 48 years, and racing from behind after a stumbling start, he still beat Satono Crown by a neck, winning both Tenno Sho races. In the Japan Cup, which he won the year before, he tried to lead all the way but was 3rd behind Cheval Grand's late run.
For his farewell his camp chose the Arima Kinen, where he had lost twice. His tactic was, of course, his trademark front-running. Setting his own pace, he stayed in front and pulled away in the straight - a textbook front-running win by a length and a half. On his third try he finally won the Arima Kinen, a perfect finale.
He missed the triple crowns in spring and autumn, but won 4 G1s that year. His 7 in all tied the record, and his earnings passed T.M. Opera O's to become No. 1 - truly a champion who walked the royal road.

* G1-Level Wins Record Broken Two Years Running
Copano Rickey was by Gold Allure, a 4-time dirt G1-level winner. He won his first graded race, the Hyogo CS, at 3, but a fracture sidelined him. After his return he kept losing, and squeezed into the February S. through a draw as last choice of 16. But he boldly raced forward and held off Hokko Tarumae and others - a shock win paying 272.1, the second-highest win payout in JRA G1 history. Amid talk of a fluke, he won the Kashiwa Kinen next and declared himself the best dirt horse. He piled up wins, including the first back-to-back February S., winning 8 G1/JpnI races by 6.
In 2017 his first race at 7 was the February S. After losses at the end of the previous year he was only 6th choice. He led briefly at the top of the straight but was passed by one horse after another, finishing 14th. He seemed finished, but in the Kashiwa Kinen he won from off the pace instead, surprising fans with a new style at 7 and winning the race for the third time. In autumn he won the Mile CS Nambu Hai again, and chose the Tokyo Daishoten, where he had lost 3 times, as his farewell. He broke well, led and held off everyone in the straight - a record 11th G1-level win, breaking the mark Hokko Tarumae had just set the year before, and a glorious send-off.
137:
* Fillies' Triple Crown and a World Record
Almond Eye was a blueblood by top sprinter Lord Kanaloa out of Queen Elizabeth II Cup winner Fusaichi Pandora. She lost her debut but won next time, then won her first graded race against colts in this year's Shinzan Kinen.
Then the first classic, the Oka Sho (from here until retirement she ran only in G1s). Unbeaten 2yo queen Lucky Lilac was favorite. Lucky Lilac raced forward while Almond Eye waited at the back. About 8 lengths behind at the top of the straight, she surged wide and swept past before anyone could react, winning easily. Jockey Christophe Lemaire's comments afterwards sounded like a Triple Crown declaration. In the Oaks she was 1.7 favorite and won by 2 lengths, taking her second crown with ease. In autumn she went straight to the Shuka Sho without a prep. Despite doubts about the schedule, she was 1.3 favorite, more heavily backed than in the Oaks - her power was on another level. In the straight she was about 10 lengths behind the leader, too far even for her believers, but she unleashed an astonishing kick, led with 150m left and won by a length and a half - the 5th fillies' Triple Crown winner.
But even that was just a milestone. For her last race of the year she chose not the fillies' Queen Elizabeth II Cup but the Japan Cup, against strong older colts. Ahead of stars like Osaka Hai winner Suave Richard and 2-time G1 winner Satono Diamond, she was again overwhelming 1.4 favorite; her 53.4% of win bets was second in the race's history only to Deep Impact in 2006. She tracked front-runner Kiseki in 2nd, drew level 200m out and pulled away to win by a length and three-quarters - a champion's performance against strong older horses. Her time, 2:20.6, was not just a race record but over a second faster than the world record for 2400m on turf. She became only the second 3yo filly named Horse of the Year, after Gentildonna in 2012.

* Lemaire: JRA Wins Record and First Jockey Quadruple
Christophe Lemaire, who won the fillies' Triple Crown on Almond Eye this year, also won the Kikuka Sho with Fierement, the Tenno Sho (Autumn) with Rey de Oro and the JBC Sprint with Graceful Leap - the first-ever G1 wins four weeks in a row, starting with the Shuka Sho (he did it again in 2020). He also set a record of 215 wins in a year (8 G1s), and became the first jockey to win four JRA Award categories.
Meanwhile legend Yutaka Take, at the top since the second racing boom, reached 4,000 JRA wins.
138:
* A Great Mare in Full Bloom
Lys Gracieux won her second start in a Hanshin 2yo record for 1800m on turf, then won the Artemis S. True to her name, French for "graceful lily," her career began brilliantly - but she then lost 7 straight G1s (four times 2nd), just short of a title. In autumn at 4, with top mare Almond Eye absent, she finally won her first G1, the Queen Elizabeth II Cup.
In 2019, at 5, near misses continued: 2nd in the Kinko Sho, 3rd in Hong Kong's QE2 Cup. She seemed to be back to "good but not quite," but showed her grit in the Takarazuka Kinen. The only filly in the field, she was 3rd choice at 5.4. Her camp planned to come late from behind, but with only favorite Kiseki going forward, she followed him in 2nd. In the straight she easily passed Kiseki and won by 3 lengths for her second G1.
From this year the Takarazuka Kinen winner got priority entry to Australia's G1 Cox Plate, with a bonus for winning. Her camp wanted to go, but her spring Hong Kong trip ran afoul of quarantine rules, and at first she had to give it up. Then Australia's agriculture department and others made the trip possible, and her long-awaited entry was confirmed. Popular there too, she waited at the back and shot up Moonee Valley's straight, just 173m long, to win - her first G1 abroad.
Back home she chose the Arima Kinen as her last race. Even in her farewell she weighed a career-high 468 kg, showing she was at her peak. Favorite was year-younger fillies' Triple Crown winner Almond Eye, fresh from winning the Tenno Sho (Autumn); Lys Gracieux was a distant 2nd choice. At a fast pace she sat in midfield, swung wide in the straight and unleashed an astonishing finish to win by 5 lengths. Almond Eye was 9th. The first mare to win both Grand Prix races in the same year, she bowed out in style. The "lily" that kept falling short at 3 and 4 bloomed beautifully this year and rose to Horse of the Year.

* Changes to the Race System
This year "listed race" status was introduced: important open races ranked just below graded races, marked "(L)" after the name.
Also, horses used to have their earned prize money halved in summer at 4 (the "demotion" system), letting them return to a class they had already won. This was abolished this year, and the 5-million, 10-million and 16-million-yen classes were renamed the 1-win, 2-win and 3-win classes.
Non-graded races' rankings and classes became easier to understand - especially welcome for new fans.
139:
* Unbeaten Triple Crowns for Colt and Filly - and a Clash
This year, unbeaten Triple Crown winners emerged among both colts and fillies.
Contrail was a son of unbeaten Triple Crown winner Deep Impact. In his second start, the Tokyo Sports Hai 2yo S., he won easily in a 2yo record for 1800m on turf despite not being fully prepared. He won the Hopeful S. clearly too and was named champion 2yo colt by a wide margin over Asahi Hai FS winner Salios. At 3 he boldly went straight to the Satsuki Sho without a prep. As attention focused on his clash with Salios, the coronavirus was raging, and the race was run without spectators. He tracked calmly at the back and passed Salios by half a length in the straight for his first classic. In the Japanese Derby he was 1.4 and Salios 4.4, with the rest in double figures - a two-horse race. But Contrail stretched the gap, winning by 3 lengths and showing his rival the difference in class. Then the last classic, the Kikuka Sho. Despite doubts about the distance, he was 1.1 favorite. Closely marked all the way by Aristoteles under Lemaire, he had a tough race, but never gave up the lead in the straight duel and won by a neck - the third unbeaten Triple Crown winner, and the first father-son unbeaten Triple Crown. A world first, it was covered by racing media around the globe.
Among fillies, Daring Tact starred. This year's fillies' classics looked wide open as the expected contenders lost their preps one after another. In her third career start, the Oka Sho, she was 2nd choice behind 2yo queen Resistencia. Morning rain made the going heavy, seemingly bad for a closer. She was about 8 lengths behind into the straight, seemingly too far, but her powerful finish ran down Resistencia and she won by a length and a half - the first to win the Oka Sho in its third start in 40 years, since Hagino Top Lady in 1980, and only the third ever. The Oaks was her first race beyond a mile, but her finish made her 1.6 favorite. As hoped, she swept from the back with a 33.1 final 600m for her second crown. Her camp judged she'd do best without a prep, and sent her straight to the Shuka Sho. Despite good-to-soft ground and the layoff, she was 1.4 favorite. She reared at the start and missed the break, but broke clear cleanly at the end to win by a length and a quarter - the first unbeaten fillies' Triple Crown ever.
Both chose the Japan Cup next. Waiting there was the undisputed queen, fellow fillies' Triple Crown winner Almond Eye, with a record 8 G1s, who had announced the Japan Cup as her last race. The first-ever clash of three Triple Crown winners had come. Almond Eye was 2.2, Contrail 2.8 and Daring Tact 3.7. As Kiseki set off in a big lead, the three raced in midfield without chasing. In the straight Almond Eye surged forward; Daring Tact and Contrail swung wide and chased but couldn't catch her. With her 9th G1 she broke her own record, was named Horse of the Year over the two unbeaten Triple Crown winners, and left the turf with the dignity of the senior champion.

* Sodashi, First G1 Win by a White Horse
In 2008 Yukichan became the first white horse to win a graded race. Then in 2019 Hayayakko won the Leopard S., and finally Sodashi reached a turf G1. Her granddam Shirayuki Hime (Yukichan's dam and Hayayakko's granddam) and dam Buchiko were both white - a pure white female line.
In her second start she raced forward and broke clear in the straight to win the Sapporo 2yo S. (G3). Since Yukichan's graded win was a JRA-local race, Sodashi was the first white horse to win a JRA graded race and a turf graded race. She then won the Artemis S. too, and rode that momentum into the G1 Hanshin JF. Breaking well, she sat in a good spot, broke clear in the straight and won a duel with Satono Reinas by a nose - the first G1 win by a white horse. Beautiful and strong, Sodashi became an undisputed idol horse.

* Gran Alegria Dominates the Sprints
The year before, Gran Alegria won the Oka Sho in race-record time. This year she raced only short distances and shone. Her first race as an older horse, the Takamatsunomiya Kinen, ended in a narrow 2nd, and she missed the Victoria Mile with a fever - not a smooth start. But in the Yasuda Kinen she upset overwhelming favorite Almond Eye.
In the Sprinters S. she sat far back, then swept past the whole field with a powerful finish to win by 2 lengths, rare in a sprint - the first sprint G1 for Deep Impact's offspring, who mostly raced longer. Her last race of the year was the Mile CS. Blocked in the straight, she switched wide, surged and ran down the leaders for a dramatic win. With 3 JRA sprint-mile G1s in a year, tying Lord Kanaloa's record, she was named champion sprinter.
140:
* Efforia: Fighting Back After a Narrow Derby Loss
By Epiphaneia (by Symboli Kris S. out of Cesario) out of a Heart's Cry mare, Efforia's pedigree is full of Japan's post-2000 stars. Nothing special at birth, he drew attention after winning his first two starts.
He won his first 3yo race, the Kyodo News Hai, as 4th choice, then went to the Satsuki Sho. Favorite was previous champion 2yo colt Danon the Kid, but Efforia broke clear perfectly from a good spot and beat Titleholder by 3 lengths. That made him overwhelming 1.7 favorite for the Japanese Derby, where filly Satono Reinas's entry also drew attention. From gate 1 he sat in midfield and closed in the straight, but Shahryar pounced just before the line, and he missed the double by a nose. By fate, like his sire Epiphaneia, grandsire Symboli Kris S. and broodmare sire Heart's Cry, he finished 2nd in the Derby.
In autumn he skipped the Kikuka Sho for the Tenno Sho (Autumn) against older horses. Favorite was 4yo unbeaten Triple Crown winner Contrail, 2nd choice 5yo queen Gran Alegria, going for a middle-distance G1 after sprints and miles. Efforia was 3rd choice. In this clash of three generations, he sat in midfield, passed Gran Alegria 200m out and held off Contrail's charge - the first 3yo to win the Tenno Sho (Autumn) in 19 years, since grandsire Symboli Kris S. in 2002.
Then the Arima Kinen. He topped the fan vote, the first 3yo to do so since Vodka in 2007. He was favorite, closely followed by 5yo mare Chrono Genesis. She had won three straight Grand Prix races since the previous Takarazuka Kinen, a first for a mare, and was going for an unprecedented fourth in her last race. Efforia tracked right behind her into the straight, dueled with Deep Bond, and held off Chrono Genesis's charge to win. He missed the Triple Crown but won two big G1s against older horses and was named Horse of the Year.

* Loves Only You: 3 G1s Abroad, Proving Her Crop-Mates Wrong
Loves Only You, a blueblood Deep Impact filly, won the 2019 Oaks in race-record time. But while crop-mates Gran Alegria and Chrono Genesis shone, she lost 6 straight graded races after the Oaks.
In 2021, at 5, she won the Kyoto Kinen, her first win in 1 year and 9 months. On a roll, she went to the Dubai Sheema Classic but was 3rd, behind Chrono Genesis (2nd) and others. Undeterred, she flew straight to Hong Kong for the QE2 Cup, won a duel in the straight with favorite Daring Tact, the unbeaten fillies' Triple Crown winner, and took her first G1 in about two years. She traveled again, to the Breeders' Cup, the pinnacle of American racing, in the Filly & Mare Turf. Against top mares from around the world, she raced from a good spot and ran them down. That same day dirt mare Marche Lorraine won the BC Distaff, Japan's first G1 abroad on dirt - two Japanese Breeders' Cup wins, a historic feat.
She then returned to Hong Kong and won the Hong Kong Cup at year's end, the first horse with 3 G1 wins abroad in a year. Once left behind by her crop-mates, she soared at the end and retired rated as a great mare to match them.
144:
* The Long-Awaited Breeders' Cup Classic Win
After running well abroad and winning races like the Tokyo Daishoten at home the year before, Forever Young went even further this year. He opened abroad in the Saudi Cup, where Hong Kong's Romantic Warrior, the world's top earner, also ran. Romantic Warrior raced skillfully for a horse trying dirt for the first time and led at the final turn, but Forever Young hung on. Seeing no room inside, jockey Sakai deftly switched him out, and he closed with every powerful stride, catching him by a neck just before the line - a first G1 abroad for both horse and rider.
He then went to Dubai for the Dubai World Cup. Overwhelming favorite and expected to win, he couldn't quicken in the straight and was 3rd. Right after, trainer Yahagi said they had been "given the away-team treatment," revealing trouble in a pre-race check that left the horse keyed up.
But his camp didn't give up, aiming for their goal from the start: the Breeders' Cup Classic, where he'd been 3rd the year before. In his prep, the Nippon TV Hai, he won easily by two and a half lengths, staying unbeaten in Japan, and set off for America. The field included last year's winner Sierra Leone and runner-up Fierceness, both of whom had beaten him. He sat near the front and held his spot, led at the final turn and tried to pull away, but Sierra Leone charged wide. Answering his rider's urging, he held on by half a length at the line. It was the first Japanese win in the race in 29 years since Taiki Blizzard first tried it in 1996 - the moment Japanese racing's long dream came true. The win took his earnings past 2.9 billion yen, passing Ushba Tesoro as the all-time leader.

* A Japanese Whirlwind in Dubai
Dubai World Cup night, a racing festival with 9 G1 and G2 races in one day, saw many Japanese horses shine this year. It began with Win Carnelian's fine 2nd in race 4, the Al Quoz Sprint on turf; then Admire Daytona won race 5, the UAE Derby. In race 7, the Dubai Turf, Soul Rush beat favorite Romantic Warrior, and in the Dubai Sheema Classic Danon Decile won with Durezza 3rd. In the final race, the Dubai World Cup, Forever Young just missed in 3rd, but it was a historic day that showed the world the strength of Japanese horses.
In Europe too, a horse made history. Satono Reve won his first G1, the Takamatsunomiya Kinen, at 6 this year, then went to Britain for the Queen Elizabeth II Jubilee S., part of the royal "Royal Ascot" meeting. Breaking from the widest gate, 16, he closed wide on Lazzat, who had broken clear, but was half a length short in 2nd. Still, it was the first top-two finish by a Japanese horse at Royal Ascot in 25 years, since Agnes World was 2nd in the King's Stand S. (now the King Charles III S., then a G2) in 2000 - and the first ever in a G1.
141:
* Equinox: An Autumn Charge Erasing Spring's Frustration
Equinox was from the first crop of 7-time G1 winner Kitasan Black. He won his second start, the Tokyo Sports Hai 2yo S., with an astonishing finish and became a leading classic contender.
At 3 he went straight to the Satsuki Sho without a prep, 3rd choice behind previous champion 2yo colt Do Deuce and unbeaten Kyodo News Hai winner Danon Beluga. He moved from midfield to a good spot and pulled clear in the straight, but was caught at the end by 5th-choice stablemate Geoglyph. He raced at the back and produced the fastest finish, but fell a neck short of Do Deuce under Yutaka Take - 2nd again.
Next, following Efforia's path from the year before, he went to the Tenno Sho (Autumn). Panthalassa, a dramatic Dubai Turf winner in spring, set off in his trademark huge lead, with Equinox tracking in midfield. As Panthalassa turned into the straight over 10 lengths clear, the stands roared, "He's going to hold on!" But Equinox unleashed an astonishing kick, closed fast and ran him down. He then won the Arima Kinen in just his 6th career start, the fewest ever, completing a father-son double. Like Efforia the year before, he turned the frustration of narrow classic defeats into triumph among the older horses.


* Stars on Earth's Double
Stars on Earth was from the second crop of double classic winner Duramente. She broke her maiden in her second start, then was favorite three times running but kept just missing.
Given that record she was only 7th choice for the Oka Sho. But she surged from midfield and drew level with Water Navillera right at the line. After a photo, Stars on Earth was crowned queen of the cherry blossoms. In the Oaks she broke well, settled in midfield and swung widest of all in the straight, powering down the middle to win clearly by a length and a quarter - the fillies' double.
But after the race a chip fracture in her right leg was found. After a break she made it to the Shuka Sho, but just missed in 3rd, falling short of the Triple Crown.
142:
* Liberty Island Wins the Fillies' Triple Crown
Liberty Island (by Duramente) showed outstanding speed from her very first race. Her final 600m of 31.4 seconds on debut tied the fastest in JRA history, and was naturally the fastest ever for a debut. She narrowly lost the Artemis S. after finding no room in the straight, but won the Hanshin JF clearly in her third start and was unanimously champion 2yo filly.
She went straight to the Oka Sho for her first 3yo race, overwhelming 1.6 favorite over the horses who came through the trials. She was a bit slow away, but unleashed a tremendous finish widest of all in the straight to win. The new jockey camera, introduced that spring, captured her astonishing run and jockey Yuga Kawada calling her "young lady" after the race. Next was the Oaks. Racing much further forward than before, she left the field behind in the straight for the double, winning by 6 lengths - beyond Gentildonna's 5 (2012), the biggest Oaks margin since graded races began (1984).
She went straight to the last leg, the Shuka Sho. Her dominant wins made her an incredible 1.1 favorite. She broke well, sat in midfield, broke clear early at the final turn and shut out the late chargers - 4 straight G1 wins and the 7th fillies' Triple Crown ever.

* Equinox Retires After 6 Straight G1s
The year before, Equinox dominated the older horses in autumn at 3. This year he tried the Dubai Sheema Classic, his first race abroad. All eyes were on how he'd do against the world's best - and he broke well and, for the first time, led. He never gave up the lead, winning easily. Lemaire never even used the whip, yet he broke the record by a second. This made him world No. 1 at 129 lbs in the international ratings (World's Best Racehorse Rankings) - the world's best horse in name and fact.
Back home he ran in the Takarazuka Kinen, which his sire never won, holding off late-improving Through Seven Seas by a neck to avenge his sire. Then he went for a second Tenno Sho (Autumn). Like Panthalassa the year before, Jack d'Or set a fast pace in front. But where Equinox had closed from midfield the year before, this time he raced near the front. As Jack d'Or and others tired, he kept going and pulled away to win easily, showing his versatility and again setting a record time - the overwhelming power of the world's best horse.
He went straight to the Japan Cup, where the entry of this year's fillies' Triple Crown winner Liberty Island made it a summit clash. With Panthalassa again in a huge lead, he raced from a good spot, shook off Liberty Island 200m out to lead with ease and won by 4 lengths. Liberty Island's jockey Kawada called Equinox "the answer of modern Japanese racing, the greatest horse in Japanese racing history." The win took his earnings past 2.2 billion yen, passing Almond Eye as the all-time leader.
Afterwards his camp announced his retirement. Having moved past his classic disappointments, he left the turf with an astonishing 6 straight G1 wins.

* Big Feats on Dirt
Panthalassa, who thrilled racing with his runaway style the year before, tried a dirt G1 for the first time in the Saudi Cup. Leading at a fast pace, he couldn't pull clear as usual, but showed tremendous grit in the straight to win - the first Japanese horse to win the Saudi Cup, and, with his Dubai Turf win, the first Japan-trained horse to win G1s abroad on both turf and dirt. He was 10th in the Dubai WC, won by Japan's Ushba Tesoro, who until autumn at 5 had won just 3 races on turf, but rose to G1 level after switching to dirt and showed his power abroad.
Lemon Pop, ridden by Ryusei Sakai, won both the February S. and the Champions C. - only the 4th horse ever to do so.
With the 3yo dirt triple crown to start the next year, a star also emerged among the 3yos: Mick Fire, who won the Haneda Hai, Tokyo Derby and Japan Dirt Derby for the Southern Kanto triple crown. He was the first to win it since these three races became the triple crown in 2002, and as it was reorganized into the dirt triple crown from 2024, he was both the first and only winner.
Many dirt heroes were born this year, raising great hopes for dirt racing's future.
143:
* Do Deuce's Shock, Regaleira's Brilliant Run
In 2024, after Equinox retired, 13 straight JRA G1s had different winning jockeys - a wide-open year. But the star was still Do Deuce, Equinox's great rival and the previous Arima Kinen winner. Unlucky with pace and going in his two spring races, he won his first autumn race, the Tenno Sho (Autumn), clearly by over a length from last year's Derby winner Tastiera. In the Japan Cup he moved up wide and won a fierce battle near the line by a neck, one step from the autumn older horses' triple crown, last done by Zenno Rob Roy in 2004. With the Arima Kinen his last race, hopes were sky-high, but two days before it he was scratched with lameness in his right foreleg, sending shockwaves through racing.
The Arima Kinen was turned into a historic occasion by Regaleira, winless since the previous year's Hopeful S. Unlike before she raced from a good spot, and in the straight fought a fierce duel with Shahryar. They hit the line together, and the photo went to Regaleira - the first 3yo filly to win the Arima Kinen in 64 years, since Star Roch in 1960, and only the second ever.

* Year One of the 3yo Dirt Triple Crown: Forever Young Shines
This year the 3yo dirt triple crown began. The first leg, the Haneda Hai, went to Amante Bianco; the second, the Tokyo Derby, to Ramjet; and the third, the Japan Dirt Classic, to Forever Young - three different winners in its first year.
Forever Young was especially brilliant abroad, winning the Saudi Derby and UAE Derby and running 3rd in both the Kentucky Derby and the Breeders' Cup Classic, America's greatest races. At year's end he beat Japan's top older horses in the Tokyo Daishoten.
200: Race ability; scales with potential.\nMatters most in this game.
201: Higher: stronger when leading or up front.
202: Higher: better on heavy going and hilly tracks.\nLower: struggles on heavy going and hills.
203: Higher: lower injury risk.\nWith Spartan trainers, also builds race sense faster.
204: Higher: faster response to jockey.\nHigher: form improves faster.
205: Higher: copes better with travel.\nLower: sensitive to changes, may underperform.
207: Higher: stronger when stalking or closing.
282: Sire of Triple Crown winner Narita Brian, Mayano Top Gun, Phalaenopsis, Tanino Gimlet and more, he hugely reshaped Japanese bloodlines from the 1990s into the 2000s, one of the "big three" sires with Sunday Silence and Tony Bin. Originally an American racehorse, he had no notable record beyond winning the Florida Derby, and went to stud in Japan on the strength of his pedigree. At the time Real Shadai's offspring were thriving in Japan, and Brian's Time was chosen as being of the same line. His first crop gave Narita Brian and Chokai Carol, the next Mayano Top Gun, and two years later Sunny Brian and Silk Justice - G1 winners one after another. He quickly became a top sire, at one point rivaling Sunday Silence. But his stars didn't succeed at stud, and apart from Tanino Gimlet siring Vodka, no notable descendants have emerged. Furioso, a dirt star, carries hopes as his heir.
284: With just 4 starts and 4 wins, he swept Europe's big three: the Derby, the King George VI & Queen Elizabeth Diamond S. and the Arc. From Nijinsky's last crop, he is the only offspring to win the Arc, which Nijinsky never did. He won a listed race on debut, then after over six months off went straight into the Derby. With just one start, he was only 6th choice, but he shot from the back like an arrow to win. In the King George he was favorite and won a tight finish by a neck. He went straight to the Arc and held off Freedom Cry's charge in the straight to complete the European Triple Crown unbeaten. With a short career and unspectacular wins, he wasn't named Horse of the Year and was rated a modest 130 lbs in the International Classification, but Britain's Timeform said "it is impossible to rate this horse's greatness." He retired right after the Arc, stood one year in Europe, then was imported to Japan. But his offspring fell short of hopes, producing only the occasional graded winner.
285: Named in hope of winning the 2000 Dubai World Cup, he did just that. He won his first 3 starts with overwhelming power, but in the Derby, partly because the trip was too long, he suffered the only defeat of his career. Then, focused on the mile to middle distances, he romped in European mile G1s like the Prix Jacques le Marois and the Queen Elizabeth II S. At 4 he had a dirt prep before the Dubai World Cup. Overwhelming favorite, he led all the way and kept pulling away - living up to expectations and prompting Dettori to call him "the best horse I've ever ridden." Back on turf, he romped in the Prince of Wales's S., then retired through injury. He died of illness after just one crop, but it included Dubawi, winner of the Prix Jacques le Marois and a hugely successful sire.
280: He won the Asahi Hai Sansai S., then the Arlington C. and the NZT Yonsai S. in spring at 3. Hailed as the best miler, he missed the NHK Mile C. through injury. After his break he ran poorly and was written off, but at 4 he won the Yonago S., his first win in a long time, winning the Kitakyushu Kinen and the Mainichi Okan. At year's end he went to Hong Kong and won the Hong Kong Mile, then returned the next April to win the QE2 Cup - and won it again the following year, G1 wins abroad 3 years running. Oddly, he lost all 8 of his older-horse G1s in Japan. At stud, no standout offspring yet.
283: A leading light of Sunday Silence's first crop, the force that swept Japanese racing. Fickle ("won't run if it's windy"), he was loved as a charming character. Early on, his moods cost him races. In the Wakaba S. he crossed the line 2nd, 5 lengths back, winning only after first-past-the-post Louisiana Boy was demoted, so he was only 3rd choice for the Satsuki Sho - but he held off the charging Tayasu Tsuyoshi, another Sunday Silence son, to win clearly. His explosive power at middle distances and shorter was real: besides the Satsuki Sho, he won the Mile Championship as an older horse. He stood at stud in Japan and Oceania, siring graded winners in the JRA and G1 winners in Oceania.
286: So strong some complained "Taiki Shuttle's races are boring." He debuted late, in spring at 3, then won 3 straight. He was beaten a neck into 2nd in the Bodaiju S., but won the Unicorn S. for his first graded title. His run continued, winning the Mile Championship and the Sprinters S. at 3. Named champion sprinter, he made it clear no one in Japan could match him at short distances. As an older horse he kept rolling, winning the Yasuda Kinen for 3 straight sprint-mile G1s. Then he set off for Europe. With Seeking the Pearl having already won a G1 abroad that year, he was a confident favorite for the Prix Jacques le Marois, and beat the world's fast horses clearly to become the world's mile king in name and fact. Back home he won the Mile Championship again. His farewell, the Sprinters S., ended in a shock 3rd, but he was the undisputed Horse of the Year. At stud he sired G1 winners like Meisho Bowler, Summer Wind and Win Kluger. He retired from stud in 2017 and died of heart failure due to old age in 2022. His stall showed no sign of struggle; a peaceful end.
281: The horse who rewrote Japanese thoroughbred bloodlines from the ground up. He produced many heirs such as Special Week and Deep Impact, nearly turning Japan's bloodlines all Sunday Silence. He was also a superb racehorse, winning the Kentucky Derby and Preakness S. He lost the Belmont S. to rival Easy Goer, but won the Breeders' Cup Classic in autumn and was Eclipse Horse of the Year. After retiring at 4 he was little valued for his pedigree in America, so he was exported to Japan for stud. His first crop gave Fuji Kiseki and Genuine, the next Bubble Gum Fellow and Dance in the Dark - a flood of G1 winners. He kept siring G1 winners every year until his last, sparking a "Sunday Silence storm" that swept the JRA's G1s. His sire sons - Fuji Kiseki, Dance in the Dark, Stay Gold, Special Week, Agnes Tachyon, Heart's Cry, Deep Impact and more - are an elite group, and successful descendants are countless. His descendants have also spread abroad, and his influence is now worldwide.
