287: Bought in America and raced by Mr. Sekiguchi, owner of the "Fusaichi" horses. His price, $4 million, the highest of his crop, made headlines. He was 2nd on debut in December at 2, then won 5 straight at 3, taking the Kentucky Derby to top his generation. He was 2nd to Red Bullet in the Preakness S. and missed the Belmont S. after hurting a leg just before, but he gave an Asian owner a first Kentucky Derby win. He later won a G2 and retired after a 6th in the Breeders' Cup Classic. Sold to Coolmore for $70 million, he went to stud in America. His best offspring include Haskell Invitational H. winner Roman Ruler and Queen Anne S. winner Haradasun, but few others did much - not results worth $70 million. Still, Roman Ruler sired a G1 winner, so his blood lives on.
288: An American idol who thrilled fans by leading and pulling away in the straight. He won 6 G1s, including the Florida Derby and Metropolitan H., in dominant style. At 2 he won his first 4, including the Futurity S. (G1). At 3 he showed some immaturity, losing when pressed early and finishing 12th after a slow start in the Kentucky Derby, but after romping in the Metropolitan H. he was unstoppable. From summer he won 3 straight G1s - the Haskell Invitational H., the Travers S. and the Woodward S. - and was named Eclipse Horse of the Year ahead of Breeders' Cup Classic winner Concern. At 4 he won a listed race easily, but was pulled up injured in the Donn H. and retired. The Donn H. winner, Cigar, went on to win a record-equaling 16 straight. At stud he sired Kentucky Derby winner Giacomo and Breeders' Cup Juvenile winner Macho Uno, carrying on the rare Himyar line. He retired from stud in 2012 and died of old age in 2017.
289: Won 10 G1s in America from 1996 to 1998, including the Breeders' Cup Classic, earning $9.61 million, then second only to Cigar. At 3 in 1996 he won no classic, but then won 3 straight G1s against older horses, outdueling the veteran Cigar in the Jockey Club Gold C., and was named Eclipse champion 3yo colt over the classic winners. At 4 he won the Jockey Club Gold C. and Breeders' Cup Classic to be champion older male. At 5 he won 5 straight G1s, including the Hollywood Gold C., and was finally named Eclipse Horse of the Year. He then tried the Jockey Club Gold C. and Breeders' Cup Classic again but lost both, retiring just short of Cigar's $9.99 million earnings record. At stud he sired graded winners like Skipshot and Skipaslew, and from horses brought to Japan came Sonoda Kinpai winner Meiner Exon.
290: Dominant from his debut, he won the NHK Mile C. unbeaten in 5. He was beaten by Silence Suzuka in the Mainichi Okan, but then crushed Air Groove, Special Week and the foreign raiders in the Japan Cup. Reigning over Japanese racing after Silence Suzuka's death, he went to France the next year. Narrowly 2nd in the Prix d'Ispahan, he then won the Grand Prix de Saint-Cloud, his long-sought G1 abroad. In the Arc, the world's summit, he lost narrowly to Montjeu after a brave run, showing the world Japan's quality. Back home, fans begged for an Arima Kinen run, but he retired, leaving the "Big Three" battle with Special Week and Grass Wonder unsettled. He died young of colic in 2002, leaving just 2 crops, which still produced dirt champion Vermilion, Kikuka Sho winner Song of Wind and Japan Cup Dirt winner Alondite.
291: A speedster who raced around the world. At 2 he won graded races like the Hakodate Sansai S. and the Zen-Nihon Sansai Yushun, but proved his huge speed in his 11th start, the Kitakyushu Tankyori S.: through the first 600m in 32.3, he never slowed, closing in 34.2 for a Japanese record of 1:06.5. Perhaps that made him, as he won the Kokura Nikkei Open next and went to France for the Prix de l'Abbaye de Longchamp. Unfazed on his first trip abroad, he held off Imperial Beauty to win his first G1 overseas. At 5 he went to Britain, was 2nd in the G2 King's Stand S., then won the G1 July C. for a second G1 abroad. That year he also tried the BC Sprint in America; whatever the result (8th), his endless challenger's spirit deserves praise. At stud he sired dirt sprinter Agnes Jedi (6 JRA-local graded wins, including the Tokyo Hai) and Falcon S. winner Kazusa Line.
292: US double classic winner of 1997. Agonizingly 2nd in the Belmont S., he won fans with his fierce will to win close duels. Never out of the top two from his debut, he held off favorite Captain Bodgit by a head in the Kentucky Derby for his first G1, then won a three-way duel with Free House by a head in the Preakness S. But in the Belmont, as he dueled with Free House, Touch Gold passed them both and he was 2nd - no first Triple Crown in 19 years since Affirmed. At 4 he won a duel with Swain in the Dubai World Cup for his third G1. In autumn he met Swain again in the Breeders' Cup Classic and beat him, but Awesome Again won and he was 2nd. At 5 he lost 4 straight and retired. After 4 crops in America he was imported to Japan, but sired no notable runners.
293: By the speedy Sakura Yutaka O out of a full sister to Tenno Sho winner Amber Shadai, this blueblood was seen as a classic contender before his debut. He won his debut by 5 lengths, then after a 2nd in the Kurotake Sho, blasted 4 lengths clear in the Sakurasou Tokubetsu. But with 2 wins from 3, he was a shock 12th in the Spring S. His camp gave up on the classics and switched him to sprints. It was a perfect fit: he won the Crystal C. next, and running mostly at 1200-1600m, won 11 of 21, including two Sprinters S. At 1400m or less he won 11 of 12, losing only his 3yo Sprinters S. His blazing speed, treating even top miler North Flight and Tenno Sho winner Yamanin Zephyr like children, truly made him "the charging king" - rarely has a name fit so well. At stud, Shonan Kampf won the Takamatsunomiya Kinen for three straight generations of Japanese-bred G1 winners. He also sired sprint stars like 2-time G1 winner Grand Prix Boss, Takamatsunomiya Kinen winner Big Arthur, She Is Tosho and Dasher Go Go. Hopes rest on sires Big Arthur and Grand Prix Boss to carry on great sire Tesco Boy's now rare Princely Gift line. Fans also noted that Kitasan Black, despite a sprinter damsire, won middle-to-long G1s like the Kikuka Sho, Tenno Sho (Spring) and Arima Kinen.
296: An heir of Mr. Prospector and sire of Dubai Millennium. In Japan his offspring Seeking the Pearl and Meiner Love won G1s, proving his suitability to Japanese tracks. He raced well from a mile to middle distances, winning two G1s, the Dwyer S. and the Super Derby. But he often fell short on the big stage, narrowly 2nd in the Breeders' Cup Classic, Haskell Invitational H. and Travers S. After a 7th in the Kentucky Derby, he took the back roads. At stud, his first crop gave 8-time G1 winner Heavenly Prize and his next champion 2yo filly Flanders, making him a hot sire. He went on to produce stars worldwide, like 2000 Dubai World Cup winner Dubai Millennium and Japanese G1 winner Seeking the Pearl, and his fee peaked at $250,000. Dubai Millennium's son Dubawi then firmly established the sire line.
297: A sire who took America by storm from the late 1990s into the 2000s. Leading sire in North America in 1999 and 2000, he was leading 2yo sire a record 7 times, and his fee peaked at $500,000 (about 60 million yen). As a racehorse he showed promise at 2, winning the Young America S. and finishing 2nd in the Breeders' Cup Juvenile, but fractures kept him from racing much and he retired. At stud he showed his true worth: his first crop's November Snow won 2 G1s, and he produced G1 winners almost every year. He sired Tabasco Cat and Hennessy, later imported to Japan as sires, and Giant's Causeway, a hugely successful heir, and his reputation soared. He had no stars in Japan, but as a broodmare sire produced many G1 winners there, including Phalaenopsis, Lord Kanaloa, Kizuna, Loves Only You and Danon Kingly.
298: Won the 1991 Derby, Irish Derby and King George VI & Queen Elizabeth Diamond S. by wide margins and was rated 139 lbs in the International Classification, the 1990s' highest. Little noticed early at 3, he was a plain 4th as 4th choice in the 2000 Guineas. But in the Derby he suddenly awoke, winning by 5 lengths from Marju, then outdueled Suave Dancer to win the Irish Derby by 3. Facing older horses for the first time in the King George as 1.7 favorite, he won by a race-record 7 lengths. He was a poor 8th in the Arc and retired, but his crushing power earned the 1990s' top rating in both the International Classification and Timeform. At stud he stood 4 years in Britain, then moved to Japan as Caerleon's heir. He sired horses like Erimo Harrier, 3-time Hakodate Kinen winner, but no G1 stars.
294: Son of "Emperor" Symboli Rudolf and winner of the 1991 Satsuki Sho and Japanese Derby. Like his sire he entered the classics unbeaten and won both as favorite, seeming the Emperor reborn. But a fracture ended his Triple Crown dream. On his return, his Tenno Sho (Spring) clash with Mejiro McQueen, then the best horse, drew huge attention: Tokai Teio, back in style after winning the Sankei Osaka Hai, against McQueen, flawless after romping in the Hanshin Daishoten. Teio was favorite, but McQueen won easily. Yet that wasn't the end: in autumn he won the Japan Cup, the first Japanese winner in 7 years. Drained by the effort, he was 11th in the Arima Kinen, but after a year off he won the next year's Arima Kinen in a miracle comeback. At stud he sired G1 winners Tokai Point (Mile CS) and Yamanin Shukuru (Hanshin JF). Lacking a sire heir, his line seemed in danger, but Leben Steel, out of a Tokai Teio mare, won 3 graded races including the 2023 St. Lite Kinen - hopes rise for the "King's" blood.
295: Until summer at 3 he was winning and losing in low classes, but as he matured in autumn he won the Kikuka Sho, then won the year-end Arima Kinen with surprise front-running. His first race as an older horse, the Hanshin Daishoten, is still legendary: he fought a fierce duel with year-older Triple Crown winner Narita Brian from the third turn to the line, losing by a head. After a 5th in the Tenno Sho (Spring) he won the Takarazuka Kinen, but in autumn ran poorly - 4th in the All Comers, 7th in the Arima Kinen - and some said he was finished. But he won the next Hanshin Daishoten easily, and in the Tenno Sho (Spring) "Big Three" clash with Sakura Laurel and Marvelous Sunday, unlike his usual forward style, he came with a miraculous late charge to win in world-record time for 3200m. Versatile, fast and tough - a great horse. At stud he sired colorful runners like turf-and-dirt Precise Machine, dirt closer Meisho Tokon and tireless stayer Chakra.
299: Won his first graded race, the Fuji S., at 3. As an older horse his speed sharpened: after a 2nd in the Keio Hai Spring C., he beat the monster Grass Wonder in the Yasuda Kinen for a G1. In autumn he boldly tried the Tenno Sho (Autumn), a fine 3rd behind Special Week and Stay Gold, then won the Mile Championship for spring and autumn mile G1s. He headed for the Hong Kong C. but developed a tendon injury there - a sad retirement just as he hit his prime. At stud he sired Yasuda Kinen winner Showa Modern, Agnes Raspberry and Nanayo Himawari, keeping the rare Princely Gift line alive.
302: A miler like his speedy sire Nihon Pillow Winner. Debuting late, in March at 3, he steadily won races and at 4 tried the Yasuda Kinen. With all 4 wins at 1200m on dirt, 11th choice was fair, but he beat Daitaku Helios and Dynamite Daddy - his first graded win was a G1. That year he was 2nd in both the Centaur S. and Sprinters S. The next year he won the Keio Hai Spring C., then the Yasuda Kinen again, cementing himself as champion miler, and in autumn tried the Tenno Sho (Autumn). The field lacked a star, but his pedigree and record raised doubts about the distance. He broke clear early in the straight, and Sekitei Ryu O charged wide; after a fierce dead heat, Yamanin Zephyr won by just a nose. Where his sire tried and failed, the son took the crown. The feat earned him three JRA Awards: champion older male, champion sire-bred-in-Japan horse and champion sprinter.
305: This crop of colts, with stars like El Condor Pasa, Special Week and Grass Wonder, was called "the greatest generation ever." Amid them, Seiun Sky, by the obscure sire Sheriff's Star, won both the Satsuki Sho and the Kikuka Sho. His power shone brightest in the Kikuka Sho: 2nd choice behind Special Week, he went off alone over 3000m and was never challenged, leading all the way in world-record time, 3.5 lengths ahead of Special Week. At that point, before the Japan Cup, he was clearly the best of his crop. But after losing the Arima Kinen to Grass Wonder and both Tenno Sho races the next year to Special Week, opinion turned. Injury then forced a long break and retirement. Somehow his name wasn't among the "Big Three." A double classic winner of the greatest crop, overlooked - his rivals were simply too strong.
308: In 1997 he won his first 8 starts, including 2 G1s, and was named Eclipse Horse of the Year at 2. Most of his wins were routs, and he won the big one, the Breeders' Cup Juvenile, by a record five and a half lengths. That stunning run earned him Horse of the Year over older stars like Breeders' Cup Classic winner Skip Away and double classic winner Silver Charm - the first 2yo Horse of the Year in 25 years, since Secretariat, rated 128 lbs on the US Free Handicap, close to the all-time best. But at 3 he lost momentum: he won a G3 first time out but was a dismal 8th in the Kentucky Derby. Turning to turf, he won a G2 mile easily, but was 8th in his main goal, the Breeders' Cup Mile, and retired. His stud record was poor, with just two G3 winners. In 2006, at 11, he died tragically in a barn fire.
310: The 1989 2000 Guineas and Derby winner, and a successful sire of horses like Swain and Bago. Watched from his debut, he won both starts at 2, then went straight to the 2000 Guineas at 3. Shrugging off the layoff, he won clearly, then romped in the Derby by 5 lengths - the first British double in 19 years since Nijinsky. He then took on older horses, winning the Eclipse S. and the King George VI & Queen Elizabeth Diamond S. back to back. In autumn he aimed for the Arc and the first European Triple Crown since Mill Reef, but lacked his usual kick in the Prix Niel prep, stumbling to 3rd, and retired. He sired many G1 winners, notably Swain, from his second crop, who won the King George twice, and late-crop Arc winner Bago.
312: A European mile star who won a then-world-record 7 straight G1s in 2001-02. He won his first G1, the Grand Criterium, in autumn at 2, then the Dewhurst S. At 3 he became only the 4th horse to win both the 2000 Guineas and Irish 2000 Guineas, added the St. James's Palace S., and beat older horses easily in the Sussex S. In autumn he beat rivals like Banks Hill in the Prix du Moulin de Longchamp for his 7th straight G1, Europe's best miler. He then went to America for the Breeders' Cup Mile as favorite, but missed the break and was hampered, closing well but only 2nd to Domedriver. He retired after this race and went to stud, siring Hong Kong C. winner Eagle Mountain, Eclipse S. winner Mount Nelson and, standing in Japan too, NZ Trophy winner A Shin Osman. He is also damsire of 2-time mile G1 winner Mikki Isle.
300: By Tolomeo out of a No Attention mare - an obscure pedigree - yet he won 11 races (nine 2nds) before retiring at 8, a great supporting actor at middle distances. A late bloomer needing 6 starts to win, he missed the classics. During a long break from autumn at 4 he grew a lot; back at 5 he was 2nd, then won 5 straight, including the Sekiya Kinen and All Comers. Leg trouble kept him winless at 6, but at 7 he won 3 graded races including the Nakayama Kinen. 3 of his 5 graded wins came at Nakayama, and he was 3rd in the Arima Kinen - a Nakayama specialist.
301: His stayer's blood bloomed in the Kikuka Sho, which he barely got into. The next year, ridden by Yutaka Take, he won the Hanshin Daishoten and the Tenno Sho (Spring) - three generations of Tenno Sho winners after Mejiro Asama and Mejiro Titan. But he was 2nd in the Takarazuka Kinen; won the Tenno Sho (Autumn) by 6 lengths but was demoted to 18th for veering; was 4th in the Japan Cup; and a shock 2nd to Daiyu Saku in the Arima Kinen. He won the Hanshin Daishoten again, then met double classic winner Tokai Teio in the Tenno Sho (Spring), "the showdown of the century" with a 150-yen quinella. Not favorite, he won clearly. So consistent was he that some joked "he always wins, so races are boring." After a year out injured he won the Osaka Hai in record time. Going for a third Tenno Sho (Spring) he lost to Rice Shower, but then won the Takarazuka Kinen. In the Kyoto Daishoten that autumn he set a stunning course record of 2:22.7, but was injured after the race and retired. At stud he sired Meguro Kinen winner Hokuto Sultan, but died in 2006. As a broodmare sire, though, his "golden cross" with Stay Gold produced Triple Crown winner Orfevre, Gold Ship and more - the champion's blood lives on.
303: It's no exaggeration to say he created the early image of Sunday Silence's runners: "fiery-tempered but fearsomely strong." From the first crop, he was called the best, even "the phantom Triple Crown winner." He won his debut by 8 lengths, beat future Derby winner Tayasu Tsuyoshi in the Momiji S., and won the Asahi Hai Sansai S. unbeaten - easy wins despite immaturely charging at rivals. He won the Yayoi Sho clearly at 3, and people debated "how many crowns," but a tendon injury forced sudden retirement. He left the turf with a sense of the miracle that might have been. At stud he thrived, siring dirt king Kane Hekili (7 dirt G1s), Dream Passport, Victoria Mile winner Koiuta, 2-time Takamatsunomiya Kinen winner Kinshasa no Kiseki, Daitaku Riva, Mile CS winner Sadamu Patek and Satsuki Sho winner Isla Bonita. He once led all Japanese-bred sires in career wins - a true great sire.
304: A big-name mochikomi with high hopes, but frail from birth and with sore shins early on, he couldn't be fully prepared or show his ability. He missed the classics, reaching open class at the end of his 3yo year. Early at 4 he won the Kimpai (East), his first graded win, then was 2nd in the Meguro Kinen but fractured a leg. At 5, back after 13 months, he crushed Satsuki Sho winner Genuine in the Nakayama Kinen. In the Tenno Sho (Spring) he brushed aside crop-mate Triple Crown winner Narita Brian and Horse of the Year Mayano Top Gun, winning his long-sought G1 and the title of best horse at once. He added the Arima Kinen and was '96 Horse of the Year and champion older male. He announced an Arc challenge, but was injured in the Prix Foy prep and came home. At stud he sired 3-time graded winner Sakura Century and Roman Empire, known for a Keisei Hai dead heat.
306: With a white blaze and smart looks, he was a "good-looking horse" watched before his debut. Needing 4 starts to win, he was called "more hype than horse," but after winning the Hiiragi Sho and Junior C. he crushed 2yo champion Ines Fujin in the Yayoi Sho. In the Satsuki Sho he was 3rd to Hakutaisei, and as Derby favorite he couldn't catch Ines Fujin, finishing 2nd. In autumn he won the Kyoto Shimbun Hai in record time and was Kikuka Sho favorite, but fellow Mejiro late bloomer McQueen beat him, and he ended the classics uncrowned. 2nd in the Arima Kinen and Nakayama Kinen, 4th behind McQueen in the Tenno Sho (Spring) - always just short. Then in the Takarazuka Kinen jockey Norihiro Yokoyama stayed ahead of McQueen and kicked early, and at last he won a G1. At stud his first crop gave 5-time G1 winner Mejiro Dober (94: Mejiro Beauty) and Tenno Sho winner Mejiro Bright (94: Reine du Temps), and he kept siring graded winners as an ace among Japanese-bred sires.
307: By Sunday Silence out of double classic winner Vega - a blueblood impossible not to get excited about. On his debut he was demoted to 4th for interference - a flashy start, in a way. He then won the Erica Sho and soon the Radio Tampa Hai Sansai S. But at 3 he was 2nd to Narita Top Road in the Yayoi Sho, then 6th in the Satsuki Sho - due to rain, or a preparation slip shown by a 10 kg weight loss. Then the Derby, a must-win. From 14th at the final turn he unleashed a powerful kick up Tokyo's long straight and caught Narita Top Road by a neck right at the line. He was 6th in the Kikuka Sho, then retired with leg trouble. He died suddenly in '04 after just 4 crops - a great loss, as he sired G1 winners like Mile CS winner Blumenblatt and Oka Sho winner Kiss to Heaven.
309: He debuted fairly late, in January at 3, but ran tough until 8, winning 12 of 38. Most remarkable was his seemingly endless capacity to improve. He won his second graded race, the Nakayama Kinen, at 7, then kept winning, finally taking the international Hong Kong International C. - a first for a Japan-bred, Japan-trained horse - and was that year's champion Japanese-sired horse.
311: He won the Asahi Hai Sansai S. but fractured a leg in training; surgery to insert bolts was so major some said he'd never return. He came back at Hakodate 82 weeks later but kept losing, and leg trouble sent him on another long break. He seemed finished, but at 6, as 10th choice in the Tokyo Shimbun Hai, he raced forward and held on - a shock first win in about 3 years. He then won the Hankyu Hai, ran 2nd in the Takamatsunomiya Kinen, and won the Yasuda Kinen, his first G1 in 3.5 years - a miracle comeback. He was also 2nd to Believe in the Sprinters S. At stud he sired Sprinters S. winner Aston Machan (04: Wrestling Cups) and sprint graded winner Majin Prosper (07: Hollywood Dream). He retired from stud in 2015 and died at 21 in 2017.
313: Seen as Storm Cat's leading heir, he sired many G1 winners like Shamardal and Aragorn and greatly boosted the Storm Cat line. Based in Ireland, he won 6 G1s. At 2 he won the Prix de la Salamandre (G1) unbeaten. At 3 he was 2nd in both the 2000 Guineas and Irish 2000 Guineas, then reeled off 5 G1s: the St. James's Palace S., Eclipse S., Sussex S., International S. and Irish Champion S. In autumn he was 2nd in the Breeders' Cup Classic, showing he could handle dirt. That year he lost Cartier champion 3yo colt to Sinndar but was Cartier Horse of the Year - a split decision. At stud his first crop included French Derby winner Shamardal, and he sired G1 winners every year; in Japan, A Shin Apollon won the Mile CS. He is damsire of Lemon Pop, 6-time G1 winner and champion dirt horse of 2023 and 2024.
314: He debuted late, in July at 3 at local Urawa, and won 5 straight with overwhelming power. 2nd in his 6th start, he won twice more, but then suffered a fracture that nearly ended his career. Back after 15 months, in May at 5, he won, and with 8 wins and a 2nd from 9 he moved to the JRA. Puzzled by turf at first, he was 2nd, then won in the 9-million class and in semi-open class, proving his Urawa record was real. In open class he lost 3 graded races, but romped in the Ireland T. over a mile, then won the Mile Championship with a late charge - his first graded win, a G1. At 7 he won the Tokyo Shimbun Hai and, after the Keio Hai Spring C., the Yasuda Kinen - autumn and spring mile G1s in a row, making him 8 for 8 at a mile including Urawa. But after the Yasuda Kinen, a dispute over the ownership name forced his retirement while still at his best - an ill-fated star whose fate was decided by people's affairs.
315: Switched to jockey Mirco Demuro, he won the Spring S., a Satsuki Sho trial, clearly. With Demuro again he ran down Sakura President to win the Satsuki Sho, then in the Derby caught front-running Zenno Rob Roy by half a length, horse and rider as one - the first Japanese Derby won by a foreign jockey. He then ran 4th in the Takarazuka Kinen, unusual for a Derby winner. Triple Crown hopes rested on the Kikuka Sho, but Demuro had used up his short-term license days. The JRA, however, made a special rule allowing a foreign jockey who had won 2 G1s on the same horse that year to ride it. Even so, he was only 3rd. The next spring he was a dismal 10th in the Tenno Sho (Spring), then developed a tendon injury and retired before settling scores with older horses. At stud his first crop gave Derby winner Logi Universe and Satsuki Sho winner Unrivaled, and his second Dubai World Cup winner Victoire Pisa - many big-name offspring.
316: At about 430 kg, slim and small like a filly, he formed a Big Three with Winning Ticket and Biwa Hayahide to light up the classics. His razor-sharp late charge from that small frame overpowered both rivals in an instant to win the Satsuki Sho. After a 3rd in the Derby he took on older horses in the Takamatsunomiya Hai (G2, 2000m), finishing 2nd. Then illness hit and he went straight to the Kikuka Sho; 3rd choice on his record, he was a dismal 17th. In his first race at 4 he regained his old finish to win the Meguro Kinen, and was 2nd to Biwa Hayahide's flawless run in the Tenno Sho (Spring). But injury forced a long break, and back after a year he was 16th in the Takarazuka Kinen, his last race. At stud he left no notable offspring.
318: He won the Asahi Hai Sansai S. easily to top his generation, then the Spring S. at 3. Just as he set off on the royal road, a fracture wiped out his spring. Back in autumn, he ignored the Kikuka Sho and stunned everyone by aiming for the Tenno Sho (Autumn). After a 3rd in the Mainichi Okan on his return, he won the big one against stars like Mayano Top Gun and Sakura Laurel - the first 3yo ever to win the Tenno Sho. He sank to 13th in the Japan Cup, but that was his only finish worse than 3rd in his career. At 4 he kept finishing a narrow 2nd and won no G1, but all agreed he was the best of his crop. At stud he sired many dirt runners, like Appare Appare, Meiner Bownot and Ono Yu. He died of pneumonia in April 2010.
319: Danzig's most successful heir. As a racehorse he did little beyond winning Britain's Sprint C., but at stud he blossomed into one of the top sires. A rare "shuttle sire" then, he covered mares in Ireland in the northern spring and Australia in the southern spring, siring Irish Derby winner Desert King and Australian champion 2yo Flying Spur and spreading his blood worldwide. Heirs like Danehill Dancer and Dansili also succeeded, forming the mighty Danehill line. From 2005 he broke Sadler's Wells's grip to be champion sire in Britain and Ireland 3 years running, and was champion sire 9 times in Australia. He stood in Japan for just one year, 1996, siring graded winners like Fusaichi Sonic and Break Time.
320: Won 4 G1s in America, including the Haskell Invitational H. and Travers S., and as a sire produced many G1 winners in America and Japan - a notable heir of Mr. Prospector. At 2 he won two G1s, the Futurity S. and Champagne S., and was Eclipse champion 2yo colt. At 3 he was narrowly 2nd to the filly Winning Colors in the Kentucky Derby and 7th in the Preakness S., but won the Haskell and Travers in summer for 4 G1s. In autumn he took on older star Alysheba but fell short, 2nd in the Woodward S. and 4th in the Breeders' Cup Classic, and retired at the end of his 3yo year. At stud he sired G1 winners from his first crop and was North America's leading sire in 1996. He was sold to Japan before that, where he sired many local stars like Meiner Select and Utopia. His American sons End Sweep and Coronado's Quest were also imported to Japan as sires, spreading his line there.
321: By great sire Mr. Prospector out of 10-time G1 winner Miesque, a blueblood and hugely successful heir to Mr. Prospector. He won the Poule d'Essai des Poulains, the St. James's Palace S. and the Prix du Moulin de Longchamp, a speedster typical of his sire. At stud his first crop included El Condor Pasa, and he sired many stars like Belmont S. winner Lemon Drop Kid, future top sire King's Best and Alkaased, who won the Japan Cup in 2005. His 2001 son King Kamehameha succeeded hugely as both racehorse and sire, and his descendants flourish in Japan, where his line is sometimes treated as a separate "Kingmambo line." Due to a chronic illness he retired from stud in 2010 and died at 26 in 2016.
323: Winner of the 1997 Arc, called one of Europe's best of the 1990s. He was 3rd in his first graded race, the Prix des Chenes at 2, but at 3 won the Prix Greffulhe, the French Derby and the Grand Prix de Paris, then after a 2nd in the Prix Niel went to the Arc. Against stars like last year's winner Helissio, Pilsudski, Swain and Oscar Schindler, he was a clear favorite. He burst clear powerfully in the straight and won by 5 lengths from Pilsudski, in a stunning record 1.7 seconds faster than before. He was named Cartier Horse of the Year and rated 137 lbs in the International Classification, second only to Dancing Brave. A tendon injury then ended his career, but at stud he had some success, siring 2004 Santa Anita Derby winner Castledale, 2006 Arc runner-up Pride and German Derby winner Dai Jin.
317: He won his debut and the Sumire S., then made the Derby his third start, chosen because he was frail and needed the shortest route. In the Derby straight, favorite Dance in the Dark surged from a good spot; just as everyone was sure he'd win, Fusaichi Concorde unleashed a "supersonic" kick and ran him down wide. Fans called the 3-for-3 Derby winner "Japan's Lammtarra." In autumn he took another odd route, the Cassiopeia S. then the Kikuka Sho, running well but losing both. He then developed periostitis and retired after just 5 races. At stud he sired stars like Blue Concorde, Balance of Game and Osumi Haruka.
325: The late trainer Tameo Toyama trained his horses with Spartan rigor, believing "you build the best horse through training." Mihono Bourbon was the ultimate masterpiece of that belief. With speed honed on the hill course, he won his debut, his powerful late burst making light of a slow start. He then led all the way in a 5-million race, and held off Yamanin Miracle by a nose in the Asahi Hai Sansai S., unbeaten 2yo champion. From 3, doubts about distance, jockey and more swirled before every race, but his power never wavered: never letting rivals near, he won the Satsuki Sho and the Derby, an unbeaten double. Triple Crown hopes rested on the Kikuka Sho, but he was 2nd to Rice Shower, who emerged as a stayer. Leg trouble then forced a break, and he never returned to the turf.
322: From Sunday Silence's first crop, he missed the classics through injury. Back in spring at 4, he won 6 straight, including 4 graded races - the Epsom C., Sapporo Kinen, Asahi Challenge C. and Kyoto Daishoten - a "late-arriving star." 4th in the Tenno Sho (Autumn) and 2nd in the Arima Kinen, he was rated in a Big Three with Sakura Laurel and Mayano Top Gun the next spring, and won the Takarazuka Kinen, shutting out Bubble Gum Fellow, Dance Partner and Taiki Blizzard. At stud he sired Silk Famous, a late bloomer just like him who won 5 straight at 4 and was 2nd in the Takarazuka Kinen, and Nikkei Sho winner Never Bouchon.
324: He won his first graded race, the Arlington C., then was 8th in the Mainichi Hai, partly due to the distance. Skipping the classics, he went to the NHK Mile C. and, as 9th choice, raced boldly forward to win. He then slumped badly and never won again on the flat. In '06 he had colic surgery and a long recovery; back in '07 he lacked sparkle, finishing in double figures. In July he switched to jumping and won a maiden hurdle, his first win in 4 years, and was 4th in the Hanshin Jump S., but retired in November. At stud he sired Ever Rose, winner of 3 straight 1000m straight-course races in lower classes.
326: On debut at Hakodate (1800m, good turf), 6th choice of 6, he came from last to win in a remarkable 2:01.6. He won the Radio Tampa Hai Sansai S., but in the classics he stuck to late charges and kept losing narrowly. At year's end, with Hiroshi Kawachi aboard for the Stayers S., he raced from a good spot and won by a distance. Now he knew how to win: the next year he took the American JCC, the Hanshin Daishoten and the Tenno Sho (Spring), beating favorite Silk Justice, last year's Arima Kinen winner - 4 straight graded wins and three generations of G1 winners after Amber Shadai and Mejiro Ryan. With the "greatest generation" a year younger starring, he won only one more G2. He went to stud but died of a heart attack in spring '04.
327: 3rd in the Satsuki Sho behind Seiun Sky and King Halo, he was still Derby favorite and won by 5 lengths. Normally that makes a horse king of his crop, but not this year: there was injured 2yo champion Grass Wonder and unbeaten NHK Mile C. winner El Condor Pasa. Then he lost the Kikuka Sho to Seiun Sky, far from the best of his crop, and was 3rd in the Japan Cup behind El Condor Pasa and Air Groove. But as an older horse he grew stronger. He won the American JCC, outdueled Mejiro Bright in the Hanshin Daishoten and won the Tenno Sho (Spring). Crushed by Grass Wonder in the Takarazuka Kinen, he won the Tenno Sho (Autumn) and the Japan Cup, then lost to Grass Wonder again after an epic duel in the Arima Kinen. Few horses have won the Derby, both Tenno Sho races and the Japan Cup; earning such honors against the greatest generation's rivals proves him a great horse. At stud he sired two queens, Cesario and Buena Vista, as a pillar of the Sunday Silence line, plus dirt stars Roman Legend and Gold Blitz and record-time Kikuka Sho winner Toho Jackal. Cesario produced three G1 winners - Epiphaneia, Leontes and Saturnalia - all fine sires too, so his excellent blood carries on.
328: The first "monster" since Maruzensky. Winning by wide margins, he took the Asahi Hai Sansai S. unbeaten in a stunning record 1:33.6. But a fracture cost him his 3yo spring. Back after a long break, he was 5th in the Mainichi Okan behind Silence Suzuka and fellow foreign-bred rival El Condor Pasa. After another poor run in the Argentina Kyowakoku Hai he was called finished, but in the Arima Kinen he beat Tenno Sho winner Mejiro Bright and Kikuka Sho winner Seiun Sky to make a comeback. The next year he lost the Yasuda Kinen by a nose to Air Jihad, then won the Takarazuka Kinen for two straight Grand Prix wins, and won the Arima Kinen again after a historic photo with Special Week. He raced on after his rivals retired but lacked sparkle and retired. At stud he sired graded stars from his first crop, and in winter 2008 Japan Cup winner Screen Hero and Asahi Hai FS winner Seiun Wonder emerged. In 2011 Earnestly won the Takarazuka Kinen, a father-son Grand Prix double. Screen Hero sired mile king Maurice, so the monster's sire line looks set to continue.
329: An Irish horse who won 6 G1s, including the Breeders' Cup Turf and Eclipse S., well known in Japan for beating Air Groove and others in the 1997 Japan Cup. He was winless at 2 and broke his maiden in summer at 3 - a slow start. At 4 he won 2 graded races, then his first G1, the Grosser Preis von Baden. He was 2nd to Helissio in the Arc and beat Singspiel and others in the Breeders' Cup Turf, joining the elite. At 5 he won 3 G1s including the Eclipse S., then came the Japan Cup. He startled Japanese fans by getting aroused in the paddock, yet still beat Air Groove, whose jockey Yutaka Take said "I rode a perfect race and still got caught." He was named Cartier champion older horse and retired to stud in Japan, but sadly sired only a few local graded winners.
330: He won his first 3 starts, including the Daily Hai Sansai S., but was 2nd by a nose in both the Asahi Hai Sansai S. and Kyodo News Hai. With master Yukio Okabe aboard he won the Wakaba S. easily, but in the classics he lost the Satsuki Sho to Narita Taishin and the Derby to Winning Ticket - 2nd both times. In autumn he won the Kobe Shimbun Hai, then in the Kikuka Sho left both rivals behind, winning by 5 lengths in record time for his long-sought classic. In the Arima Kinen he was 2nd again, to Tokai Teio's miracle comeback, but at 4 he grew to win 4 straight graded races, including the Tenno Sho (Spring) and Takarazuka Kinen. Aiming for both Tenno Sho races, he developed a tendon injury during the autumn race, finishing 5th, and it ended his career.
331: In 1991 he won 4 French and American 2yo G1s and became Horse of the Year at 2 in the first Cartier Awards. He won in his second start, then 2 graded races, then France's 2yo G1s: the Prix Morny, Prix de la Salamandre and Grand Criterium. He then went to America and won the Breeders' Cup Juvenile on dirt for the first time, earning Cartier Horse of the Year in Europe and Eclipse champion 2yo colt in America. But at 3 he faded: 8th in the Kentucky Derby, then 5th back in Europe in the St. James's Palace S. He won a G2 in autumn, was well beaten in the Breeders' Cup Mile and retired. At stud he sired 5-time G1 winner Congaree, but little else; in Japan his best was imported son Dollar Arabian, winner of the Oi Kinen. He stood in Japan from 1998 without success, was exported to Switzerland 5 years later, and died at 32 in Australia in 2021.
332: A blueblood, half-brother to Breeders' Cup Turf winner Theatrical. Rated highly from his arrival at the stable, he won his first 2 starts but then kept finishing 2nd - in the Mainichi Hai, Radio Tampa Sho and Hakodate Kinen - showing talent but a soft finish. The next spring he won the Tanigawadake S., his first win in about a year, but kept falling short, and his first graded win came only in spring at 5, in the Osaka Hai. At 6 he tried the Yasuda Kinen a third time after a 3rd and a 2nd. Unfazed by A Shin Berlin's fast pace, he ran with a champion's strength to beat Genuine by a neck for his long-sought G1. He also boldly raced abroad, including the BC Classic at 5 and 6. Results didn't follow, but the know-how laid the foundation for stablemate Taiki Shuttle's G1 win abroad.
333: He won the Kisaragi Sho and Yayoi Sho to become the top classic contender, but was a close 3rd in the Satsuki Sho and 2nd by a neck in the Derby - narrow losses. 2nd by a neck again in the Kyoto Shimbun Hai, he went into the Kikuka Sho with his back to the wall. Racing boldly from 4th, he beat T.M. Opera O by a neck for his long-sought G1. But as Opera O matured, Top Road ran well without winning, ending his 4yo year winless. He won 4 more middle-to-long graded races and was always a contender in G1s, but never won another, retiring at the end of his 6yo year. He died young of heart failure in '05, leaving only 3 crops, yet his first included Bella Leia (04: Maristar II), Flora S. winner and Oaks runner-up.
336: 3rd in the Yayoi Sho earned him a Satsuki Sho ticket, but he was a poor 4th in the Wakaba S. and only 11th choice for the Satsuki Sho. Yet he took the lead at the third turn and no one could catch him. As the favorites watched each other behind, he held on - a shock Satsuki Sho win. Called a fluke, he was only 6th choice for the Derby. Freed by the low expectations, jockey Onishi and Sunny Brian took the lead from Silence Suzuka and set their own pace. The favorites, sure he'd tire, only panicked after the final turn. Silk Justice and Mejiro Bright closed in the low 34s, but too late - another shock wire-to-wire win and a double, at the top of his generation. But injury ended his career after the Derby. His true worth remains unknown - maybe he'd have won the Triple Crown with ease.
337: He won in his third start, but in his next he threw jockey Minai and failed to finish. He kept falling short, winning again only in his 9th start, in October at 3. That win was by 7 lengths, but he was still just an ordinary allowance horse. Switched from dirt to turf, though, he was strong. He won his next special by 8 lengths, then the Naruo Kinen by 6 in course-record time. Three straight wins drew sudden attention and an Arima Kinen run was mooted, but he went instead to the Kimpai (West). Slowly away and last, he passed 15 horses in the straight alone - so strong some said he'd have romped in the Arima Kinen too. Despite doubts about the distance, he dead-heated with Dyna Carpenter in the Hanshin Daishoten. In his first G1, the Tenno Sho (Spring), he shut out stars like Mejiro Durren, and in the Takarazuka Kinen he beat "mile emperor" Nippo Teio - 7 straight wins, 5 graded. In autumn, in the much-hyped grey clash in the Tenno Sho (Autumn), he beat the younger "grey monster" Oguri Cap, becoming the first to win both Tenno Sho races. In the Japan Cup outsider Pay the Butler ended his streak, but he was 2nd by half a length, the best Japanese finisher - strong in defeat. In his farewell Arima Kinen, his third grey duel, Oguri Cap finally beat him by half a length - a changing of the guard between two great greys. From a modest sire, and surviving his birthplace farm's bankruptcy, Tamamo Cross returned to Hokkaido as the last great horse of the Showa era. A steady sire and leading Japanese-bred stallion, he sired graded winners like Mysore Sound and Kanetsu Cross, but died of colic on April 10, 2003.
341: He won his first 2 starts, but back trouble kept him from showing his ability and he went on a long break. On his return he ran with new power and rose fast, winning 3 graded races within a year. At 5, as the ace of Kanto's older horses in the Yasuda Kinen, he lost by a nose to foreign raider Heart Lake, but in the Tenno Sho (Autumn) he swooped from far back to become a G1 winner.
342: One of the most brilliant horses of the Fairway line. He won the Derby by a record 10 lengths, then the Irish Derby and King George VI & Queen Elizabeth S. He was Britain's Horse of the Year at 3, rated 140 lbs in the International Classification, equal to the best then. In autumn he aimed for the Arc and the European Triple Crown, but was 4th in the St. Leger prep and retired to stud. Great things were expected, but after his first season he was kidnapped, leaving just one crop. The kidnappers wanted money; after the ransom demand was refused, Shergar was never seen again. That single crop included Irish St. Leger winner Authaal, but he failed at stud, and the direct line died out.
334: After winning his first graded race, the Mainichi Hai, his camp paid a supplementary fee to enter the classics - and he won the Satsuki Sho. He ran well after that: 3rd in the Derby, 2nd in the Kikuka Sho, 3rd in the Arima Kinen. The next year was stunning. He won the Kyoto Kinen and Hanshin Daishoten, then the Tenno Sho (Spring) for his second G1, and the Takarazuka Kinen to cement himself as No. 1. In autumn he won the Tenno Sho (Autumn), Japan Cup and Arima Kinen, an unprecedented autumn sweep - 8 straight graded wins, unbeaten all year. The next year, perhaps tired, he was 4th in the Osaka Hai, but beat Meisho Doto by half a length in the Tenno Sho (Spring) for a third straight Tenno Sho. He then had three G1 2nds, adding no more titles, and retired with 7 G1s, equal with Rudolf. Lacking routs, he isn't always called the greatest, but he's a historic great. At stud his offspring did poorly: no flat stars, just two jump graded winners, T.M. Toppazure and T.M. Ace.
339: Steady - 4th in the Satsuki Sho and Derby, 3rd in the Kikuka Sho - but rarely a winner, he was called "the bronze collector." His first graded win was the Nikkei Sho at 4, on extremely heavy ground, as 3rd choice. He was also 2nd on heavy ground on debut at 2, in the Yayoi Sho at 3 and the Niigata Kinen at 7 - never out of the top two on soft going. Placed in the Tenno Sho (Spring) and Diamond S., he was a true stayer at heart.
340: A blueblood, half-brother to Air Dublin and full brother to Dance Partner, seen as a leading classic contender before his debut. He won the Yayoi Sho as hoped, but a fever forced him out of the Satsuki Sho just before. Recovered, he won the Principal S. and went to the Derby, but lost narrowly to Fusaichi Concorde's late swoop. In autumn he won the Kyoto Shimbun Hai, then in the Kikuka Sho waited far back, 12th at the final turn - seemingly hopeless - and unleashed an ultimate 33.8 finish to win his long-sought classic. A tendon injury followed and he retired to stud. He has sired G1 winners like That's the Plenty, Delta Blues, Turu Maru Boy and Three Rolls, and more recently Dark Shadow and Clarente - one of the most successful heirs of the late Sunday Silence.
335: A turf middle-distance horse with a sharp kick, best off the pace. Blooming at 4, he won 3 straight, was 2nd in the Niigata Kinen, then won the Keihan Hai as 2nd choice.
338: He won the Hanshin Sansai S. and was champion 2yo colt, but leg trouble kept him out of the Satsuki Sho and he was 15th in the Derby. He then ran down Satsuki Sho winner Yaeno Muteki in the Chunichi Sports Sho Yonsai S. and won the Hakodate Kinen in Japanese record time for 2000m. Leg trouble ruled out the Kikuka Sho, so he ran in the Mile Championship and crushed top older milers by 4 lengths. He was a close 3rd behind Oguri Cap and Tamamo Cross in the Arima Kinen. Duels with crop-mate Oguri were expected, but leg trouble forced retirement - "if only he'd stayed sound." He became a very successful sire.
344: Won 7 G1s, including two US classics and the Breeders' Cup Classic, and was 1988 Eclipse Horse of the Year. One of Alydar's best, he ranked 42nd in The Blood-Horse's "Top 100 US Racehorses of the 20th Century." Until spring at 3 he kept finishing 2nd and 3rd, but as 6th choice in the Kentucky Derby he finally won a G1 and graded race. Favorite for the Preakness S., he won that too for a double. He was 4th in the Belmont S., but won the Super Derby in autumn for a third G1. At 4 in 1988 he was even better, winning G1 after G1 from the Charles H. Strub S., and took the Breeders' Cup Classic to be Horse of the Year. He retired after that race. At stud he sired Moonlight Dance, winner of France's Prix Saint-Alary (G1), but fell short of expectations.
347: Maturing at 5, he won 4 G1s, including the King George VI & Queen Elizabeth Diamond S. and Breeders' Cup Turf, honored on both continents as Cartier Horse of the Year and Eclipse champion turf male. At 3 he ran over a mile, winning the Poule d'Essai des Poulains, but then kept finishing 2nd and 3rd. At 4 he stepped up in distance, winning the 10-furlong Eclipse S. and the Man o' War S. in America. At 5 he won 3 straight G1s: the Coronation C., the King George and the Irish Champion S. He was 9th in the Arc, far behind Montjeu and El Condor Pasa, but won the Breeders' Cup Turf to be Cartier Horse of the Year, and was the first champion of the new World Series Racing Championship. At stud his first crop included Irish Derby winner Grey Swallow, but little followed, and he was exported to South Africa.
348: 2nd in his first two maidens, he won in his third start. Then as 5th choice he won the Asahi Hai Sansai S. in record-equaling time. At 3 he led all the way to win the Kyodo News Hai Yonsai S. by 3 lengths and went to the Yayoi Sho as top classic contender, but sank to 4th behind Mejiro Ryan, partly due to the ground. That year's classics were billed a Big Three: "front-running Ines Fujin, stalker Hakutaisei, closer Mejiro Ryan." As Satsuki Sho favorite he was bumped by White Stone at the start and caught near the line by Hakutaisei, losing by a neck. Slightly less fancied in the Derby, he broke well and jockey Nakano set a perfect pace, holding off Mejiro Ryan and White Stone to win in race-record time. For his "wind god" run and the superb ride of the hard-working Eiji Nakano, 200,000 fans roared "Nakano! Nakano!" - the origin of the chants still heard at G1s today. Leg trouble followed, and he retired after the Derby to stud.
350: 5th on debut, he won next time out, then won 4 straight including the Yayoi Sho to become the classic favorite. But in the Satsuki Sho he fought his rider, his famous finish misfired, and he was 4th to Narita Taishin. Losing as overwhelming favorite shocked his camp, but it only strengthened their resolve to win the Derby. Favorite again on Derby day, he focused on settling, saving ground inside, and bet everything on the straight. He held off the charging Biwa Hayahide to cross the line first, giving jockey Masato Shibata his long-dreamed title of "Derby jockey." In autumn he was 3rd in both the Kikuka Sho and the Japan Cup, but a dismal 11th in the Arima Kinen. Winless after that, he retired with leg trouble to stud.
351: By great sire Alydar. He won his debut by 8 lengths and, with 2 wins from 3, won the Asahi Hai Sansai S. as favorite in 1:34.0, 0.4 seconds faster than Maruzensky's record - stunning for the time. Jockey Hitoshi Matoba said excitedly, "He may be better than Maruzensky." At 3 he won the Hyacinth S. easily by 4 lengths, but was 2nd to Ibuki Maikagura's late run in the Yayoi Sho. As a foreign-bred barred from the classics, he trained for the Crystal C., but injury forced retirement. With 4 wins and two 2nds from 6, he left the turf with his true worth hidden and went to stud.
352: From 2 to 7, an essential supporting player in the sprint division, winning 4 graded races including the Swan S. and CBC Sho. His Swan S. time of 1:19.3 was then the Japanese record for 1400m on turf. But in G1s his best was 2nd in the Sprinters S. at 4.
353: A French horse well known in Japan for beating El Condor Pasa in the 1999 Arc. As a sire he produced many stars like Hurricane Run and Motivator, greatly boosting the Sadler's Wells line. At 3 he romped in the French and Irish Derbies, then after the Prix Niel went to the Arc. Co-favorite with Japan's El Condor Pasa, he pulled clear of the field in the straight in a two-horse battle, catching the front-running El Condor Pasa by half a length. He then went to the Japan Cup, short of preparation, and was 4th. At 4 he won 4 straight G1s, including the Tattersalls Gold C. and the King George, but lacked sparkle in autumn, 4th in the Arc, and retired at year's end. At stud his first crop gave Hurricane Run and Motivator, making him France's leading sire, and later Derby and Irish Derby winner Camelot. Montjeu died in 2012, but his grandchildren include Motivator's Arc winner Treve, Pour Moi's Derby winner Wings of Eagles and Camelot's Irish Derby winner Latrobe - his blood lives on.
354: By great sire Sunday Silence out of Oka Sho winner Agnes Flora - a true blueblood. Slow to mature, he missed 2yo racing, but won his debut at 3. He lost next time, then won the Wakakusa S. and Kyoto Shimbun Hai to earn a Derby ticket. In the Japanese Derby, as 3rd choice, he chose his usual late charge - risky in a big G1 field - but surged sharply, dueling with Air Shakur, who also came from the back. Slightly behind entering the straight, he won the fierce battle by a nose to take the Derby. It was jockey Hiroshi Kawachi's first Derby, on his 17th try. Winning with the son of a horse he once rode to a G1 win, with the same owner and trainer, felt like a strange bond of fate.
355: Sunday Silence sired countless G1 winners, but only one was ever called "the genius": Agnes Tachyon. Full brother to Derby winner Agnes Flight, he won his first 4 starts, always with ease, becoming an unbeaten Satsuki Sho winner - a true genius. Trainer Hiroyuki Nagahama even declared a Triple Crown, but just before the Derby a severe tendon injury struck, and he retired to stud without waiting to recover. "Tachyon" is a hypothetical particle faster than light. True to his name, he flashed through his career, and the brothers' Derby double and the Triple Crown stayed hypothetical as he left the turf. A superb sire, he produced Daiwa Scarlet (Oka Sho, Shuka Sho, Queen Elizabeth II Cup, Arima Kinen), double winner Deep Sky, Satsuki Sho winner Captain Thule and Hanshin JF winner Reve d'Essor. A leading heir to the late Sunday Silence, he died suddenly of heart failure in June '09.
356: The greatest rival of seven-G1 winner T.M. Opera O. They first met in the Takarazuka Kinen at 4: Doto came in after winning the Kinko Sho, Opera O on 3 straight graded wins including the Tenno Sho (Spring). In his first G1, Doto was 2nd by a neck. In autumn he won the All Comers and went into the Tenno Sho (Autumn) fully prepared, but lost to Opera O again in 2nd - and the same in the Japan Cup and Arima Kinen: 4 straight G1 2nds, a perfect foil to Opera O's march. At 5 he won the Nikkei Sho, then took on Opera O in the Tenno Sho (Spring), only to trail him yet again - a strange record of the same 1-2 in 5 straight G1s. After a full year of chasing him, in the Takarazuka Kinen he raced aggressively, with sheer tenacity, and finally beat Opera O. But the win didn't reverse their roles; both declined from there.
358: "The grey monster" who flashed through just 10 races with explosive speed and power on turf or dirt. He won the NHK Mile C. in spring at 3 for his first crown, then ran in the Japanese Derby, the first foreign-bred ever to do so, finishing a fine 5th. In autumn, after a 3rd in the Kobe Shimbun Hai, he was excluded from the Tenno Sho (Autumn), and instead ran in the Musashino S., beating Eagle Cafe by 9 lengths - stunning for his first dirt race - in an astonishing 1:33.3, 1.2 seconds under the record. In the Japan Cup Dirt he treated the best from home and abroad like children, winning easily in another record. Many hoped he'd go abroad, but a tendon injury ended that dream. At stud he sired many G1 winners, led by 2-time sprint G1 winner Curren Chan, plus Sleepless Night, Whale Capture and Fusaichi Richard. Recently his filly Aerolithe won the NHK Mile C. leading at a fast pace and ran well in many G1s against colts. He also sired Sodashi, the first white turf G1 winner, and white graded winner Yukichan. He retired from stud in 2019; his last crop's Mamakocha won the Sprinters S., giving him JRA graded winners 19 years running (the streak ended in 2024). He died of old age at 23 in 2021.
343: Until spring at 4 he was an unremarkable horse, winning and losing dirt sprints in lower classes. But in his first turf race, the semi-open Dotonbori S., he won as 6th choice, was 3rd in the Silk Road S. (OP) and went to the Yasuda Kinen. Only 10th choice, he won by a length and a half - his first open win, in his 18th start. He later dueled Oguri Cap in the Mile Championship and won the first G1 Sprinters S., a top sprinter.
345: He won his first graded race, the Sapporo Kinen, at 4, then couldn't win and switched to jumps in November. Winning 1 of 2, he returned to the flat and led all the way to win the Niigata Daishoten as 7th choice. He then breezed in front to win the G1 Takarazuka Kinen ahead of Kamino Cresse. Half a year after jumping fences, he was the Mejiro crop's third G1 winner after McQueen and Ryan. As 15th choice in the Arima Kinen, his "second wind" held off Tokai Teio and the rest - a shock Grand Prix double, earning champion older male and champion Japanese-sired horse. His sire Mejiro Eagle was also a famous front-runner.
346: Based at local Iwate. He won his debut at 2, then developed a tendon injury in his left foreleg. After 19 months off he returned at 4 and won race after race, 18 straight from his debut, then a Japanese record. After one 2nd he won 11 more, including the Michinoku Daishoten, Tohoku Thoroughbred Daishoten, Kitakamigawa Daishoten, Nambu Hai and Toka Sho. At 7 he suffered his second loss to rival Moriyu Prince in the Michinoku Daishoten, then won 8 more. Leg trouble kept him from racing outside Tohoku, but 39 wins, three 2nds and a 3rd from 43, never out of the top two in 41 straight - worthy of "the Iwate monster."
349: He debuted early in the year, won 3 straight, then won the Satsuki Sho by 5 lengths. A father-son Triple Crown seemed certain, but a fracture after the Satsuki Sho ruled out the Derby, and on his return he was a dismal 5th in the rain in the St. Lite Kinen. Still, he won the Kyoto Shimbun Hai by 2 lengths and was a confident Kikuka Sho favorite, winning clearly with the bottomless stamina of his sire. He was 2nd to Symboli Rudolf in the Arima Kinen, but no one doubted his future. Yet at 4, partly due to a fracture, he went winless all year. Just when he seemed done, at 5 he won 2 graded races and then the Tenno Sho (Spring) by a whisker in a photo - a father-son Tenno Sho double.
357: Northern Taste's last star. Injury-prone, he had many long breaks, but at 5 he won 4 straight to reach open class, and at 7 won his first graded race, the Fuji S., giving his sire a record 20 straight crops with a graded winner.
359: Talented but forever falling short: by the Tenno Sho (Spring) in April at 6 he had run 37 times without even an open win, yet was 2nd 7 times and 3rd 7 times in graded races, including four 2nds and two 3rds in G1s. "The best horse never to win a graded race" fit him, and trainer Ikee naturally longed to get him one. In the Meguro Kinen, with Yutaka Take replacing regular jockey Shigefumi Kumazawa, he finally won a graded race in his 38th start. At 7 he won the Nikkei Shinshun Hai, then the Dubai Sheema Classic, beating future BC Turf winner Fantastic Light. In his farewell, the Hong Kong Vase, he won again - his long-sought G1, abroad. "The best never to win a graded race" retired as "a G1 winner unbeaten abroad." At stud he sired brothers Dream Journey and Orfevre, 6-time G1 eccentric Gold Ship, Arc runner-up Nakayama Festa, dirt star Silk Mobius and Hanshin JF winner Red Riviere, establishing himself as a key Sunday Silence heir before dying in 2015.
360: Unbeaten in 8 at local Oi, including the Tokyo Okan Sho, he joined the JRA after winning the Tokyo Daishoten at the end of his 3yo year. He lost his first 2 races, but in the Tenno Sho (Spring), as 4th choice, he beat Mr. Cyclennon by 5 lengths in record time. He then brushed aside rival Yaeno Muteki in the Takarazuka Kinen. In autumn he narrowly lost the Mainichi Okan to Oguri Cap, then ran poorly: 6th in the Tenno Sho and 11th in the Japan Cup. In the Arima Kinen, billed as Oguri Cap vs Super Creek, just as Super Creek caught the tiring Oguri Cap, Inari One swooped wide with a devilish kick to win. He won only 3 races in the JRA, but all were G1s - and fittingly, he was never favorite.
361: At 2 he kept falling short, and the Asahi Hai FS was his 9th start. But as if his narrow losses had never happened, he won in a record 1:33.5, 0.1 seconds faster than Grass Wonder. At 3 he won the Yayoi Sho and ran a good 3rd in the Satsuki Sho. But after a 10th in the Derby, at a distance that didn't suit him, he lost his rhythm, ran poorly and left the JRA without another win. Moved to local Oi, he won the Oi Kinen and was 6th in the JBC Classic, retiring after a 4th in the '07 Sumidagawa Open.
362: "The demon of Fuchu," with outstanding aptitude even among Tony Bin's many Tokyo specialists. He was perfect at Tokyo, 3 for 3 including 2 G1s, the Japanese Derby and the Japan Cup. His Japan Cup at 3 was stunning: he ran down reigning champion T.M. Opera O in the straight and caught him right before the line, with a dignity rare in a 3yo. Peslier's ride was superb, but the horse himself seemed to say "no one beats me at Tokyo." Hopes for the first back-to-back Japan Cup were high the next year, but with the race moved to Nakayama, he was 5th. He retired at the end of his 4yo year to stud. As if answering hopes as heir to the late Tony Bin, he sired Kikuka Sho winner Oken Bruce Lee, Tenno Sho winners Jaguar Mail and Tosen Jordan, full sisters Tall Poppy (Oaks) and Aventura (Shuka Sho), and abroad NZ Oaks winner Jungle Rocket.
363: After 2 G1 wins in Italy he raced worldwide, winning G1s in Britain, France, Japan and Hong Kong, and is known for winning the 2002 Japan Cup. Just a graded contender until 3, at 4 he won the G1 Premio Presidente della Repubblica and Gran Premio di Milano. Spreading his wings, he went to the Japan Cup in autumn and beat Symboli Kris S. and others. Shadai then bought half of him, and he was set to stand in Japan after racing. At 5 he moved to Britain, winning the Prix d'Ispahan, Eclipse S., International S. and Queen Elizabeth II S., then was a close 3rd in the Breeders' Cup Turf. He ended his career with the Hong Kong C., his 8th G1. At stud in Japan he sired no superstar, but steady graded winners like Hakodate Kinen winner Transwarp and Fillies' Revue winner One Carat, and as a damsire produced Harp Star and Stelvio.
366: He began on turf, but in spring at 3 won a 5-million race and an open special on dirt, first showing his talent. He then ran a close 5th in the Derby, his last turf race before switching to dirt. He won the Japan Dirt Derby and Derby Grand Prix back to back for an early G1 - surprisingly, the first dirt G1 by a Sunday Silence son. 5th in the Japan Cup Dirt, he bounced back to win the Tokyo Daishoten and February S. - 4 G1s in about six months. A Dubai trip was planned, but worsening roaring ended his career early. At stud until his sudden death in 2017, he sired dirt kings Espoir City, Smart Falcon and Copano Rickey, and in 2019 Chrysoberyl won the Champions C. unbeaten in 6, proving his blood's quality again.
370: One of Brian's Time's best. His record falls short of stars like Narita Brian and Mayano Top Gun, but in pure ability he was their equal - true super-G1 class. He narrowly lost his debut over 1000m on dirt, then won easily next time, won the Shinzan Kinen, and with the Arlington C. and Spring S. won 4 straight, becoming the top classic contender. In the Satsuki Sho he had the field's fastest finish but a poor position, finishing 3rd, and was 3rd again in the NHK Mile C. In the Derby, his revenge match, he finally won his G1, topping his crop. But a tendon injury before autumn ended his career before showing his true worth, and he went to stud. His first crop included Vodka, a filly who won the Derby - the first father-daughter Derby winners ever. He also sired Aoba Sho winner Hiraboku Royal and Derby runner-up Smile Jack. As Brian's Time's heir, a star colt is hoped for.
372: He debuted in January at 3. As a son of great sire Nureyev he was highly rated, and at 4 he won 3 straight, including his first graded race, the Lord Derby Challenge T. But after just 1 win in the next 18 months, jockey Norihiro Yokoyama suggested "1200m would suit him better." In his first 1200m race, the Sprinters S., he beat Agnes World by a neck for his long-sought G1. But his reign atop the sprint world was brief: he kept falling short, 2nd 5 times in graded races, earning the unwanted nickname "silver collector." At 7 he finally won again in the Yasuda Kinen - as 9th choice, with 15th-choice Break Time 2nd, a wild 120,000-yen quinella. At stud he sired Keeneland C. winner Couverture and Kyoto Himba S. winner Celebrita.
374: A great supporting player who fought many epic battles with rivals like Mihono Bourbon and Rice Shower, always livening up G1s. Racing until the end of his 6yo year, he won 8 of 32, including 4 graded races like the American JCC and Meguro Kinen, but in G1s always fell just short, his best a 3rd in the Kikuka Sho. Perhaps that soft finish won sympathy - many fans loved him to the end.
375: Gifted, but lacking a sharp turn of foot, he kept falling short, and tendon injuries forced many breaks. Late in his career, as his leg troubles eased, his running changed, and at 7 he showed remarkable form, winning 2 graded races in a row. In the Tenno Sho (Autumn), amid the drama of front-runner Silence Suzuka's breakdown, he broke clear of the pack and won a duel with Stay Gold.
376: By great sire Sadler's Wells out of Arc winner Urban Sea - a true blueblood, top-class on the track and at stud. Unbeaten in 4, he won the Derby, then romped in the Irish Derby, and brushed aside older horses in the King George VI & Queen Elizabeth Diamond S., Europe's best by summer at 3. In autumn he tried the Irish Champion S. at middle distance and the Breeders' Cup Classic on dirt, losing both, but retired as Cartier champion 3yo colt. At stud his first crop gave 4 G1 winners including Red Rocks, followed by New Approach, Frankel and more, and he was champion sire in Britain and Ireland 11 years running from 2010 - the most powerful branch of the Sadler's Wells line. His grandchildren include 11-time G1 winner Enable and Derby winner Masar, and in Japan Frankel's Soul Stirring and Mozu Ascot. He died in 2021 at the height of his success, but in 2024 Content's Yorkshire Oaks win made him the sire of 100 G1 winners. With heirs like Frankel, his blood's march goes on.
364: A born sprinter, all his wins at 1400m or less. His first 3 starts on dirt came to nothing, but switched to turf his speed blossomed and he won twice. Wins then dried up, but he reached open class at the end of his 5yo year, and at 6, as 16th choice, last in the betting, he beat Agnes World and others in the Sprinters S. - his first graded win a G1. He also won the Swan S. and Hankyu Hai. A late bloomer.
365: With natural speed he set three records, including a Japanese one. At 3 he missed the spring classics, but won his first graded race, the Chunichi Sports Sho Yonsai S., in record time for Kyoto's 1800m. He ran in the Kikuka Sho in autumn but suffered atrial fibrillation mid-race and finished last. The next year, in his prime, he won the Osaka Hai and then the Keihan Hai in record time. He was 5th to Biwa Hayahide in the Takarazuka Kinen, but set a Japanese record for 1800m on turf in the Mainichi Okan in autumn and won his long-sought Tenno Sho (Autumn), a middle-distance speedster.
367: A sprinter who bloomed late. He struggled at 3 and 4, but from autumn at 4 began winning, took his first graded race, the CBC Sho, then held on by a neck in the Silk Road S., and won the Takamatsunomiya Kinen with an overwhelming late run to become sprint king. After a 14th in the Yasuda Kinen he won the Sprinters S. in autumn in a record 1:07.0, a spring-autumn sprint G1 double. He never won again and retired at the end of his 6yo year.
368: It took 3 starts to break his maiden, but the next year he won the Kyodo News Hai Yonsai S. and went to the NHK Mile C. Using Tokyo's long straight, he came from the back to beat Toyo de Hair, who used the same tactics, by a nose - a G1 winner. He then slumped, and even a Dubai trip didn't help; he went over 2 years without a win. But at 5 he won the Tanabata Sho, his first win since the NHK Mile C., and in the Japan Cup Dirt, with a fine ride by Dettori, he shot up the rail in the straight to beat the world's best for another G1. It was his last win, but shedding the "early bloomer" label meant a lot to his camp.
369: A character who led with head high, mouth open and tossing, racing steadily from 2 to 5. After a heavy loss in the Spring S. he switched to sprints: he won the Crystal C., his first graded race. The second half of his 3yo year was dull, but the next year he won the Milers C. and came into his own, 2nd in the Yasuda Kinen, winner of the Takamatsunomiya Hai (G2, 2000m), 2nd in the Mainichi Okan, then won his first G1, the Mile CS. He was a fine 5th in the Arima Kinen. The next year he won the Mainichi Okan and Mile CS in record times and had great duels with Daiichi Ruby. At stud he sired '00 Sprinters S. winner Daitaku Yamato.
371: 10 wins from 12 at local Kasamatsu, he joined the JRA with overwhelming power and won 6 straight graded races from the Pegasus S. to the Mainichi Okan. Then in the Tenno Sho (Autumn) he met Tamamo Cross, the best horse in training, and suffered his first defeat. He trailed him again in the Japan Cup, but avenged himself in Tamamo Cross's farewell Arima Kinen. The next year he started in autumn, winning the All Comers and Mainichi Okan, then narrowly lost the Tenno Sho (Autumn) to Super Creek. Then the Mile Championship and Japan Cup on back-to-back weekends. He won the Mile Championship with a furious finish, then dueled foreign mare Horlicks in the Japan Cup, losing by a neck in a then world record 2:22.2. At 5 he won the Yasuda Kinen in spring, but in autumn slumped - 6th in the Tenno Sho, 11th in the Japan Cup. "Oguri is finished," people said, and he was 4th choice for his farewell Arima Kinen. But first past the post was Oguri Cap. With that Arima Kinen, racing became not "gambling" but "drama." The "Oguri Cap story" had the happiest ending.
373: A king of the sand who won dirt G1s in spring and autumn. At 3 he was crushed in his first turf race, the Principal S., and from then on raced only on dirt. He won the Shobu S. with a charge from 13th at the final turn, then the Nagoya Yushun for his first graded win. He kept rolling, winning 5 straight including 4 graded races - the Grand Chariot C., Unicorn S. and Super Dirt Derby -. As an older horse he often lost narrowly, but at 5 won the February S. for a G1, then crushed the foreign raiders by three and a half lengths in the new Japan Cup Dirt, the first JRA dirt G1 double in a year. The next year he was 2nd in both races.
377: Based at local Funabashi. Unbeaten in his first 8, he won the Southern Kanto triple crown and the national G1 Japan Dirt Derby - a superhorse. The first triple crown winner since the great mare Rosita was big news for dirt racing, but after the Japan Dirt Derby a fracture was found and he rested 5 months. On his return his old dominance was gone, but he still ran 2nd to Agnes Digital in the February S. and won the Kashiwa Kinen. From 5 he ran well only now and then, finishing 12th in another February S., showing decline. He raced until 7 but never regained his shine.
378: A versatile star, top-class on both turf and dirt, with a multi-surface career beyond all convention. At 2 he won the Zen-Nihon Sansai Yushun. At 3 he went the turf mile route in spring without winning, then won 2 graded races on dirt. Seen as a future dirt leader, he ran in the turf Mile Championship instead. With all his wins on dirt, he was 13th choice, but a powerful late charge from the back beat the older horses - his first turf win, a G1. The next autumn he returned to dirt to win the Nambu Hai, then back on turf beat seven-G1 winner T.M. Opera O in the Tenno Sho (Autumn), and at year's end won the Hong Kong Cup. He then won the February S., 4 straight G1s across local, JRA turf, overseas and JRA dirt. Trips to the Dubai World Cup and Hong Kong's QE2 Cup brought no wins, and injury cost him a year, but the legend wasn't over: after a poor comeback run, he won the Yasuda Kinen in race-record time. There may never be another like him. At stud he sired a varied group: dirt runners Daishin Orange, Ubiquitous and Kaze no Ko, turf middle-distance Yamanin Kingly and turf sprinter Grand Prix Angel.
380: A leading figure of the In Reality line. He was the first to win the Breeders' Cup Classic twice, and as a sire produced many stars like Colonel John. He debuted late, in April at 3, and won his first graded race only after the classics ended. In autumn he won his first G1, the Super Derby, then won the Breeders' Cup Classic after a fierce duel with Giant's Causeway, earning Eclipse Horse of the Year. At 4 he won the Santa Anita H. for a third G1, but then kept losing narrowly and was less fancied when he returned to the Breeders' Cup Classic. Against stars like Sakhee and Galileo, he won a duel with Sakhee in the straight by a nose - the first to win the race twice. He retired after it. At stud his first crop included Dubai World Cup winner Well Armed, and G1 winners kept coming - a central force of Man o' War's direct line.
383: Little as a racehorse, but a huge success at stud, champion sire in Argentina 10 times - called "the Sunday Silence of the Southern Hemisphere" in Japan. Racing in America he won no graded race; his best were 2nds in the G1 Swaps S. and Super Derby. But valued for his Halo bloodline, then booming, he went to stud in Argentina, where he sired G1 winners one after another and was champion sire 8 seasons running from 94/95, plus 03/04 and 07/08 - 10 in all. Hailed there as greater than the historic sire Congreve, his line now dominates more than Sunday Silence's does in Japan. As a shuttle sire he also produced G1 winners in North America like More Than Ready. He was leased to Japan for a year as a relative of Sunday Silence, but sired no stars there.
385: He showed ability at 3, finishing 4th in the NHK Hai (G2, 2000m turf), but then stalled, reaching open class only in spring at 5 - a late bloomer. At 6 he won the Nakayama Kimpai on his 8th graded try, then, as if defying his low 6th-choice rating, beat Taiki Sherlock and others by 4 lengths in the February S. for a G1. He went to stud but sired no stars.
386: The best son of top sprinter Sakura Bakushin O, in whom his sire's genes truly bloomed. Raced only on dirt early, he was erratic and slow to rise, but switched to turf as an older horse he showed overwhelming speed, as if his past were a lie, leading all the way to win the Yamashiro S. and Ocean S. with ease. Riding that momentum into the sprint G1 Takamatsunomiya Kinen, his superior speed let him lead all the way, never letting anyone near - a G1 winner. He went to Hong Kong at year's end but, perhaps unsettled by travel and tired from a hard year, ran unlike himself and was 10th. At stud he sired NZ Trophy winner Shonan Achieve.
389: Often mistaken for a son of Lyphard because of his name, his sire was actually Relaunch, of the Man o' War line. He won 3 graded races on turf and dirt, but fell just short in G1s. He went to stud, but his offspring did poorly.
390: Repeated fractures cost him chance after chance. When he overcame his third, he was already in autumn at 5, late in a racehorse's career, but in his comeback, the Mile Championship, he ran as well as ever, then beat sprint queen Flower Park in the CBC Sho in record time. Then came the Sprinters S.: after a long photo, he lost to Flower Park by just 1 cm, missing his long-sought G1 - an epic struggle for the history books.
379: Slow to rise, he missed the spring, but emerged in summer and went to the Kikuka Sho. Outsider Meiner Despot seemed set to win unchallenged in front, but Manhattan Cafe caught him at the line for his first crown. He then beat strong older horses like T.M. Opera O with a powerful finish in the Arima Kinen. The next year he beat crop rival Jungle Pocket to win the Tenno Sho (Spring). That autumn he tried the Arc but was injured during the race and finished 13th. At stud he had no stars at first, but went on to sire NHK Mile C. winner Joe Cappuccino, Tenno Sho winner Hiruno d'Amour, Red Desire, who beat Buena Vista in the Shuka Sho, and 2013 February S. winner Grape Brandy. He was leading sire in 2009.
381: He won his first 2 starts, but a fracture cost him 10 months. Back, he won twice, then a tendon injury cost him another 13 months. Returning at 5, he won a semi-open race and then the Keihan Hai, his first graded win. In the Takarazuka Kinen he was 2nd choice as "the late-arriving star," and won his first G1 in record time. Sadly for him, Rice Shower broke down fatally in that race, leaving the winner little remembered.
382: He ran in all three classics, finishing 6th, 9th and 6th. Improving after the Kikuka Sho, he won the Kimpai (East) early at 4. That autumn he fought a legendary 300m duel with Yamanin Zephyr in the Tenno Sho (Autumn). He lost by a nose, but it was the race where his true ability showed best. The next year he won the Tokyo Shimbun Hai, but in another Tenno Sho (Autumn) he lost to Nehai Caesar, 2nd again.
384: Based at local Iwate. He won 9 straight including the Tohoku Derby, then was crushed in the Derby Grand Prix and Super Dirt Derby. Growing steadily, in autumn at 4 he beat Southern Kanto king Abukuma Poro in the Nambu Hai for a G1. Next year he overpowered Taiki Sherlock, M.I. Blanc and others in the JRA's February S. - the first JRA G1 won by a local horse. After 5 more wins including the Teio Sho, he was 11th in the Tokyo Daishoten, but was still '99 NAR Horse of the Year. Trying to repeat in the February S., he was 4th behind new JRA stars Wing Arrow and Gold Tiara.
387: By European champion Dancing Brave out of Goodbye Halo, a 7-time US G1 winner - a true blueblood. After winning his first 3, a G1 seemed imminent, but his temper held him back, with narrow losses led by a 2nd in the Satsuki Sho. Older, he won the Tokyo Shimbun Hai and Nakayama Kinen, but was crushed in the Yasuda and Takarazuka Kinen, then 2nd in the Mile Championship and 3rd in the Sprinters S. At 5 he finally won the Takamatsunomiya Kinen, on his 11th G1 try. At stud he sired fillies' double winner Kawakami Princess (03: Takano Secretary) and 2-time sprint G1 winner Laurel Guerreiro (04: Big Ten Bee).
388: After a 7th in the Derby he won 3 straight, including the Kobe and Kyoto Shimbun Hai, the year's top late improver. There were doubts about the Kikuka Sho distance, but a slow pace set up a sprint in the straight. His astonishing 33.9 finish outran closers Mejiro Bright, Silk Justice and Tokio Excellent, and he became a classic winner on a 4-race streak. He never won again, retiring after the Takarazuka Kinen at 6.
391: His first win came in March at 3, in his 7th start. He then won the Wakakusa S. and Kyoto Yonsai Tokubetsu and went to the Derby, just failing to catch Sunny Brian but finishing 2nd, ahead of favorite Mejiro Bright. After winning the Kyoto Daishoten, he was 5th in both the Kikuka Sho and Japan Cup, his late charges leaving him short. In the Arima Kinen he moved early from the third turn and powered through from midfield, beating strong older horses clearly - a G1 just 9 months after his first win.
392: A leading classic contender, but 2nd in the Satsuki Sho, 2nd in the Derby, 5th in the Kikuka Sho, then 5th in the Mile Championship - a supporting role. After a 2nd in the next Yasuda Kinen, he finally won his long-sought G1 in the Takarazuka Kinen. A tendon injury the next year seemed to send him to stud, but in autumn '04, 16 months later, he suddenly returned at local Arao. Winless in 4 starts, he retired in June '05.
394: A rare graded winner by Miho Shinzan. With the "hatchet-sharp" kick of grandsire Shinzan, he romped in the NHK Hai (G2, 2000m) and was 5th in the Derby. Just as he seemed set to rise as his sire's heir, leg trouble forced a long break. He still won the Asahi Challenge C., showing real ability, but leg problems forced retirement at 5. At stud he left no heir... Shinzan's line ended here.
393: From Fuji Kiseki's first crop, he crushed A Shin Preston by 4 lengths on debut, then won the Shinzan Kinen and Spring S. and was Satsuki Sho favorite. Breaking clear from a good spot, he was outdueled by the charging Air Shakur, a narrow 2nd. After a heavy defeat in the Derby he ran well at a mile, winning 3 graded races including the Naruo Kinen and two Kyoto Kimpai, but lost narrowly to Agnes Digital in the Mile Championship - no G1.
395: Brian's Time's third Satsuki Sho winner, after Narita Brian and Sunny Brian. Many called that win a fluke, and he was never rated highly; indeed it was his only graded win, and he never won again. But he was hit by mishaps - a fracture, a fall that stopped him mid-race, a tendon injury - and never had a smooth career. It's also true he never got to show his real ability.
396: He won his debut as expected, then finished 2nd, 3rd and 3rd, missing the Satsuki Sho. He won the Yamabuki Sho in his 4th start, romped in the Aoba Sho and went to the Derby, losing to Tanino Gimlet in 2nd. In autumn he won the Kobe Shimbun Hai, then skipped the Kikuka Sho for the Tenno Sho (Autumn) against top older horses, beating Narita Top Road by three-quarters of a length - and won it again the next year. He also won the Arima Kinen twice, only the 4th to do so, taking 4 JRA Awards: Horse of the Year twice, champion 3yo colt and champion older male. Fearsome as an older horse, in his farewell Arima Kinen he crushed Tap Dance City by 9 lengths, repaying his Japan Cup defeat.
