"The best horse of recent years" retired with plenty left, to much regret. Syndicated for 1.95 billion yen, he sired many graded winners: February S. winner Success Brocken, Yasuda Kinen winner Strong Return, 4-time graded winner Sun Carlo and more. Epiphaneia, out of Cesario, won the Japan Cup by 4 lengths, fulfilling the dream of his sire, twice 3rd in it. In 2018 Le Vent Se Leve won the Champions C. at just 3.
397: Offered at a training sale, he stood out in neither pedigree, build nor workout, selling for just 6.5 million yen. Not much was expected; he debuted in August at 2 but kept running poorly, breaking his maiden only 9 months later, at the end of May at 3, in his 10th start. That win changed everything. He improved amazingly, his running far more consistent. That autumn he stepped up to the Kikuka Sho and, as 10th choice, won - a "miracle" true to his name that left fans stunned. The next year, again lightly fancied, he won the Tenno Sho (Spring) and Takarazuka Kinen. All 3 of his graded wins were G1s, and all paid 10,000-yen-plus quinellas. But injury sidelined him in autumn at 4. Back in the next Tenno Sho (Autumn), he kept losing heavily, and another injury forced retirement.
398: Sunday Silence's great rival on the track. They fought fiercely in all three US classics: 2nd to Sunday Silence in the Kentucky Derby and Preakness S., he finally beat him in the Belmont S. for the last classic. In their 4th clash, the Breeders' Cup Classic, he lost by a neck, so Eclipse Horse of the Year went to Sunday Silence. At 4 he won the Suburban H. and retired with 14 wins, five 2nds and a 3rd from 20. While Sunday Silence, retiring about the same time, was sold to Japan, Easy Goer, by Alydar out of a Buckpasser mare, went to stud in America with high hopes. He died at 8 after just 4 crops, which included CCA Oaks winner My Flag and Travers S. winner Will's Way, who went to stud.
399: He combined rare speed with a strong finish, and inherited the Tokyo-course aptitude of many Tony Bin runners. At Tokyo he won 5 of 20, with four 2nds, including the NHK Mile C., but elsewhere he managed just one 2nd from 17, never winning. He raced abroad boldly - 3rd in the Prix Jacques le Marois, 13th in the Prix du Moulin, 7th and 14th in the Hong Kong Mile - without results; his clumsy late-charge-only style likely cost him. He raced until 7 but never won after the Mainichi Okan at 5, and retired to stud. His first crop included Niigata 2yo S. winner Meine Isabel.
400: Won 6 G1s, including the Derby, Irish Derby and two Breeders' Cup Turfs, and sired stars like So You Think - a great legacy. Emerging at 2, he won the Racing Post T. for his first G1. At 3 he won twice, then went to the Derby as 2nd choice behind stablemate Hawk Wing, but beat him clearly by 2 lengths. He romped in the Irish Derby too, then went straight to the Arc, finishing 3rd. But he won the Breeders' Cup Turf to end his 3yo season in style. At 4 he won the Irish Champion S. and tried the Arc again, but struggled on heavy ground and was 3rd once more. Still, he went back for the Breeders' Cup Turf and dead-heated for the win with Johar after a thrilling finish, retiring in glory. 10 wins from 13, losing only a 2nd on debut and two Arc 3rds - very consistent. He stood as a shuttle sire in Europe and Oceania, siring stars in both; in Oceania, notably 10-time G1 winner So You Think.
405: In the star-studded 1988 crop, Nice Nature was a standout character loved by fans. He had the guts to match any rival, but a soft finish that let lesser horses beat him, and after winning the Naruo Kinen in autumn at 3 he went 2 years and 7 months without a win. Meanwhile he set odd records like 3rd in the Arima Kinen three years running, earning unwanted nicknames like "Mr. Close Second" and "bronze collector." He raced until 8 thanks to a strange charm that made you think "maybe next time," and fans' warm support. He stood 5 years at stud, then retired as an honored horse. From 2017 a retired horse association held "birthday donation" drives for him, and from around 2021, with a revival of popularity, donations far exceeded the goals. He died peacefully at 35 in 2023.
410: His sire Tudenham King was a fine supporting player who won the Nakayama Kinen and more. The late trainer Tameo Toyama, who adored the sire, raised Dojima Muteki with great care as his best son. He ran tough until 10, winning 4 of 57, and raced not only in the JRA but at local tracks and abroad - a pioneer of his time. But big titles eluded him: no G1, and his only graded win was the Keio Hai Autumn H. at 5, a record short of his fame. In later years his form faded, but the sight of him racing happily among young horses inspired and moved many fans.
411: Twin Turbo thrilled fans by dashing to the lead and setting off in a reckless, all-or-nothing runaway. His extreme style made his record anything but steady, but when it worked, his wins were pure joy. His best race was the All Comers at 5. All the leading runners had question marks that year, a wide-open race. As the others watched each other, he built a huge lead at his own pace until it was a safe one, cruising home as the other jockeys went pale - fooling stars like Rice Shower and Sister Tosho. He never won again, but many fans loved his single-minded front-running. After moving to local Kaminoyama, he retired to stud.
413: The one-hit wonder whose shock win in the 1991 Arima Kinen stunned everyone. Last and over the time limit on debut, he was never a big hope, but gradually improved from 3. At 6 he won the Kimpai (West), his first graded win, and ran in that year's Arima Kinen. With the dominant Mejiro McQueen the favorite, he was ignored at 14th choice of 15. But in the straight he unleashed the kick of his life, overpowering McQueen to win - in record time. The announcer's cry, "Daiyu Saku, to everyone's amazement!", summed up every fan's feelings. He died of old age in 2013.
414: One of America's best of the 1990s. He won 11 G1s, including the Breeders' Cup Classic, matched legendary Citation's 16 straight wins, earned a then-record $9.99 million, and ranked 18th in The Blood-Horse's "Top 100 US Racehorses of the 20th Century." Until late at 4 he raced mostly on turf without success, but after winning on dirt at the end of his 4yo year, he was transformed. He won his first G1 in the NYRA Mile H. (renamed the Cigar Mile H. after his retirement), and at 5 won all 10 starts, including 8 G1s like the Jockey Club Gold C. and Breeders' Cup Classic. At 6 he won the first Dubai World Cup and the Citation Challenge, equaling the record of 16 straight. He lost his next race, ending the streak, but was Eclipse Horse of the Year at 5 and 6. Syndicated for $25 million, he went to stud but was found infertile, leaving no offspring, and died in 2014.
415: Won the 1987 Derby and King George VI & Queen Elizabeth Diamond S. and was Britain's Horse of the Year. 3rd on debut, he won his next 2, including the William Hill Futurity S. (G1), becoming the 2yo to watch. At 3 he won a G2, then went to the Derby as favorite, beating Most Welcome and others. In his first race against older horses, the Eclipse S., he was narrowly 2nd to Mtoto, but won the King George to prove he was No. 1. In autumn he won the St. Leger and took on the Arc, but sank in the straight after a fast pace, a heavy-beaten 8th. Named British Horse of the Year, he retired after the Arc. He died young at 7, leaving few offspring, including Italian Oaks winner Ivyanna.
401: He trailed Fusaichi Zenon in the Yayoi Sho, but as 2nd choice in the Satsuki Sho his late charge from the back made him a classic winner. Going for a double in the Derby, he lost to Agnes Flight by a nose, then boldly went to Britain's King George VI & Queen Elizabeth Diamond S., 5th against Montjeu. 3rd in the Kobe Shimbun Hai, he still won the Kikuka Sho narrowly as 2nd choice - two classics plus a nose 2nd in the Derby, a "near Triple Crown." Winless after, he went to stud at the end of '02. But the next spring, out at pasture, he kicked the paddock fence, fractured a leg and was put down.
402: US double classic winner of 2002. After retiring he went to stud in Japan as a hoped-for successor to Sunday Silence, but his extreme pickiness limited his matings, and he didn't greatly succeed. As a racehorse he was erratic: early at 3 he was crushed when intimidated by the pack, then won his next 2 easily at his own pace. In the Kentucky Derby, only 9th choice, he romped again, then won a tight Preakness for a double. But a slow start in the Belmont left him a heavy-beaten 8th, no Triple Crown. He won the Haskell Invitational H. easily, but was crushed by older horses in the Pacific Classic S. and Breeders' Cup Classic. Bought by the Shadai Group, looking for Sunday Silence's successor, he went to stud in Japan. But he showed interest only in certain mares, so covering was a struggle; in 12 years he left under 100 offspring. Still, they included Shuka Sho winner Black Emblem and other graded winners, hinting at his quality as a sire.
403: 16 starts, 9 wins, his only G1 the Takarazuka Kinen. By the numbers, not enough to be called great. But his fearsome ability to win in record time just by running his own race made him a true monster, and his career is full of legends: ducking under the gate in the Yayoi Sho; an unprecedented 6 straight wins, 5 graded, after Yutaka Take took over at 4; winning the Kinko Sho by a distance; the switch to jockey Minai in the Takarazuka Kinen because Take rode Air Groove; toying with year-younger El Condor Pasa and Grass Wonder in the Mainichi Okan; and the Tenno Sho (Autumn) that ended the legend... Ending unfinished through a fatal breakdown, his reputation is not settled; some say "tragedy has glamorized him." On records, perhaps. But no one can deny the impact of his running or the thrill it brought. That makes him a legend.
404: Called "the black assassin from Kanto" and "the last stayer," he was loved by fans. He debuted early, in August at 2, and won the Fuyo S. in his third start. Then injury cost him 6 months; back in the Spring S. he was 4th, then 8th in both the Satsuki Sho and NHK Hai (G2, 2000m turf), and only 16th choice for the Derby. But perhaps helped by the longer trip, he held on for 2nd to Mihono Bourbon. In autumn he was 2nd in both Kikuka Sho trials, the St. Lite Kinen and Kyoto Shimbun Hai. In the Kikuka Sho itself, his stayer's power finally beat Mihono Bourbon, shattering his Triple Crown dream for his first crown. The next year he denied Mejiro McQueen a third straight Tenno Sho (Spring) and Yutaka Take a fifth, beating the champion by two and a half lengths. A long slump followed, but at 6 he won the Tenno Sho (Spring) again, his first win in two years. Voted first for the Takarazuka Kinen, he he broke down in the race and had to be put down. By fate, that Takarazuka Kinen was held at Kyoto. The greatest stayer bloomed at Yodo, and fell at Yodo.
406: Half-brother to Tenno Sho winner Biwa Hayahide, the best horse of the 1990s, "the shadow-roll monster." He ran some poor races early, but from the Kyoto Sansai S., when the shadow roll went on, he won race after race. He won the Satsuki Sho by three and a half lengths, the Derby by 5 and the Kikuka Sho by 7 - a Triple Crown by huge margins. He then beat Hishi Amazon and Rice Shower by 3 lengths in the Arima Kinen. But after winning the next spring's Hanshin Daishoten, things darkened. A hip inflammation cost him 7 months; back in the Tenno Sho (Autumn), the old sparkle was gone and he was a dismal 12th. Things never came right, and he retired after the Takamatsunomiya Hai at 5. He went to stud but died young after just 2 crops - the greatest Triple Crown winner, dogged by tragedy at the end.
407: Debuted at local Oi. Ordinary at 3, he came into his own after moving to Funabashi at 4, winning 7 straight including the Oi Kinen. At 5 he won the JRA's Tokai Winter S. and kept improving, and from 6 he was a monster, with 10 wins and a 3rd from 11. In JRA-local races packed with stars like Kyoto City, Meisei Opera, Taiki Sherlock and M.I. Blanc, he showed overwhelming power, winning 9 graded races (4 G1s), and was NAR Horse of the Year in 1997 and 1998. In his prime, among Japan's best ever on dirt. A Dubai World Cup trip was naturally hoped for, but it never happened for various reasons - still a cause for regret.
408: Brother of Sakura Chiyono O, by Tosho Boy - a blueblood watched from the start. As hoped he won 3 straight, including the Asahi Hai Sansai S., but as favorite in the Yayoi Sho he sank to 12th, then a dismal 19th in the Satsuki Sho. Many blamed the heavy ground, but he was 9th in the Derby on good going too. In autumn he won the St. Lite Kinen and went all in on the Kikuka Sho. But at the final turn he ran wildly off course. Into the straight he charged boldly along the outside rail with a tremendous kick, but the lost ground was too much and he could only finish 5th. Gifted, he ended the classics uncrowned.
409: Losing his dam soon after birth, Sakura Star O was raised by hand - an unusual start. He won the Yayoi Sho and became a classic favorite. 2nd choice behind Material in the Satsuki Sho, he won with overwhelming power, but leg trouble forced a long break and he missed the Derby. His preparation fell further behind, and he returned after six months in the Kikuka Sho itself - an unheard-of route. But he blew away all doubts, winning to announcer Kiyoshi Sugimoto's famous call, "Cherry blossoms in full bloom in chrysanthemum season!" - "the miracle double winner." Then the Arima Kinen, where he topped the fan vote, brought tragedy: he caught a leg in a hollow in the track, fractured it and was pulled up. Devoted treatment followed, but in vain; 4.5 months later he was put down.
412: He won twice at 3, was 2nd in the Chunichi Sports Sho Yonsai S. and ran in the Kikuka Sho, finishing 11th. At 4 he won his first graded race, the Kokura Daishoten, then the Chukyo Kinen. At 5 he won the Tanigawadake S., was 2nd in the Kitakyushu and Kokura Kinen, won the Fukushima Minpo Hai and went to the Tenno Sho (Autumn). With Tokai Teio a clear favorite, Let's Go Turkin was 11th choice. Held up, he won with a sharp late kick.
416: His temper was extraordinary (he'd bite horses alongside him) so despite his ability he lost many close races. Still, in autumn at 3 he won his first graded race, the Unicorn S., and the next year the Heian S. Then in the February S., newly a G1 that year, he ran a good time on Fuchu's dirt, turned to mud by rain, and won the JRA's first-ever dirt G1. Then long injury breaks and a worsening temper kept him from winning again.
418: Named after yokozuna Akebono for his huge frame of nearly 560 kg. It took 6 starts to win, but then his speed carried him through 4 straight wins into open class. After winning the Swan S. he lost to Trot Thunder's powerful finish in the Mile Championship, but romped in the Sprinters S. as favorite, sprint king at 3. He never won as an older horse.
419: A late bloomer who reached open class by winning the Fukushima Kinen in autumn at 3. Winless at 4, at 5 he was 2nd to Tamamo Cross in the Tenno Sho (Spring). The next year his talent bloomed, winning the American JCC and Nikkei Sho in a row.
420: With an astonishing finish he won the King George VI & Queen Elizabeth Diamond S. and the Arc, earning a world-best 141 lbs in the International Classification. Ratings were later reviewed and his was cut to 138, but his crushing power is still legendary. He won his first G1 in the 2000 Guineas, then in the Derby, though 2nd, closed from last over the final 2 furlongs to within half a length of Shahrastani, showing his potential. He won the Eclipse S. and King George, and was a solid favorite for the Arc, where his explosive late kick swept past the whole field in a flash for a record win. He retired at year's end to stud, but after his first season contracted Marie's disease, and with his runners doing little, the farm sold him. The JRA bought and imported him to Japan, and then his remaining offspring produced stars like Commander in Chief and White Muzzle, changing his image. In Japan he sired Kyoei March, King Halo, T.M. Ocean and more, a top-ranked sire. He died at 16 in 1999; Commander in Chief, White Muzzle and King Halo carried on, but his direct sire line is near extinction in Japan.
423: 3rd choice in the NHK Hai (G2, 2000m turf), he was 2nd to Rugby Ball, then 7th in the Derby. The Kyoto Kinen at 4 was his only graded win. His best offspring was Asahi Challenge C. winner Shinkaiun (92: Shin Miss Brown).
424: The 1990 Satsuki Sho winner. He won 5 straight including the Kisaragi Sho, was a Satsuki Sho contender, and beat favorites Ines Fujin and Mejiro Ryan for the crown - a father-son double after his sire Haiseiko. 2nd choice in the Derby, he couldn't quicken and was 5th to Ines Fujin. A tendon injury followed, and after a long break he retired without racing again.
425: Raced mainly on dirt from his debut, he shone in JRA-local races, winning the Derby Grand Prix by a distance. In 2001 he won the Kawasaki Kinen in record time, a race his granddam Rosita had won; two years later his uncle Kanetsu Fleuve won it too - a family race. He kept running hard on dirt, including a Dubai trip (10th), and won the first JBC Classic. Yet oddly he flopped in JRA graded races: 10th and 14th in two Japan Cup Dirts and 15th in the February S. Apart from a 5th in the Unicorn S. at 3, he never even made the top five. At stud he sired 2009 Tokyo Derby winner Silent Stamen. He covered mares until 2010 and died in July 2017.
426: Unbeaten in 3 from his debut, he won the Asahi Hai FS, a G1 double with his brother Admire Vega. At 3 he struggled in the classics - 7th, 6th and 4th - so, given his pedigree too, he switched to dirt. In his first dirt race, the JBC Classic, he won by 7 lengths as 2nd choice. He lost the Japan Cup Dirt and February S., but after a break swept Japan's big dirt G1s - Nambu Hai, Teio Sho, February S. - building an era as dirt king. He never won the Japan Cup Dirt, but had no real rivals. Declaring "we're done with dirt," his camp ran him in the Arima Kinen, his first turf race in 2 years 2 months; he was 7th. Taking that back, he ran in the February S. and was a dull 5th, then 6th in the Sankei Osaka Hai and 4th in the Kashiwa Kinen, and retired to stud. He was exported to Korea in 2011, but his Japanese offspring include graded winners Admire Deus and Albert.
427: Too late for the spring classics, he improved rapidly and won the Kobe Shimbun Hai, his first graded race. In the Kyoto Shimbun Hai he then beat double classic winner Narita Brian by a neck - a huge upset. Even in a prep, beating Narita Brian made Starman a household name. He was 5th in the Kikuka Sho, but brushed aside older horses for the first time in the Naruo Kinen, proving his ability. Then a fracture cost him 18 months. Back in summer at 5, after a dirt race, he was 2nd in the Kokura Kinen and Asahi Challenge C., showing signs of recovery, but a third injury ended his career.
436: He won the Aoba Sho and went to the Derby, losing to Neo Universe by half a length in 2nd. He won the Kobe Shimbun Hai in autumn but was 4th in the Kikuka Sho. Near misses continued: 3rd in the Arima Kinen, 2nd in the Nikkei Sho and Tenno Sho (Spring), 2nd in the Kyoto Daishoten. Then in the Tenno Sho (Autumn), with Peslier aboard, he showed new power and won his long-sought G1. As if releasing his frustration, he won the Japan Cup too, and in the Arima Kinen beat Tap Dance City, who had beaten him in the Takarazuka Kinen - the autumn older horses' triple crown, the best in training. In '05 he went straight to the Takarazuka Kinen, finishing 3rd, then was 2nd in the International S. in summer; 2nd in the Tenno Sho (Autumn), 3rd in the Japan Cup and 8th in the Arima Kinen followed as his form faded, and he retired. At stud he sired Oaks winner Saint Emilion and many middle-distance stars like Perusa, Animate Bio, Cosmo Mnemosyne and Trailblazer.
438: 5th on turf on debut, he won his second start on dirt by 9 lengths. He won the Cyclamen S. too, then the Zen-Nihon 2yo Yushun to reign as dirt champion of his crop. In spring at 3 he tried the NHK Mile C., finishing 4th. Back on dirt he won the Unicorn S. and Derby Grand Prix. Then he went about a year without a win, until in the Nambu Hai at 4 he beat dirt king Admire Don to bounce back, and won it again the next year. In '06 he went to Dubai and romped in the Godolphin Mile, prompting a sudden sale to Dubai's Godolphin and a move abroad. Fans hoped he'd return to race in Japan, but he retired in December '07 and went to stud in America.
417: Debuting in Hokkaido local racing at 2, he emerged in Southern Kanto, 2nd in all three legs of its triple crown: the Haneda Hai, Tokyo Derby and Tokyo Okan Sho. He then won the Hochi Grand Prix C., Kinpai and Mile Grand Prix. Best of all was the 20th Teio Sho, the first as a national G1, where he held off stars like Abukuma Poro and JRA dirt regular Battle Line by a neck.
421: His maiden win came on turf, but all 12 other wins were on dirt - a sand specialist. Running in many JRA-local races, he won the Hokkaido Sprint C. at 5, then 5 graded races at 6 including the Garnet S. and Kashiwa Kinen, and 8 dirt graded races by retiring at 9.
422: He emerged at 5, stepping up from the 10-million class to finish 3rd in the Nikkei Shinshun Hai; until then he had won 2 of 15. After 2 more wins he was a close 2nd in the Nikkei Sho. That autumn he won the Asahi Challenge C. in record time and was 2nd in the Arima Kinen with a bold forward run. The next year he won the Kinko Sho, was 3rd in the Takarazuka Kinen and won the Kyoto Daishoten. In the Japan Cup, against the best in training, Symboli Kris S., he won a legendary wire-to-wire race by 9 lengths for his first G1. After a heavy loss in the Arima Kinen, he romped in the '04 Takarazuka Kinen and announced an Arc bid. But his plane broke down and he flew in on a replacement just before the race; the punishing schedule left him 17th. He was 2nd to rival Zenno Rob Roy in the Arima Kinen. Racing on at 8 in '05, he won a third straight Kinko Sho but was 7th in the Takarazuka Kinen, and after more heavy losses retired that year.
428: A late-blooming middle-distance dirt horse who changed the image of his sire Soccer Boy. Lacking punch early, he was 2nd 3 times before winning his 5th start, and only took off in summer at 4. He then won the Winter S. and local Nagoya's Nagoya Daishoten, and in JRA-local races battled stars like Hokuto Vega, Lively Mount and Amazon Opera, showing fans the fun of dirt racing. At 5 he won the Tokyo Daishoten, and was 2nd in it the next year as a G1. At 7 he was 6th in the Dubai World Cup, and ran tough on dirt until 8, winning 13 races.
429: 5th in the Asahi Hai Sansai S., 2nd in the Keisei Hai, 3rd in the Yayoi Sho, 8th in the Satsuki Sho, 3rd in the NHK Hai (G2) and, as 12th choice, 3rd in the Derby - always running well, never quite winning. In autumn he won the St. Lite Kinen, his first graded race. 2nd in the Kikuka Sho, he was 4th in the Japan Cup, best of the Japanese ahead of Oguri Cap, and 3rd as favorite in Oguri's farewell Arima Kinen. He ran in 28 straight graded races from the Asahi Hai Sansai S., slipping year by year, yet remained an essential supporting player.
430: The monster of local Utsunomiya, whose 43 wins set a local thoroughbred record. At 9 he was entered in the All Comers as "North Kanto's best," but in his first turf race was 7th. He went to stud but retired in '07 for poor results, and has since lived quietly at Araki Training Farm in Hokkaido.
431: He won 3 straight from the Hiiragi Sho, including the Keisei Hai, but leg trouble ruled out the NHK Mile C. Coming back in the Yasuda Kinen, he was a fine 3rd at 3 behind Taiki Blizzard and Genuine, and 3rd to Bubble Gum Fellow in the Mainichi Okan, but then ran poorly as if burned out.
432: He debuted late, in September at 3, and was 15th in his hyped debut, but improved steadily, reaching open class with 3 straight wins by the end of his 3yo year. At 5 he won the Aichi Hai, Kitakyushu Kinen and Mainichi Okan in a row, then was a fine 3rd behind T.M. Opera O and Meisho Doto in the Tenno Sho (Autumn), ahead of Narita Top Road and Stay Gold. But an injury to his right foreleg followed, and despite long treatment he never returned.
434: Crushed in the Spring S., he missed the classics. After 6 months off he won 3 straight in autumn, and just 3 months after returning won the Nakayama Kimpai. At 5 he won the Nakayama Kimpai and Tokyo Shimbun Hai, but a tendon injury forced him to retire to stud. His daughter Gina Fontaine (Empress Hai winner) is the dam of Funabashi star Casino Fontaine, who led all the way to beat JRA horses in the 2021 Kawasaki Kinen.
435: At 3 he was a fine 3rd against older horses in the Takarazuka Kinen. The next year he won the Nakayama Kinen, his first graded race, then the Milers C. in record time, and in France was 2nd by half a length in the Prix du Moulin de Longchamp. Erratic like many front-runners, he also had many heavy defeats. Winless in autumn at 5, he tried dirt again in the Japan Cup Dirt but blasted off in front and collapsed. At 6 he won the Milers C., his first win in 2 years, and in his first race of '07 led to win the Nakayama Kinen easily. When it worked, he was formidable. At stud his second crop's Logotype won the Asahi Hai FS and Satsuki Sho, with fellow son Gottfried 3rd in that Asahi Hai FS.
437: Favorite for the Asahi Hai FS, he lost by a neck to A Shin Champ's record 1:33.5. A close 2nd to Neo Universe in the Satsuki Sho, he was crushed in the Derby and Kikuka Sho. But he won the Sapporo Kinen against older horses like Air Eminem, and the next year crushed Lohengrin and others in the Nakayama Kinen in record time - hard to beat at middle distances. In autumn at 4 a tendon injury forced retirement. At stud he sired Ocean S. winner Sakura Gospel and Flower C. winner Sakura Plaisir.
433: "The demon of Kyoto": all 8 of his wins came at Kyoto. He won his debut and the Shiragiku Sho, but injury cost him the spring classics; he was 3rd in the Kyoto Shimbun Hai and 10th in the Kikuka Sho. At 5 he won the Subaru S., then the Kyoto Kinen from the front for his first graded win, and the Kyoto Daishoten in autumn. In the Takarazuka Kinen at 6, as others swung wide off the torn-up inside, he alone dove to the rail, a thrilling 3rd.
439: The 1988 Arc winner, who went to stud in Japan and built an era alongside Sunday Silence and Brian's Time. Until 3 he only ran well in graded races, emerging at 4: he won 4 straight including the Gran Premio di Milano and Gran Premio del Jockey Club, then was 2nd in both the Grand Prix de Saint-Cloud and the Arc. At 5 he won the Premio Presidente della Repubblica and Gran Premio di Milano, and in autumn finally won the Arc. He then went to Japan for the Japan Cup as favorite but was 5th to Pay the Butler, retiring after it to stud in Japan. His first crop gave Derby winner Winning Ticket, fillies' double winner Vega, mile queen North Flight and Tenno Sho winner Sakura Chitose O, and he was leading sire in 1994. Later came Air Groove, Jungle Pocket and many more - a huge success. But heirs were scarce; Jungle Pocket and Miracle Admire sired G1 winners, yet his direct line is now declining.
440: In his first graded race, the Derby, he was a fine 2nd to unbeaten double winner Tokai Teio. That autumn he held off Ibuki Maikagura by a length and a half in the Kikuka Sho for his first G1 - in his 7th start, then the fastest ever. But his brilliant career ended there. The incurable tendon injury struck his glass legs, and like many of his sire's runners, he couldn't escape leg trouble. Back a year later in the Arima Kinen, he was a dismal 13th, ran once more and retired to stud.
441: A highly rated foreign-bred, he won his debut but injury cost him his 2yo year and spring at 3. Returning in May at 3, he raced mainly in his class and matured in autumn at 4. Stepping up in the Keisei Hai Autumn H., he won easily in a Japanese record 1:31.5. Favorite for the Sprinters S., he was 10th, but then won the Mile Championship for a G1. Little followed, and he retired at 5 to stud, siring Fuji S. winner Meiner Seagull and Asahi Hai FS runner-up Meiner Robust.
442: Top two in 70% of his races, never out of the top five, and outside the top three only once (5th in the Derby) - yet just 5th choice for the Satsuki Sho. At 2 he was 2nd to Daishin Fubuki in the Asahi Hai Sansai S., then 3rd to filly Dyna Fairy in the Keisei Hai and narrowly beaten by Daishin Fubuki again in the Yayoi Sho, so fans saw him as a horse who couldn't win. But in the Satsuki Sho he held off Fresh Voice by a neck, shedding that image. 5th to Dyna Gulliver in the Derby, he then beat future great miler Nippo Teio by a length and a half in the Radio Tampa Sho. Leg trouble then ended his career, and he went to stud. Though minor, he sired perfect miler Trot Thunder (89: La Seine Wonder), unbeaten at a mile with 2 G1s, the Yasuda Kinen and Mile Championship, and Kabutoyama Kinen and Kokura Daishoten winner One More Love Way (89: Zengi Ghost) - a fine effort.
444: Strongly carrying the blood of Lyphard, sire of many fast horses, he starred from a mile to middle distances. The turning point was the NZT Yonsai S. at 3: after 8ths in the Satsuki Sho and NHK Hai, he switched to the mile and won by three and a half lengths with his speed. He won the Hakodate Kinen and Swan S., lost the Mile Championship as heavy favorite by a nose to Takara Steel, and was named champion sprinter. At 4 he was 2nd in the Yasuda Kinen and Takarazuka Kinen, then led all the way to win the Tenno Sho (Autumn), and avenged himself in the Mile Championship by 5 lengths - champion sprinter again, plus champion older male.
445: 2nd on debut, he won his next 3 including the Kyodo News Hai Yonsai S., becoming a classic contender. He was a disappointing 10th in the Satsuki Sho, but won the Japanese Derby by half a length from Grandpa's Dream to reach the top of his crop. He showed his class with a 2nd in the Kikuka Sho, then beat seasoned older horses like Miho Shinzan and Gallop Dyna in the Arima Kinen, earning Horse of the Year and champion 3yo colt.
446: Unbeaten in 3, including the Kyodo News Hai Yonsai S., he was a classic star, but injury cost him the whole spring. He was 4th in both the Kyoto Shimbun Hai and Kikuka Sho on his return. At 4 his talent bloomed: he beat crop rival Suda Hawk in the Osaka Hai; ran out of stamina in the Tenno Sho (Spring); crushed mile king Nippo Teio in the Mainichi Okan; and beat double winner Miho Shinzan and other greats in the Tenno Sho (Autumn) for a G1. Every fan regretted his early retirement that year, but given his success at stud it was the right call: he sired Sakura Bakushin O (89: Sakura Hagoromo) and many graded winners.
447: With an astonishing finish he won 3 graded races, including the Hanshin Sansai S. His fiery temper meant he always raced from the back, but his all-or-nothing charges thrilled fans. At 3 he beat Asahi Hai winner Lindo Shaver in the Yayoi Sho, then met Tokai Teio for the first time in the Satsuki Sho, finishing 4th. He won the NHK Hai (G2, 2000m) clearly, hoping for revenge in the Derby, but was injured just before it. In autumn he was 2nd in both the Kyoto Shimbun Hai and the Kikuka Sho, just short. After 3 more races, leg trouble ended his career without glory.
448: He finally won in his 7th start, in May at 3, then took off, winning 3 straight up to the Yamayuri S. After summer he was 2nd in the Kobe Shimbun Hai, his first graded try, then in the Kyoto Shimbun Hai swept past Derby winner Winner's Circle and improver Osaichi George for his first graded win, and was Kikuka Sho favorite. His sire Bamboo Atlas won the Derby but was injured after the Kyoto Shimbun Hai and went to stud before the Kikuka Sho. Carrying his sire's regret, Begin moved up from midfield and pulled away in the straight to win. Trainer Fuse, who also trained Bamboo Atlas, said, "Winning the Kikuka Sho with an Atlas foal was my dream." But injury followed, and the Kikuka Sho was his last race.
449: A leading miler of 1980s Europe and America, she won 10 G1s, including two Prix Jacques le Marois and two Breeders' Cup Miles, and as a broodmare produced Kingmambo and East of the Moon - a legendary great mare. She won 2 G1s at 2 and was France's champion 2yo filly. At 3 she won the English and French 1000 Guineas, the Prix Jacques le Marois and Prix du Moulin, then won the Breeders' Cup Mile in America in record time. At 4 she won the Prix d'Ispahan, then both the Jacques le Marois and Breeders' Cup Mile again. Dominant at a mile with 9 wins and two 2nds from 11, she retired that year. Her first foal, Kingmambo, was a huge success on the track and at stud. Her granddaughter Loves Only Me, imported to Japan, produced two G1 winners: Loves Only You and Real Steel.
451: Called the greatest mare in American history by some. Unbeaten in 13, with 8 G1s including the Breeders' Cup Distaff, she was nicknamed "Miss Perfect." A serious injury in autumn at 2 cost her until autumn at 3, but at 4 she won G1 after G1 as if making up for it, beating 7-time G1 winner Gulch and other males in the Whitney H. Then came the Breeders' Cup Distaff. Among great mares like Winning Colors and Goodbye Halo, she was a clear 1.5 favorite. Far behind leaders Winning Colors and Goodbye Halo at the top of the straight, she shrugged off the sloppy track and ran them down to complete her unbeaten legend. She retired after the race. A superb broodmare, she produced 3 G1 winners including My Flag, and second foal Our Emblem, though no G1 winner, succeeded at stud.
452: Won 7 G1s in America, including the Kentucky Oaks, an idol whose battles with Derby-winning filly Winning Colors made her popular. Dominant from her debut, she won 2 G1s at 2, the Demoiselle S. and Hollywood Starlet S. At 3 she clashed with the unbeaten Winning Colors, winning the Las Virgenes S. but losing the Santa Anita Oaks. She then won the Mother Goose S. and CCA Oaks, meeting Winning Colors again in the Breeders' Cup Distaff, but older star Personal Ensign won, with Winning Colors 2nd and her 3rd. Despite 4 G1 wins that year, champion 3yo filly went to Winning Colors. At 4 she won the La Canada S. but lost narrowly in G1s, retiring after a 6th in the Breeders' Cup Distaff. As a broodmare in Japan she produced Takamatsunomiya Kinen winner King Halo.
453: From his debut on turf he kept finishing 2nd to 4th, losing 12 straight, before finally winning in his 13th start in autumn at 3. He still struggled on turf, but switched to dirt in summer at 4 he was transformed, quickly winning 3 to reach open class. In his first graded race, the Heian S., he charged from last to win. He was 11th in his first G1, the February S., but then won the Tokai S. and Elm S. After a 4th in the Japan Cup Dirt he won JRA-local races like the Nagoya Daishoten and Breeders' GC, then was 2nd to Kane Hekili in the Japan Cup Dirt. Among the best in a deep dirt division, but as a closer he dropped more races than front-runners, and won nothing from '09.
454: She ran in 35 G1s in six countries, including Japan and America, winning 8 - then a record for a European mare - and was called "the Iron Lady" for her toughness. From 3 she ran a punishing schedule: the 1000 Guineas, an Irish 1000 Guineas trial, the Irish 2000 Guineas and Irish 1000 Guineas, four weeks running, then the Oaks and Irish Derby. Her only title was the Irish 2000 Guineas - the first ever won by a filly. At 4 she won just one G1 in 11 races in six months. At 5 she matured, winning 4 G1s: the Prix Ganay, Coronation C., International S. and Phoenix Champion S. She was 3rd in both the King George and the Arc, then 4th in the Japan Cup, but won the Fuji S. with an otherworldly finish, stunning fans. At 6 she won the Coronation C. again and retired. Great things were hoped of her as a broodmare, but she died in an accident right after her first covering, leaving no offspring.
455: Raced mainly on turf until 6, winning 6 and placing 3rd in the CBC Sho at 5, but he plateaued and switched to dirt at 7. He won the Garnet S. and then the Negishi S., and in autumn added the Tokyo Hai and Hyogo Gold T., becoming a top dirt sprinter. At 8 in '07 he raced mostly in JRA-local races, winning 3 graded races including a second Tokyo Hai. From '08 he won the Sakitama Hai and was 3rd in the JBC Sprint, showing no decline, and retired after a 7th in the Tokyo Sprint in April 2010, at 11. 14 wins from 63 - a horse who truly paid his owner back.
456: A filly who matched or beat the colts, winning the Tenno Sho (Autumn), and was called "the Empress." Talented early, she was the classic star. A fever kept her out of the Oka Sho, but she romped in the Oaks to prove herself best of her crop. After a fracture, she showed her true power on returning at 4: she won the Mermaid S. and Sapporo Kinen, then beat a strong field in the Tenno Sho (Autumn). 2nd to Pilsudski in the Japan Cup, best of the Japanese, and 3rd to Silk Justice in the Arima Kinen, she became the first female Horse of the Year since Tomei. The next year she was 2nd again, close behind El Condor Pasa, in the Japan Cup. As a broodmare she produced Admire Groove, Forgettable and Rulership, cementing her status as the greatest of great mares, before dying in April 2013.
458: At a US 2yo training sale he clocked under 11 seconds for a furlong and sold for a fair $120,000 despite an obscure pedigree. He debuted in October in a 1200m dirt race at Kyoto, winning by 7 lengths, then, stepping up in distance, dominated the Hyogo Junior Grand Prix and Zen-Nihon 2yo Yushun to top his crop on dirt. At 3 he aimed for the classics, starting on turf in the Arlington C., but did nothing and finished 12th. Back on dirt he struggled to beat Nathaniel, already beaten before, in the Fukuryu S., and lost a duel by a neck to Golden Ticket in the Hyogo Championship, his first dirt defeat. After a 6th in the Japan Dirt Derby and 2nds in the Leopard S. and Tokyo Hai, he won the JRA-local G1 JBC Sprint against older horses, breaking clear from up front like a champion. But in the Japan Cup Dirt he couldn't get his usual forward position and was 14th. At 4 he lacked sparkle in JRA graded races - 4th in the Negishi S., 9th in the February S. At local tracks he won the Kurofune Sho and Tokyo Sprint, then went over a year without a win despite running well. In summer at 5, carrying 58.5 kg, he romped by 4 lengths in Saga's Summer Champion, then won the Tokyo Hai. In the big one, the JBC Sprint, against 3-time sprint graded winner Seikrimson, defending champion Summer Wind and turf convert Dasher Go Go, he unleashed a powerful finish to win it again after 2 years. He also won the Hyogo Gold T. at 5 and was 3rd in the JBC Sprint at 6 - a star of recent dirt sprinting.
459: After making her name in Argentina, she moved to America and won 12 G1s, including two Breeders' Cup Distaffs - then the record for a mare - and was Eclipse champion older mare in 1989 and 1990. In Argentina she just missed in G1s, then won the Gran Premio Palermo (G1) by 12 lengths in November at 3, earning a move to America. She struggled to win in her first year there, but showed her true worth from 1989, at 5, winning 7 G1s from the Santa Margarita Invitational H. to the Breeders' Cup Distaff. At 6 she won 5 more G1s, including another Distaff, and was champion older mare again. At 7 her form faded, and after 3 losses she retired. Her 4 foals disappointed - 2 unraced, 1 maiden, 1 single winner - but her grandchildren include G1 winners Affluent and Fort Larned.
457: Small at around 420 kg, she won her debut by 9 lengths, then the Sazanka Sho and Elfin S. After a 4th in the Tulip Sho, she beat London Bridge in the Oka Sho for her first classic. The longer trip told in the Oaks, where she was 3rd, but in autumn she won the Shuka Sho for a fillies' double. As an older mare she struggled against colts, but won the Queen Elizabeth II Cup at 5, her first win in 2 years, her class showing. Her half-brother Kizuna, 15 years younger, won the 2013 Japanese Derby.
460: She won the Suzuran Sho by 6 lengths and the Hakodate Sansai S. by 5 - called a sure classic bet. But her temper was the miscalculation. At 3 she refused to enter the gate for the Sumire Sho, had to retake a training exam and missed the Oka Sho. After the Yonsai Himba Tokubetsu (East) she made her long-sought Oaks, finishing 3rd. Winless at 3, she slumped in spring at 4 too. But teamed with master Yukio Okabe, she tried a late charge for the first time in the Keio Hai Autumn H. and won in a time equal to the then world record. She lost the Tenno Sho (Autumn), Japan Cup and Arima Kinen, but at 5 won the Sprinters S. (G2) and Keio Hai Spring C.. In the Yasuda Kinen she dueled Nippo Teio, losing by just 0.2 seconds in 2nd. After a 4th in Tamamo Cross's Tenno Sho (Autumn), she retired. As a dam she produced Stage Champ (90: Real Shadai).
443: He won 4 straight from his second maiden race, including the NHK Mile C., then lost over six months to injury. After a long slump he won the Keisei Hai Autumn H. at 4. At 5 he was hurt acting up in the gate before the Lord Derby CT and put down.
450: She won 3 straight including the Sapporo Sansai S., then had two long breaks. In autumn of the next year she won the Autumn Sprint S. and Himba Tokyo Times Hai, then was 5th in the Mile Championship despite a slow start.
461: Winner of the 1993 Arc and dam of 4 G1 winners including Galileo and Sea the Stars - a historic great mare of unmatched success. On the track she drew little attention: 6th in the Prix de Diane, 3rd in the Prix Vermeille, and just 2 G3 wins until midway through her 4yo year. Then in the Arc, as 11th choice, she beat stars like Hernando, Opera House and User Friendly, the first mare to win in 10 years. Perhaps seen as a fluke, she was only 10th choice for the Japan Cup, the lowest ever for an Arc winner, and finished 8th. She raced until 5, winning one G2. As a broodmare she produced future greats Galileo and Sea the Stars, plus 2 more G1 winners and 2 graded winners - unprecedented success, her blood now spread worldwide.
462: By double classic winner Neo Universe, brother of Derby winner Fusaichi Concorde - a blueblood. In a much-watched debut in October at 2 he beat Reach the Crown and Buena Vista. In the Kyoto 2yo S. bold tactics backfired and he was 3rd as favorite. At 3 he won the Wakakoma S. with a sharp run, then in his first graded race, the Spring S., beat Asahi Hai FS runner-up Fifth Petal and future NHK Mile C. runner-up Red Spada, becoming a classic contender. In the Satsuki Sho, billed as a Big Three with Logi Universe and Reach the Crown, his powerful late charge won it, making him the best of his crop. But in the Derby the heavy going blunted his kick and he was a shock 12th. Back from a break, he was 4th as favorite in the Kobe Shimbun Hai, then crushed in the Kikuka Sho and Arima Kinen, and developed a tendon injury. Back after 18 months, he was a good 5th to Rulership in the Kinko Sho as 9th choice, but the injury recurred and he retired to stud.
463: She won her debut and the Fukushima Sansai S. easily. 3rd to Nishino Flower and Saneisankyu in the Hanshin Sansai Himba S., her outstanding ability was still clear. But as a foreign-bred she couldn't run in the classics, racing mainly at a mile. Never flashy but always efficient and consistent, she won 10 of 15. Of her 5 losses, all but a 6th on her first comeback in the Carnation C. were top-three finishes, and many fans loved her steady strength. Surprisingly, her first G1 came only in her farewell, the Mile Championship at 4 - finishing a career with a win is hard enough, yet she did it with her first crown. It was also the first G1 for "the great trainer of Heisei," Kazuo Fujisawa. As a dam she produced graded-class runners like '01 Chukyo Kinen winner Lord Cronos (95: Tony Bin) and Treasure (98: Brian's Time).
464: Unbeaten in her first 3, including the NZT Yonsai S., she was overwhelming NHK Mile C. favorite but finished 14th. After a break she went straight to the Shuka Sho and held off Erimo Chic for a G1. In the Japan Cup, a 3yo filly against world stars like Singspiel, she was a superb 2nd and highly rated. But she was 10th in the Arima Kinen and retired after just 7 races. As a dam she produced Hanshin Daishoten winner Gustave Cry (08: Heart's Cry).
465: Frail from birth, she took time to debut, finally running at 3 and winning by a distance. 2nd in the St. Paulia Sho and 3rd in the Flower C., she missed the Oka Sho. But she won the Wasurenagusa Sho by 4 lengths, was a confident 2nd choice for the Oaks and won clearly, though by three-quarters of a length - the first fillies' G1 for Brian's Time. In the Queen Elizabeth II Cup she lost a nose-to-nose battle with top mare Hishi Amazon. As an older mare she won the Chukyo Kinen and was 2nd in the Keihan Hai, holding her own against colts. She retired in spring at 4 but left no notable offspring.
466: She won 7 G1s in America, including the Breeders' Cup Juvenile Fillies, losing only twice, both 2nds. So consistent she was called "the second Ruffian," she broke down fatally in her last race, the Breeders' Cup Distaff. Champion 2yo filly after winning the Juvenile Fillies, at 3 she won the Ashland S. by 5 lengths. She was 2nd to front-running Seaside Attraction in the Kentucky Oaks, then reeled off 5 straight G1s including the Mother Goose S. and Test S. In the big Breeders' Cup Distaff she was co-favorite with Bayakoa, an Argentine import with 11 US G1 wins. They dueled into the straight, but in the final furlong she fell, was found beyond saving and put down - remembered as the Breeders' Cup's greatest tragedy.
467: She beat Nippo Teio in the Keisei Hai and was 2nd choice for the Oka Sho, but finished 17th, then a narrow 4th in the Queen Elizabeth II Cup. At 4 she won 3 graded races against colts - the Epsom C., Niigata Kinen and All Comers - proving her talent. As a broodmare she produced Aoba Sho winner Summer Suspicion (92: Sunday Silence) and Rosenkavalier (93: Sunday Silence), winner of the St. Lite Kinen, American JCC, Nikkei Sho and Meguro Kinen.
469: Just 11 starts, but 8 wins, two 2nds and a 5th - nearly perfect, top two in over 90%. At a mile she never lost, whatever the grade, winning both mile G1s, the Yasuda Kinen and Mile Championship - the only mare to do so. She also ran 2nd to Hokuto Vega over 2400m in the Queen Elizabeth II Cup. Truly a modern great, "the Queen of the Mile." Retiring at the end of her 4yo year, she produced Fukushima Kinen runner-up Miscast (98: Sunday Silence), who went to stud despite no graded win and sired Tenno Sho winner Beat Black.
470: He struggled to get out of the lower classes, but his camp believed in him, stepping him up into graded races early, even the Argentina Kyowakoku Hai as a 2-time winner at 3. Reaching his prime with 5 wins, he ran 2nd to Admire Fuji in the Nikkei Shinshun Hai at 5, his third graded try against older horses. After a break he won the Kokura Kinen in record time and was 2nd in the Tenno Sho (Autumn), his peak. From '07 his best was a 2nd in the Kinko Sho, and he retired to stud in May '09.
471: A New Zealand mare who won the 1989 Japan Cup in a world record for 2400m on turf after a fierce duel with Oguri Cap. By Three Legs out of a Moss Trooper mare, a typically local pedigree, she won 3 G1s in New Zealand and Australia, then came to the Japan Cup at 6 in 1989. The field was stellar - Arc winner Carroll House, world-record holder Hawkster, and Japan's best: Oguri Cap, Super Creek, Inari One - and she was overlooked as 9th choice. But she tracked the fast pace from a good spot, broke clear in the straight and held off Oguri Cap's charge by a neck in an astonishing world-record 2:22.2, burning her image into Japanese fans' minds. Back home she won 2 more G1s and retired. As a broodmare she produced G1 winner Brew and more down to her grandchildren, and is in her country's Hall of Fame.
472: She romped in the Tulip Sho (OP) in her third start, then won the Oka Sho with more in hand than the margin showed. In the Oaks she stayed rock solid for a double. Hopes rose for the fillies' Triple Crown, but leg trouble struck just before, and she went straight to the Queen Elizabeth II Cup, finishing 3rd. She retired after a 13th in the next Takarazuka Kinen. As a dam she produced three sires: Derby winner Admire Vega (96: Sunday Silence), dirt king Admire Don (99: Timber Country) and Admire Boss (97: Sunday Silence). Her only daughter and last foal, Historic Star, never raced due to frailty, but produced Harp Star, winner of the Hanshin JF and Oka Sho. Queen Vega was top-class as a broodmare too.
473: At 3 she won the Sweet Pea S. and went to the Oaks, then was 3rd in the Shuka Sho and won the Turquoise S. In '05 she won her first graded race, the Nakayama Himba S. After a slump she was 2nd in the '07 Kyoto Himba S. and 2nd again in her farewell, the Nakayama Himba S. - no win, but back-to-back graded 2nds as a proud exit.
474: By Pegasus Tosho Boy out of the lady Hagino Top Lady, she sold for 100 million yen and drew attention from the start. Debuting late, in February at 3, she was excluded from the Oka Sho trial, won the Anemone Sho but lost the Oka Sho entry draw, and was a shock 2nd in the Wasurenagusa Sho instead. In the Oaks a costly slow start left her 5th - a 3yo year of unmet hopes. But at 4 she found her path in sprints, fighting many great duels with her "eternal rival" Daitaku Helios and winning two G1s, the Yasuda Kinen and Sprinters S. She seemed a pampered blueblood, but reportedly had more grit than the colts.
476: He won in his 4th start, then as 12th choice ran a good 4th in the Asahi Hai FS. At 3 he won the Shinzan Kinen clearly by 3 lengths, breaking clear from up front. He was to run in the Spring S. but was slow to recover condition, going straight to the Satsuki Sho, where he was 13th, far behind Victoire Pisa, then 15th in the NHK Mile C., and gave up the Derby. He later won the Tokyo Shimbun Hai and Lord Derby CT, was 5th in the Yasuda Kinen, and as 14th choice 2nd in the Hanshin C. at 5 - steady around a mile. At 7 he moved to sprints, and in the Hakodate Sprint S., with Straight Girl, 3rd in consecutive G1s, a heavy favorite, he surged from midfield for his first graded win in about 2 years. He met crop-mate Cosmo Sensor in over 10 races, and in 2012 they finished 1-2 in both the New Year S. and Tokyo Shimbun Hai.
477: Unbeaten in 4 after winning her debut by 10 lengths, Agnes Flora went to the Oka Sho. Her dam was Oaks winner Agnes Lady. Wanting to "win the Oka Sho her dam couldn't," the owner bred Lady to Royal Ski, proven at middle distances, and Flora was born. She won the Oka Sho as hoped. Going for a dam-daughter double in the Oaks, she was 2nd to A Shin Sunny, then developed leg trouble and retired. But Flora had a bigger role: passing her talent on. Her 4th foal was an elegant chestnut by Sunday Silence - Agnes Flight, who gave jockey Kawachi, rider of her and her dam, his long-sought Derby. The next year she produced unbeaten Satsuki Sho winner Agnes Tachyon, mother of two classic winners.
478: The first and best of Mejiro Ryan's offspring, a great mare who starred in the fillies' division from debut to retirement. Outstanding from the start, she won the Hanshin Sansai Himba S. with 3 wins from 4. Her temper showed then, sometimes fighting her rider and losing. In the classics she battled Kyoei March: beaten by 4 lengths in the Oka Sho, she got revenge in the Oaks, then won the All Comers against older colts and beat Kyoei March clearly in the Shuka Sho, earning champion 3yo filly. Unlike Air Groove she didn't battle the top colts, but she won a G1 every year: the Hanshin Sansai Himba S. at 2, the Oaks and Shuka Sho at 3, and two Queen Elizabeth II Cups at 4 and 5 - 5 G1s, then a record for a mare - and JRA Awards 4 years running, 1996-99. In fillies' races she was beaten only 3 times (two 2nds, one 3rd), by just 4 horses in all, and beat Air Groove head-to-head in the Queen Elizabeth II Cup at 4 - truly "the greatest of great mares."
481: She won her debut by 2 lengths, then as 8th choice was 2nd by half a length in the Sapporo 2yo S., going on to the Hanshin JF. At 3 she was 2nd in both the Tulip Sho and Oka Sho. She kept running well without winning until her second win, the Kyoto Himba S. Winless after that, she retired after a 6th in the '07 Oro C. to become a broodmare.
482: She won her debut, the Sapporo Sansai S. and Daily Hai Sansai S., all by three and a half lengths or more. In the Hanshin Sansai Himba S. she beat talented rivals like Saneisankyu and Shinko Lovely, and was champion 2yo filly. The next year, with the authority of a 2yo queen, she won the Oka Sho by three and a half lengths from future Oaks winner Adorable - a true "child prodigy." But in the Oaks and the Queen Elizabeth II Cup the distance stopped her, 7th and 3rd, and she lost her crown. Yet that wasn't the end. Targeting sprints to use her abundant speed, she beat strong older horses like Daitaku Helios and Yamanin Zephyr in the Sprinters S. as a 3yo filly - a comeback win, her second G1 that year, and champion 3yo filly. JRA Awards two years running - simply superb. She retired after a 3rd in the next Sprinters S., with 7 wins from 16. As a broodmare she produced Satsuki Sho and Derby runner Nishino Seiryu (96: Brian's Time) and Aichi Hai runner-up Nishino Manamusume (04: Agnes Tachyon).
483: She romped in the Yonsai Himba Tokubetsu (West) trial by 7 lengths and went to the Oka Sho with 4 wins and a 3rd from 5. Letting Mini Skirt lead, she tracked in 2nd and pulled away to beat Mejiro Dober by 4 lengths - a perfect race. Going for a double in the Oaks, she was 11th, partly due to the distance, but won the Rose S. in autumn. In the Shuka Sho, though, she lost again to Mejiro Dober. Focusing on shorter races, she was 2nd to Taiki Shuttle in the Mile Championship. As an older mare she won the Hankyu Hai and Kyoto Kimpai but never an older-horse G1. She also tried dirt, finishing 2nd in the JRA-local G1 Nambu Hai, and raced until 6. As a broodmare she produced Satsuki Sho runner-up Triumph March (06: Special Week). She died in spring 2007, but her granddaughter Sanbure Muse (10: Daiwa Major) won the Fuyo S. (OP) - her speed lives on.
475: At 3 she was 6th in the Oaks, 2nd in the Shuka Sho and 8th in the Queen Elizabeth II Cup. A sharp closer, but at the mercy of the pace, she fell just short of a crown. At 4 she started in spring, improved through summer and was 2nd to Air Groove in the Sapporo Kinen. In her second Queen Elizabeth II Cup, her powerful kick caught favorite Dance Partner near the line for a G1.
479: Debuting late in October at 3, she steadily won races and the next May took the Takamatsunomiya Hai (now Kinen), newly a sprint G1 - the fastest older-horse G1 win ever, 6 months after her debut. In that year's Sprinters S. she chased down front-runner A Shin Washington in a thrilling finish. With no result for a long time after the photo, Nakayama buzzed, "The first G1 dead heat?" She won by just 1 cm. In Japan's sprint scene, she is the only filly or mare to win both sprint G1s in one year. She retired after a 4th in the Sprinters S. at 5. Her best offspring are 5-time winner Firenze (01: Sunday Silence) and Vincennes (09: Deep Impact), Tokyo Shimbun Hai winner and Yasuda Kinen runner-up.
484: A bargain under 10 million yen, she won her debut and the Phoenix Sho. But in the classics she was 11th in the Oka Sho, 9th in the Oaks and 4th in the Queen Elizabeth II Cup At 4 she won the Coral S. (OP) for her first win in a while, then the Keihan Hai, her first graded race At 5 she won the Emerald S. and Kinko Sho in a row, plus the Kokura Kinen and All Comers. The next year she was 2nd to Yamanin Zephyr in the Yasuda Kinen as 14th choice and 2nd to Mejiro McQueen in the Takarazuka Kinen, becoming the top-earning mare. Running 51 races safely from 2 to 6, she won 4 graded races and was twice 2nd in 11 G1s - a tough mare called "the Iron Lady."
468: Half-sister to Sakura Chitose O. A late improver, she won a 5-million race and the Queen S. In the Queen Elizabeth II Cup, as 10th choice, she outdueled Bright Sandy to win, and later won the Fuchu Himba S.
480: Steady and rarely out of the top five, she won the Hanshin Himba Tokubetsu at 4 and ran in the Japan Cup and Arima Kinen before retiring. As a dam she produced classic runner She's a Chance (93: Sunday Silence).
485: Half-sister of the monster Oguri Cap. She debuted at local Kasamatsu like her brother, won 6 of 7 with a 2nd, and moved to the JRA. Puzzled by turf, she was 9th in the Elfin S., but 2nd in the Tulip Sho earned an Oka Sho spot - the classic road her brother never took. Ridden by Yutaka Take, who rode her brother's farewell, she saved ground in midfield and unleashed an Oguri-like kick to win by a nose. Brother and sister, both local-bred, G1 winners - simply superb. But she was crushed in the Oaks and slumped as if her Oka Sho never happened; racing to the end of her 3yo year, the Oka Sho was her only JRA win.
486: She won her debut, then ran poorly 4 times. But in the Tulip Sho (OP) she beat 2yo queen Nishino Flower by three and a half lengths and was 2nd in the Oka Sho, living up to early hopes. In the Oaks she held off Saneisankyu by half a length to be crowned. With leg trouble in autumn she went straight to the Queen Elizabeth II Cup, a solid 4th, having raced in all three legs of a chaotic fillies' classic year. She retired after it, producing '99 Kyoto Kinen winner Emocion (95: Tony Bin) and Sumire S. winner Salire (96: Tony Bin).
487: 2nd in his first 2 starts, he then won 3 straight - a maiden, the Junior C. and the Kyodo News Hai. His first graded win beat future NHK Mile C. winner Danon Chantilly and Spring S. winner Arrivee, and big things were expected. But he was last (18th) in the Satsuki Sho and 16th in the Derby. He returned the next year but couldn't regain his early-3yo shine and retired. Close relatives include great sires Woodman and New England.
488: JRA-raised, he sold for 27.3 million yen, the top price at the JRA Breeze-Up Sale, and was highly rated. 2nd on debut, he won his maiden by 6 lengths, then the Niigata 2yo S. by a length despite racing wide on heavy ground. Skipping the Tokyo Sports Hai 2yo S. with a hoof inflammation, he went straight to the Asahi Hai FS and won it like his sire - 2yo champion. At 3 he was 8th in the Yayoi Sho after the break, then 3rd in the Satsuki Sho under Hiroyuki Uchida. 3rd choice for the Derby, he was 13th on heavy ground. In autumn he was 3rd in both the Kobe Shimbun Hai and Kikuka Sho, showing G1 quality. At 4 he won the Epsom C., his first win in 18 months, but was 16th in the Takarazuka Kinen, then went on a long break and retired without returning.
489: She won her debut in January at 3, was 2nd in the Tulip Sho and Oka Sho, then won the Oaks. In autumn she went to France: 2nd in the G3 Prix de la Nonette, she was favorite for the G1 Prix Vermeille but, hampered in the straight, finished 6th behind Carling. Back home she tried the Kikuka Sho, again favorite (5th). As an older mare she won the first Queen Elizabeth II Cup under its new conditions - a great mare who tried everything. Her broodmare career brought steady runners but few graded winners, until her 6th foal Federalist won the Nakayama Kimpai and Nakayama Kinen, proving her quality.
490: Named after a red Hawaiian bird. 3rd on debut, she won her next 2, then, as 2nd choice from the widest draw, slipped up the inside in the straight to win the Hanshin JF - 2yo queen and her sire King Kamehameha's first G1 winner. At 3 she fought her rider and was 2nd in the Tulip Sho, but won the Oka Sho from up front in race-record time. Doubts about the Oaks distance, her dam Salty Bid being a sprinter, were dispelled: she dead-heated for the win with trial winner Saint Emilion. After summer and a 4th in the Rose S., she won the Shuka Sho, passing northern assassin Apricot Fizz and holding off trial winner Animate Bio - the first fillies' Triple Crown in 7 years, since Still in Love. Older, she won the Victoria Mile against Buena Vista. One more, the Queen Elizabeth II Cup, would have swept the fillies' G1s, but British mare Snow Fairy beat her at 3 and 4. As a broodmare, crossed with Deep Impact - two Triple Crown winners, 12 crowns combined - she produced Jinambo and Akaitorino Musume.
492: Mejiro Ramonu won the TV Tokyo Sho Sansai Himba S. with 2 wins from 3. 4th in the Queen S. at 3, she then won 6 straight to take the fillies' Triple Crown. From the start of the streak, the Yonsai Himba Tokubetsu (West), she was ridden by Hiroshi Kawachi, later famed as "Kawachi of the fillies." Winning that by a neck, she broke clear to win the Oka Sho by a length and three-quarters. After the Yonsai Himba Tokubetsu (East), people said "no filly can beat Ramonu now," and she won the Oaks as heavy favorite. But in autumn she won the Rose S. by just a neck, and in the Queen Elizabeth II Cup Super Shot closed steadily, held off by half a length - the first fillies' Triple Crown ever. Mr. C.B. and Symboli Rudolf had won Triple Crowns 3 and 2 years before; how good was a fillies' Triple Crown winner? The year-end Arima Kinen was the stage to test it - beat the older horses and colts and the title "best" was hers. But as 2nd choice she was a dismal 9th. Retiring after it, she is remembered as the first fillies' Triple Crown winner, but without the fame of Air Groove, who matched the colts. Her title stayed "best filly."
494: She won the Elfin S. and Pegasus S. and went to the Oka Sho, but drew the widest gate, 18 - seen as a big disadvantage. Some say jockey Yutaka Take missed the break on purpose to overcome it; no one knows. Slow away, she headed for the rail and reached 6th by the final turn, then unleashed an otherworldly kick to catch Hokuto Venus by a head for a G1. In the Oaks she lost to outsider Light Color in 2nd. She won the Rose S. in autumn, but leg trouble struck; nursed through training, she tried the Queen Elizabeth II Cup, long announced as her farewell. Favorite, she broke down fatally mid-race. Take sensed it and tried to pull her up, but her fighting spirit wouldn't let her stop; dragging her injured leg, she finished last by a distance, but finished.
496: Whether for his pedigree - by great sire Mr. Prospector out of Sinezita, a daughter of US Triple Crown winner Secretariat - or his lucky name, he was always heavily backed: favorite in a remarkable 14 of 24 starts, given his record. He had ability, chasing Genuine to half a length in the Mile Championship at 5, and won 7 races. But his graded wins were just two G3s against fillies and mares - a little underwhelming.
497: After a 3rd in the Anemone S., she was only 10th choice for the Oka Sho, without a graded win. But with hot favorite Air Groove out, any horse had a chance, and she cleanly ran down the field to become a G1 winner. In the Oaks she ran a fine 2nd to favorite Air Groove, proving her Oka Sho was no fluke. But as if she'd used it all up, after a 7th in the Rose S. she was injured, never won again and retired after another injury. As a dam, Pegasus Fight (02: El Condor Pasa), a 6-time winner, is her best so far.
500: From the famous Star Roch family; her dam Shiba Sky was a sister of Machikane Tannhauser. With a razor-sharp finish she won 9 of 20, including 4 graded races - all against colts, beating stars like Taiki Blizzard, Rice Shower and Nice Nature. She also gave Olivier Peslier, now a G1 regular, his first graded win in Japan. She became a broodmare but produced no standout.
502: Debuting late, in April at 3, she needed 7 starts to win. Then she won 4 straight, and even her first graded race, the Heian S. Her form then dipped, and after a winless spell and long break, her retirement to stud was announced in '08.
505: Trainer Hashiguchi, who developed many greats, hailed him as "on the level of Dance in the Dark or Heart's Cry." 2nd in a strong debut in October at 2, he won his maiden by a distance 3 weeks later. After an easy win in the Senryo Sho, some said "this is the classic horse," but he was beaten 4 lengths by unbeaten Logi Universe in the Radio Nikkei Hai 2yo S. and lost the lead role. He won the Kisaragi Sho easily at 3, but the pace didn't suit him in the Satsuki Sho, 13th. In the Derby he shrugged off heavy going, raced forward and held on for 2nd to Logi Universe. 2nd in the Kobe Shimbun Hai in autumn, he led by a mile in the Kikuka Sho but was 5th, then flopped in the Japan Cup and Arima Kinen. At 4 he switched to the mile: 10th in the February S. on dirt, he won the Milers C. next, becoming a top miler. But in the Yasuda Kinen he was jostled and finished 15th; a fracture followed, and back he managed little beyond a 3rd in the Nakayama Kinen. Undeniably first-class, but strength and fragility lived side by side.
507: A filly with beautiful lines, but as tough as any colt, she won the Sapporo Sansai S. by three and a half lengths. In the Hanshin Sansai Himba S. she led all the way at a perfect pace, beating Air Groove, a future Tenno Sho winner, and was unbeaten champion 2yo filly. But at 3 Air Groove beat her by 5 lengths in the Tulip Sho, she was 15th in the Oka Sho, and then boldly ran in the Derby, a filly against colts (13th). After a long injury break she won the Kyoto Himba Tokubetsu at 5. As a broodmare she was a huge success, producing 6 graded winners: Keisei Hai winner Admire Japan, Yayoi Sho winner Admire Aura, Horse of the Year Buena Vista, Epsom C. winner Tosen Reve, Hanshin JF winner Joie de Vivre and Flora S. winner Sangreal. She retired from breeding in 2015 with 12 foals and died of old age at 29 in 2022.
508: A star of the 1991 fillies' classics. Unbeaten in 5, she was Oka Sho favorite, but lost a shoe just before the race and finished 5th. In the Oaks she led all the way, as if venting her frustration, holding off Oka Sho winner Sister Tosho by a nose. In autumn she went for the third leg, the Queen Elizabeth II Cup, but wasn't at her best and finished 16th behind Linden Lily. An injury followed and she retired. As a broodmare she produced Isono Winner, 2nd in the 1999 Garnet S.
509: Led by a 2nd in the Oka Sho, she had 8 seconds and 5 thirds - many near misses - and won little after her debut. But at the end of her 3yo year she won the CBC Sho from a good spot, her first graded race. The next year she was 2nd by a head to Sunningdale in the Hankyu Hai, a fine 5th in the Takamatsunomiya Kinen, then won the Hakodate Sprint S. In '05 she won it again, and at 6 in '06 won the CBC Sho and Centaur S., becoming the first champion of the new Summer Sprint Series.
491: She won her debut, then injury cost her six months. 2nd on her return, she won 3 straight, and in her 6th start, her first graded try, beat colts by 2 lengths in the Nikkei Shinshun Hai. She later won the Nakayama Himba S. at 5.
493: Ridden by "Tsunoda of the fillies," she won her first 3 with overwhelming power, beating Scarlet Bouquet by two and a half lengths in the Tulip Sho. But that year's fillies' classics were a wide-open, unusually strong field. Unbeaten Isono Roubles (5 for 5) was Oka Sho favorite, Northern Driver, who beat colts in the Pegasus S. (G3, 1700m), 2nd choice, and Sister Tosho only 4th choice behind Scarlet Bouquet, whom she'd beaten. Isono Roubles lost a shoe just before the start. Sister Tosho tracked the leaders, led at the final turn and burst clear, winning by 2 lengths - an unbeaten Oka Sho winner. Isono Roubles got revenge in the Oaks, but Sister Tosho dispelled doubts about the distance in 2nd and was named champion 3yo filly. Injury followed, and she retired without another win.
495: Along with A Shin Washington, a year older, she cemented the image "A Shin = foreign-bred, sprinter, front-runner." She won her debut by a distance in record time, and at 3 won two G3s, the Queen C. and Arlington C. After an 18-month break she slumped, but at 5 won the Kyoto Himba Tokubetsu and Silk Road S. She was 2nd in the Takamatsunomiya Hai (now Kinen), never winning on the big stage. As a broodmare she retired without producing a star with her speed.
498: After beating Daiichi Ruby in a trial, she was 6th in the Oaks and ran poorly in autumn. But in a wide-open Queen Elizabeth II Cup, she was 8th choice at 13.6, a fancied outsider. Waiting at the back, she closed in the straight and crossed the line to Kiyoshi Sugimoto's famous call: "Number 18, one week late!" The week before, her jockey Norihiro Yokoyama had lost the Kikuka Sho as favorite on Mejiro Ryan - also number 18.
499: 3rd in the Oaks and Queen S., she was consistent. In the Queen Elizabeth II Cup, with the betting focused on fillies' double winner Max Beauty, she was 4th choice, but swooped on Max Beauty in the straight and won by 2 lengths. She was put down in '08 due to old age.
501: She ran a gutsy 3rd in a debut hailed as "the strongest maiden race ever." Her jockey said "she'll win a G1," and she did in her 3rd start, the Hanshin JF. With amazing finishes she won the Oka Sho and Oaks, earning the nickname "the female Deep Impact." An Arc trip was planned, but after a 2nd in the Sapporo Kinen she stayed home. Going for the fillies' Triple Crown in the Shuka Sho, she trailed rival Red Desire and was demoted to 3rd for interference. In the Queen Elizabeth II Cup lightly-fancied Queen Spumante and T.M. Precure held on in front, leaving her 3rd, and in the Arima Kinen she was 2nd to Dream Journey's sharp finish. At 4 she proved herself world-class with a 2nd in the Dubai Sheema Classic, won the Victoria Mile with a devilish kick for her 4th G1, was 2nd to outsider Nakayama Festa in the Takarazuka Kinen, then won the Tenno Sho (Autumn) by 2 lengths - her long-sought G1 against colts. In the Japan Cup she crossed the line first but was demoted to 2nd behind Rose Kingdom for interference, and in the Arima Kinen she just failed to catch Victoire Pisa, 2nd by a nose - frustrating defeats. Still she was named Horse of the Year, the 4th female ever, after Vodka the year before. At 5 she was 8th in the Dubai World Cup, her first heavy defeat. In the Victoria Mile she met year-younger fillies' Triple Crown winner Apapane; Apapane perhaps suited the mile better, and she was 2nd. She was 2nd again to Earnestly's record run in the Takarazuka Kinen, and 4th to Tosen Jordan trying to repeat in the Tenno Sho (Autumn) - over a year without a win. In the Japan Cup, for the first time not favorite in Japan (Arc winner Danedream was), she raced a little closer than usual, unleashed a 33.9 finish and won, avenging last year. In the Arima Kinen, a summit clash with Triple Crown winner Orfevre, she couldn't quicken from midfield and was 7th. If Vodka was a queen with the strength to keep challenging, Buena Vista was a queen with the strength to keep reigning.
503: She led all the way to win her debut by 5 lengths and a 5-million race by 6, then won the Fantasy S. from a good spot with a 34.0 finish - speed on another level. But leg trouble ruled out the Hanshin Sansai Himba S. Back at 3, she raced forward and faded to 4th in the Yonsai Himba Tokubetsu (West), and was caught by Phalaenopsis at the end of the Oka Sho, 2nd. After a 10th in the Oaks, which didn't suit her, a tendon injury ended her career. On paper, 3 wins from 6 and one G3 - but a speedster who starred in the classics. As a broodmare she produced Oaks winner Daiwa El Cielo (01: Sunday Silence), her daughter fulfilling her classic dream, then 2-time graded winner Big Planet (02: Brian's Time), and Greater London (12: Deep Impact), born when she was 17, who was 4th in the Yasuda Kinen after 6 wins from 7.
504: Debuting in January at 3, she missed the Oka Sho. She won the Wasurenagusa Sho and, with 2 wins from 4, won the Oaks with a sharp run from midfield. Later she won 3 graded races at 4.
506: He improved rapidly late at 4. At 6, though, he powered past future Takamatsunomiya Kinen winner Ore wa Matteruze to win the Tokyo Shimbun Hai, a graded winner at last. Poor runs followed, and he retired after a 13th in the '09 CBC Sho.
510: Leading in nimble style, she won the Flower C., her first graded race. 2nd choice in the Oka Sho, she was hampered and finished 14th, and her injuries kept her out of the Oaks. 17th in the Queen Elizabeth II Cup on her return, she then won the Turquoise S. The next year she won the Nakayama Himba S., then beat hot favorite Mejiro Ryan in the Nakayama Kinen. Retiring at 4, she produced '98 Queen C. winner Eidai Queen (95: Mejiro McQueen).
511: An extreme front-runner: good when she got the lead, crushed when she didn't. After winning the Hakodate Sansai S. and TV Tokyo Sho Sansai Himba S., she won the Yonsai Himba Tokubetsu (West) at 3, with Royal Cosmo half a length behind. 2nd choice in the Oka Sho, she led again, and though Royal Cosmo closed at the end, held on. She was 15th in the Oaks, beaten by the distance - proven when she led all the way against older horses in the Keio Hai Autumn H. After a 2nd in the Rose S., her camp chose the 2400m Queen Elizabeth II Cup. She got the lead but finished 11th, and with an injury, left the turf.
512: A filly who won the Southern Kanto triple crown: the Haneda Hai, Tokyo Derby and Tokyo Okan Sho. She ran in the Japan Cup as a local representative, but an international turf race was too much for a 3yo filly, and she lost by a distance. But at year's end she beat seasoned older horses in the Tokyo Daishoten - arguably the greatest filly ever on dirt. The next year she was retired to breed, choosing the Kawasaki Kinen at home as her farewell. Her 1.0 odds were no surprise; astonishingly, every other horse paid over 100 to 1. She swept forward down the backstretch and won easily, living up to mythical odds and leaving a legend. Breeding began chapter two: Ibuki Government (96: Commander in Chief) won 8 including 2 G3s, Kanetsu Fleuve (97: Paradise Creek) won the Teio Sho and Kawasaki Kinen, and her first foal Sister Sono (91: Nasr El Arab) produced Regular Member (97: Commander in Chief), winner of 3 dirt G1s - the Derby Grand Prix, Kawasaki Kinen and JBC Classic.
513: The only star by her sire Tosho God. Tough, she raced until 6, winning a graded race every year: the Sapphire S., Asahi Challenge C., Kitakyushu Kinen, Aichi Hai and Kyoto Himba Tokubetsu. She twice tried the Tenno Sho (Autumn), finishing 5th and 6th, holding her own against top colts. She often met fellow tough mare Ikuno Dictus in local graded races - true rivals. Sadly she produced no notable offspring.
514: With her fine pedigree she was always a classic contender, but fell just short: 4th in the Oka Sho, 5th in the Oaks, 3rd in the Queen Elizabeth II Cup. Her ability held up as an older mare, and racing to the end of her 4yo year she won 6 of 21, including 4 graded races - more than enough for a filly. But her success didn't end there. Her son Daiwa Major (01: Sunday Silence) won 5 G1s including the Satsuki Sho and Tenno Sho (Autumn), and his sister Daiwa Scarlet (04: Agnes Tachyon) won the Oka Sho, Shuka Sho and Queen Elizabeth II Cup - a top-class dam.
515: A mochikomi by great sire Raise a Native, watched from before her debut. Debuting late, in July at 3, she broke her maiden, and after a 2nd won 3 straight up to the open Autumn Sprint S. After an 8th in her first graded race, the Swan S., leg trouble sent her on a break, but back in July the next year she won 3 straight including the Sekiya Kinen and Centaur S. Another injury cost her a year; back in the Centaur S. she couldn't win, and retired after 3 races. Much was hoped of her as a broodmare, but her best was 5-time winner Win Gloria (99: Sunday Silence).
516: Out of Alcea, 1983 US Eclipse champion 2yo filly, by great sire Danzig - a true blueblood. She won her first 3 in record time: 1:08.2 for 1200m at Chukyo on debut, 1:34.7 for 1600m at Tokyo in the Icho S., and 1:34.7 for 1600m at Hanshin in the Hanshin Sansai Himba S. She slumped after, but as a dam produced '02 Keisei Hai winner Yamanin Seraphim (99: Sunday Silence) and '03 Hanshin JF runner-up Yamanin Alcyone (01: Sunday Silence).
519: With one win, she ran a close 2nd to Peace of World in the Hanshin JF. The next year she won the Fillies' Revue and ran a fine 4th in both the Oka Sho and Oaks. In autumn, after a 2nd in the Rose S., she was 3rd in the Shuka Sho.
521: Remarkably consistent: at 3 in 5 G1s he was 2nd in the Satsuki Sho, 3rd in the Derby, 2nd in the Kikuka Sho, 2nd in the Japan Cup and 4th in the Arima Kinen. Wins in the Kisaragi Sho and Kobe Shimbun Hai set him apart from the usual silver collector. He was also famous for changing jockeys: 7 riders in 16 starts, a different one in each of those 5 G1s - unheard of for a horse this good. In '07 Katsumi Ando rode him again for the first time since the Kisaragi Sho, 2nd in the Hanshin Daishoten, but a fracture then sidelined him. Back in autumn for a G1, he was 14th in the Japan Cup and 6th in the Arima Kinen, his steadiness gone. In '08 he ran as if burned out, and his retirement was decided.
522: Won the Sweet Pea S. and improved over middle distances on turf, winning the Aichi Hai at 4.
523: Debuted at local Oi. A Southern Kanto fillies' classic contender, she was 3rd as favorite in the Urawa Oka Sho, then boldly ran 4th in the Tokyo Derby against colts. Winning 4 straight as an older mare, she moved to the JRA. A closer at the mercy of the pace, her form was erratic, but she won two graded races, the Niigata Kinen and Hakodate Kinen - both narrow wins grabbed by grit at the very end.
524: Winless except on dirt, she couldn't even make the top five in the 9-million class - then, lucky to get into the Queen Elizabeth II Cup by draw, she won it. Last choice of 20, she paid 430.6 to win, still the record payout for a graded race. Naturally called a fluke, as an older mare she was 3rd in the Kyoto Daishoten and 2nd in the Kyoto Kinen - oddly good only over 2400m on Kyoto turf. As a dam she produced Tamamo Strong (95: Scan), 4-time dirt graded winner, and died of old age in June 2007.
525: He won the Shinzan Kinen and Yayoi Sho, was 4th as Satsuki Sho favorite and 3rd in the Derby. His path mirrored Admire Moon, a year older, of the same owner, and growth was expected, but a fracture ruled out the autumn classics. Back with a 3rd in the Naruo Kinen, he then beat Derby-winning crop-mate Vodka in the Kyoto Kinen. Following Admire Moon, he tried the Dubai Duty Free but was boxed in all the way, 9th. More bad luck, including a fracture, kept him from returning to form. At stud he sired dirt runners like first-crop Procyon S. winner Novo Baccarat, Nambu Hai winner Arctos and Leopard S. winner Cross Krieger, but sadly died young in 2015 after fracturing a leg at pasture.
526: She won in her 8th start, then as 14th choice ran a stunning race to win the Flora S., paying a 250,000-yen exacta. She ran a fine 3rd in the Oaks as an outsider, but then did nothing and retired after heavy defeats.
529: At 2 he was 2nd in his first 3 starts, then won his maiden as favorite at 3. In the Kisaragi Sho he showed a sharp kick, just holding off Reve d'Orient's charge for his first graded win. After a refreshing break he went straight to the Satsuki Sho, but, keyed up, faded from a good spot to finish 17th of 18. He later won the Miyakooji S. (OP) twice and was a regular in middle-distance open and graded races. Close relatives include 3-time graded winner Tuscata Sorte.
