To secure an Oka Sho spot, her camp ran her a week later in the Flower C., and she won. 3rd choice for the Oka Sho, she led alone and nearly won, caught only by Apapane, 2nd. In the Oaks she was held up and stayed on for 5th. In autumn she did little in the Rose S. and Shuka Sho, but a week later, as 17th choice in the Tenno Sho (Autumn), she charged to 4th against seasoned older horses.
902: He won in his 3rd start, was 2nd in the Principal S. and 16th in the Derby, then crushed in the Kikuka Sho. After a slump he won his 3rd race in summer at 4 and quickly improved, winning the '07 Nakayama Kimpai, 4th in the Nakayama Kinen and 2nd in the Osaka Hai. Then abroad he won the Singapore Airlines International C. - an international G1! (2nd was previous winner Cosmo Bulk, a Japanese 1-2.) Later he surprised fans by leading and holding on in middle-distance graded races when least expected.
903: He won the Kyoto Shimbun Hai and was 2nd in the Derby, though 5 lengths behind monster Deep Impact. But hoof cracks forced repeated long breaks, and he only raced steadily from autumn '06. He was 7th in the Kyoto Daishoten and 15th in the Tenno Sho (Autumn), then 2nd in the Chunichi Shimbun Hai, a local graded race with easier rivals, still a shadow of his old self. In autumn '07 he won the Asahi Challenge C. and Kyoto Daishoten, suddenly a G1 contender, but was 10th in the Japan Cup and 9th in the Arima Kinen. From '08, apart from a 3rd in the Takarazuka Kinen, he was always out of the top five, retiring after finishing last, 15th, in the '10 Kokura Daishoten.
868: His dam Air Deja Vu won the Queen S.; uncle Air Shakur was the 2000 double classic winner; sister Air Messiah starred in the '05 classics, winning the Shuka Sho - a superb family. Often close but winless, he finally won the American JCC at 7, and was 3rd in the Arima Kinen in both '08 and '09, steady in G1s despite his age. A fracture in the '10 Tenno Sho (Spring) ended his career; he went to stud in Korea.
871: No good in the classics or on dirt, he bloomed in sprints, winning 4 straight to the Keihan Hai at 3. He then ran poorly, adding only the Fukushima Minpo Hai, often unplaced in graded races.
900: Based at local Nagoya. Won 11 races, incl. the Kakitsubata Kinen over Novo True and Utopia.
904: An Australian sprinter, winner of 7 G1s from 2004 to 2009 - a gelding who came to Japan in 2006 and won the Sprinters S. Debuting late, in April at 4, he won 7 straight to his first G1. In 2006, at 6-7, he contested the Global Sprint Challenge: he won the Lightning S. at home, then the King's Stand S. (G2) in England, and in autumn came to Japan, 2nd in the Centaur S. and winner of the Sprinters S., clinching the series. Back in Australia he won 3 more G1s - the Doomben 10,000, TJ Smith S. and Goodwood H. - the last in May at 9. Age then caught up and he retired at the end of his 9yo year. He was bought for just A$1,250 (about 110,000 yen) by owner-trainer Joe Janiak, who worked as a baker in the morning, trainer by day and taxi driver at night to make ends meet; the horse's big earnings let him become a full-time trainer.
907: After 2 turf runs did nothing, he switched to dirt. Injury cost him 17 months, but on his return he won 4 straight that summer, including the Sirius S., and was 2nd in the JBC Sprint. He then ran poorly and retired without more success.
908: Two long breaks slowed his rise, but back at the end of his 4yo year he won 3 straight, then was 2nd, a length behind Meisho Kio, in the Chukyo Kinen. He was a fine 5th in the Tenno Sho (Spring), then in autumn beat Zenno Rob Roy by a neck in the Kyoto Daishoten for his first graded win. At 6 he won the Kyoto Kinen and the next year was 2nd in the Takarazuka Kinen, but then a tendon injury forced his retirement.
909: Raced only on dirt from her 2nd start, in spring at 5 she won Funabashi's Marine C., then 3 straight graded races: Sparking Lady C., Empress Hai and Queen Sho. The next year she was 3rd in both the Kawasaki Kinen and February S., then won the Tokai S. and the Teio Sho, a G1 title. She won the Empress Hai again and the year-end Tokyo Daishoten, retiring at 7 with 15 wins, including 9 graded races.
911: Winner of the 2011 NHK Mile C. A sprinter with the blood of sire Sakura Bakushin O, he loved 1400-1600m. At 2 he won 3 of 4, including the 2010 Asahi Hai FS, and was champion 2yo colt. At 3 he aimed for the NHK Mile C., running well in the Spring S. and NZ Trophy, and won it in a tight finish after a stewards' inquiry. He then tried England's St. James's Palace S., 8th. At 4 he was 2nd in the Yasuda Kinen, won the Swan S. and was 2nd in the Mile CS. At 5 he won the Yomiuri Milers C., his 5th graded win. Then he kept missing the top five, and in his 3rd Yasuda Kinen at 6, off a layoff and poor form, he was second-last choice despite being a G1 winner. Yet from midfield he surged as others struggled on heavy ground, nearly giving jockey Kosei Miura his first G1, but heavy favorite Just a Way caught him by a nose. His last race, the Hong Kong Cup, brought a fine 3rd. Surely one of the stars of recent sprint-mile racing. Retired to stud, he carries high hopes of extending Japan's proud Tesco Boy sire line.
912: Debuted at local Nagoya and won the Nagoya Yushun. Moved to the JRA without success and returned.
913: She won her debut, but was crushed in the Flower C. Switched to dirt, she was always in the top five, winning the JRA-local Sparking Lady C. in summer at 4. 2nd in the '05 Empress Hai and Marine C., she improved from summer, winning 3 straight JRA-local graded races - Hakusan Daishoten, Queen Sho and TCK Jo-o Hai - then the Marine C., ruling local dirt racing. Losing form, she retired at the end of '06.
914: A dirt horse who left the lower classes only at 5, then starred in JRA-local races. He won the Hakusan Daishoten at 7, the Mercury C. at 9, and raced 77 times until 11.
915: He won Kanazawa's Thoroughbred Challenge C. impressively at 3, then struggled to win. At 5 he regained form, winning a 16-million race and an open special. 3rd in the Musashino S. at 6, he was steady at the top of dirt racing, won Kochi's Kurofune Sho at 8, and the Hyogo Gold Trophy at both 8 and 9.
916: A foreign-bred by Valid Appeal, of the In Reality line. A sprinter on turf or dirt, 2nd in the Falcon S. at 3. Moving to local racing in summer at 5, he won the Sakitama Hai and Kakitsubata Kinen. Winless in '07, he retired after the Platinum C. in late July.
917: On dirt alone, 10 wins and three 2nds from 20 - very consistent. He won the Musashino S. easily after 10 months off. In '05 he won the Antares S. and Mercury C., then ran poorly. Retired in '08.
918: He won his first 2 and was 2nd in the Shinzan Kinen. Switched to sprints from summer at 3, he beat older horses by a head in the Swan S. in autumn. Inconsistent, often beaten badly, he still livened up sprint racing, winning the Silk Road S. at 5.
919: Consistent from his debut win, he won the Spring S. Out of the frame for the first time in the Satsuki Sho, he was 2nd in the Derby as 12th choice, showing his class. In autumn he lacked his spring spark, 16th in the Kikuka Sho. Moving to miles, at 4 he closed for 3rd in the Tokyo Shimbun Hai and raced forward for 3rd in the Milers C., showing versatility, but was 7th as favorite in the Keio Hai Spring C. and a disappointing 9th in the Yasuda Kinen, though he stumbled in the straight. He won the Sekiya Kinen, his first win in a year, but was 11th in the Tenno Sho (Autumn) and 6th in the Mile CS. He was 3rd in the Yasuda Kinen 2 years running, always just short in G1s. He moved to local racing in autumn at 8, then retired to stud.
921: With a sharp finish, she was 2nd in the Queen C. and Flower C. in spring at 3 and 3rd to Symboli Indy in the NHK Mile C. Crushed in the Shuka Sho, she then won the Fuji S., and the Nakayama Himba S. the next year.
922: Winner of the 2009 Asahi Hai FS and 2010 Japan Cup. Descended from Rosa Nay, Rose Color and Rose Bud - the "Rose family" - he was its great hope. He won his first 3, including the Asahi Hai FS, and was a classic favorite, but was only 4th in the Satsuki Sho, 2nd in the Derby and 2nd in the Kikuka Sho. In the Japan Cup he was promoted to the win when Buena Vista, first past the post, was demoted. A worthy rival to his strong crop-mate Victoire Pisa. From 4 he won only the Kyoto Daishoten and retired in 2013.
923: Very consistent at a mile or less. Rarely beaten badly, but often 2nd or 3rd. She won the Hanshin Himba S. twice and was 3rd against colts in the Yasuda Kinen - not to be underestimated. After a 13th in the '09 Keeneland C., she fractured a leg preparing for the Swan S. and retired to breed.
924: A late developer, winning first in her 8th start in summer at 3. She stepped up steadily but faded from the front to 8th in a 16-million race and 6th in the Nakayama Himba S. It looked like she'd hit a wall, but in the Fukushima Himba S. on heavy ground, as 7th choice, she led before the final turn and won an upset. On good ground in the Victoria Mile she was 2nd, well beaten by Vodka, proving it no fluke. She kept running well in fillies' graded races on turf and dirt.
925: She won her debut and the Shiraume Sho, but was 7th in the Tulip Sho and 4th in the Fillies' Revue, missing the Oka Sho. But she unleashed her sharp kick in the Flora S. for her first graded win, then as 3rd choice closed for 3rd in the Oaks. After a fracture, at 4 she was 3rd in 5 straight graded races including the Victoria Mile and Queen Elizabeth II Cup - "the bronze collector." She won the '07 Kyoto Himba S. and the year-end Aichi Hai, but struggled in '08 and retired to breed. Her 2nd foal Dia de la Madre (10: King Kamehameha) won the Fuchu Himba S. and her 5th, Dreadnoughtus (13: Harbinger), the Kyoto 2yo S. - her kick lives on.
926: He won 4 races, mostly at a dirt mile, and the Unicorn S. by 7 lengths over Silk Big Time. Expected to shine, in autumn '08 he lost 3 straight as a heavy favorite under 2.0. Winless in '09, he tried a local comeback but, with a breathing problem, ran just once and retired.
927: She outdueled Rosado to win the Keio Hai Sansai S., then was 6th in the Hanshin Sansai Himba S. She beat favored Red Chili Pepper by a neck in the Queen C., but was 6th again in the Oka Sho. Talented but not quite strong, with a great burst that often misfired - that was Umeno Fiber's image. Even after her powerful finish caught favorite To the Victory by a nose to win the Oaks, that image held: she was never favorite in all 16 starts. After the Oaks her fickle kick brought occasional good runs but many double-figure finishes, and she retired to breed without another win.
928: Injured in spring at 3 and out for a long time, he won on his return and the next race too, but injury struck again. Winning his 3rd race back, he kept running well and won the '05 Niigata Daishoten. A 3rd long break followed; back in the '07 American JCC, he did little more and retired.
929: A talented filly who won 2 graded races, the Hakodate Sansai S. and Shinzan Kinen, in the strong 1991 crop. While many dropped out, she ran in all 3 fillies' classics but did nothing: 15th in the Oka Sho, 16th in the Oaks, 17th in the Queen Elizabeth Cup. As a broodmare she produced Run for the Dream (94: Real Shadai), winner of the Mermaid S. and Asahi Challenge C. and 2nd in the Queen Elizabeth II Cup - a fine dam.
930: She won her debut as 5th choice, then in the Hakodate 2yo S. held off Kyoei Ashura's storming charge by a head - 2 straight and a graded win. But she did nothing in the Fantasy S., Hanshin JF or the next year's classics.
931: Half-sister of NHK Mile C. winner Taiki Fortune. A turf sprinter, she won the Crystal C. at 3. Her only graded win, but she was 2nd in the Hanshin Himba Tokubetsu and Kyoto Himba S. at 4-5.
932: Needing 6 starts to win, she missed the spring classics, and in autumn just made the Queen Elizabeth Cup, 10th. But she improved with racing, and at 4, in 14 starts, won 2 fillies' graded races - the Himba Tokyo Times Hai and Hanshin Himba Tokubetsu - and was named Best Older Filly or Mare. Retired to breed in spring at 5, she had no stars but steady runners like Little Harmony (95: Commander in Chief).
933: He won his first 2, but leg trouble cost him 6 months, and he ran just 4 times at 2-3. At 4, finally racing regularly, he ran mainly at 1800m on turf, winning once in the 10-million class but stuck after. A strong win in a 10-million mile race moved him to a mile or less, and he won at 1400m next, but injury again forced a long break. Back after 11 months, his kick exploded in the Christmas C., reaching open class. At 6 he closed for a narrow 2nd in the New Year S., then was 4th in the Tokyo Shimbun Hai and 3rd in the Milers C., and won the Keio Hai Spring C. in record time, his first graded win. In the Yasuda Kinen he beat Hong Kong hero Silent Witness, great mare Sweep Tosho and others with authority - in just 6 months he had risen to the top of the mile. Winless after, he retired to stud in autumn '07.
935: At 2 she won her debut and the Fantasy S. 4th in the Tulip Sho at 3, she went to the Oka Sho and, 13th at the final turn, charged past stars like Fusaichi Airedale and To the Victory to win by a length and a half - a classic winner. In the Oaks she closed again but was beaten by Umeno Fiber's career-best charge, 3rd. After that, long injury breaks left her unable to shine.
936: Winner of the 2006 Takamatsunomiya Kinen at 6. Debuting late, he reached open class only at 5, then kept falling short: 2nd in the Keio Hai Spring C., 2nd in the Tokyo Shimbun Hai and 3rd in the Hankyu Hai the next year. Dropping back in trip for the Takamatsunomiya Kinen worked perfectly, and he won it, then the Keio Hai Spring C. But beaten badly as Yasuda Kinen favorite, he ran poorly after and retired. At stud his first crop's Hana's Goal won an Australian G1.
937: A closer with a brilliant kick. Dependent on the pace, she often fell short, but at 4 won the Kyoto Himba Tokubetsu. Racing on until 6, she stubbornly stuck to her last-to-first style - a true character.
938: Slow to win, she missed the classics, but came good in summer, winning 2 allowance races and then the Queen S. She ran a fine 3rd in the Queen Elizabeth II Cup. She never won again, even after dropping in class.
939: Consistent from her debut, at 4 she won the Shinsaibashi S. to return to open class, then led all the way in the Hanshin Himba S., her first graded race and win. In the Victoria Mile she broke clear in the straight and held off Vodka and Blumenblatt to win a valuable G1. She rested afterward but never got back into condition, gave up defending the Victoria Mile, and retired.
905: He won the Aoba Sho with a sharp kick. 8th in the Derby, he was a good 4th in the Kikuka Sho. His temper cost him wins; gelded at 4, he still couldn't win, but at 6 switched to jumps and won for the first time since the Aoba Sho.
906: Debuting in Hokkaido racing, he won twice and moved to the JRA. Good when sitting handy, poor when too far forward or back. He quickly won through the 5 and 10-million classes, but class drops held him back until he settled in open class at the end of 4. He led all the way to win the All Comers at 6, and held on for 2nd from the front in the '05 Tanabata Sho. He later moved to Australia.
910: A son of Kako Esees bred in Aomori. Debuting at Kawasaki, he ran in the Haneda Hai and Tokyo Derby. Older, a JRA-local graded regular, he improved from the end of 4, winning 3 straight to the Kawasaki Kinen in record time. Retired in '05.
920: The "Monster of Tohoku," based at local Iwate. He won his debut on heavy ground and went unbeaten in 9. After two 2nds, he won 6 more, including the Derby Grand Prix. At the end of 3 he moved briefly to Oi for the Tokyo Daishoten, 2nd to Rosita. Back in Iwate he built the "SG era" with rival Great Hope, and ran in the Tokyo Daishoten again the next year, 2nd to Daiko Garudan. At 5 he also ran in the JRA's All Comers (5th).
934: From the first crop of sprint champion Durandal, she debuted at Kokura in summer at 2. She won a maiden by 3 lengths, then as 2nd choice won the Kokura 2yo S. from up front, holding off Dasher Go Go. After a break she led in the Hanshin JF but was 11th. She later ran well in turf sprints and came close in open races.
942: Tried on turf and dirt, he came good after focusing on dirt from summer at 3. Overcoming 2 injuries, at 5 in '05 he won the Tokai S., then the Breeders' Gold C. and Nippon TV Hai. When half-brother Vermilion became dirt champion, he answered by winning the '08 Mercury C., showing big-brother pride. Steadily in the top five in JRA-local races, he retired in autumn '09.
943: She won in her 2nd start and was 2nd to Biwa Heidi in the Sapporo Sansai S., but a long break followed and she never left the lower classes. As a dam she produced 4-time graded winner Admire Kiss (03: Sunday Silence).
944: Despite a late debut in February at 3 and a break, he won 3 straight and was 3rd in the Kikuka Sho. Running well after, at 4 he won the Meguro Kinen in a course-record 2:29.8 for his first graded win.
945: She won her debut at Hanshin in July at 2. 2nd in the Dahlia Sho, she won the Niigata 2yo S. from last with an astonishing 32.9 finish. Favorite for the Hanshin JF on that showing, her kick misfired, 5th. In the classics she was dull, 6th in the Oka Sho and 11th in the Oaks, but in her first dirt race, the Kanto Oaks, she raced forward and burst clear to become 3yo dirt queen. Hailed as an all-rounder, she was soon found to have a chip fracture. Winless after her return, in the Queen Elizabeth II Cup, as rank outsider at 343.7, she led by a wide margin and held on for 7th, 0.8s behind Snow Fairy, thrilling the crowd.
947: Out of Chansonnette, half-sister of '96 Japan Cup winner Singspiel, he won his debut at Kyoto in autumn at 2, then was 3rd to Victoire Pisa in the Radio Nikkei Hai 2yo S., a classic gateway. At 3 he started in the Kyodo News Hai, closing in the fastest 33.5 but losing by a nose to Hansode Band. With another fastest finish he won the Mainichi Hai in his 4th start. Avoiding tight tracks, he skipped the Satsuki Sho for the NHK Mile C., where as 2.6 favorite he swept down from behind to win in 1:31.4, a Japanese turf mile record. A leading Derby fancy, he was found the day before to have fractured his right hind leg. Back after 6 months, a tendon injury forced his retirement to stud. His first crop's Smart Odin won the Tokyo Sports Hai 2yo S. and 3 graded races incl. the Kyoto Shimbun Hai; hoped to succeed great sire Fuji Kiseki, he retired from stud in 2020.
948: Winning in summer, she just made the Shuka Sho as 14th choice, and though she couldn't catch Phalaenopsis, closed fastest for 2nd, setting up a huge payout. 9th in the Queen Elizabeth II Cup, she was 5th in the Hanshin and Kyoto Himba Tokubetsu, then in the Nakayama Himba S., 9th choice of 11, ran a perfect race and, helped by her weight, beat Mejiro Dober by 2 lengths - a big upset.
949: Small at about 430kg but with rare fighting spirit, she starred in the classics. After winning the Shinzan Kinen and Yonsai Himba Tokubetsu (West), she was 2nd in the Oka Sho, 5th in the Oaks and Shuka Sho, and 2nd to Mejiro Dober against older mares in the Queen Elizabeth II Cup - always near the top against fillies. The next year she won the Lord Derby Challenge T. and Mermaid S. and was 2nd again in the Queen Elizabeth II Cup, but never won a G1 and retired at year's end. As a dam she produced '05 Queen C. winner Lailaps (02: French Deputy) and '05 Asahi Hai FS winner Fusaichi Richard (03: Kurofune) - a fine broodmare.
950: Winning 3 straight at 3, he was 13th in the Shuka Sho, then won the Turquoise S. At 4 he beat Black Hawk in the Sekiya Kinen in a stunning Japanese record 1:31.6. Winless after, he was 2nd in the next Sekiya Kinen.
951: She won her dirt debut but was mediocre on turf. Trying the dirt graded Unicorn S., she won by 2.5 lengths. Racing mainly on dirt, she won the Sirius S. and was half a length 2nd in the next February S. Focusing on JRA-local races, she won the Kakitsubata Kinen and Procyon S., and in autumn the Nambu Hai, a long-sought G1. That was her peak; she never won again. As a dam she produced Golden Hind (06: Kurofune), a familiar front-runner in long open races. How such a pure stayer came from mile-to-middle-distance parents shows the depth and fun of breeding.
954: Raced on dirt early, he was a fine 5th in his first turf race, the Spring S. As 14th choice he was 2nd in the Radio Nikkei Sho, a key part of an upset, and 3rd as an outsider in the St. Lite Kinen - a rare longshot specialist, it seemed. A chip fracture cost him a year. Winning his comeback in his own class, he then ran to form in graded races and won the Argentina Kyowakoku Hai. In the Japan Cup, while all eyes were on 3 Derby winners, he swept past them to win, a hero overnight. 5th to Daiwa Scarlet in the Arima Kinen and 4th in the Hanshin Daishoten at 5, he lacked stamina in the Tenno Sho (Spring), 14th. 5th in the Takarazuka Kinen, in the autumn Tenno Sho he gave way only to Company's kick, holding off Vodka for 2nd. Expected to repeat in the Japan Cup, he was 13th, and a tendon injury led to his retirement to stud. His first fee was just 300,000 yen, a quiet start, but his first crop's Maurice won 6 G1s, including 3 in Hong Kong, and Gold Actor won the Arima Kinen on a 4-race streak. Other runners include Shinzan Kinen winner Guanciale and Keisei Hai and St. Lite Kinen winner Generale Uno, and in 2022 Win Marilyn won the Hong Kong Vase. A rising non-Sunday Silence sire, he retired from stud in 2023 and lives at his birthplace, Shadai Farm.
955: At the end of 3, running above her class in the Hanshin Himba Tokubetsu, she beat crop stars Scarlet Bouquet and Yamano Casablanca - a shock graded win from a mere allowance runner. She never won again.
956: Montjeu's best son, he won the 2005 Arc and was Cartier Horse of the Year. Unbeaten in 3 incl. a graded win, he was a neck 2nd to Shamardal in the French Derby, then won the Irish Derby as 1.8 favorite. In autumn he won the Prix Niel (G2), then the Arc, crushing English Derby winner Motivator, previous winner Bago, Irish Oaks winner Shawanda and others by 2 lengths - top of Europe. At 4 he won the Tattersalls Gold C., then the King George VI & Queen Elizabeth Diamond S. after a fierce duel with Japan's Heart's Cry. After that he declined: 2nd in the Prix Foy, he was promoted to 3rd in the Arc when Deep Impact was disqualified, 3rd in the Champion S., and 6th in the BC Turf, his last race. Hoped to succeed Montjeu at stud, he sired only a few graded winners like Criterium International winner Ectot, and died in 2016.
957: A great mare from local Utsunomiya. She won her first 5 with ease, then ran in the JRA's Flower C. (6th). Back home she won 5 more, incl. the Kita-Kanto Derby, and returned to the JRA for the Unicorn S., 2nd to Gold Tiara, proving her potential. Older, she won the Tokyo Hai at 4 and was 4th in the JRA's Negishi S., and at 5 beat Preeminence in the TCK Jo-o Hai.
958: Often close but winless, she reached open class only at 5 with the Dotonbori S. Three starts later she won the Mermaid S. by 3.5 lengths. She kept trying fillies' graded races without another win.
959: An Australian mare who starred over long distances, winning 3 straight Melbourne Cups from 2003 to 2005. She came to Japan for the Tenno Sho (Spring) but couldn't show her best, 7th to Suzuka Mambo. From her 2nd start she won 6 straight, including the Queen Elizabeth S. (G2) in November at 3. At 4 she tried G1s and won the Melbourne Cup, Australia's greatest race, then the 3200m Sydney Cup, named Australia's champion stayer. At 5 she won 3 G1s including a second Melbourne Cup. In April she came to Japan, 7th as a fancied runner in both the April S. and Tenno Sho (Spring), but was still Australia's Horse of the Year. At 6 she won the Cox Plate, a middle-distance highlight, showing she had speed too, then under top weight won an unprecedented 3rd Melbourne Cup. She retired after it, Horse of the Year 2 years running. Bred to top sires like Galileo, she produced no notable runners.
960: Her sire Kurofune ("black ships") recalls the old verse about Perry's ships: "Four cups of Jokisen tea and no sleep at night" - so she was named Sleepless Night. Like her sire she handled turf and dirt, but her sprinting stood out: never out of the top five, with 9 wins and two 2nds at 1200m. In '08 she won 4 straight incl. the CBC Sho and Kita-Kyushu Kinen, then won the Sprinters S. as 2.4 favorite for her first G1 - the first mare named champion sprinter since Flower Park 12 years earlier. Setbacks delayed her, but in her first race in 6 months, the '09 Takamatsunomiya Kinen, she was 2nd. 2nd in the Centaur S., she aimed to repeat in the Sprinters S. but retired with a tendon injury.
961: A stayer by Admire Vega, who died young at 8. Winning the Sumire S., he showed promise early at 3, but came good from that autumn: 3rd against older horses in the Kyoto Daishoten and 2nd to Asakusa Kings in the Kikuka Sho. 2nd in the next Meguro Kinen, always a contender over long trips, he won the Nikkei Sho in spring at 5 and was a neck 2nd to Meiner Kitz in the Tenno Sho (Spring). The next summer a tendon injury ended his career.
962: His first 2 runs, on turf, brought a 4th and an 11th, beaten over 2 seconds in a maiden. Then Kane Hekili tried dirt and won by 7 lengths, then a 5-million dirt race by a mile. Trying turf in the Mainichi Hai, he was 7th, but back on dirt won by 9 lengths. In his 4th dirt race, the Unicorn S., he won as favorite, then the Japan Dirt Derby and Derby Grand Prix with ease. A slow start cost him the Musashino S. (2nd), but he won the Japan Cup Dirt, and the next February S. for his 4th G1. As Japan's representative he went to the Dubai World Cup, 4th. Back home he was 2nd to local star Adjudi Mitsuo in the Teio Sho, below his best. A tendon injury forced a long break, and his comeback was in doubt, but his team's efforts paid off: he returned in the '08 Musashino S. after 2.5 years (9th). Then in a star-studded Japan Cup Dirt he beat crop champion Vermilion and the rest - a miracle comeback. In the year-end Tokyo Daishoten he beat Vermilion again to regain his crown. In '09 he won the Kawasaki Kinen, his 7th G1, but fractured a leg in the Kashiwa Kinen. Back in the '10 Teio Sho after a year, he was a good 2nd to Furioso, but a recurring tendon injury ended his career and he went to stud.
964: 2nd in her first 2 starts, she won her 3rd, then often fell just short. At 4, with a light 51kg, she ran on from a good position to win the Aichi Hai. Mostly unplaced after, she retired in a slump.
965: A New Zealand mare who won 13 G1s from 1998 to 2002. She was New Zealand's Horse of the Year 4 years running, from 3 to 6, and Australia's from 4 to 6. Unbeaten in 7 to her first G1, she beat older horses and colts in the Doncaster H. at the end of 3. She won the Cox Plate at 4 and 5, and at 5 won the Hong Kong Mile. In the Dubai Duty Free she was a close 3rd to Jim and Tonic. At 6 she was 2nd going for a 3rd Cox Plate, but then won 4 G1s in a row. She retired at 7 after a 4th in her 4th Cox Plate. Her career earnings of $11.69 million were then a world record for a mare. She had 4 foals, none successful.
966: A Hong Kong gelding who won 3 G1s: the Dubai Sheema Classic, Hong Kong Cup and Queen Elizabeth II Cup. Originally named Subscribe, he raced in New Zealand, winning his 2nd start at 2 and finishing 5th in the G1 Sires' Produce S. Sold at 3 to Hong Kong, he began a new career as Vengeance of Rain. Slow to win at first, he got his first Hong Kong win late at 4, then won 3 straight up to the Hong Kong Derby, and then the Queen Elizabeth II Cup, his first G1. At 5 he won the Hong Kong Cup, but heart trouble forced a long break. Back nearly a year later at 6, he won the Hong Kong Gold Cup and Dubai Sheema Classic, Hong Kong's Horse of the Year. Heart trouble returned at 7 and he retired to New Zealand, dying in 2011 at 10.
967: Rarely beaten badly even in graded races. He won the Keihan Hai at 4 and the Osaka Hai at 5, a long, steady career. In '07 he won the Sekiya Kinen after a break and was 3rd in the Tenno Sho (Autumn). At 7 in '08, with Norihiro Yokoyama aboard, he switched from closing to racing forward, winning the Nakayama Kinen and Milers C. A fine supporting actor in G1s, 4th in the Tenno Sho, he took the lead role in autumn '09: he ran down top mare Vodka in the Mainichi Okan, beat her again in the Tenno Sho (Autumn) for his first G1 at 8, and won the Mile CS for 3 straight, a perfect finale. Can he carry on sire Miracle Admire's line at stud?
968: Debuting late, in summer at 3, she raced mainly in sprints, rarely running badly. She boldly tried middle-distance graded races, 3rd in the Nakayama Himba S. and 2nd in the Aichi Hai, and won the Keeneland C. at 6.
969: Apart from a 4th in the NZ Trophy in spring at 3 he did little, but at 5 won the Suzaku S. with the fastest 33.6 finish. On that run he won the Keio Hai Spring C., beating Tosho College, Fallichat and others. In the Yasuda Kinen, from the inside draw, he dropped back and swung wide in the straight, losing ground, 12th behind Vodka. Racing mainly in sprints after without success, he retired to stud.
970: 2nd in the Yayoi Sho, he was crushed in the Satsuki Sho (9th) and Derby (17th). After a long slump he won in autumn at 4, his first win in 18 months, ran well after and won the Epsom C. at 5. Dull again, he retired at 7.
971: Consistent but often just short, she changed in autumn at 4, winning an allowance race and an open special, then 3rd in the Victoria Mile the next spring. In the Fuchu Himba S. she ran down Kawakami Princess, who had broken clear from 2nd, for her first graded title. Choosing her best distance over fillies' races, she went to the Mile Championship and outdueled Super Hornet for her first G1 - the first mare to win it in 14 years, since North Flight. She retired after it and became a broodmare at her birthplace from '09.
973: She won her debut with the field's fastest 34.2 finish. Beaten in the Kikyo S. and Daily Hai 2yo S., in the Fantasy S. she swept down the outside past Best Cruise, Grenadine, Ranunculus and others. 3rd choice for the Hanshin JF, her kick misfired, 6th, and she was beaten badly in the fillies' classics. Still, only 3 of her crop ran the Hanshin JF and all 3 fillies' classics: Apapane, Animate Bio and her.
974: 17th on debut, she gave up turf for dirt, which paid off with 6 wins. Her only graded win was Kawasaki's Empress Hai, but she was 2nd in Funabashi's Queen Sho and Oi's TCK Jo-o Hai. She raced until 7.
975: Winless on turf, but a sand specialist with 9 dirt wins. She won the Sparking Lady C. in autumn at 5, then toured the country in JRA-local races, winning the Summer Champion at 6.
976: A JRA-local graded star who won the Sakitama Hai and Hyogo Gold T. at 6.
977: A hyped foreign-bred, he needed 8 starts to win. But from spring at 3, racing mainly in turf sprints, he bloomed, winning the Sakurasou Tokubetsu and Aoi S., and was 3rd in the Falcon S. 8th over 1800m in the Radio Tampa Sho, he returned to sprints and won the Aurora C. and CBC Sho. Winless since, he has done well in sprints: 2nd in the Swan S. and 3rd in the Mile CS.
940: Still in the lower classes, she closed powerfully for 3rd in the Shuka Sho. Injured after, she rested long, but at 5, with a light 51kg, won the Niigata Kinen, then was 4th in the Queen Elizabeth II Cup.
941: A closer: good when her charge worked, poor when it didn't. Her only graded win, the Rose S., came from behind with a 34-second finish. But in the Shuka Sho and Queen Elizabeth II Cup, faster finishers beat her.
946: She won 4 straight allowance races in summer at 4, then beat Erimo Excel and others in the Hanshin Himba Tokubetsu. 2nd in the Fuchu Himba S., steady in fillies' graded races.
952: A front-runner who won every race by leading. Winning a debut race and another, she went to the Oka Sho, but a slow start forced her to race from behind, a good 4th. In the Yonsai Himba Tokubetsu (East) she beat Sakura Clear and others by over 3 lengths. In the Oaks she was swallowed up at an extreme pace, 9th. At 4 she won the Nakayama Himba S. As a dam she produced Tokyo Derby winner Grade Shori (89: Mogami).
953: Three weeks after her debut win she won the Akamatsu Sho, then a week later the Hanshin Sansai Himba S. by 2 lengths as 3rd choice - a G1 just 28 days after her debut, a record. A slow start left her 12th in the Oka Sho, and she was 4th in the Oaks. In autumn she took the unusual route for a 3yo filly of the Mainichi Okan, Tenno Sho (Autumn) and Japan Cup, 4th in the first two. At 4 she moved to miles, winning the Kyoto Himba Tokubetsu. The Keio Hai Spring C. drew 7 G1 winners, incl. Grass Wonder, but Stinger won easily from last with a devilish 33.6 finish. She won it again the next year in 1:20.1, equal to Taiki Shuttle's record - a true speedster.
963: Like many Mori stable runners, he raced hard in JRA-local graded races, winning 6: Saga's Summer Champion, Oi's Tokyo Hai, Urawa's Sakitama Hai, Hokkaido's Hokkaido Sprint C. twice and Morioka's Cluster C. He went to Dubai in '06 and '07 without success, then kept shining at home.
972: Full sister of Hishi Amazon, who led the 1994 crop with Narita Brian. Injured in spring at 3, she came good in autumn, winning the Rose S., and was 2nd choice for the Shuka Sho, but 3rd behind 2 outsiders. She then ran poorly and retired.
979: He debuted at Oi, won the Southern Kanto Triple Crown and more, then moved to the JRA at 5 (old age system), winning the 1968 Tenno Sho (Spring) and Takarazuka Kinen as champion older horse. In a class of his own from the start, at 3 he won 5 of 7, incl. the Zen-Nihon Sansai Yushun. At 4 he won the Haneda Hai, Tokyo Derby and Tokyo Okansho - the first Southern Kanto Triple Crown winner - and despite a 2nd in the Tokyo Daishoten was named local racing's best. Moving to the JRA in spring at 5, after 3 open races he won the Tenno Sho (Spring) by a huge margin, then the Takarazuka Kinen in record time - truly top class. Leg trouble forced a long break; back at 6 he won just one open race and retired at year's end. Yuji Nohira, his rider in both big wins and later one of Japan's great horsemen, summed him up in one word: "strong." At stud he sired local graded winner Mobster but little else, and died in 1990 at 27.
980: A bold traveler in the 1960s, he was the first Japan-trained horse to run in the King George VI & Queen Elizabeth S. and the Arc. As broodmare sire of Symboli Rudolf, he laid the foundation of Symboli Farm. He emerged in autumn at 4 (old age system), a nose 2nd as 14th choice in the Kikuka Sho and 3rd in the Arima Kinen, best of the 4yos. At 5 he won 3 straight to the Tenno Sho (Spring). That autumn he went to America for the Washington DC International, a good 5th but clearly short of the Americans. At 7 he raced in Europe, 5th in the King George and unplaced in the Arc; those defeats are said to have changed jockey (later trainer) Yuji Nohira's view of racing. Back home he won the Arima Kinen, and again at 8 - the first 8yo to win one of the 8 big races. He retired to stud that year. Apart from Diamond S. winner Pure Symboli, his runners were modest, but his daughter Sweet Luna produced Symboli Rudolf, making him a great broodmare sire.
981: The 1969 Kikuka Sho winner. His rapid rise from summer at 4 (old age system) earned him the name "the greatest late improver of the postwar era." Debuting at the end of 3, he needed 7 starts to win, in spring at 4. He won 3 straight allowance races over summer, then the St. Lite Kinen as 7th choice. 2nd in the Kyoto Hai, he was favorite for the Kikuka Sho and won by 4 lengths from Riki Eikan, the next year's Tenno Sho winner. In the Arima Kinen he was a nose 2nd to Speed Symboli. At 5 he was 5th and 3rd in the Tenno Sho races, but won the Nihon Keizai Sho and was again a close 2nd to Speed Symboli in the Arima Kinen. At 6 he won the American JCC and Meguro Kinen (Autumn), and at 7 the Tokyo Shimbun Hai. He never won the Tenno Sho in 4 tries, but retired with 6 graded wins. He had no success at stud.
986: Half-brother of double classic winner Tanino Moutiers, he won the 1973 Tenno Sho (Autumn) and 1974 Arima Kinen, and his crushing wins rank him among the greatest ever. Famous before his debut thanks to his brother, he won his 2nd start, but a fracture kept him out 20 months, missing the classics; he returned in summer at 5 (old age system). He won 3 allowance races easily, then the Asahi Challenge C., then the Hollywood Turf Club Sho (now Kyoto Daishoten) over 2 Tenno Sho winners, Yamanin Wave and Mejiro Musashi, and then the Tenno Sho (Autumn) - a big-race winner in no time. In the Arima Kinen, too wary of favorite Haiseiko, he was 4th. At 6, after spring 2nds in the Kyoto Kinen and Sankei Osaka Hai, he won 3 straight in autumn from the Kyoto Daishoten to the Arima Kinen - this time running his own race, leading all the way to beat Haiseiko by 5 lengths. At 7 he won the Kyoto Kinen (Spring) by a huge margin under 63kg, prompting race caller Sugimoto to say "the strongest horse I've ever seen." After one more open win, he ran despite leg trouble in the Milers C. (3rd) and retired. He died of a ruptured aorta after only 5 years at stud, siring Hanshin Shogai S. winner Shiba Ricky and local graded winners.
988: The Derby winner of the TTG crop (Tosho Boy, Ten Point, Green Grass). That year's classics centered on Tosho Boy versus Ten Point, who ran 1-2 in the Satsuki Sho, but in the Derby Climb Kaiser broke in and took the title. His win was forceful, almost worthy of an inquiry, and caused controversy: as favorite Tosho Boy hit the front off the final turn, Climb Kaiser swooped from outside as if to bump him, got ahead of the flinching Tosho Boy and held on. It was said to exploit Tosho Boy's weakness of flinching when challenged. Some even renamed the "Climb Kaiser" the "Crime Kaiser." He never won again, but rarely out of the top five, he gave the TTG trio many good fights. Retired with injury, he had little success at stud; apart from Kyodo News Hai winner Meiner Brave, no notable runners.
989: Debuting at local Utsunomiya and unbeaten in 4, she moved to the JRA, was 2nd in the Flower C. and ran a bold 4th in the Oaks, leading at the final turn. From autumn she ran mainly on dirt, 2nd in the Winter S. and 3rd in the next February H. (G3). She also won on turf, never shy against colts, and at 5 won the Kimpai (East). Racing on in graded races on turf and dirt, she ran 36 times before retiring at 6.
992: Winner of the Tenno Sho (Spring), Takarazuka Kinen, Kyoto Kinen and more, but you never knew when he would win. Beaten badly when fancied and winning easily when not, he was called "Fickle George." 3rd in the Hanshin Sansai S. (old age system), at 4 he won the Shinzan Kinen as favorite, a classic contender. But no match for legendary front-runner Kaburaya O, he was 3rd in the Satsuki Sho and 12th in the Derby. After a slump, at 5 he was 3rd in the Sankei Osaka Hai and Naruo Kinen, then won the Tenno Sho (Spring) as 12th choice, stunning fans. Losing and falling out of favor, he won the Hakodate Kinen easily under 60kg; fancied again, he flopped in the Kyoto Daishoten; ignored again, he won the Kyoto Kinen in record time. At 6 he slumped as the TTG crop rose, but at 7 won 3 straight - Kyoto Kinen, Naruo Kinen and Takarazuka Kinen. Jockey Yoichi Fukunaga said happily, "the horse is finally complete." As if mocking him, the horse never placed again, though often fancied, and retired after the Takarazuka Kinen at 8. Even master Fukunaga gave up: "If anyone knows when he'll run, please tell me." At stud, many foals shared his bad temper; the only notable one was Paris Bembe, a 5-time allowance winner who ran in the Tenno Sho.
993: Winner of the 1980 Arima Kinen and 1981 Tenno Sho (Autumn). Injured after his debut win, he rested about 2 years, then returned at 5 (old age system) and won allowance race after allowance race. At 6 he was 2nd choice for the Tenno Sho (Autumn), but let Pretty Cast run away and was 7th. He gained revenge in the Arima Kinen, beating Katsurano Haiseiko by a nose after a fierce duel, and was named Horse of the Year. Injured in spring at 7, he aimed for the Tenno Sho (Autumn), where he and Monte Prince broke clear and dueled, winning by a nose on the photo. He then ran in the first Japan Cup, 6th, the 2nd-best Japanese horse, and retired after a 2nd to Amber Shadai in the Arima Kinen. He died during his first breeding season, leaving only one crop; the best was Hokkaido Kinen winner Best Boy.
994: Winner of the 1981 Satsuki Sho and Derby. The road was not smooth: named for "Top" and "Ace," he was still stuck in the 8-million class when the classic season came. He only got into the Satsuki Sho because leading horses withdrew, and was 16th choice of 17. But from the inside draw he broke well, led and never gave it up. Jockey Osaki was amazed: "I only led because we were in gate 1." Seen as a fluke with no strong rivals, he was only 3rd choice for the Derby despite being Satsuki Sho winner. Again he defied the doubters: racing forward, he broke clear with favorite San Ei Solon and won by a nose for the double. Injury ended his career, but he left his name in history. At stud he was disappointing, siring only a few allowance winners.
998: The legendary front-runner who won the 1983 Takarazuka Kinen. Half-brother of Hagino Top Lady, he sold for 185 million yen, then a staggering price. He lived up to it, winning his first 3 to lead the classic crop. But in the Satsuki Sho he dueled fellow front-runner Gail Sport and both collapsed, and the same happened in the NHK Hai - a lost spring. In autumn he won the Kobe Shimbun Hai and Kyoto Shimbun Hai and was Kikuka Sho favorite, but again led and faded, 14th - no luck in the classics. He showed his worth at 4, leading all the way in the Swan S., Takarazuka Kinen and Takamatsunomiya Hai, suddenly a star. He didn't win again, but his bold runaway in the 3rd Japan Cup is remembered as Japan's pride against the foreign stars.
1000: He moved from local racing to the JRA and won the 1982 Arima Kinen. Racing in Southern Kanto and Tokai until mid 5, he joined the JRA that autumn with little fanfare, given his modest record. But in his first race, the Asahi Challenge C., he closed to win as 7th choice, drawing attention. He was 2nd to Mejiro Titan in the Tenno Sho (Autumn), 5th in the Japan Cup (best Japanese horse) and won the Arima Kinen over Mejiro Titan and Amber Shadai - Horse of the Year. The next year he won the Osaka Hai, but broke down in the Tenno Sho (Spring) and retired.
1001: Winner of the 1981 Kikuka Sho and the Argentina Kyowakoku Hai at 4 and 5. 14th choice in the Kikuka Sho, he won by 4 lengths from favorite San Ei Solon, Shinzan's first classic winner as a sire. His 2nd Argentina Kyowakoku Hai at 5 is famous: in a blanket finish with long-distance favorite Amber Shadai and previous Kikuka Sho winner Hollyskey, he edged ahead by a nose at the line - a race for the history books.
1002: Winner of the 1983 Arima Kinen. Overshadowed in the classics by Triple Crown winner Mr. C.B., he represented his crop in the year-end Arima Kinen in Mr. C.B.'s absence, beating older stars like Amber Shadai and Mejiro Titan. But an injury found right after ended his career - the Arima Kinen was his first and last open-class win.
1003: The 1970 Satsuki Sho and Derby winner. He had a fierce rivalry with crop-mate Arrow Express, beating him on the track, but was left far behind at stud. Tough, he ran 9 times at 3 (old age system), winning 7 including the Hanshin Sansai S., top of the Kansai crop, and at 4 his clash with Kanto's best, Arrow Express, was eagerly awaited. He beat him in the Spring S. and narrowly again in the Satsuki Sho. Off form and mistaking the finish post, he was 2nd to him in the NHK Hai, but repaid him in the Derby for the double. During a summer break he developed a breathing problem; he returned in autumn anyway but was beaten badly 3 times, and after an 11th in the Kikuka Sho, chasing the 3rd Triple Crown ever, he retired. At stud he sired few stars beyond open winner Tanino Cyrus and local graded winner Hello King, overtaken by the very successful sire Arrow Express.
1004: With part-bred blood on his dam's side, he wasn't recognized as a Thoroughbred, yet raced as a part-bred with great success. Raised beside a farmhouse, untrained, he was bought cheaply for 1.5 million yen - but rose to win the Satsuki Sho and Derby, a true rags-to-riches story. Starting without basic training, he won his first 3 by wide margins, and at 4 (old age system) the Kisaragi Sho. Hot-tempered and erratic, he was 4th choice for the Satsuki Sho but won brilliantly. Still not trusted, 2nd choice for the Derby, he came from last of 28 with a stunning straight-long charge to win. In autumn he was 3rd in his first race and 9th in the Kyoto Shimbun Hai, then a tendon injury ended his Triple Crown dream and his career. At stud his part-bred status kept mares away, and he sired no stars.
1005: The 1977 Kikuka Sho winner. Winning 3 straight at the end of 3 (old age system), he drew attention, but was mediocre in graded races: 13th in the Satsuki Sho and 7th in the Derby. In autumn he came good, 2nd in the Keio Hai Autumn H., then winning the St. Lite Kinen and Kyoto Shimbun Hai, given a single-bracket entry for the Kikuka Sho. Behind only Derby winner Lucky Ruler in the betting, he powered home to beat Tenmei and others for his classic title. In the Arima Kinen he faced TTG and was 4th, flying the flag for his crop. Older, he was a middle-to-long distance force: he failed to finish in the Tenno Sho (Spring) clash with Green Grass, but in autumn won the Mainichi Okan and was 2nd in the Tenno Sho (Autumn). Fetlock trouble followed, and he retired after a 4th in the Mainichi Okan at 6. He sired no notable runners and after 10 years was exported to Korea.
1006: A rare carrier of the Tom Fool branch, a side line of the Phalaris line that makes up about 80% of all Thoroughbreds. Bred in America, he was named Buckpasser - one who dodges responsibility - after his sire Tom Fool. Despite the name, he had a superb build and temperament: "every horse has 100 faults, but this one has none." He won 25 of 31, and at 3 won 13 straight, incl. the Woodward S. and Jockey Club Gold C., US Horse of the Year. At stud he sired Buckaroo, Egg Toss and others, his male line surviving faintly today. He is famous above all as a broodmare sire of Maruzensky, Miswaki, Woodman, Seeking the Gold and more, his blood spread widely.
978: With Tosho Boy and Green Grass he formed the "Big Three" of 1976-77, known as "TTG" from their initials. His beautiful chestnut coat and blaze earned him the name "the Shooting Star Prince." He emerged early, winning the Hanshin Sansai S. (old age system), and his clashes with Tosho Boy in the classics were the talk of racing. He was 2nd to Tosho Boy in the Satsuki Sho, 7th in the Derby, and 2nd to late bloomer Green Grass in the Kikuka Sho - no classic. But older, he showed his true worth: winning 3 straight to the Tenno Sho (Spring), then, after a 2nd to Tosho Boy in the Takarazuka Kinen, 3 more in autumn to the Arima Kinen, avenging himself on Tosho Boy. That year of battles among the three, above all that Arima Kinen, is told as one of racing's greatest duels. Then at 6 came tragedy: in the Nihon Keizai Shinshun Hai, a prep for a trip abroad, he broke a leg and had to be put down. Many fans laid flowers at his grave at Yoshida Farm, his birthplace. In 1990, 12 years after his death, he was added to the JRA Hall of Fame for contributions beyond his record.
982: Winner of 4 graded races incl. the 1973 Yasuda Kinen and Sapporo Kinen, he was from the last crop of Hindostan, 7-time champion sire - "his final masterpiece." Best at 1200-2000m, at 4 (old age system) he won the Kabutoyama Kinen and was 2nd in the NHK Hai, Sprinters S. and Kumohata Kinen. At 5 he won the Yasuda Kinen, Sapporo Kinen and All Comers. A fracture in that year's Tenno Sho (Autumn) ended his career. At stud he sired local graded winners, and Hakuho Queen, holder of local racing's record 161-race losing streak.
983: The 1974 Derby winner, with 4 wins from 11, always in the top 3. At 3 (old age system) he won 3 allowance races; at 4 he was 2nd in the Keisei Hai, 3rd in the Yayoi Sho and 2nd to Kitano Kachidoki in the Satsuki Sho. In the Derby he beat Kitano Kachidoki in a record 2:27.4. Injury ended his career after it. At stud he sired local graded winner Seven Lancer and others, and in 1984 was presented to the President of South Korea.
984: Winner of the 2009 Tenno Sho (Spring). A late bloomer, he reached open class at 5 and grew stronger in G2s and G3s. At 6, after a 2nd in the Nikkei Sho, he won the Tenno Sho (Spring) at 46.5 to 1, a huge upset: favorite Asakusa Kings and 2nd choice Screen Hero were swallowed by the pack, and he won a tight finish by a neck. The next year he won the Nikkei Sho and was 2nd in the Tenno Sho (Spring), and the year after won the Stayers S., a long-distance force for years until retiring in 2013 at 10.
985: She won 4 straight allowance races from late 4 into spring at 5, then was 5th in the Victoria Mile. She finally won the Hakodate Sprint S. in summer at 6. She retired to breed after a 10th in the '08 Hankyu Hai. All 8 wins came at 1500m or less - a pure sprinter.
990: She finished behind Mejiro Ramonu 6 times: Yonsai Himba Tokubetsu (West), Oka Sho, Yonsai Himba Tokubetsu (East), Oaks, Rose S. and Queen Elizabeth Cup. After that she won the Hanshin and Kyoto Himba Tokubetsu, and at 4 the Swan S., holding her own against colts.
991: Based at local Oi, she won 6 at 3 and 3 at 4. At 5 she won the Queen Sho, Kanto Hai and Tokyo Hai in a row, then moved to the JRA, winning only the Kokura Nikkei Sho at 6. Often a narrow 2nd.
995: Son of Tomei, hailed as the greatest mare, he made the first mother-son Tenno Sho double. Late at 3 he showed his stamina with 2nds in the Kikuka Sho and Hanshin Daishoten. In autumn at 4, as 5th choice, he won the Tenno Sho (Autumn), the race his dam had won. He won the Kyoto Daishoten at 5, then raced in Iwate until 8.
996: The first Japanese horse to go toe-to-toe with foreign horses in the Japan Cup. At 5 he won the Diamond S. and was 4th in the Takarazuka Kinen. In autumn at 6 he finally won a big race, the Tenno Sho (Autumn). With Triple Crown winner Mr. C.B. absent, he was Japan's main hope in that year's Japan Cup, and ran a superb 2nd, beaten a head - the best by a Japanese horse. He retired after the race, the first to give Japan real hope of winning the Japan Cup.
997: The most-watched horse of the 1981 classics. He won all 3 trials - the Spring S., NHK Hai and Kyoto Shimbun Hai - as favorite, yet was scratched from the Satsuki Sho and 2nd in both the Derby and Kikuka Sho - the "Trial Triple Crown winner." But all agreed on his ability: older, he won the Sankei Osaka Hai and was 2nd in the Takamatsunomiya Hai and Mainichi Okan. At stud he sired local stars like Tokyo Daishoten winner Bold Face and Takasaki Derby winner San Ei Speed.
999: The 1980 Satsuki Sho winner. Strong on dirt and heavy ground, he was at his best in the Satsuki Sho, run in a downpour: 4th choice, he sat handy and held off Opec Horse in the straight. 14th in the Derby, he then won Fukushima's Radio Tampa Sho, Fukushima Kinen and the Local Racing Invitational, and raced until 7.
987: As 12th choice she won the Rose S., beating favorite Elps. After a 13th in the Queen Elizabeth Cup and an 18-month break, she ran a few times and retired to breed. Her foals include Shingun Opera (98: Opera House).
1007: A French great who won the 1965 Derby and Arc and was rated 145 lbs by Timeform, then the highest ever - unbeaten for 47 years until Frankel's 147 in 2012. At 2 he won 2 of 3, rated behind Grey Dawn. At 3 he won the Prix Greffulhe and Prix Lupin, then the Epsom Derby in England, the Grand Prix de Saint-Cloud, and the Arc by 6 lengths - European Horse of the Year. He retired after the Arc, was leased to America for 7 crops, and died soon after the start of his first season back in France. His short stud career produced French fillies' Triple Crown and Arc winner Allez France, and his male line continues faintly through Arctic Tern and Bering.
1008: Winner of 11 G1s, then the most by an American mare, she ran 32 times at 3-4, earning the name "Iron Lady." Often beaten until spring at 3, she then won 8 straight, beating Triple Tiara winner Mom's Command in the Test S. and winning the Maskette S. by 5.5 lengths for her first G1. 2nd in the BC Distaff, she lost the champion 3yo filly title to Mom's Command. At 4 she took on males, winning the Whitney H. - the first mare to do so in 38 years - and ran well in the Metropolitan H. and Woodward S. With a record 8 G1s that year, she was Eclipse Horse of the Year. From 5 she won just 2 allowance races and retired. Her foals disappointed, but granddaughter Sound Barrier won the Fillies' Revue, and her foal Sound Chiara won 3 graded races in a row and was 2nd in the Victoria Mile - her family thrives in Japan.
1010: Two long injury breaks limited him to 18 starts by 7. Hard to keep sound, but talented, with 6 wins incl. the Tanabata Sho at 6. He retired to stud after a 16th in the '06 Niigata Kinen.
1011: Winning 6 dirt allowance races, he went to the Japan Cup Dirt at 4 (8th). 2nd in the Negishi S., he won the Tokai S. at 6, then the Breeders' Gold C., but broke down in the year-end Tokyo Daishoten and was put down.
1012: A strong mare who won the English fillies' Triple Crown and held her own against older horses and colts. Unbeaten in 5, she won the 1000 Guineas, then the Oaks by 6 lengths from Triptych, later winner of 9 G1s. In summer she was 2nd in the King George VI & Queen Elizabeth Diamond S. and Benson & Hedges Gold C., proving herself against older horses and colts. In autumn she won the St. Leger, the 9th fillies' Triple Crown winner and first in 30 years. She retired after it to breed: 7 wins and two 2nds from 9, favorite every time. Her 2nd foal Shaima won a US G2, her 3rd, Rosefinch, the French G1 Prix Saint-Alary, and Shaima's son Shantou the St. Leger and Gran Premio di Milano - a fine broodmare.
1014: Debuting fairly early, in September at 2, he was slow to win and long stuck in the lower classes. At 4 he won the Korea Racing Authority Hai to reach open class, then made the top three in the Japan Cup Dirt 2 years running. At 6 he won the Kawasaki Kinen over Furioso and other local stars for his first title, but broke down in the February S. Back after 8 months, he was 5th in the JBC Classic and 4th in the Urawa Kinen, then rested again for about 2.5 years. On his return he lost his rider at the start of the Antares S. and was scratched from the Tokai S., but as 8th choice he was a fine 5th in the Teio Sho - a veteran's grit.
1015: 9 wins from 44, mainly at a dirt mile to middle distances, with eleven 2nds. He liked the Procyon S. (2nd in '05, 3rd in '06) but usually ran poorly in other dirt graded races. A dirt supporting player who won the Enif S. (OP) in '07, he retired after that year's Aldebaran S.
1017: Long in the lower classes, he reached open class at 5 and was 2nd in the Tokai S., then won the Antares S. the next spring. At year's end he beat Meisho Tokon in the Nagoya Grand Prix - he had come good at 6. At 7 he won the Heian S. by a neck from Espoir City, later Kashiwa Kinen winner. 2nd to improvers in the Nagoya Daishoten and Antares S., in his 3rd Tokai S. he swept past Japan Cup Dirt winner Alondite to win. He won the Nagoya Grand Prix again but never bettered 3rd in G1s - yet in 2012 his half-brother Wonder Acute won the JBC Classic, fulfilling his big brother's G1 dream.
1018: Little noticed at first, he needed 9 starts to win. Steadily working through the classes, he showed his staying power: 3rd in the Stayers S. and Manyo S., then the '08 Nikkei Shinshun Hai, and the Diamond S. over later Tenno Sho winner Admire Jupiter and others. In autumn he was 2nd in the Kyoto Daishoten and 2nd to Daiwa Scarlet in the Arima Kinen, with more to come - but after a 5th in the Nikkei Shinshun Hai, a fractured sesamoid ended his career. He became a riding horse.
1019: Out of form after a big loss in the Hanshin JF, at 3 she took on older horses in the Ibis Summer Dash and won with a sharp finish as 7th choice. She kept running hard as a turf 1200m specialist without results, retiring to breed in summer '07.
1020: He won 3 straight to the Sapporo 2yo S., then the Kyodo News Hai and Yayoi Sho, a heavy classic favorite - but 4th in the Satsuki Sho and 7th in the Derby. In autumn he beat older horses in the Sapporo Kinen and, putting distance first, chose the Tenno Sho (Autumn) over the Kikuka Sho, a fine 3rd. His last race at 3, the Hong Kong Cup, brought a 2nd. Even stronger at 4, he beat veteran Pop Rock in the Kyoto Kinen, then won the Dubai Duty Free over world stars including Daiwa Major - his first G1, abroad. Back home he beat Meisho Samson in the Takarazuka Kinen, the best horse in training. He then made news with a rare trade to a new owner. 6th in the Tenno Sho (Autumn) off a break, he won his farewell, the Japan Cup, proving himself among the best. His first crop debuted in 2011: Fine Choice won the Hakodate 2yo S. at once, followed by graded winners like Leo Active and Hakusan Moon, and in 2018 Fine Needle won both sprint G1s. A big hope among sires standing in Hidaka.
1021: Won the Flower C. but retired injured after one more race. Dam of '07 February S. winner Sunrise Bacchus (02: Hennessy).
1022: A speedster who won the Lord Derby CT. Dam of 6-time winner Golden Rodrigo (97: Rodrigo de Triano).
1023: His first 4 races on turf brought 6th at best. Switched to dirt, he emerged at once, much like crop rival Kane Hekili. In the Derby Grand Prix he was 2nd, 2.5 lengths behind Kane Hekili, but next in the Musashino S. he beat the previously unbeaten-on-dirt Kane Hekili for his first graded win. In '07 he won the February S., his first G1. Winless since, he kept running well on dirt and later moved to local racing.
1025: He won 3 straight on dirt from a maiden, then the Unicorn S. As the JRA's best 3yo dirt horse he went to the Japan Dirt Derby, but was a well-beaten 3rd to local stars Furioso and Ampersand. Against older horses he was 3rd to Meisho Tokon in the Elm S., then 9th in the Musashino S. He won the Topaz S. and was 2nd in the year-end Nagoya Grand Prix. Older, he was 4th in the February S. at 4, but repeated long breaks followed, and he retired in 2011 at 7.
1026: Poor in the Yayoi Sho and Mainichi Hai, he missed the Satsuki Sho, but won the Kyoto Shimbun Hai to make the Derby (11th). 9th in the Kikuka Sho, he returned to middle distances, 3rd in the Chunichi Shimbun Hai, then won the Chukyo Kinen and Sapporo Kinen. In '09 he was a fair 5th in Singapore's Airlines International C., and in '10 was 2nd in the Chukyo Kinen as 12th choice, a popular supporting player. He broke down in the Kinko Sho and was put down.
1027: She won her debut and the Kokura Sansai S. easily, but after an 8th in the Hanshin Sansai Himba S. she ran poorly and retired. Her first foal Alluring Voice (03: French Deputy) also won the Kokura 2yo S., and also fell away after the Hanshin JF.
1028: Winning 4 straight incl. the Kokura 2yo S. and Fantasy S., she was Hanshin JF favorite but finished 14th. At 3 she was 4th in the Fillies' Revue and 7th in the Oka Sho, and early-bloomer talk, like her dam, began. A fracture forced a long break; back in April '07 she didn't win, though she ran well against males in sprints, retiring to breed after the '08 Ibis Summer Dash.
1030: Dam of Monte Prince and Monte Fast, the 4th pair of brothers to win the Tenno Sho. Talented herself, she won 9 races, mainly in allowances, and was 2nd in the Nakayama Himba S. 2 years running. Racing until spring at 7 (old age system), she went straight to stud, breeding until 20 and leaving 9 foals. The best were her 3rd and 4th. Monte Prince starred in the classics, 2nd in the Derby and Kikuka Sho, then won the Tenno Sho (Spring) and Takarazuka Kinen at 6. Monte Fast struggled in allowances until 6, scorned as the lesser brother, but won the Tenno Sho (Spring) at 7, silencing critics. Thanks to the two, Monte Okan's place as a great mare was secure. She also produced Monte Japan, 3rd in the Tokyo Shimbun Hai and Nakayama Kinen.
1031: Winning 2 straight at 5, he was 2nd in the Kokura Kinen, then narrowly beat Erimo Harrier and others in the Asahi Challenge C. Twice 3rd in graded races after, he never won again; his last race was the Nakayama Kimpai at 10.
1032: She won the Queen C. and was 3rd in the Oka Sho, but pulled up in the Oaks. Back in the Shuka Sho, she was 17th. After more poor runs, at 4 she was 2nd against males in the Lord Derby Challenge T., then as 12th choice won the Victoria Mile with a sharp finish - a shock G1. She went to the US for the CashCall Mile (9th), then slumped again in autumn: 11th in the Sprinters S., 8th in the Fuji S., 14th in the Mile CS. She retired to breed after a 10th in the '08 Tokyo Shimbun Hai.
1034: Half-brother of 2006 Kobai S. (OP) winner Touch the Peak. A slow developer, winless in the JRA, he moved to local racing in autumn at 3 and won 4 of 5. Back in the JRA in spring at 4, he climbed the classes and won the Amethyst S. at 5 to reach open class. Improving with placings in local graded races, he was a close 3rd to Curren Black Hill in the star-studded Mainichi Okan at 6, ahead of Derby winner Eishin Flash. Then in the Nakayama Kimpai he won with a sharp late kick - his first graded win at 7.
1035: Seen as a classic contender at 4 (old age system), she was 5th in the Oka Sho as 4th choice and 19th in the Oaks as 3rd choice. Moving to miles and middle distances, she won the Himba Tokyo Times Hai (now Fuchu Himba S.). At 5 she was 2nd in the Kimpai (East), and at 6 won the Sekiya Kinen. As a dam she produced Himba Tokyo Times Hai winner Lovesick Blues - a mother-daughter double.
1036: He needed 3 starts to win and was 2nd in the Tokyo Sports Hai 2yo S. and Kisaragi Sho, slow to win a graded race. When he won the Spring S. and went to the Satsuki Sho it was already his 10th start - heavily raced for a classic horse. But his wins in the Satsuki Sho and Derby, breaking clear from a good position, were dominant, and a Triple Crown seemed possible. Then he slipped to 2nd in the Kobe Shimbun Hai, 4th in the Kikuka Sho and 5th in the Arima Kinen, and his stock fell. At 4 he won the Osaka Hai and Tenno Sho (Spring); 2nd to Admire Moon in the Takarazuka Kinen, he regained, even raised, his reputation. An Arc plan was wiped out by an equine flu epidemic. Venting his frustration, he crushed top domestic rivals like Admire Moon and Daiwa Major in the Tenno Sho (Autumn), leaving many fans wondering "what if he had run in the Arc?" That "if" came true in '08: winless since, but strong in defeat with 2nds in the Tenno Sho (Spring) and Takarazuka Kinen, he went to the Arc, but was 10th in the rough European race. Back home he was 6th in the Japan Cup and 8th in his farewell Arima Kinen, ending 4 years of racing. He went to stud at Shadai Stallion Station from '09. His first crop included Principal S. (OP) winner Samson's Pride, and in 2015 Denko Ange won the Artemis S. as 12th choice, his first graded winner.
1037: He won the Yurikamome Sho and was 2nd to Higher Game in the Aoba Sho. 9th in the Derby, he showed early aptitude for the classics and staying trips. 2nd in the St. Lite Kinen, he closed strongly from midfield for 2nd to Delta Blues in the Kikuka Sho. A long break with leg trouble followed; in his 2nd race back he won the All Comers. But leg trouble persisted, and he retired at 6 after a cycle of slumps and breaks.
1038: The 1979 Oaks winner. Her daughter was Oka Sho winner Agnes Flora, whose sons were Derby winner Agnes Flight and Satsuki Sho winner Agnes Tachyon - classic winners for 3 generations. Consistent from her debut, she was 2nd choice for the Oka Sho at 4 (old age system) but 6th, her first time out of the top five. After a 2nd in the Yonsai Himba Tokubetsu she won the Oaks as favorite, breaking clear from a good spot, jockey Kawachi's first big-race win. In autumn she was favorite for the Queen Elizabeth Cup but narrowly 2nd to Miss Kabura-ya. Older, she won the Kyoto Kinen and Asahi Challenge C. against colts. Bred to British great Mill Reef, she produced a foal injured before racing, but 5 years later, bred to Royal Ski, came Agnes Flora, founding a great family.
1039: She won her first 3, incl. the Hakodate Sansai S. (old age system), a contender for the spring classics at 4. Crushed in the Oka Sho (15th), she won the Yonsai Himba Tokubetsu right after, and the Hanshin Himba Tokubetsu in autumn. At 5 she beat crop Derby winner Katsurano Haiseiko and others in the Kyoto Daishoten and was 3rd choice for the Tenno Sho (Autumn), partly due to a jinx of a mare winning it every 9 years. Another mare, Pretty Cast, won instead, and Silk Ski was 10th, retiring after the race. Her best foal was Silk Maria, 2nd in the Chunichi Sports Sho Yonsai S.
1040: The 1982 Oka Sho winner. Victoria Crown was that year's classic favorite but was injured, and in the open Oka Sho, Riesen Gross won. After a 2nd in the Hanshin Yonsai Himba Tokubetsu, as 2nd choice she won by 5 lengths. She was 2nd in the Oaks, then missed the autumn through fatigue, retiring at the end of 4 without ever meeting Victoria Crown.
1041: Switched to dirt in his 9th start, he took off, winning 5 straight to reach open class. Racing forward, he was consistent but kept just missing graded wins, until at the end of 6 he won the JRA-local Nagoya Grand Prix - 3 years after reaching open class in autumn at 3. He kept livening up middle-distance dirt races from the front, winning the Hakusan Daishoten in 2013 and 2014.
1042: Won the 1980 Oaks by 5 lengths as 10th choice. Never well fancied after, she won the Chukyo Kinen and was 2nd in the Kyoto Kinen (Spring), Kokura Daishoten and Hankyu Hai - a dogged runner. She died in May 2011, aged 34.
1009: Gelded before his debut, he bloomed in summer at 4. Inconsistent but powerful, he won the '05 Hakodate Kinen and again the next year. After a 5th in the Sapporo Kinen, a tendon injury cost him nearly a year, but in his 2nd race back he won the Hakodate Kinen a 3rd time. 3rd in the All Comers and 4th in the Mainichi Okan, he was 4th going for a 4th Hakodate Kinen in '08, showing his age.
1013: In her first graded race, the Shuka Sho in autumn at 3, she stayed at the back, 12th. Stuck in the lower classes for 18 months, she reached open class at 5, leading all the way in the Minami Hokkaido S. on a light weight. 9th in the Kyoto Daishoten, she then set her own pace in the Queen Elizabeth II Cup and held off Buena Vista - the first Kanto-trained winner since Mejiro Dober in '99. In her last race, the Hong Kong Cup, she led but tired, last of 10.
1016: A tough mare who ran 48 times on turf and dirt. She settled in open class only at 6, then the next spring won the Fukushima Himba S. with a powerful late charge - her first and last graded win.
1029: Slow to rise, he emerged in spring at 5, winning the Niigata Daishoten in a tight finish, then 2nd in the Epsom C. and Asahi Challenge C. After a 10th in the Tenno Sho (Autumn) he faded, retiring after the '09 Kyoto Kimpai.
1033: The 1973 Oaks winner. Polished early, with 5 wins and two 2nds from 7 at 3 (old system), she was 2nd in the Yonsai Himba Tokubetsu, then won the Oaks over its winner Lady Sport and Oka Sho winner Nittoh Chidori, who beat her in the Victoria C. in autumn. Older, she won the Niigata Kinen at 5 and Keio Hai Autumn H. at 6, then retired. Her 6 foals incl. Niigata Daishoten runner-up Nasuno Prince and Meguro Kinen runner-up Nasuno Taizan.
1044: He won 3 straight at 3, but was 2nd in the Kokura Daishoten, 4th in the Chukyo Kinen and 5th in the Niigata Daishoten, graded-winless through 4. At 5 he was 2nd in the Kyoto Kimpai and Kokura Daishoten, then won the Hankyu Hai and the Keio Hai Spring C., a mile contender. 3rd in the Yasuda Kinen, he never won again.
1045: A foundation mare of Mejiro Farm whose family produced Mejiro McQueen, Mejiro Durren, Mejiro Phantom and many more. She bred 16 foals over 18 years, from 6 (old age system) to 23, building a great family. A daughter of sire Bostonian, she raced poorly but made her sire's name as a broodmare. She won just 2 allowance races from 25, retiring at the end of 4. Eleven of her foals won, and sons Mejiro Suisei and Mejiro Hawk won graded races. Her daughter Mejiro Iris produced Mejiro Aurora, dam of 2 G1 winners, Mejiro McQueen and Mejiro Durren. Mejiro Harima produced graded winners Mejiro Phantom and Mejiro Jupiter, and later descendants include Shonan Kampf and Shonan Tachyon. Mejiro Farm closed in 2011, but Asama Yuri's blood lives on as a native Japanese family.
1046: Dam of 1980 Satsuki Sho winner Hawaiian Image and graded winners Meiwa Kimiko and Pro Maid. Imported from America, she began breeding in 1973 at 5 (old age system). Her first foal Meiwa Kimiko won the Sprinters S. in 1977 and 1978, and her 3rd, Hawaiian Image, won the Satsuki Sho, one of the 8 big races. He also won the Radio Tampa Sho and Fukushima Kinen - an unusual classic winner who starred at local meetings and on dirt. Her 6th foal Pro Maid won the Kabutoyama Kinen, her 3rd graded winner. After her 7th, Out Power (unraced), she was bred every year until 22 without another foal. Meiwa Kimiko carried on the family, her great-grandson King Joy winning the Nakayama Daishogai twice.
1048: The 1972 Oaks winner; her half-brother a year younger was Derby and Tenno Sho (Spring) winner Take Hope. She won her debut and was 3rd in the Keisei Hai Sansai S., her only 2 starts at 3 (old age system). At 4 she struggled in allowances, won once and went to the Yonsai Himba Tokubetsu as 12th choice, but was 2nd to Takai Homa, rising to 3rd choice for the Oaks. There she beat favorite Takai Homa clearly for her only title. She never won again, placing in some open races but crushed in graded races, e.g. 12th in the Lord Derby Challenge T. and 11th in the Kimpai (East). She retired at 6 with 3 wins from 20. Of her 9 foals none won a graded race, but Take Masaru was 2nd in the Kabutoyama Kinen and Take Fighter 2nd in the Mainichi Hai, and 3 daughters carry on her family.
1049: Winning 4 straight to the Hanshin Yonsai Himba Tokubetsu (old age system), she was Oka Sho favorite but 7th to Titania. In autumn she was 5th as 3rd choice in the Queen Elizabeth Cup. Older, she was 3rd in the Azuma Kofuji Sho and Fukushima Daishoten, then 2nd choice for the Yasuda Kinen, which she won by 3.5 lengths - a big-race win at last. She retired after it. A prolific dam with 15 foals, she produced no stars.
1050: A mare who won 10 G1s, including the King George VI & Queen Elizabeth S. twice. She won it at 3 and 4; at 3 she crushed stars like Roberto and Rheingold by 6 lengths, still the race's widest margin, and she is often called the greatest mare. She also won the Benson & Hedges Gold C. twice, the Irish Oaks and Grand Prix de Saint-Cloud, and in America the Washington DC International and Man o' War S. But her crop included Allez France, French fillies' Triple Crown and Arc winner, and in 8 meetings she never beat her. She raced until 6, retiring with 15 wins from 48. At stud she had 13 foals, incl. G1 winners Dahar, Riverman's son Rivlia and Delegant. Rivlia sired Satsuki Sho winner Narita Taishin in Japan, and Dicky Dream sired Sengoku Silver there - a family of note.
1051: A legendary horse who excelled on turf and dirt at any distance. Emerging early, he won 6 straight from autumn at 3 (old age system) to spring at 4, by 7 lengths in the Asahi Hai Sansai S. and 8 in the Tokyo Yonsai S. (now Kyodo News Hai), the top classic hope. But then came a frustrating run of 2nds: Yayoi Sho, Spring S., Satsuki Sho, NHK Hai and Derby - no spring title. In autumn he went to America for the Washington DC International, last of 8. At 5 he showed his true worth, winning 8 straight incl. the Tokyo Shimbun Hai (dirt 2100m), Kyoto Kinen (Spring), Tenno Sho (Spring), Mainichi Okan (dirt 2100m) and the British Fair Commemorative (now Sprinters S.) - 4 in record time, the Tenno Sho with a sprinter's kick. Unstoppable. In autumn he went back to America for the DC International, but fell ill and finished last. Still tired on his return, he retired. Excluding America, he won 16 of 27 in Japan, his losses ten 2nds and one 3rd - superbly consistent. At stud, in an era hard on Japan-bred sires, he produced many graded winners like Dokan Yashima and Ajishiba O, and local stars like Hatsushiba O.
1052: The sire who ruled Japanese racing in the 1970s-80s with Symboli Rudolf, Mejiro Asama, Sakura Shori and more. An Irish racehorse, he won only 2 of 14, but ran respectably even over long trips, 6th in the Irish Derby and 4th in the Irish St. Leger. Bought jointly by Tomohiro Wada of Symboli Farm and Toyokichi Kitano of Mejiro Farm, he was imported to Japan to stand. His son Mejiro Asama soon won the Tenno Sho (Autumn), followed by Derby winner Sakura Shori and 7-time G1 winner Symboli Rudolf. Mejiro Asama led via Mejiro Titan to Mejiro McQueen, Sakura Shori to Sakura Star O, and Symboli Rudolf to Tokai Teio - the great Partholon line. His male line is now nearly gone, but as a broodmare sire of Sirius Symboli, Mejiro Dober and others, his blood lives on widely.
1053: While TTG captivated fans in 1976-77, an astonishing speedster appeared a year behind them: Maruzensky, a Nijinsky colt conceived abroad. Such horses then faced many limits, including a ban from the classics, so after the Asahi Hai Sansai S. he went at 4 (old age system) to the Nihon Tampa Sho, the "consolation Derby." Along the way he faced Satsuki Sho favorite Hishi Speed and later Kikuka Sho winner Press Tosho and toyed with them. Far beyond the classic crop, his jockey Nakanowatari famously pleaded: "Put him in the widest gate. He won't get in anyone's way and needs no prize money. Just let him run in the Derby to test his ability." It never happened, and after 8 wins from 8 with extraordinary power, injury ended his career - the dreamed-of Arima Kinen clash with TTG never came. At stud he sired many G1 winners, including Derby winner Sakura Chiyono O, Kikuka Sho winners Hollyskey and Leo Durban and Takarazuka Kinen winner Suzuka Koban. As a broodmare sire he produced Special Week, Winning Ticket, Mejiro Bright and many more - an extraordinary record as a sire too.
1054: Winner of the 1974 Satsuki Sho and Kikuka Sho. At 3 (old age system) he won his first 4, incl. the Hanshin Sansai S., showing talent early. At 4 he won the Kisaragi Sho and Spring S., and as heavy Satsuki Sho favorite - one of the first horses given a single-bracket entry, introduced that year - he won with authority from a good spot, unbeaten in 7. In the Derby he lacked his usual kick, 3rd to Cornell Lancer. In autumn he won the Kobe Shimbun Hai and Kyoto Shimbun Hai, then the Kikuka Sho as favorite for his 2nd classic, Horse of the Year. At 5 he beat Arima Kinen winner Tanino Chikara in the Milers C., but the trip beat him in the Tenno Sho (Spring), 2nd. Troubled by his legs, he ran anyway in the Arima Kinen, 8th; a fracture was found and he retired. At stud he had no stars but steady graded winners like Kyoto Yonsai Tokubetsu winner Takano Kachidoki and Kinko Sho winner Towa Kachidoki. Sumo wrestler Kitakachidoki (active 1987-2000) took his name after this horse's strength.
1055: Imported to Japan amid the 1970s Northern Dancer boom, this son of his was a huge success, siring G1 winners like Amber Shadai, Dyna Gulliver and Gallop Dyna and transforming Japanese pedigrees. He overturned the dominance of sires like Tesco Boy and Never Beat, champion sire 10 times in 11 years from 1982. As a broodmare sire he was just as dominant, with countless stars like Sakkah Boy, Sakura Bakushin O, Air Groove and Daiwa Major. He was also famous for his durability, standing 25 years from 1975 to 1999. A fine racehorse too: 4th in the 2000 Guineas and 5th in the Derby, he won a G1 in France, the Prix de la Foret.
1056: Winner of the 1973 Tenno Sho (Spring). Talented early, he won no classic (7th Satsuki Sho, 3rd Derby, 2nd Kikuka Sho) but won the trials: Spring S., Kobe Shimbun Hai and Kyoto Shimbun Hai. Older, he won the Milers C., then the Tenno Sho (Spring) as favorite, and retired after a 2nd in the Takarazuka Kinen. At stud he sired graded winners like Kimpai (West) winner Western George and Nakayama Kinen winner Kosei - a fair success for a Japan-bred sire in hard times.
1057: With Ten Point and Green Grass he defined 1976-77, beloved as "TTG." His solid build and flying stride earned him the name "Pegasus." His duels with Ten Point are still told as classics. The first came in the Satsuki Sho: Ten Point was Kansai's star, while in Kanto Tosho Boy rose as his rival after 3 straight wins - a much-anticipated clash. Tosho Boy won by 5 lengths with superior speed. They met again in the Derby and Kikuka Sho, neither winning but both fighting as favorites. In the Arima Kinen they swept aside the older horses to finish 1-2, Tosho Boy winning again to be the best horse at 4 (old age system). After a break, he faced Ten Point in the Takarazuka Kinen on his return; Ten Point, in steady form, was favored, but Tosho Boy won again. Their final clash came in the Arima Kinen, ending with Tosho Boy a narrow 2nd after a fierce duel, and Ten Point took Horse of the Year. Green Grass was 3rd in both races. At stud he sired Triple Crown winner Mr. C.B. and G1 winners like Sakura Hokuto O, Daiichi Ruby and Sister Tosho, showing the potential of Japan-bred sires in an era of imports.
1058: Sire of Tosho Boy, Sakura Yutaka O and more, the great sire of 1970s Japan. A British racehorse whose main win was the Queen Anne S., on a disqualification, he was imported to Japan and rewrote its racing history. His first crop gave Satsuki Sho winner Land Prince, his 3rd Kitano Kachidoki, his 4th Tesco Gabby and his 5th Tosho Boy - top runners almost every year. Later came Inter Gushiken, Hagino Kamui O and Sakura Yutaka O, and he was champion sire 5 times from the 1970s to the early '80s. Tosho Boy and Sakura Yutaka O succeeded at stud too, producing Mr. C.B., Sakura Hokuto O, Sakura Bakushin O, Air Jihad and others - the great Tesco Boy line that continues today.
1059: A French horse famous as sire of Sakkah Boy. Though from stayer bloodlines, he starred at a mile, winning the G1 Prix Jacques le Marois. At first he raced over long trips, but after a big loss in the Grand Prix de Paris (then 3100m) and a 4th in the Champion S. (about 2000m), he switched to miles. At 4 he won the G3 Prix d'Evry, then the summer highlight, the Jacques le Marois. In the Queen Elizabeth II S. he met superstar Brigadier Gerard and was well beaten, 8 lengths 2nd, and retired. Not quite top class as a racehorse, he was a gifted sire, soon a regular near the top of the French sire table. Bought by the Shadai group in 1980, in Japan he sired Asahi Hai Sansai S. winner Scrum Dyna and 2-time G1 winner Sakkah Boy, among many. His male line has faded, but as broodmare sire of Stay Gold his blood lives on.
1060: The 1972 Derby winner, who with crop-mates Land Prince, Tai Tem and Ishino Hikaru lit up 1972.
