Debuting at 4 (old age system), he won his first 5, incl. the Yayoi Sho, beating Land Prince into 2nd in both his 4th and 5th starts. Satsuki Sho favorite, he was 3rd behind Land Prince and Ishino Hikaru. In the Derby he gained revenge, edging Land Prince and Tai Tem in a 3-way straight duel in a record 2:28.6. From autumn he lost his spark: 6th to Tai Tem in the Kyoto Shimbun Hai, 5th to Ishino Hikaru in the Kikuka Sho and 8th in the Arima Kinen, his last race. At stud his 2nd crop produced Takarazuka Kinen winner Teruten Ryu, plus graded winners Speed Hero and Wide O. Not a leading sire, but a fair success for a Japan-bred sire in hard times.
1061: In the late 1970s-80s, when imported sires ruled, he led the Japan-bred sires, producing 2-time classic filly Titania, Oka Sho winner Riesen Gross and more, and in 1980 and 1981 became only the 2nd Japan-bred champion sire, after Kumohata. On the track he had a fierce rivalry with Tanino Moutiers in the 1970 classics. At 3 (old age system) he won his first 5, incl. the Asahi Hai Sansai S., and a clash with Kansai's Hanshin Sansai S. winner Tanino Moutiers was eagerly awaited. In the classics he was 2nd to him in the Satsuki Sho and 5th in the Derby, but beat him in the NHK Hai. Both flopped in their last meeting, the Kikuka Sho, after which Tanino Moutiers retired. Arrow Express ran on in the Arima Kinen and next year's Sprinters S., 4th in both, and retired. At stud his first crop gave Titania, plus many graded winners, and his son Lead Wonder succeeded as a sire, building a sire line - turning the tables on the less successful Tanino Moutiers.
1062: In 1964 he became only the 2nd Triple Crown winner, then won the Tenno Sho (Autumn) and Arima Kinen as an older horse - the first "5-crown" horse, a legend of Japanese racing. 15 wins and four 2nds from 19. His wins were never flashy, so his image as the greatest is a little fainter than later Triple Crown winners', but his way of doing just enough to win with plenty in hand hinted at boundless strength. His four 2nds came only in open races and preps: he hated training, so trainer Takeda used races as workouts. Horse of the Year at 4 (old age system) and at 5, his feats made "Beat Shinzan" Japanese racing's catchphrase. He retired at the end of 5 to stud. In an era hard on Japan-bred sires he got few good mares, yet sired graded winners like Shingun, Sugano Homare and Silver Land, ranked among the imports every year, and later produced 2 big-race winners, Minagawa Manna and Mihoshinzan. His male line is gone, but his legend will be told for ages.
1063: He moved from Oi to the JRA and won 10 straight, including the Satsuki Sho, sparking a national boom - an idol known even to people who knew nothing of racing. Debuting at Oi in summer at 3 (old age system), he won all 6 starts by 7 lengths or more. At 4 he joined the JRA - "the local monster storms the JRA" - and won the Yayoi Sho, Spring S. and Satsuki Sho, quickly famous nationwide, then the NHK Hai for 10 straight. But in the Derby, with an astonishing 66% of the win betting, he lost to Take Hope, his lifelong rival, 3rd. In autumn he beat Take Hope in the Kyoto Shimbun Hai but lost a duel to him in the Kikuka Sho, 2nd, and won no more titles. Older, he won the Nakayama Kinen, Takarazuka Kinen and Takamatsunomiya Hai, but was 6th to Take Hope in the Tenno Sho (Spring). In their shared farewell, the Arima Kinen, he beat Take Hope but was 2nd to Tanino Chikara, retiring as a horse strong up to middle distances but never a winner beyond 2400m. At stud he was a huge success for a Japan-bred sire, producing Derby winner Katsurano Haiseiko, Satsuki Sho winner Hakutaisei, Queen Elizabeth Cup winner Sand Piaris and many more - easily beating Take Hope, a flop at stud.
1064: With Tosho Boy and Ten Point he ruled racing in 1976-77 as the "Big Three," or "TTG" from their initials. The latest bloomer of the three, he burst onto the stage in the Kikuka Sho in autumn at 4 (old age system), beating hugely popular Tosho Boy and Ten Point. Winning as 12th choice remains an unmatched upset. Older, he raced at the top with the other two, and at 5 the three finished 1-2-3 in both the Takarazuka Kinen and Arima Kinen - that Arima Kinen is called the greatest race ever by many fans. After Tosho Boy and Ten Point left the turf at 6, he fought on as the last of the Big Three, winning the Tenno Sho (Spring) at 6 and the Arima Kinen at 7, a fitting farewell. Fragile and lightly raced, he was out of the top five only once after reaching open class. At stud he sired Queen Elizabeth Cup winner Reward Wing and American JCC winner Tosho Falco, among others.
1024: She won the Flora S. and, with 3 wins from 4, was Oaks favorite without Vodka and Daiwa Scarlet, but lost by a nose to Robe Decollete. 2nd in the Rose S. and 4th in the Shuka Sho, at 4 she was 3rd in the Fuchu Himba S. and Queen Elizabeth II Cup. With a powerful kick, always among the fastest finishers yet falling short, she was frustrating. In her last race, the '09 Fuchu Himba S., Mood Indigo outkicked her. Her G1 dream passes to her foals.
1043: He won his debut, the Daily Hai 2yo S. and Kyoto 2yo S. impressively, but injury kept him out of the Satsuki Sho. He made the Derby but was 4th. After that his best was a 2nd in the Naruo Kinen, below expectations. After a stable move he suffered a twisted intestine; surgery succeeded but meant a long break. Back after about a year, he led all the way in an open special, then won the Sekiya Kinen in summer. He later thrilled mile fans with last-to-first charges after slow starts, but never won another graded race, retiring to stud at the end of 7.
1047: 4th in the Oka Sho and 3rd in the Oaks, she was 2nd in the American Oaks. In autumn she was 2nd in the Shuka Sho and 4th in the Queen Elizabeth II Cup. Older, she was 2nd in the Victoria Mile, then won the Queen S., and was 2nd in the Fuchu Himba S. After nearly a year off, she was last in the '08 Fuchu Himba S., a fracture was found, and she retired to breed.
1065: Winner of the 1975 Satsuki Sho and Derby and Horse of the Year. His 9 straight wins, from his debut at 3 (old age system) to an open race in spring at 5, are the JRA record. But more than records, Kaburaya O is remembered for his wild front-running, called "killer laps" and "insane pace." After winning the Tokyo Yonsai S. (now Kyodo News Hai) and Yayoi Sho, he led the Satsuki Sho at a blistering 58.9 for the first 1000m and pulled away in the straight for a record win. Lake Sprinter, who dueled him, broke a leg in the race and was put down, giving rise to the feared names. After the NHK Hai, he led the Derby even faster, 58.6 for 1000m. Surely he couldn't last 2400m - yet, mouth open and wandering in the straight, he held everyone off and won, amazing fans. No horse has since won the Derby leading at such a pace. Injury ruled out the Kikuka Sho; back in spring at 5 he won 2 dirt races and 1 on turf, but another injury forced his retirement. At stud he sired Queen Elizabeth Cup winner Miyama Poppy and Derby runner-up Grandpa's Dream. His camp later revealed his front-running was a tactic born of his timid nature and rare heart-lung capacity.
1066: Winner of 6 G1s incl. the English and Irish Oaks, and familiar in Japan for winning the Queen Elizabeth II Cup in 2010 and 2011. Little rated at first, at 2 she won just a maiden from 6 starts. At 3 she won a Listed race easily, then the Oaks for her first stakes win - a G1. She won the Irish Oaks by 8 lengths, top of her crop. In autumn she came to Japan and won the Queen Elizabeth II Cup by 4 lengths from Meisho Beluga, then won the Hong Kong Cup, Cartier champion 3yo filly. At 4 she suffered near misses - 2nd in the Irish Champion S. and 3rd in the Arc - but came back to Japan to win the Queen Elizabeth II Cup again. At 5 she won the Irish Champion S. for her 6th G1, then retired with leg trouble. Her 3rd foal, John Leeper by Frankel, made headlines running in the Derby.
1067: The best son of Takeshiba O. Debuting at Oi, he won the 1978 Southern Kanto Triple Crown: Haneda Hai, Tokyo Derby and Tokyo Okansho. After 5 straight wins from autumn at 3 (old age system), he won the Haneda Hai by 2.5 lengths, then the Tokyo Derby by 6 for 7 straight. 3rd in the Tokyo Hai in autumn, he won the Tokyo Kinen, then the Tokyo Okansho by 5 lengths for the Triple Crown, and the year-end Tokyo Daishoten too. At 5, after a 2nd in the Teio Sho, he moved to the JRA, but was 12th in the Arima Kinen, his first big defeat, and retired. His best foal was Asahi Challenge C. winner Hatsushiba Ace.
1068: A star of the 1965 classics: after 2nds in the Satsuki Sho and Derby, he won the Kikuka Sho, in a fierce rivalry with Derby winner Keystone. Emerging late at 3 (old age system), he won the Kisaragi Sho at 4 and beat Keystone, on a 6-race streak, in their first meeting in the Spring S. But outsider Chitose O beat him in the Satsuki Sho, and after winning the NHK Hai he lost the Derby duel to Keystone - no spring title. Owner Ueda, obsessed with winning the Derby, had bought him just before the race, and his narrow defeat popularized the saying "the Derby can't be bought." In autumn he won the Kobe Hai (now Kobe Shimbun Hai) and an open race, then beat Keystone in the Kikuka Sho for his classic title. After a 4th in the Hanshin Daishoten, he slumped from 5, switched to jumps at 7, won once and retired. At stud he sired many graded winners like Nishino Raiden, Kitano Rikio and Hoshu Missile, leading Japan-bred sires in hard times and ranking 4th on the sire list in 1981.
1069: The great heir who developed Mill Reef's blood in Japan. He sired many local stars like Rocky Tiger, Inari One and Rosita, and JRA G1 winners like Osaichi George and Linden Lily, and in 1989 was champion sire of JRA and local racing combined, ahead of Northern Taste. An American racehorse, he won his 3rd start, then a 9-furlong dirt allowance in a good 1:50.8, showing promise, but a fracture soon after ended his career. Standing in Japan, his first crop gave local star Rocky Tiger, followed by Inari One - who starred at Oi, then won 3 JRA G1s - Takarazuka Kinen winner Osaichi George and Southern Kanto star Rosita. Many excelled on dirt, and he was local racing's champion sire from 1987 to 1989. But he lacked successful sons, and his male line died out.
1070: The 1978 Derby winner, who also won the Takarazuka Kinen at 5 (old age system). Emerging early, he won the Tokyo Yonsai S. (now Kyodo News Hai) and was 2nd choice for the Satsuki Sho, 3rd to Fantast. He gained revenge in the Derby, breaking clear from a good spot and holding on by half a length. In autumn he won the St. Lite Kinen and was 2nd in the Kyoto Shimbun Hai, then favorite for the Kikuka Sho, but 5th to Inter Gushiken. Still, he was a respectable 5th in the Arima Kinen for his crop. Older, he won the American JCC and Meguro Kinen (Spring), was 2nd in the Tenno Sho (Spring), and won the Takarazuka Kinen as favorite, a Grand Prix winner. Winless after, he retired after the Meguro Kinen in February at 6. At stud he succeeded too, siring double classic winner Sakura Star O.
1072: A sire who took Japan by storm from the late 1980s to early '90s. As Northern Taste's blood spread, the Shadai group bought him in America as a new line to cross with it. Carrying the "Shadai" name, he raced in France until 3, winning the Grand Prix de Deauville (G2), 2nd in the French Derby and 5th in the Arc, then went to stud in Japan from 1984. His first crop gave graded winners Muguet Royal and Free Talk, his 2nd Oka Sho winner Shadai Kagura, then Hanshin Sansai S. winner Ibuki Maikagura and Rice Shower, 3-time G1 winner incl. the Kikuka Sho and Tenno Sho (Spring). In 1993 he beat Northern Taste to be champion sire. Other graded winners include Monsieur Shekel, Stage Champ and Hagino Real King. His runners were mostly strong stayers, and as a broodmare sire he produced Tenno Sho (Spring) winners Ingrandire and Admire Jupiter - a renowned source of stamina.
1073: His name means "blushing groom," inspired by his dam Runaway Bride. He won 5 G1s incl. the French 2000 Guineas and sired many heirs like Nashwan and Rainbow Quest. His 2yo season was brilliant: from his 2nd start he won 5 straight, sweeping all 4 French 2yo G1s, an undisputed champion. The streak continued at 3: after a G3 prep he won the French 2000 Guineas by 3 lengths. In England he was 3rd in the Derby, and after a 2nd in the Jacques le Marois that summer he retired. At stud in America he sired 24 G1 winners, incl. Derby winner Nashwan, Arc winner Rainbow Quest, and Crystal Glitters and Arazi, later imported to Japan as sires. As a broodmare sire he produced Lammtarra, T.M. Opera O, Goldikova and many more, leading broodmare sire in Britain and Ireland in 1988 and 1995.
1074: Famous as the great rival of crop-mate and US Triple Crown winner Affirmed. He was 2nd to Affirmed in all 3 legs, and in the Belmont S. the two fought a fierce match race, 13 lengths clear of the rest. In 10 meetings he won only 3, but his ability was highly rated: 27th in The Blood-Horse's "Top 100 US Racehorses of the 20th Century." He won 14 of 26, incl. 6 G1s. At stud he sired G1 winners Alysheba, Easy Goer, Strike the Gold and many more, and was US champion sire in 1990, far surpassing Affirmed, who disappointed at stud. As a broodmare sire his blood reached Lure, Peintre Celebre and others, a strong branch of the Raise a Native line, though behind Mr. Prospector's.
1075: With Sadler's Wells and Nijinsky, one of Northern Dancer's most successful sire sons. Leg trouble limited him to 3 races, a maiden and allowances, but at stud he showed his worth. His first crop gave 8-time G1 winner Chief's Crown, followed by Danehill, Green Desert, Dayjur, Adjudicating and more. US champion sire 3 years running from 1991, he also sired Japanese stars like Agnes World and Yamanin Paradise. Many sons succeeded at stud, especially Chief's Crown, Danehill and Green Desert, with many G1 winners. At one point his branch made up about half of the Northern Dancer line, and it is now seen as an independent line: the Danzig line.
1076: America's 9th Triple Crown winner, all 3 legs in record time. In the Belmont S. he won by 31 lengths in a legendary world record 2:24.0. Not only unbroken, no horse has since even run 2:25 - called an unbeatable time. He raced until the end of 3, winning 16 of 21, Eclipse Horse of the Year at 2 and 3, and 2nd only to Man o' War in The Blood-Horse's "Top 100 US Racehorses of the 20th Century." At stud he sired 11-time G1 winner Lady's Secret, incl. the BC Distaff, and dual classic winner Risen Star, but few others; his male line is fading. As a broodmare sire, though, he produced great sires like Storm Cat, A.P. Indy and Gone West, deeply influencing today's pedigrees.
1077: An Irish horse who, like his great-grandsire Ribot, won the Arc twice. Those were his only G1s, but trainer O'Brien called him "on a par with Nijinsky, or better." At 2 he ran once, winning his debut. At 3 he won graded races steadily aiming for the St. Leger, where he was 2nd, then won the Arc as favorite, a star. At 4 his preparation was disrupted, winning just 2 graded races before the Arc, which he won again as favorite, retiring with 2 Arcs. 9 wins from 10, his only loss a 2nd in the St. Leger. At stud in America he sired many G1 winners like BC Turf winner Miss Alleged and Irish Derby winner Law Society; son Fair Judgement was imported to Japan as a sire.
1078: From Northern Dancer's 2nd crop, he was outstanding as both racehorse and sire, and did much to establish the Northern Dancer line. Unbeaten, he won the English Triple Crown and crushed older horses in the King George VI & Queen Elizabeth S. He was 2nd in the Arc, missing the European Triple Crown, but no horse has won the English Triple Crown since him, the first in 35 years. His dominance led to a then-record $5.44 million syndication, and he went to stud in America the next year. His first crop gave Green Dancer, then Maruzensky, Ile de Bourbon, Yamanin Ski and others who became successful sires. With his most successful son Caerleon and Lammtarra too, he built the great Nijinsky line. His male line is becoming a minority, but through dams his blood runs widely in stars like Dance in the Dark, Special Week, Taiki Shuttle and Buena Vista.
1079: He established the Mr. Prospector line through heirs like Miswaki, Woodman and Kingmambo - with Northern Dancer, one of the two giants of modern pedigrees. On the track he was an ordinary sprinter, never winning a stakes race, just setting 2 records over 6 furlongs. But at stud he sired Fappiano in his 2nd crop, Miswaki in his 3rd and Conquistador Cielo in his 4th, and with Gulch, Gone West and Seeking the Gold starring he was champion sire in 1987-88. His sons succeeded at stud too, building a great empire. In Japan, Kingmambo's son King Kamehameha was champion sire, and his son Lord Kanaloa sired Almond Eye and many G1 winners - a force rivaling the Sunday Silence line.
1080: A Northern Dancer sire son who produced many stars: 6-time US G1 winner Theatrical, Miesque with 10 G1s in Europe and America, and 5-time European G1 winner Soviet Star. A miler who won 2 G3s, in his 3rd start he crossed the line first in the 2000 Guineas but was disqualified for interference. Then an infection ended his career with little to show. At stud his first crop gave Theatrical and his 3rd Miesque and Soviet Star, plus Arc winner Peintre Celebre and Japanese G1 winners Heart Lake and Black Hawk - a big success. Champion sire in France in 1987 and 1997. He never founded his own line, but through Miesque, dam of Kingmambo, he is a major broodmare sire.
1081: From Northern Dancer's 4th crop, he excelled mainly at sprint-mile trips, and at stud sired Dancing Brave, Mogami and others, a key branch of the Northern Dancer line. He ran in the classics, incl. the English and Irish Derbies, without success, then switched to shorter races: he won the G1 Jacques le Marois, was 2nd in the Moulin and won the Prix de la Foret, showing great aptitude. He retired at the end of 3 with 6 wins from 12. At stud he was French champion sire 2 years running from 1978, when his first crop turned 3, and US champion sire in 1986. With Dancing Brave and Mogami succeeding as sires, he founded the Lyphard line. His male line is fading, but his son Alzao sired Wind in Her Hair, dam of Deep Impact, spreading his blood widely.
1082: The first unbeaten US Triple Crown winner, also a great success at stud. Through his heir A.P. Indy he carries on the Bold Ruler line, still a strong force. Brilliant at 2, he won the G1 Champagne S. easily, Eclipse champion 2yo. At 3 he won 2 more G1s and, unbeaten in 6, won the Kentucky Derby, Preakness S. and Belmont S. with ease - the first unbeaten Triple Crown winner. The next year he met Affirmed, the Triple Crown winner a year younger. He beat him decisively in the Marlboro Cup H., but in their 2nd meeting, the Jockey Club Gold C., though ahead of Affirmed, he was beaten a nose by outsider Exceller. 14 wins from 17, 8 G1s. At stud he sired A.P. Indy, Slew o' Gold, Capote and others, and in Japan Taiki Blizzard and Dantsu Seattle; he is also broodmare sire of Kawakami Princess, Seeking the Pearl, Hishi Akebono and Agnes World.
1083: America's 11th Triple Crown winner. With Seattle Slew, a Triple Crown winner a year older, their rare clashes made headlines. At 2 he fought rival Alydar fiercely, the two running 1-2 almost every time; Affirmed won 4 of 6 and was Eclipse champion 2yo colt. At 3 they met in every Triple Crown leg, and he won all 3 narrowly, Alydar 2nd each time. He then met Seattle Slew in the Marlboro Cup H., the focus of the nation, but was beaten 3 lengths, 2nd. Still, he was Eclipse Horse of the Year, and the next year won 6 G1s to repeat the title. He retired with 22 wins from 29, 14 G1s, 12th in The Blood-Horse's "Top 100 US Racehorses of the 20th Century." At stud he sired Arlington Million winner The Tin Man and Canadian Triple Crown winner Peteski, but lacking successful heirs, his line is in decline.
1084: Winner of the European Triple Crown - the Derby, King George VI & Queen Elizabeth S. and Arc - and 8th in Timeform's "100 Greatest Racehorses." At stud he founded the Mill Reef line through many heirs - one of the greats. At 2 he was rated 2nd, behind My Swallow, but at 3 became the first European Triple Crown winner and Horse of the Year. A clash at 4 with crop-mate Brigadier Gerard, the unbeatable miler, was eagerly awaited, but equine flu prevented it. He then suffered a severe fracture, survived and retired safely, with 12 wins and two 2nds from 14. At stud he sired Shirley Heights, Mill George, Magnitude and more, and was twice champion sire in Britain - the most successful sire of the Never Bend line, forming the Mill Reef line. From the mid-2010s it has faded, with only a few European successes like Shakeel, winner of the 2017 Grand Prix de Paris.
1085: Sire of Real Shadai, Brian's Time, Kris S. and more, he did much to establish the Hail to Reason line - and as a racehorse was resented as "the villain of the century." First, he won the Derby after a ruthless jockey switch: regular rider Williamson was replaced just before the race by master Lester Piggott, and he won amid loud boos. Second, he beat British hero Brigadier Gerard, ending his bid for a European-record 16th straight win. That great upset was not welcome at all, and he lost his spark afterward and retired. At stud he was a huge success, also siring Sunshine Forever, Silver Hawk, Dynaformer, Red Ransom and many other successful sires. In Japan today, his sire lines are firmly rooted: Kris S. to Symboli Kris S to Epiphaneia, and Silver Hawk to Grass Wonder to Screen Hero.
1086: An American horse, US champion sire in 1983 and 1989, who sired Sunday Silence and transformed Japanese pedigrees. Not a standout racehorse, he struggled to win a stakes race until the Lawrence Realization on turf in autumn at 3. Late maturing, at 5 he won the turf United Nations H., a G1 title. At stud his first crop gave Canadian Horse of the Year Glorious Song. In 1983 Sunny's Halo won the Kentucky Derby and Devil's Bag was champion 2yo, and he was champion sire. He later sired 7-time G1-winning mare Goodbye Halo and Sunday Silence, exported to Japan, deeply influencing pedigrees. He had a fierce temper to match his sire Hail to Reason's, and his habit of biting people is famous.
1071: A fast grey known as sire of Tamamo Cross, called "the White Lightning" for his sharp late charge. At 4 (old age system) he was 5th in the Satsuki Sho and 7th in the Derby. In autumn he was 2nd in the Lord Derby Challenge T. but 10th in the Arima Kinen. At 5 he won the Kimpai (East), was 3rd to Kashu Chikara in the Tenno Sho (Spring), and in autumn won the Mainichi Okan and Meguro Kinen. Retired to stud at 8, he sired 3-time G1 winner Tamamo Cross, White Stone, Inazuma Cross and more.
1087: The horse with the greatest influence on modern Thoroughbred pedigrees - his blood runs in most horses worldwide. With Northern Dancer's arrival, a landscape divided among the Nasrullah, Nearctic, Hyperion and St. Simon lines was repainted in Northern Dancer colors. He sired great sires who became champions - Nijinsky, Northern Taste, Lyphard, Nureyev, Sadler's Wells, Danzig, Storm Bird and more - each founding its own line, building a vast Northern Dancer empire. Beyond his male line, many fine daughters spread his blood through dams too. Northern Dancer was also top class on the track: the first Canadian-bred to win the Kentucky Derby and Preakness S., and winner of Canada's great Queen's Plate.
1088: His talent was spotted before his debut, and he received elite schooling from Wada of Symboli Farm, trainer Yuji Nohira and jockey Yukio Okabe. He debuted over 1000m at Niigata and won 3 low-key races, the Icho Tokubetsu and an open race; through these Okabe is said to have taught Rudolf how to race. After a break, his first race at 3 was the Yayoi Sho. Untested against top rivals, he was 2nd choice behind Bizen Nishiki, but by crushing that highly rated favorite he cemented his status. In the Satsuki Sho, the first classic, he drifted out in the straight and bumped Bizen Nishiki, still green, yet won by a length and a quarter. Already sure of the Triple Crown, Okabe famously raised one finger - "the first of three." By the Derby he was already a complete racehorse: ignoring his rider's urging to go early, he raced his own way and won comfortably. He won the St. Lite Kinen easily in autumn and the Kikuka Sho with ease - Japan's first unbeaten Triple Crown winner. For his steady dominance he was called "the Emperor." In the Japan Cup he lost for the first time to Katsuragi Ace's bold runaway, but won the year-end Arima Kinen by a wide margin - 4 G1s at 3 and Horse of the Year. The next year he was a shock 2nd to Gallop Dyna's surprise charge in the Tenno Sho (Autumn), but won the Tenno Sho (Spring), Japan Cup and Arima Kinen - a monumental 7 G1s. The following year he went to America, but was injured and beaten badly, and retired. At stud he sired Tokai Teio, 2-time Stayers S. winner Airton Symboli and unfulfilled talent Tsurumaru Tsuyoshi, and died in autumn 2011.
1089: Winner of the 1980 Oka Sho and Queen Elizabeth Cup, half-sister of Hagino Kamui O and dam of Daiichi Ruby. She won her debut by a mile in record time, was 3rd in an open race, and in only her 3rd start won the Oka Sho, leading at a fast pace and holding on. 17th in the Oaks on heavy ground, she won the Kyoto Himba Tokubetsu in autumn, then the Queen Elizabeth Cup, champion 4yo filly (old age system). A trip abroad at 5 was planned but dropped after a 4th in the Takarazuka Kinen. In summer she won the Takamatsunomiya Hai, then fought a fierce match race with Brocade, Oka Sho winner a year younger, in the Tomoe Sho - a race fans remember. She retired after an 8th in the Mainichi Okan. As a dam she produced Yasuda Kinen and Sprinters S. winner Daiichi Ruby.
1090: The JRA's 3rd Triple Crown winner, after St. Lite and Shinzan. His sire Tosho Boy and dam C.B. Queen had met in their debut (Tosho Boy 1st, C.B. Queen 5th) - a match made by fate. Fans loved his bold style: sweeping forward from near last and charging home in the straight. In the Kikuka Sho he launched a long run up the 3rd-turn hill and swept forward on the downhill, then held on - breaking Kyoto's outer-course golden rule - to win the Triple Crown. At 4 he missed the spring with injury, returned with a 2nd in the Mainichi Okan, then won the Tenno Sho (Autumn) in record time from last with a fierce kick, his 4th big title. But his glory faded as Triple Crown winner Symboli Rudolf emerged a year behind him. He was 10th to Katsuragi Ace in the Japan Cup (Rudolf 3rd), 3rd to Rudolf in the Arima Kinen and 5th to Rudolf in his last race, the Tenno Sho (Spring) at 5. Never beating Rudolf, he retired to stud. He sired Yamanin Global (Meguro Kinen) and Shako Grade (2nd, Satsuki Sho), but none to match himself.
1093: A great French mare who won the 2008 French fillies' Triple Crown and the Arc, unbeaten in 7. She won her first G1, the Prix Marcel Boussac for 2yo fillies, and at 3, after a G3 prep, won the French 1000 Guineas in record time. She won the French Oaks easily as favorite, then went straight to the Prix Vermeille in autumn to complete the Triple Crown unbeaten - after missing the break badly, swinging wide and sweeping past them all. Then the Arc: she was favorite over Duke of Marmalade, on a 5-G1 streak, and previous runner-up Youmzain. Waiting in midfield, she split the field powerfully in the straight to beat Youmzain by 2 lengths. She retired unbeaten after it. As a broodmare she produced Grand Prix de Saint-Cloud winner Zarak and others, retiring from breeding in 2024.
1094: Unbeaten in 8 in 2009 in America, including 5 straight G1s like the Kentucky Oaks and Preakness S., she was Eclipse Horse of the Year. Up and down at 2, she changed after a stakes win at year's end, won 4 straight and took the Kentucky Oaks by over 20 lengths. In the Preakness she beat colts, the first filly to win it in 85 years. Instead of the Belmont she ran in the fillies' Mother Goose S., winning by 19 lengths, then won the Haskell Invitational, the summer's top 3yo race, by 6 lengths from Belmont winner Summer Bird - the best of her crop, colts included. She then beat older males narrowly in the Woodward S. - 5 straight G1s - and became the first 3yo filly named Eclipse Horse of the Year. At 4 a clash with unbeaten Zenyatta, 2 years older, was awaited, but she lost form with two early 2nds and they never met. After a graded and a Listed win, she retired after a 2nd in the Personal Ensign H. She produced G1 winner Rachel's Valentina, but after being badly hurt foaling she was no longer bred.
1095: Known as dam of Hishi Amazon, plus graded winners Hishi Nile and Hishi Pinnacle - a great broodmare. An Irish racehorse, she won the Irish 1000 Guineas, then the Coronation S. (G2), and retired after graded 2nds. She had 3 foals in America and, in foal with her 4th, was bought by Japanese owner Masaichiro Abe; her later foals raced in Japan under the "Hishi" prefix. Her 5th foal, Hishi Amazon, starred in races like the Queen Elizabeth Cup and Hanshin Sansai Himba S., making her name, followed by Fairy S. winner Hishi Nile and Rose S. winner Hishi Pinnacle. Their descendants didn't flourish, but her first, American-born foal Katies First was imported as a broodmare, producing grandsons Admire Moon and Efforia. Her 3rd foal What Katy Did was imported too, producing Sleepless Night - her family thrives in Japan.
1096: A blueblood by champion sire Northern Taste, she won her debut by 5 lengths as favorite and won 3 straight at 2, incl. the Sansai Himba S., champion 2yo filly. In spring at 3 she was 5th and 2nd in the preps, then favorite for the Oka Sho, but on heavy ground and slow away was 3rd to Shadai Sophia. In the Oaks, 2nd choice, she drew level in the straight; with 50m left five horses were in a line, and she won a blanket finish with the first five on the same time. Skipping the Queen Elizabeth Cup, she won the Turquoise S. (OP) and was 4th in the Arima Kinen as 9th choice, champion again that year. She ran well but never won another big race and retired injured at the end of 6. A superb dam, she produced Tenno Sho (Autumn) and Oaks winner Air Groove (93: Tony Bin) and Curly Angel (90: Judge Angelucci). Air Groove produced Admire Groove and many G1 winners, and in 2015 great-grandson Duramente won 2 classics. Curly Angel produced graded winner Egao wo Misete and Takamatsunomiya Kinen winner Ore wa Matteruze. Her family is now one of Japan's great families.
1097: Just 1 G1 win on the track, but a huge success at stud: North American champion sire 2014-2016, with a fee once reaching $300,000 - a great modern sire. He won his first 2 impressively and was a Kentucky Derby fancy at 3, but with an infection was 6th in the Florida Derby. He won the Wood Memorial S., a G1, but did nothing in the Kentucky Derby, 9th. Aiming for the Belmont, he hadn't fully recovered and needed a long break. Back in autumn, he was 9th in the Pennsylvania Derby and retired to stud. His first crop gave Eclipse champion 2yo filly Stardom Bound, and G1 winners came almost every year. In 2014 his runners earned a record $16.8 million, and he led North America for 3 years. In Japan his son Testa Matta won the February S.
1098: The 1982 Derby winner. A close 6th in the NHK Hai trial, he went to the Derby and won in 2:26.5, then a race record. Injured after the Kobe Shimbun Hai that autumn, he retired after just 8 starts. At stud he sired Kikuka Sho winner Bamboo Begin, El Casa River, Agnes Parade and many graded winners.
1100: Unbeaten in 4, he won the Kyodo News Hai Yonsai S.; his margins totaled over 10 lengths. A clash with fellow unbeaten Rudolf was keenly awaited. In their first meeting, the Yayoi Sho, the margin was small, but everyone saw it as "Rudolf by a mile." He regained his confidence in the Spring S., then sought revenge in the Satsuki Sho, but bowed to the Emperor again. After winning the NHK Hai he was beaten badly in the Derby, injured in autumn, and retired that year. Called an early bloomer, he seemed to collapse against the wall that was Rudolf. Either way, he was born in the wrong era.
1101: Winner of the 1982 Tenno Sho (Autumn), making a father-son Tenno Sho double. Emerging with a St. Lite Kinen win in autumn at 3, he won the Nikkei Sho by 10 lengths the next year to join the top older horses. But he often either won big or lost big, rated a fickle horse. Even on his biggest day, the Tenno Sho (Autumn), he was only 4th choice, yet won clearly in record time. Retired to stud at 5, he sired 4-time G1 winner Mejiro McQueen, who also won the Tenno Sho - 3 generations of Tenno Sho winners: Mejiro Asama, Mejiro Titan, Mejiro McQueen.
1102: A great miler unbeatable at a mile or less. He won the Mile Championship twice and the Yasuda Kinen, and was champion sprinter 3 years running, 1983-85. Unbeaten in 3 to the Daily Hai Sansai S., he was narrowly 2nd to Daizen King in the Hanshin Sansai S. He won the Kisaragi Sho at 3 and was a classic contender, but after a 6th in the Spring S. he was 20th of 20 in the Satsuki Sho, hurt by the trip or the heavy ground (the winner, Mr. C.B., went on to the Triple Crown). He skipped the Derby and gave up the classics, but in 1984 graded races arrived with a proper sprint division, and his run began: from '84 he won 7 and was 2nd once in 8 races at 1600m or less. Many fans wanted to see him meet 1984 Triple Crown winner Rudolf, "the Emperor," and it happened only once, in the 92nd Tenno Sho (Autumn), where he finished behind him (Rudolf 2nd, Winner 3rd, outsider Gallop Dyna winning). Many said at a mile Winner would have had the edge. At stud he sired speedsters like Flower Park and Towa Winner, while Yamanin Zephyr won the Tenno Sho (Autumn), overcoming the distance barrier his sire never could.
1103: 2nd on debut, he won a debut race and the Hakodate Sansai S., a classic hope, but a chipped left knee sidelined him. Back in the Spring S. at 3, he charged into 2nd off the layoff, belatedly raising the "beat Rudolf" flag. But leg trouble struck again, costing 6 months. In autumn he was 8th in the Kyoto Shimbun Hai and 9th in the Kikuka Sho. He then focused on middle distances, but with repeated breaks ran just once at 4, and retired at 5 after his only graded win, the Tanabata Sho. At stud he sired fast Tenno Sho winner Nehai Caesar (90: Nehai Tesco) and others.
1104: One of Mr. Prospector's leading sons. He sired world-class mare Urban Sea and BC Classic winner Black Tie Affair, and as a broodmare sire produced Galileo, Sea the Stars and many more - his blood spreading worldwide. Not a standout racehorse, his main results were a win in the Prix de la Salamandre (G1) and a 2nd in the Prix Morny (G1) at 2. At 3 he raced on dirt in America, winning no stakes race, and retired. At stud his first crop gave G1 winner Papal Power, followed by Black Tie Affair, Misil and Japanese star Marvelous Crown. His daughter Urban Sea produced world-beating sires Galileo and Sea the Stars, making him a great broodmare sire, leading in Britain and Ireland in 1999 and 2001. In Japan, Silence Suzuka and That's the Plenty carry Miswaki as broodmare sire.
1105: At 3 (old age system) he won the Fuchu Sansai S. (now Tokyo Sports Hai 2yo S.) and was 2nd in the Asahi Hai Sansai S. He slumped at 4 and had a long break. 2nd in an allowance race at 5, he climbed steadily at 6 and won the Lord Derby Challenge T. in its first year as a graded race. At 7 he won the Nakayama Kinen and was 2nd in the Mile CS, a new G1 the year before. At stud he sired February S. winner Gourmet Frontier and 1992 2yo queen Suehiro Jo-o.
1106: At 2 he won the Asahi Hai Sansai S., 3 wins and a 2nd from 4, but Sakkah Boy took the champion 2yo colt title. He meant to avenge it in the classics, but was 4th in the Kyodo News Hai. In the Yayoi Sho he beat old foe Sakkah Boy. 2nd choice in the Satsuki Sho, he was 3rd to Yaeno Muteki - the top was within reach. 3rd choice for the Derby, he won a tight duel with Mejiro Ardan - top of his crop at last. But leg trouble then cost him a year. Back, he was 16th in both the Yasuda Kinen and Takarazuka Kinen, and as crop-mate Oguri Cap ruled and fueled the racing boom, he quietly retired.
1107: The 47th Derby winner in 1980, but then lost 32 straight until retiring - "the weakest Derby winner ever." At 2 he won 2 of 4, 4th to Laughon Tace in the Hanshin Sansai S. At 3, 5th in the Mainichi Hai, he won the Nanohana Sho, then was narrowly 2nd to Hawaiian Image in the Satsuki Sho. After a 2nd in an open race, in the Derby he won a duel with Monte Prince near the line to claim the title. But from then their fortunes split: Derby loser Monte Prince won the Tenno Sho (Spring) and Takarazuka Kinen at 5, while Opec Horse's best was a 2nd in the Asahi Challenge C.; barely making the top five in graded races, he couldn't win even in plain open races or on dirt, and retired without another taste of victory.
1109: At 2-3 he won 3, all on dirt, but also ran well on turf, 3rd in the Keisei Hai and Spring S. At 4, after a turf allowance win, he set a record in a Nakayama 1800m dirt open race. At 5 he lowered his own record by 0.5s in his first race, then won the Niigata Daishoten, Yasuda Kinen and Keio Hai Autumn H. - a big year. From 6 he did little and retired after an 11th in the Sprinters S. at 7. His 1:48.5 for 1800m on dirt at 5 stood as the Japanese record until Premium Thunder beat it by 0.1s in 1997 - a truly valuable mark.
1110: He won his debut, the Daily Hai Sansai S. and Hanshin Sansai S., champion 2yo colt. Hopes were high for the classics, but injury kept him out of the Satsuki Sho and Derby. Back in autumn, he was 13th in the Kyoto Shimbun Hai and 17th in the Kikuka Sho. A middle-distance graded regular after, he won just one open race and retired at the end of 6. Named after a perfume (chypre), his kick charmed fans at 2, but his fragrance may have faded during his injury absence.
1091: 53 races until 7 (old age system), 8 wins. Her only graded win was the Niigata Kinen at 7, but she was 2nd in the Mainichi Okan and Himba Tokyo Times Hai (now Fuchu Himba S.). At 4 she was 11th in the Oka Sho, but a fine 5th to Toko Elsa as 16th choice in the Oaks, and 2nd to Toko Elsa in the Victoria C. (forerunner of the Queen Elizabeth Cup). Also the dam of Tenno Sho winner Pre Classny.
1092: She won the Niigata Kinen and Himba Tokyo Times Hai (now Fuchu Himba S.) in 1984, the first year of graded races. At 4 (old system) she won 3 allowance races to reach open class but kept falling short; dropped back the next year, she won again, then both graded races in a row. As a dam she produced Broad Mind, JRA champion jumper twice. Her full sister Dyna Shoot is granddam of Rhein Kraft.
1099: A late-maturing stayer carrying Northern Taste's blood. Long in the lower classes, he bloomed in autumn at 4, winning the Meguro Kinen (Autumn) and Arima Kinen. The next year he fell short - 2nd in the Tenno Sho (Spring), 5th in the Tenno Sho (Autumn), 2nd in the Arima Kinen - but at 6 he won the Tenno Sho (Spring). He shone even more at stud: son Mejiro Ryan, and grandchildren Mejiro Bright and Mejiro Dober, built a G1 dynasty - a hope for Japan-bred sires as imports grew stronger.
1108: A leading contender in the 1981 fillies' classics. She won the Flower C., was 5th in the Yonsai Himba Tokubetsu and 4th in the Oaks, won the Radio Tampa Sho, and was 4th in the Himba Tokyo Times Hai and Queen Elizabeth Cup. At 5 she beat colts in the Kimpai (East) and Nakayama Kinen, and after 10 months off won the Nakayama Kinen again at 6. Apart from the Arima Kinen (10th), always in the top five. As a dam she produced Mother Tosho.
1111: 5th on debut at 2, he won 3 straight incl. the Chukyo Sansai S. Hopes were high, but after a 7th in an open race at 3, he was switched to sprints in view of his pedigree. At 4 he won 3 races at 1400m or less, and at 5 won the Hankyu Hai clearly - his first meeting with lifelong rival Nihon Pillow Winner, who beat him into 2nd in the CBC Sho after a 6-month break. At 6, graded races arrived and the JRA's sprint division was organized, a turning point for sprinters long overshadowed by middle-distance stars. When Nihon Pillow Winner, who had beaten him again in the Yodo Tankyori S. (OP), was injured, Happy Progress had no rival, winning 3 straight graded races up to the Yasuda Kinen. In autumn, with Nihon Pillow Winner back, he lost the Swan S. and Mile Championship to him, but beat Oka Sho winner Shadai Sophia in the year-end CBC Sho, and the pioneer of the new sprint era retired after that win.
1112: 4th on debut, he won a maiden in his 4th start, then often fell short and missed the classics. Leg trouble kept him in his class at 4, and next to full brother Monte Prince, "Emperor of the Sun," winner of the Tenno Sho (Spring) and Takarazuka Kinen, Monte Fast came to be called "the lesser brother." But at 5 he was 3rd in the Hakodate Kinen, 4th in the Tenno Sho (Autumn), then won the Meguro Kinen, his first graded win. In spring at 6, after a 4th in the Nikkei Sho, he went to the Tenno Sho (Spring). Favorite was Hollyskey, Kikuka Sho winner a year younger, at 1.5. Monte Fast was only 6th choice, but sat in midfield and held off Hollyskey's late charge to win - a historic brothers' Tenno Sho double. No one called him "the lesser brother" again.
1113: Racing until 8 (old age system), he won 2 graded races, the February H. (then a G3 handicap) and the Winter S. (now Tokai S.). At 4 he won 4 straight to reach open class, and at 5 was 2nd in both the Kabutoyama Kinen and Negishi S., good on turf or dirt. He won the year-end Winter S., then into 6 won the Alexandrite S. (OP), February H. and Keiyo S. (OP). Then came heavy weights, and his only other win was the Times Hai (OP) at 7. He retired after a 6th in the February H. at 8. At stud he sired Winter S. winner Laurier Andre and others.
1114: Winning his first 3, at 4 (old age system) he was 3rd in the Shinzan Kinen and Kisaragi Sho, then won the Mainichi Hai. But in the classics he was 5th in the Satsuki Sho and 14th in the NHK Hai. Racing mainly at middle distances, he was 3rd in the Keihan Hai and Kimpai (West), then won the Times Hai on dirt in summer. In autumn he won the Kyoto Kinen and Keihan Hai as an outsider, and at 6 won the Nikkei Shinshun Hai (then on dirt) and retired. At stud he had very few foals and none of note.
1115: Debuting at Funabashi, he won the Teio Sho at 8 (old age system). He only reached big races at 7: 11th in the Kawasaki Kinen, 6th in the Teio Sho, 9th in the Tokyo Daishoten. At 8 he improved, 5th in the Kawasaki Kinen and 2nd in the Diolite Kinen, then in the Teio Sho beat local stars Countess Up and Rocky Tiger and JRA invitee Rikisan Power as 10th choice. He won the Tokyo Kinen that autumn and retired after racing until spring at 10.
1116: Winner of the 1981 Asahi Hai Sansai S. After 2 straight wins and a 2nd in the Keisei Hai Sansai S., he was favorite for the Asahi Hai and beat Tosho Pegasus by a head, champion 2yo colt. Then injury sidelined him for 2 years. Back, he was 2nd in the Lord Derby Challenge T. and Tokyo Shimbun Hai, showing his class, and retired at 5.
1117: From Maruzensky's first crop. Debuting late, in January at 3, he won a dirt maiden by 9 lengths, and ended the spring with a 9th in the Derby. After one allowance race, he went to the Kikuka Sho as 9th choice, took the lead in the straight off Hagino Kamui O's fast pace and held on in a record 3:05.4, giving Maruzensky - barred from the classics himself - a classic win. He never won another big race, but was 2nd and 3rd in the Tenno Sho (Spring) and 3rd in a nose-and-nose finish with Minagawa Manna and Amber Shadai in the Argentina Kyowakoku Hai - a true stayer.
1118: The middle-distance king who became the first Japan-trained winner of the Japan Cup (4th running), beating crop-mate Triple Crown winner Mr. C.B., "absolute Emperor" Symboli Rudolf and world stars like Bedtime. He won his debut over 1200m at Hanshin by 8 lengths, a classic hope. With 2 more wins he headed east as Kansai's ace alongside Mejiro Monsnee, but lost to Mr. C.B.: 11th in the Satsuki Sho, 6th in the Derby. In autumn he was 2nd in the Kobe Shimbun Hai, then beat C.B. in the Kyoto Shimbun Hai for revenge. But as 2nd choice in the Kikuka Sho he was second-last of 21 (C.B. won the Triple Crown). At 4 he came good, winning the Osaka Hai, Keihan Hai and Takarazuka Kinen - a G1 winner. He beat C.B. again in the Mainichi Okan, but was 5th behind him in the Tenno Sho (Autumn), sealing his image as strong in preps, weak on the day. Then in the Japan Cup he boldly ran away and held on - his first win in a G1 that C.B. also ran in.
1119: He shocked fans by running down "absolute Emperor" Symboli Rudolf to win the 92nd Tenno Sho (Autumn) in 1985. After winning his debut he lost race after race and couldn't even run in the classics, won by Mr. C.B. and Mejiro Monsnee. At 4 he ran well in allowances, and only at 5 raced regularly in open and graded races. In the Tenno Sho (Autumn) at 5, with 6 of his wins on dirt, he was 13th choice of 17. But from last at the final turn he unleashed a furious charge, running down overwhelming favorite Rudolf in record time - the only horse ever to do so. No match for Rudolf in the Japan Cup and Arima Kinen, at 6 he won the Tokyo Shimbun Hai, was 4th in the Keio Hai Spring C., and won the Yasuda Kinen, his 2nd G1. He went to France for the Jacques le Marois and Moulin, beaten badly in both. Back home he was 4th in the Tenno Sho (Autumn) and 10th in the Japan Cup, but in his final race, the Arima Kinen, ran 2nd as 11th choice, showing a G1 winner's pride. At stud he sired Osumi Diner, who won a Hokkaido graded race at 13 - Japan's oldest graded winner.
1120: A mare from the crop of Mr. C.B. and Katsuragi Ace. No G1 win, but very consistent in many graded races, rarely unplaced. At 5 she won the Kokura Daishoten, Kita-Kyushu Kinen and Hanshin Himba Tokubetsu, champion older mare. She ran in the Queen Elizabeth Cup and twice in the Takarazuka Kinen, making the top five every time.
1121: A forerunner of the "Sakura stable" boom of the mid-1980s, followed by Sakura Toko a year later, Sakura Yutaka O and Sakura Sunny O 2 years later, Sakura Chiyono O 4 years later and Sakura Hokuto O 5 years later. A late bloomer, his first graded win was the American JCC early at 6 (old age system). He was 2nd in the Tenno Sho (Spring) and Takarazuka Kinen, strong over long trips. He sired no notable runners.
1122: In 1983, as Mr. C.B. became the 3rd Triple Crown winner, Southern Kanto racing had one too: San O I. He won the Haneda Hai by 4 lengths and Tokyo Derby by 7, then the Tokyo Okansho by 1.5 lengths as favorite; Celebration was 2nd in all three. Older, he moved to the JRA, 3rd in the Yasuda Kinen, showing aptitude for turf. In autumn he met Mr. C.B. in the Mainichi Okan and Tenno Sho (Autumn), 3rd and 6th. He returned to local racing and retired at the end of 7 (old age system). He left only 3 crops, incl. Kasamatsu star Tomishino Porunga.
1123: By Northern Taste out of a daughter of US great sire Bold Ruler. Her graceful bearing had people calling her "a million-dollar horse" from a young age, and she won her debut in record time. After 2 wins from 3 at 2, she was 3rd in a prep, then 3rd choice for the Oka Sho behind Shadai Farm stablemate Dyna Carle, and won from a good position. In the winner's circle she posed for photos with 3rd-placed Dyna Carle. For the 2nd classic, her camp surprised all by choosing the Derby over the Oaks, but she was 17th behind future Triple Crown winner Mr. C.B. In autumn, despite distance doubts, she was 2nd to Long Grace in the Queen Elizabeth Cup. At 4 she was repelled by G1 colts Happy Progress and Nihon Pillow Winner and slumped badly. Late in the year she showed signs of recovery, and at 5 won the Coral S. (OP), her first win in 18 months, then the Hankyu Hai by 2.5 lengths under top weight 56.5kg. In autumn at 5 she was favorite for the Swan S., her Mile CS prep, fully recovered - but fell in the race and had to be put down.
1124: A stayer of the 1980s. At 4 (old age system) he ran above his class in the Kikuka Sho, 3rd to Mr. C.B., and won the Hanshin Daishoten (then in December), his first open win. The next year graded races began, and he won the Hanshin Daishoten again as a G2, his first graded title, and later a 3rd time. He did little at stud, but his brothers include Kyoto Kinen winner Shin Chest and 2-time graded winner T.M. Jumbo.
1125: A fine supporting actor of Mr. C.B.'s crop. At 3 he won the Kobe Shimbun Hai as 7th choice, then often fell short. In autumn at 4 he won the Kyoto Daishoten by 4 lengths, but as 4th choice in the Tenno Sho (Autumn) was 7th behind C.B. His big chance came in the Takarazuka Kinen at 5: Emperor Symboli Rudolf's entry shrank the field to 11, but on the day Rudolf was scratched with leg trouble. 2nd choice, Suzuka Koban held off Tenno Sho (Spring) runner-up Sakura Gaisen to win his long-sought G1. He won the next Kyoto Daishoten and ran well in graded races, but that was his only G1.
1126: Based at Oi, he ran in the JRA's All Comers at 7 and 8 (old age system), 3rd as favorite at 7. Debuting late at 3, he was 6th in the Tokyo Okansho, a Southern Kanto classic, at 4, and won the Tokyo Daishoten at 5. At 6 he was 2nd in the Kawasaki Kinen, 4th in the Teio Sho and 3rd in the Tokyo Daishoten, and 2nd to Rocky Tiger in the Tokyo Kinen, missing a Japan Cup spot. At 8 he won the Teio Sho and his farewell Tokyo Daishoten, retiring at his peak. No notable runners at stud.
1127: At 4 (old age system) he ran 17 times, won the Lord Derby Challenge T., and thrilled fans with a 2nd as an outsider in the Arima Kinen. In 1984, the first year of graded races, he won the Nakayama Kinen. 17th as 2nd choice in the Tenno Sho (Spring), he was 2nd to Mr. C.B. in the Tenno Sho (Autumn), then over 2000m for the first time. At stud from 1987 for 6 crops, his best was sprinter Dojima Muteki.
1128: Racing steadily from 3 (old age system) to 8, he won a graded race 6 years running: the Keisei Hai Sansai S. at 3, Hakodate Kinen at 4, Nakayama Kimpai at 5, Tokyo Shimbun Hai at 6, Asahi Challenge C. at 7 and Kyoto Kimpai at 8. From 4 he won just once a year, suddenly running big between poor runs - "once-a-year Dokan Yashima." Winning both the East and West Kimpai is another rare feat. At stud he sired Southern Kanto runner Kinko Batora and others, and was retired in 1995.
1129: A rare member of the Blandford line, from Mr. C.B.'s crop. Injury kept him out of the classics, but older he won the Nikkei Sho (2500m) and Sekiya Kinen (1600m), and was 5th in the Tenno Sho (Spring) (3200m) - good at any distance. Of about 70 foals, only Utsunomiya's Shimotsuke Oaks winner Dokan Satsuki stood out, and his male line died out.
1130: Mr. C.B.'s chief rival in his Triple Crown year. In the Satsuki Sho he dueled C.B., 2nd by half a length; in the Derby he swooped from outside on the early leader but fell short, 2nd again. A fracture kept him out of the Kikuka Sho, but he lit up the classics. Back as an older horse, he won the Takamatsunomiya Hai. At stud he had no notable runners and retired in 1995.
1131: Debuting late, in January at 3, she ran 3rd, 2nd and 3rd that month, then rested, missing the spring classics. Back in June she won a maiden and a 4-million race, and improving over summer won the Rose S. over Oaks winner Dyna Carle and 3rd-placed Mejiro Heine, a Queen Elizabeth Cup favorite. Dyna Carle skipped it, but Oka Sho winner Shadai Sophia, Rose S. runner-up Global Dyna and Mejiro Heine ran. Long Grace waited in midfield and kicked sharply in the straight to win as favorite. The next year she won the Kimpai (West), was 2nd to Katsuragi Ace in the Osaka Hai, 2nd to Suzuka Koban in the Kyoto Daishoten and 3rd to Mr. C.B. in the Tenno Sho (Autumn), running well against top colts, and was 1985 champion older mare.
1132: He left the lower classes in November at 4 (old age system). Racing in graded races from 5, he won the Tokyo Shimbun Hai in his 2nd try, then after a 5th in the Meguro Kinen won the Diamond S. 4th in the Takamatsunomiya Hai, he won the Mainichi Okan in autumn and was favorite for the Tenno Sho (Autumn). But a 7th there marked a sudden decline. Mostly unplaced after, he raced until 8, breaking down in the Meguro Kinen and having to be put down.
1133: 2nd in the Asahi Hai Sansai S. at 2, he won the Keisei Hai after a duel with Nippo Swallow. In the Yayoi Sho he met Symboli Rudolf for the first time since the Icho Tokubetsu and was crushed, over 8 lengths behind in 5th. From then things went wrong: 9th in the NHK Hai, 16th in the Derby. After resting in autumn, he did nothing in graded races, but ran well in occasional dirt races and found his way on sand. At 5 he won the Ginrei S., his first win in 2 years, then the February H. by a nose. From 7 he raced at Mizusawa, winless, until 9.
1134: At 3 he met Symboli Rudolf, 3rd in the Yayoi Sho and 5th in the Satsuki Sho. He won the NZ Trophy Yonsai S. by 3.5 lengths, but 2 breaks cost him 3 years in all. Back at 6, he moved to local Nakatsu and Kochi, winning 23 races and racing at the top until 10.
1135: He won his debut, then leg trouble cost him 5 months. Back, he won 2 straight, showing great promise. 4th in the Hanshin Sansai S., he won the Shinzan Kinen at 3 and the Kyoto Yonsai Tokubetsu, but then, as if avoiding Rudolf, switched to sprints. 2nd in the NZ Trophy Yonsai S., he looked set to shine there, but fractures and other injuries left him without another win.
1141: In the classics with Rudolf he was 4th in the Yayoi Sho, Satsuki Sho and Derby - just short. But winning the Radio Tampa Sho in summer started his run: after an open special he won the Fukushima Kinen, then the Kimpai (East) at 4. Injured in the Nakayama Kinen, he rested 7 months, won the Lord Derby Challenge T. in his 2nd race back, was injured again, and back again won 2 more graded races incl. the Nakayama Kinen. At 6 he beat Nippo Teio in the Takarazuka Kinen, a Grand Prix win. Undeterred by injuries, he won 8 graded races. Apart from Rudolf, he was the only one of his crop to win an older-horse G1.
1142: He beat future Oaks winner Tokai Roman by 5 lengths in the Wakana Sho, was 2nd in the Kisaragi Sho, and won the Mainichi Hai by 2.5 lengths. But he flopped in the classics, then ran poorly with occasional surprise good runs - a punter's nightmare. In the end he was simply erratic, running well on dirt or turf, long or short, only when he felt like it. He raced over jumps from spring at 7 until 10, then went to stud.
1143: She won her debut by 3 lengths, then made the top five without winning. Winning the Shiraume Sho at 3, she squeezed into the Oka Sho and charged from behind for 2nd to Diana Solon. In autumn she won the Rose S., but was 7th as 7th choice in the Queen Elizabeth Cup. She later won the Topaz S., but her temper made her inconsistent. As a dam she produced no notable runners.
1144: He won his 2nd start and the Wakatake Sho, then was 3rd in his first graded race, the Spring S. 7th in the Satsuki Sho behind Symboli Rudolf and graded regulars, he was 6th in the NHK Hai behind Bizen Nishiki, Nishino Raiden and others. He barely made the Derby as 20th choice, second-last - yet only Rudolf beat him: a proud 2nd. In autumn he was a fair 4th in the Kikuka Sho, and ran in the Arima Kinen, a superb 4th behind the Big Three. Older he was sometimes beaten badly, but won the Epsom C. and was 2nd in the Yasuda Kinen at 4.
1136: A horse of Rudolf's crop who thrilled classic fans with a sharp late charge. After his debut win he often fell short: at 2, 2 wins from 9. At 3 he was 2nd in the Shinzan Kinen and won the Kisaragi Sho, but was well beaten by Bizen Nishiki in the Spring S. and swallowed up in the Satsuki Sho. A long break cost him the Derby, but in the Kikuka Sho, when all others had given up, he alone chased Rudolf down the straight, closing to 3/4 of a length. His later highlight was the Mainichi Okan at 4, but that kick, which for a moment touched the Emperor's back, left a deep impression on fans.
1137: Unbeaten in 4 to the Queen C., she was crushed in the Oka Sho (20th) and Oaks (25th) and retired to breed. All her placings came from leading - a classic front-runner. Sister of Niigata Kinen runner-up Aino Lady.
1138: She won a debut race at 2, but her first graded win, the Niigata Daishoten, came at 6 - rare longevity for a filly. Free of major injuries, she won specials every year and ran 42 times before retiring to breed at 6.
1139: Debuting at 2, she won the Flower C. with just 1 win. At 3 she was 2nd in the Queen S. and Rose S., and in the '85 Yasuda Kinen a fine 3rd. Alternating good and poor runs, she ran 20 times before retiring to breed at 5.
1140: A moody front-runner, strong when allowed his own pace. At 2-3 he was 2nd in the Hakodate Sansai S. and Kyodo News Hai Yonsai S., but after finishing last in the Satsuki Sho he kept losing badly. At 4, 2nd in the Kimpai (East), he switched to leading every time, and results followed: the Azuma Kofuji Sho, then the Sapporo Kinen. Mainly a dirt star, his last win was the February H. at 6.
1145: The leading lady of the '84 fillies' classics. Beaten badly in the Yonsai Himba Tokubetsu (West), she was only 3rd choice for the Oka Sho but won by 5 lengths from Long Leather. In the Oaks she was 2nd, 0.2s behind Tokai Roman, and 3rd in the Queen Elizabeth Cup after Kyowa Thunder's swoop - a fine classic campaign. Champion 4yo filly that year, she ran twice in spring at 4, then retired to breed.
1146: The '84 Oaks winner. 8th in the Tulip Sho trial, she was 4th in the Oka Sho. After the Oaks win she was 5th and 6th in the autumn trials but 4th in the Queen Elizabeth Cup. Missing some races but delivering when it mattered - just like her nephew Tokai Teio. Winning the Kyoto Daishoten "out of nowhere" at 6, long after the Oaks, must run in the family too.
1147: After 2 straight wins she was 3rd in the Sansai Himba S. (OP), then rested with leg trouble. Back, she won the Yonsai Himba Tokubetsu (East), but fell ill before the Oaks and was 12th. Often injured, she raced until 4, winning 4 of 9.
1149: After her debut she lost 11 straight maidens; half her 23 starts were maidens. Her first win came in late April, after the Oka Sho. Winning in summer, she began autumn with the Sapphire S., promoted to 2nd when Long Kitty was demoted, earning a Queen Elizabeth Cup spot. There she was 14th choice of 21, barely noticed. Waiting at the back and charging in the straight, she slipped past classic stars Tokai Roman and Diana Solon and crossed the line first. Her only notable win, yet it left a huge impression - a true one-hit wonder.
1150: Just 9 starts, but her brilliant burst and sharp finish left a vivid memory. She won her first 2 but illness cost her the spring classics. A close 3rd in the Sapphire S. raised hopes; she won an allowance race, then the Queen Elizabeth Cup, with no clear favorite, became a duel with Kyowa Thunder - 2nd. That race sparked her rise: she won the Aichi Hai and the Hanshin Himba Tokubetsu by over 3 lengths. At 4 she won the Chunichi Shimbun Hai, looking like the ace of middle distances, but retired after it with leg trouble.
1151: She lit up the fillies' classics, winning the Tulip Sho and Queen S., but her only G1 was the Queen Elizabeth Cup, where she pulled up before the 3rd turn. Injury-free, she ran 47 times before breeding at 7. Only 5 wins, but she was 3rd against colts in the Niigata Kinen, Kabutoyama Kinen and Fukushima Kinen. As a dam she produced 3-time winners Elegant Bouquet (90: Ile de Bourbon) and Daigo My All (91: Russian Bond).
1152: A late debut, but he kept running well, aiming for the Kikuka Sho; 4th in the St. Lite Kinen, he missed out. He then won the Argentina Kyowakoku Hai, outdueling Dyna Carle and others. No more wins.
1153: Winning his late debut in May at 3, he did little after, reaching open class only after summer at 5 - a classic late bloomer. At 6 he won the Kimpai (East), then starred in graded races, an all-rounder at home on dirt too.
1154: Struggling at 3, he came good in spring at 4, winning allowances, then the Sekiya Kinen and Keio Hai Autumn H. Outclassed in spring miles at 5, he won summer specials and set a Japanese 1200m record - a renowned speedster.
1157: Indecisive at 3-4, in summer at 4 she led into the straight in the Kinko Sho (G3: 1800m) on soft ground and powered home with authority. From 6 she raced at Mizusawa, in the top three 12 times in 15.
1158: He won his debut, but his 2nd win came in his 6th start. 4th in the Hanshin Sansai S., he was 12th in the Shinzan Kinen. He won the Kisaragi Sho, but again couldn't follow up - inconsistent. He later ran over jumps.
1159: A front-runner who broke so brilliantly that people joked "wasn't that a flying start?" Building his record at local middle-distance meetings, at 4, still in allowances, he won the Kabutoyama Kinen. But that was Kippoushi's last win. In allowances his fast pace gave others no chance, but in open class it didn't work at all - the classic "TV horse" who only shines early. Still, his bold front-running, undeterred, moved many fans. He moved to local racing at 6.
1160: After an injury, he showed his talent from autumn at 3, winning allowances, then the Kimpai (East) at 4. His camp saw him as a middle-distance horse and planned to skip the Tenno Sho (Spring), but favorite Mihoshinzan and other leaders withdrew injured, so he ran. To save stamina, he was ridden easily early and asked only late; jockey Okabe's superb ride paid off and he won.
1162: He came good at 5, winning an allowance and then the Milers C., his first graded win. 4th to Fresh Voice in that year's Yasuda Kinen, he was expected to do more, but repeated injuries held him back.
1163: Talented but weak on big days - that was Sunny O. He won his first 2 and was 3rd to Scrum Dyna in the Asahi Hai Sansai S. At 3 he won the Keisei Hai and was 2nd in the Yayoi Sho, a classic hope, but was 3rd to Mihoshinzan in the Satsuki Sho and 7th in the Derby, and 3rd to Mihoshinzan again in the Kikuka Sho. Older, he won the Argentina Kyowakoku Hai and more, but in G1s was 5th in the Tenno Sho (Autumn) at 4 and 3rd in the Yasuda Kinen at 5. A tendon injury in summer at 5 ended his career without a G1. In racing, that last step can be impossibly far.
1164: The Derby winner Symboli Farm produced after Rudolf. Trained alongside Rudolf from 2, he was tipped for greatness early. But a feud between owner and trainer drew more attention than his ability. Perhaps partly to escape it, after his Derby win he raced in Europe for 2 full years, laying a precious foundation for Japanese horses abroad, now common. He didn't win, but his 14 hard races against Europe's best, incl. a 2nd in the Prix Foy, were a great asset to Japanese racing.
1167: He won his debut by 10 lengths, then the G1 Asahi Hai Sansai S. by about 2. But at 3, though unbeaten 2yo champion, he was only 2nd choice for the Spring S.; unbeaten Mihoshinzan was favorite. Masato Shibata, who rode both, had chosen Mihoshinzan. As Shibata judged, Mihoshinzan won, and Scrum Dyna suffered his first loss. He was well beaten by Mihoshinzan again in the Satsuki Sho, 2nd. With Mihoshinzan resting, he was 3rd in the Derby behind Sirius Symboli and Suda Hawk, a fracture was found, and he retired.
1168: Winning the Yayoi Sho, he earned a classic spot. In the Satsuki Sho he raced from behind as usual but lost the finishing duel, 6th, narrowly behind runner-up Scrum Dyna. In the Derby he was 2nd to Sirius Symboli. Beaten in both autumn trials, he was 2nd choice for the Kikuka Sho as a stayer, but 2nd again to Mihoshinzan. 6th, 2nd, 2nd - frustrating classics. His ability was clear: older he won the American JCC and Kyoto Kinen. But in G1s he fell short, 5th in the Takarazuka Kinen and 3rd in the Tenno Sho (Spring).
1169: Debuting in March at 3, he won 3 straight, then was 10th in the NHK Hai (G2: 2000m). After a break he won the Kobe Shimbun Hai, then was 2nd to Mihoshinzan in the Kyoto Shimbun Hai and 9th as 3rd choice in the Kikuka Sho. From 4 he kept running well in graded races. Graded-winless at 5 after a long break, at 6 he won the Nikkei Shinshun Hai, sitting handy and powering home, defying his age.
1170: Raced only in sprints from his debut; his only run beyond a mile was the 1800m Kokura Daishoten in spring at 4. The plan worked: he won 2 graded races, the Hankyu Hai and CBC Sho. Above all, he was a horse of 2nds - 13, over a third of his career. In graded races too, he was 2nd in the Milers C., Sprinters S. (then G2), Swan S. and Mile Championship - almost every major sprint-mile race. A heartbreakingly good loser.
1173: He won his first 3, incl. the Hanshin Sansai S., but all by a length or less - not dominant, and not a leading figure in a strong classic crop. At 3 he was 3rd in the Kisaragi Sho and 4th in the Spring S., then 18th as 8th choice in the Satsuki Sho. After a break he was 7th in the Kobe Shimbun Hai, developed a tendon injury and retired.
1174: A small mare under 400kg. She won the Kokura Sansai S. but never won again, retiring in spring at 4. As a dam she produced Superine (87: Real Shadai), dam of Derby runner-up Bold Emperor (95: King Glorious).
1175: Winning the Queen C. in spring at 3, her 4th win, she was an Oka Sho contender in the Yonsai Himba Tokubetsu (West), but couldn't catch front-running Elps, 3rd - 0 for 3 against her. Yet she was Oka Sho favorite over Elps, showing how highly she was rated. While Elps led all the way, she faded in the straight to 15th and had to leave the classic path. Unfazed, she won 2 specials, then the Sekiya Kinen easily as a 3yo filly. Older, she ran well in graded races, and the climax came in the Mile Championship in autumn at 4, where she swooped on mile king Nippo Teio in the straight to win a G1.
1177: A classic front-runner: good when leading, hopeless when not. 10th in the Yayoi Sho at 3, he won the NHK Hai (G2: 2000m) impressively. In autumn he beat older horses in 2 open specials, the Tokyo Sports Hai and Fuji S. He seemed to be coming good, but missed the break in the Lord Derby Challenge T., 14th. A month later he was 3rd in the Kimpai (East) - erratic like many front-runners.
1178: Apart from a 2nd in the Kisaragi Sho he did little, until his talent suddenly bloomed at 5: 2nd in the Kimpai (West), he won the Fushimi Tokubetsu, then the Kokura Daishoten as favorite. Next, in the Chukyo Kinen, he beat runner-up Knockout by 2.5 lengths - a true KO. Rarely beaten badly after, he won the next Kokura Daishoten and Keihan Hai, racing at the top until 7.
1179: A stayer with great stamina who powered through long races. His debut at 3 was over 1600m, but from autumn, when he came good, every race was 2000m+. He won the Kujukuri Tokubetsu (9M) and was a fine 5th in the Kikuka Sho, 2nd to Hokkai Pegasus in the Stayers S., then at 4 won the Diamond S. from a good position, holding off Ron Spark. He rested after his next race, hurt his right hind at pasture and retired.
1148: The best of Daikoter's runners, strong when things went his way. 6th in the Satsuki Sho and 5th in the Derby, he won the Kyoto Shimbun Hai and was 3rd to Rudolf in the Kikuka Sho. He won the Naruo Kinen, Hanshin Daishoten and more. But in the Asahi Challenge C., having beaten Wakao Raiden, he became the first horse disqualified from first in a graded race, for veering. In the Tenno Sho (Spring), 2nd to Mihoshinzan, he was disqualified again for veering. A strong winner of 4 G2s, he is best remembered for "veering" and "disqualification" - a quirky horse.
1155: After his debut win and the Shiragiku Sho, a knee fracture cost him 6 months. Back, he was 3rd in the NZ Trophy and won the All Comers against older horses. After the Kimpai (East) he broke his knee again, and a tendon injury ended his career.
1156: She won a maiden easily in April at 3, then 2 allowance races. A blueblood bred much like Derby winner Sakura Shori, she already raced with authority. After a short break, she won the Queen S. by 5 lengths and entered the Queen Elizabeth Cup unbeaten. Waiting in midfield, she easily passed front-running Elps at the final turn and kicked on. Just as an unbeaten queen seemed born, Reward Wing swooped wide and snatched it near the line - her first defeat. She won the Turquoise S. and retired at year's end, her limits never found.
1161: She won her debut, but after a 10th in the Daily Hai Sansai S. had shin trouble. Back, she won, then chipped her right knee. She won the Sapphire S. in autumn, but injuries kept coming.
1165: Leg trouble forced 6 months off after his debut. Back at 3, he was 2nd in the Naruo Kinen at 4, then won the Keihan Hai and was 3rd in the Takarazuka Kinen, but leg trouble struck again. After racing in Hokkaido, he went to stud.
1166: Debuting at Morioka, he won 4 and joined the JRA at 2. 4th in the Yayoi Sho, he closed for 5th to Mihoshinzan in the Satsuki Sho, but a fracture cost him 9 months. Back, he won the Niigata Daishoten and Epsom C., then broke a leg again. After 13 months off he did little and returned to Iwate at 6.
1171: Debuting in March at 3, she won 3 straight, then the Radio Tampa Sho. Hailed as the star of the autumn fillies, her chronic left foreleg trouble flared in the Queen S. and she retired. A fast front-runner.
1172: At 3 he was 2nd to Windsor Knot in the Hakodate Kinen and won the St. Lite Kinen, then retired injured.
1176: After a big loss in the Satsuki Sho, he went a year winless, then won the Sprinters S. (G3) by half a length from Long Hayabusa. Breathing trouble and temper hurt him later, but his speed was first-class.
1180: The '84 champion 2yo filly. She won her first 2, was 2nd to Tanino Bouquet in the Daily Hai Sansai S., then beat her by 2.5 lengths in the Radio Tampa Hai Sansai Himba S. After a long break she did little and retired to breed at 4.
1182: A foreign-bred, then still rare. Debuting late, in February at 3, he ran 5th, 2nd and 2nd, then a fracture sidelined him until the next February. Beaten badly in 2 dirt races, he won his 3rd race back, a 2600m turf allowance. With his weak hindquarters now strong, he went on a tear: 3 allowance wins and a 2nd in the Tanigawadake S. Reaching open class, he went straight to the summer Grand Prix, the G1 Takarazuka Kinen, and in his first graded race beat top older horses like Suda Hawk and Kushiro King. After his first win: 4 wins and a 2nd from 5 - perfect. A tendon injury forced his retirement right after, sadly.
1184: Won the Sapporo Kinen (G3: dirt 2000m) by 11 lengths. A dirt specialist: 6 of his 8 wins came on dirt.
1185: 4th to Mihoshinzan in the Satsuki Sho, he was 13th in the Derby. Two fractures followed, and his graded wins, the Fukushima Kinen and Niigata Kinen, fell short of his ability.
1186: Only 4 wins, but 2nd in the Kyoto Shimbun Hai and 3rd in the Tenno Sho (Spring). He won his only graded race, the Nikkei Shinshun Hai, by 2 lengths. Chronic leg trouble forced an early retirement.
1187: At 5 he won a special, then ran above his class for 2nd in the Hanshin Daishoten and 4th in the Tenno Sho (Spring). He won the Kinko Sho at 7. A stayer, but versatile enough to handle dirt.
1189: From local Kasamatsu, he won 7, including his first 6, and moved to the JRA at 3. 12th in the Kobe Shimbun Hai, he did little at first, but winning in summer at 4 he came good, holding on for 7th in the Mile Championship. Steady in open class at 5, he won the Centaur S., and the Milers C. the next year, starring around a mile. From 7 he raced in Iwate until 9.
1190: A dirt king, unbeaten in 6 on dirt incl. 2 graded races. At 4 he beat Fate Northern, later a local star, in the Winter S., champion dirt horse that year. Good on turf too, he won the Shinzan Kinen at 3 and was 2nd in the Asahi Challenge C. at 4. Without leg trouble, he could have done much more.
1191: Winning the Kyoto Yonsai Tokubetsu, he ran a fine 4th to Sirius Symboli in the Derby. Then hoof cracks and a knee fracture cost him over 2 years. Back, he was 2nd in an allowance, won a 14-million special, then won the Takamatsunomiya Hai (G2: 2000m) over Pot Tesco Lady - a comeback graded win. He was later 2nd in the Osaka Hai and won the Nikkei Shinshun Hai at 7, fully overcoming his injuries.
1192: In '85 the Queen Elizabeth Cup ended in an upset, just like the Oaks: as Noano Hakobune had won the Oaks fresh from a 4-million win, Reward Wing had just won the Nagatsuki Tokubetsu (9M) 2 months earlier, and was well beaten (8th) in the Rose S. trial. As Elps led at a fast pace, she waited at the back and swept past Asakusa Scale and the rest in the straight. The next year she held her own against colts, 4th in the Kyoto Daishoten.
1193: Often 2nd - 5 times at 3, 7 at 4 - he couldn't win, until the Argentina Kyowakoku Hai in autumn at 4. After a 6th in the Arima Kinen, he won the American JCC and Kyoto Kinen. Injury then forced a long break, and he never won again.
1194: He won his debut and the Kaede Sho, then the Hanshin Sansai S. as favorite, a classic hope. But as 2nd choice he was 4th in the Kisaragi Sho and 8th in the Spring S., then 18th in the Satsuki Sho. He retired after 2 more races.
1195: Won his debut by 4 lengths and stayed unbeaten in 5 to the Yayoi Sho, always by a length or more until a neck win over Dyna Cosmos there. Satsuki Sho favorite, he broke down in the race and retired.
1196: Firm or rain-soaked heavy ground, his finishing kick was always sharp. In his 2nd race at 3, the Mainichi Hai, snow fell - bad news for a closer - yet he exploded in the straight to win by 3.5 lengths. In the Satsuki Sho he charged from last for 2nd. A wound kept him out of the Derby, and in autumn he was 4th in the Kobe Shimbun Hai and 6th in the Kikuka Sho. At 4 he won the Nikkei Shinshun Hai, but was 4th in the Hanshin Daishoten, so his camp skipped the Tenno Sho (Spring) for the Yasuda Kinen over a mile. It proved a lucky choice: rain made the ground heavy, with water standing. Mile favorite Nippo Teio led from the start while Fresh Voice was slow away. At the final turn everyone thought he was beaten, but he charged and swept past Nippo Teio for his first G1. As if he had spent everything in that run, he did little after, apart from a 2nd in the Takarazuka Kinen at 6, and retired after that year's Arima Kinen.
1197: Half-brother of Mejiro McQueen. His first win came late, in May at 3, but he grew strong over summer, winning allowances and reaching the Kikuka Sho. Behind Rugby Ball and Legend Teio in the betting, he beat Derby winner Dyna Gulliver by half a length - a G1 winner. Hopes were high when older, but he kept losing; still, at the end of 4 he won the Arima Kinen as 10th choice for his 2nd G1.
1198: After winning his debut and the Sawarabi Sho, Rugby Ball won the NHK Hai (G2: 2000m) by 2 lengths from Shin Chest, and was Derby favorite. But Dyna Gulliver swooped and he was 4th, 0.5s back. His camp chose the Takamatsunomiya Hai (G2: 2000m) next; meeting older horses seemed early, but he beat Wakao Raiden and others by 1.5 lengths. In autumn he was 5th in the Kyoto Shimbun Hai and 3rd in the Kikuka Sho. In the Japan Cup he swooped wide for a fine 4th, but the effort perhaps cost him: leg trouble ended his career after the race.
1199: Tipped as a star before her debut, she won just 1 of 3 at 2. At 3 she came good, winning the Kobai Sho by 2 lengths, the Violet S. by 5 and the Tulip Sho by 2. In the Oka Sho she beat runner-up Kosei by 8 lengths, then won the Yonsai Himba Tokubetsu (East) by 1.5. In the Oaks she sat 15th of 24, moved up from the 3rd turn and unleashed a fierce kick to beat Kuri Rotary by 2.5 lengths for the double. In autumn she beat colts in the Kobe Shimbun Hai and won the Rose S. - 8 straight. Then came her bid to match Mejiro Ramonu, the first fillies' Triple Crown winner a year earlier, in the Queen Elizabeth Cup. A sure thing, it seemed; she took the lead at the final turn, but outsider Talented Girl caught her - 2nd. The crown slipped away at the very end. Burnt out, she ran poorly after, winning one open special in autumn at 4, and retired to breed. As a dam she produced no graded winner, but steady runners like Max Jolie (90: Real Shadai), 3rd in the Oka Sho and Oaks, and 8-time winner Chokai Raijin (93: Dancing Brave).
1201: A flashy chestnut with flaxen tail, 4 white socks and a blaze, he became an idol overnight. Not just looks: he won the Hanshin Sansai S. - but that was his last win. In the classics he was 2nd in the Satsuki Sho, 4th in the Derby and 2nd in the Kikuka Sho, and raced steadily until 5 without another win. Lacking pedigree appeal, he was retrained as a riding horse, but broke a leg at pasture and was put down.
1203: He did little on turf early, but switched to middle-distance dirt late at 4. At 5 he won 5 races, all on dirt, incl. the Sapporo Kinen (G3: dirt 1700m) and Negishi S., and was champion dirt horse - a leader of dirt racing before it had today's structure. After winning the Musashino S. (OP) at 6, he oddly went back to turf, 2nd in the Fuji S. (OP). He retired after the Kimpai (East) at 7 and went to stud.
1204: "The horse Yutaka Take loved" was actually a cheap horse who went unsold at auction. But his broodmare sire was famed stayer Intermezzo: his breeder, after talks with Okada of Ruffian, had bred a super stayer to win the Kikuka Sho. A fracture just before the Derby cost him the spring. In autumn, aiming for the Kikuka Sho, he ran in the Kobe Shimbun Hai and Kyoto Shimbun Hai, but a 6th left his entry hopeless. Young Yutaka Take, his rider so far, turned down other mounts and kept himself free for Super Creek, though he might not even get in. As if in answer, Okada withdrew his own horse, Meiner Frisse, saying "the strong horse should run," and Creek got in. Creek repaid Take's devotion and Okada's faith, winning the Kikuka Sho. He was then disqualified in the Arima Kinen, a humiliation, and leg trouble returned for a long break. The next autumn he won the Kyoto Daishoten in record time, then the Tenno Sho (Autumn), thought too short for him, beating champion Oguri Cap, Inari One and others. 4th in the Japan Cup and a nose 2nd to Inari One in the Arima Kinen, he neared his peak, and at 5 won the Tenno Sho (Spring) - back-to-back autumn and spring Tenno Sho. Leg trouble struck again and he retired to stud with a 1.5-billion-yen syndicate. High hopes for foals with his ability went unmet: his best was Sweet Pea S. runner-up Hadashi no Megami, with no graded stars.
1207: Running above her class in the Queen Elizabeth Cup, she was 9th, but as a turf sprinter that 2400m defeat was no surprise. The next year, at her distance, she was 2nd in the Kyoto Himba Tokubetsu and Milers C. After a dip, at 5 she won the CBC Sho in record time, was 2nd in the Swan S., and as 10th choice won the Mile Championship, outfoxing top miler Bamboo Memory - a big shock.
1208: That year's classics had no clear star - an age of warring states. Winner's Circle was a highly rated prospect, but 4th as favorite on debut, then favorite but 2nd repeatedly in maidens, winning only in his 4th start, and needing 3 more to win a 4-million race. In the Satsuki Sho he was 2nd to Doctor Spurt, then went to the Derby. Favorite Long Symphony was a shaky 6.0, Meiner Brave 6.1 and Winner's Circle 3rd choice at 7.3 - a truly wide-open Derby.
